We show how a controller can stop after a local edit while an earlier occurrence, regenerated statement or context-dependent
match remains. We introduce a completion check that covers the final editable
region and invalidates stale judgments, and use it in a verified fixed-boundary
controller. A second published procedure, Thought Anchors, accepts locally different replacements that can recover the target later. On Qwen3-32B safety tasks,
verified removal reduces prohibited actions by 12.02–15.69 percentage points relative to continuation without erasure, while native remains within three points.
Matched-content controls separate target removal from additional regeneration.
On a new eighty-trace panel, a multiclass replication of the Thought Branches
category comparison recovers its native ordering but reverses the plan-generation
versus self-preservation gap after complete-region removal. We also derive computable attribution bounds from shared execution records, allowing decisions before every continuation finishes. The results identify intervention completion as a
measurable condition for reasoning attribution and provide a procedure for checking it.

Cryo-electron tomography (Cryo-ET) allows high resolution reconstruction of biological structural in context, but carries and inherent limitation. The limited tilt range of the microscope results in a missing wedge of information in Fourier space. Previous deep learning approaches to missing wedge correction train to repair the artifacts in an individual tilt series. We instead pre-train a tilt autoencoder on a corpus of experimental tilt series, with a single pass latent-space 3D correction to impute the missing wedge. On simulated and experimental tilt series, we demonstrate competitive generative capabilities with iterative refined approaches. We demonstrate that our pre-trained approach sustains its performance on out-of-distribution data while the iterative, per-experiment models do not and our single-pass inference allows for dramatically faster reconstruction after pre-training.

A simulated agent can keep discussing the same topic while changing how it
supports its claims. A plausible individual post cannot show whether the agent
uses the same arguments later. We study this problem through the recorded posts
and discussions of LLM agents on Moltbook. For each post, we distinguish its
topics, its ways of supporting a claim, and which ways are applied to which topics.
We then compare these pairings across early and late parts of each agent’s history
and examine their association with participation in different discussion threads.
Topic stability often masks a change in argument form. Explicit reasons within
posts do not by themselves imply stable argument patterns over time. Participation
in actively discussed threads is more closely associated with later change than
participation in highly voted threads, and threads with critical replies show the
clearest match to arguments used later. These findings describe observable text
histories and recorded participation; they do not establish changes in agents’ private
beliefs or causal social influence.

Monitoring chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is a foundational safety technique for large language model (LLM) agents; however, this oversight is compromised if models learn to conceal their reasoning. We explore steganographic CoT—where models hide secret reasoning within innocuous text—to inform risk assessment and deployment policies. Steganographic reasoning requires two skills in a single forward pass: computing an intermediate result, and embedding it into a coherent cover that answers an unrelated question. Drawing on our taxonomy of steganographic and non-steganographic CoT types, we systematically evaluate the limits of prompt-elicited steganographic CoT capability across 34 models, ranging from past generations to the current frontier. We measure monitor evasion, refusal rates, encoding fidelity, and hidden task accuracy across five datasets, comparing against plain reasoning, direct answer, and filler-token baselines. The two experiments isolate the two sub-skills: a reasoning tasks sweep tests joint reason-and-embed, while a counting task hands the model a known numerical sequence and tests embedding alone—a necessary precondition for stego reasoning. Current frontier models cannot sustain joint reason-and-embed: a paired McNemar comparison shows the steganographic channel is dominated by a filler-token baseline on every (model, family) cell. The encoding-only floor, by contrast, is cleared—Claude Opus~4.6 reaches 96% per-number partial accuracy (61% exact-match)—establishing that the binding constraint on stego CoT is the joint reasoning-plus-encoding load, not raw channel capacity. Separately, GPT-5.2 issues an explicit refusal to the steganographic instruction yet still produces partial valid encoding in 6 of 644 trials. Our findings underscore the need for continuous evaluation of steganographic risk and provide a methodology to preemptively detect and evaluate hidden reasoning that might empower misaligned scheming and deceptive behavior.

TL;DR: We decompose steganographic reasoning into compute-the-answer and embed-into-cover; under prompting, 34 LLMs reach the embedding floor (Opus 4.5: 92% on 4-digit acrostics) but the joint reason-and-embed channel is bounded by a filler-token baseline.

Long-sequence single-cell Transformers are constrained by the quadratic cost of self-attention. We show that physical-interaction structure is recoverable from pretrained dense scGPT attention and contextualized gene embeddings, and that masking physical partners produces a larger mean change in masked-value predictions than masking matched controls. Motivated by this evidence, we construct STRING-derived hard block-sparse attention layouts using Reverse Cuthill--McKee ordering and $128\times128$ blocks, computing query--key scores only within active blocks. To reduce block density and sparsify the attention matrix, we introduce edge-ratio and confidence-score-sum criteria for block activation, yielding active-block densities of $0.146$--$0.177$ on a 10k-gene panel. Separate scaling benchmarks up to 20k tokens achieve up to $3.74\times$ isolated full-layer forward speedup over FlashAttention-2. A two-epoch 10k-gene pretraining run delivers $2.4\times$ higher end-to-end throughput, using a fourfold larger micro-batch than the memory-constrained dense baseline. Under matched fp16 precision, initialization, data, optimization, and reported update budgets, both low-density models increase validation MSE by approximately $3\%$ while retaining zero-shot linear-probe accuracy within $2.0$ percentage points and fine-tuned accuracy within $0.7$ percentage points of dense attention across three datasets. These results show that protein-interaction-guided block-sparse attention substantially reduces long-context training cost while maintaining zero-shot and fine-tuned accuracy comparable to that of the dense-attention baseline.

TL;DR: We introduce protein-interaction-guided block-sparse attention that accelerates single-cell foundation model training while retaining competitive zero-shot and fine-tuned accuracy.

An imperfect demonstration includes both errors and their corrections. Selecting transitions by how much their states resemble expert states may discard the correction along with the mistake. We study this failure-recovery aliasing: a trajectory can visit the same state during failure and recovery, although the two visits should receive different training weights. We introduce AFTER (Avoid Failure, Train on Error Recovery), which infers an ordered sequence of normal, failure, and recovery phases from an expert-likeness score and coarse trajectory-level supervision. A mistake label supplies a contains-failure constraint; a terminal outcome, when available, supplies an ending-phase constraint under a domain-specific interpretation; and changes in the score help locate the transitions between phases. Exact inference gives a posterior probability of failure at each timestep, which supplies weights for behavior cloning. We prove a selection-error floor for state-only weights and a localization bound showing when a score-based boundary is reliable. On D4RL and Adroit, AFTER  outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on average return. The method trains offline without timestep-level phase labels, per-step rewards, or a learned critic.

TL;DR: This paper addresses failure–recovery aliasing in offline imitation learning by separating mistakes from corrective behavior using temporal structure and coarse trajectory supervision.

We analyze dynamic Schrodinger bridges from a Gaussian source to a
bounded, possibly singular target. Matching the entropic endpoint coupling
to the Brownian bridge noise makes the clean-endpoint posterior mean (PM)
both the population regression target and the only field the forward SDE
needs, and its martingale structure ties numerical error to posterior
covariance. Under a covering-number exponent $k$ for the target, we
separate cutoff-time KL error into discretization, approximation,
population excess risk, and pairing mismatch, and prove three results.
The discretization term is an exact posterior-covariance identity of order
$\widetilde O(k/N)$, so cutoff-time total-variation accuracy $\epsilon$
costs $\widetilde O(k/\epsilon^2)$ steps. A two-scale posterior quadrature
represents the PM by one softmax-attention layer over $O(P/d)$ prototypes
at rate $(d/P)^{1+2/k}$ with polynomial constants. One terminal PM
evaluation converts cutoff-time accuracy into target-$W_2$ accuracy with
an intrinsic residual $\widetilde O(\eta k(1-b))$ instead of the ambient
stopping bias of the raw cutoff sample. Entropy-dependent limits connect
the bridge to optimal-transport flow and rescaled denoising diffusion.
These guarantees take population prediction and pairing accuracy as
inputs.

Agentic option trading requires an autonomous policy to select complex option strategies based on nuanced market conditions. We present SOTA (Stock Options Trading Agents), a language-model post-training framework for dynamic option strategy selection. SOTA represents market conditions using features of the option-implied return distribution and selects among nine structured option-strategy families. SOTA is first supervised on frontier-model trading trajectories and then optimized through reinforcement learning on portfolio performance. We evaluate SOTA on options on nine large-cap U.S. equities and SPY against non-LLM-based option strategy-selection, and demonstrate that SOTA achieves superior out-of-sample performance. We also find an asymmetric role of news: news improves frontier-teacher trajectories, but retaining news during reinforcement learning provides little additional benefit.

TL;DR: SOTA trains language models to dynamically select option strategies based on market conditions, achieving superior out-of-sample performance. News helps generate high-quality training examples but adds little benefit during reinforcement learning.

Black-box jailbreak evaluation usually relies on repeated target-specific search or a transfer library built before deployment. We consider a setting in which attack factors are known, while the best configuration for a new model is not. We introduce PolyJigsaw, a single-turn multilingual parallel-fragment reconstruction prompt. POLY is the accompanying acquisition and deployment method. It crosses PolyJigsaw’s structural controls with response frames to define a registered 160-action space, acquires a shallow source library with a fixed schedule that does not branch on observed outcomes, and shares evidence across factors and one-coordinate transitions. POLY compiles these statistics into provenance-preserving cards and, during deployment, appends transition events derived from response text without observing endpoint labels. Across independently rebuilt source libraries, factor sharing improves attack success rate at one call (ASR@1) relative to flat-arm estimation. On 17 targets, a frozen prior built with Q = 300 source calls improves ASR@1 over prior-free factorized Thompson sampling by 8.82 and 22.57 percentage points in the two transfer directions. This advantage narrows or reverses by eight calls. Under canonical HarmBench evaluation, continual memory improves matched frozen ASR@8 by 1.27 and 6.63 percentage points on average in the two directions. Selected mismatch stress tests show larger recoveries. The evidence establishes stronger cold-start transfer and conditional mismatch recovery. It does not establish dominance at every budget.

TL;DR: PolyJigsaw and POLY enable cold-start black-box jailbreak transfer by sharing attack-factor evidence across models, improving early-call ASR and adapting under distribution mismatch.

Large vision-language models have advanced radiology report generation, yet single-pass decoding entangles candidate finding discovery, evidence assessment, and report composition. Conservative decoding may omit findings documented in reference reports, whereas broader sampling may introduce claims unsupported by those reports.
We introduce RRG-MRPA (Radiology Report Generation with Multi-Role Policy Agents), an inference-time optimization framework that decomposes report generation into three coordinated roles—\textit{Explore}, \textit{Verify}, and \textit{Compose}—without retraining the report-generation backbone. \textit{Explore} samples complementary candidate reports and extracts structured observations to broaden finding coverage. \textit{Verify} selectively admits evidence by combining conservative anchors with calibrated image–text scoring, targeted visual checks, and conflict arbitration. \textit{Compose} reconstructs the final report from the admitted evidence. Together, these roles separate broad candidate discovery from selective evidence admission and final report composition. 
We evaluate RRG-MRPA with three backbones on MIMIC-CXR and IU X-Ray.
The consistent label-level gains across diverse backbone-benchmark settings support multi-role evidence selection and report reconstruction as an effective approach to inference-time optimization for radiology report generation.

TL;DR: Our proposed RRG-MRPA improves radiology report generation through multi-role inference-time optimization that decouples candidate exploration, evidence verification, and report composition without retraining the backbone.

Scientific progress depends on research that is conducted soundly and reported faithfully. As AI scientist systems increasingly automate the research process, final reports and benchmark scores alone are insufficient to establish the credibility of their findings. We call behaviors that create a gap between apparent success and actual research practice \emph{research integrity violations}. In this work, we introduce RIDAR, a framework for auditing and safeguarding research integrity in AI scientist systems. First, we develop RIVT, a taxonomy of 14 violation types spanning the research lifecycle, together with RIV-Gold, a human-annotated reference set of 60 trajectories. Second, RIDAR audits collected trajectories post hoc using an Analyzer--Verifier architecture that grounds every accepted finding in exact trajectory evidence. On RIV-Gold, it achieves 60.9\% instance-level recall with 96.4\% precision. Applied to RIV-Wild, which contains 300 trajectories from six harness--model configurations across metric-guided optimization and open-ended discovery tasks, RIDAR identifies 2,487 accepted findings across 99.3\% of trajectories, with scientific reporting manipulation and contribution inflation as the most widespread types. Third, we extend auditing to runtime: a resident Analyzer monitors the growing trajectory, while a Supervisor delivers findings back to the agent. On RIV-Live, intervention reduces the mean number of findings remaining at completion from 9.22 to 5.23, a 43.2\% decrease relative to matched runs without intervention. We will release our code and data.

TL;DR: We introduce RIDAR, a framework for auditing and safeguarding research integrity in AI scientist systems.

One-step real-world super-resolution can initialize restoration from a low-quality
(LQ) image or generate from noise conditioned on that image. These choices expose different balances between observation fidelity and perceptual quality. We
investigate a dual-origin formulation in which LQ tokens serve both as an explicit
restoration origin and as a condition for a noise-origin stream. A shared QwenImage2.1 transformer uses token-specific low-rank adapters to predict two restoration endpoints. Directional attention permits the noise-origin stream to read the
LQ representation while preserving a fidelity anchor. Reconstructed endpoints can
be combined without mixing velocities defined at different origins. On RealSR
and DRealSR, the two endpoints exhibit complementary metric profiles; latent
interpolation improves PSNR over both endpoints in the evaluated configuration.
We additionally study same-origin interpolation between independently restored
and adapted LQ endpoints. It increases no-reference quality at the expense of
paired perceptual fidelity, but does not yet establish an improvement attributable to
reverse cross-stream interaction. Our results motivate treating attention direction,
conditioning, and the number of transformer evaluations as explicit experimental
variables when studying controllable one-step restoration.

Cross-platform user identity linkage (UIL) aims to identify accounts belonging to the same individual across different social networks. Despite the rich identity signals in user-generated content, effectively integrating content representations with incomplete, structurally heterogeneous social graphs remains challenging. A key difficulty lies in the long-tailed nature of social networks: Euclidean representations may suffer from neighborhood crowding around high-degree users, while mapping all users into hyperbolic space can introduce unnecessary geometric transformations for locally sparse regions. To address these issues, we propose a degree-gated hyperbolic--Euclidean mixed-space framework for cross-network user alignment. A lightweight content encoder first derives task-oriented user representations from user-generated content. Based on local structural characteristics, a degree-aware routing mechanism selectively assigns hub-centered users and their one-hop neighborhoods to a hyperbolic branch, where the exponential volume growth of Poincar\'e space provides additional capacity for crowded neighborhoods. In contrast, other users follow a direct Euclidean pathway. The two geometric branches are jointly optimized through common-space training with cross-network alignment supervision, allowing identity information to guide mixed-space representation learning. During inference, a geometry-aware matching module computes space-specific similarity. It uses a tangent-space bridge to align candidates represented in different geometries, producing a unified correspondence score without discarding geometry-specific information. A joint tangent-space visualization protocol places the two branches in a shared view for direct comparison. On two cross-network UIL datasets, the method improves both classification and candidate-ranking results over the compared structural and multimodal baselines. Controlled ablations and sensitivity analyses examine the contributions of routing, neighborhood expansion, and mixed-space comparison.

Code is available in an anonymous repository at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/degree-gated-mixed-space-CC0B.

TL;DR: We propose a degree-gated hyperbolic–Euclidean framework that adaptively models heterogeneous social structures for accurate cross-platform user identity linkage.

Long-horizon coding agents can make locally correct edits that are globally inconsistent. We propose modification-induced dependency mismatch: an agent's edits change repository dependencies and invalidate previously correct beliefs, even when the original evidence remains in context. We hypothesize that this mismatch, rather than context length, is a proximate predictor of cross-file consistency errors. Because program semantics and latent model state are not fully observable, we define an operational mismatch over previously observed, aligned dependencies by comparing checkout-grounded structur

Speech deepfake detection increasingly demands robust generalization across unseen generators, languages, and recording conditions. While recent detectors achieve strong performance, they differ substantially in how frame-level representations are aggregated into an utterance-level embedding. Despite its importance, the impact of temporal aggregation on cross-generator robustness remains largely unexplored. We present Indic-Forge, a large-scale multilingual benchmark for Indic speech deepfake detection, comprising $5.1$ million utterances across seven Indian languages, five held-out speech generators, and diverse neural codec conditions, as well as genuine compressed speech. Using this benchmark, we conduct a systematic study of utterance-level pooling by evaluating mean, percentile, top-$k$, and hybrid aggregation strategies across $300$ model configurations while keeping the detection pipeline unchanged. We explore lightweight detectors such as MLP, which achieves a $4.61\pm{0.17}$\% equal error rate on the codec group with only $0.27$M parameters, outperforming a $300$M parameter XLS-R baseline under the same evaluation protocol. Thus, we establish temporal aggregation as one of the key fundamental factors for building efficient and generalizable speech deepfake detectors, yet overlooked in the literature. We assert that this provides an efficient pathway toward speech deepfake detectors that generalize reliably across unseen generators and compression conditions.

An agent memory card can help one policy and hurt its successor, but measuring its effect under the new policy requires costly continuations with and without the card. We ask whether the policies' different responses to the same card can guide which new-policy outcomes to measure. Our acquisition rule averages changes in the memory-versus-empty scoring contrast across first assistant messages; a comparator receives the same scores and all 28 pairwise absolute differences. On fixed software-repair failure states and cards, the rule lowered held-out target-effect mean squared error relative to this comparator for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct to Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct by 0.0100 (paired 95\% confidence interval $[0.0030,0.0170]$) and for Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct to Qwen3-Coder-Next by 0.0059 ($[0.0014,0.0104]$). With 256 purchased target tasks, paired regression fell by $0.80$ and $0.60$ percentage points, respectively; both updates met the prespecified one-point recovery noninferiority margin, while neither established recovery superiority. The second update reuses failure states and cards created with the original 7B policy, so it tests a second Qwen update under fixed conditions rather than a new failure distribution. In the original update, uniform purchases cost less and equal-cost extra agent computation recovered more tasks. These results support lower paired regression at this budget and about 25\% memory acceptance, subject to the fixed library, learner, and interface.

When should decentralized agents imitate a privileged teacher? Reproducibility-based weighting favors teacher actions that a local auxiliary policy can predict, but predictability alone need not make an imitation update beneficial. In a two-agent cooperative game with an optimal teacher and an exact auxiliary, we show that discrepancy-weighted Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) imitation yields strictly lower team return than constant weighting after a sufficiently small update of equal joint-logit norm. The weighting shifts update mass toward the agent whose change is harmful to the current team. Yet the ordering reverses at the limiting policies under continuous-time pure JSD imitation. The counterexample thus rules out a general local-improvement guarantee for this weighting rule, without implying that it harms learning in general. Separately, exact-reference calibration shows how auxiliary capacity and fitting affect discrepancy at fixed information. A five-task neural study compares combined quality/discrepancy weighting with quality-only weighting and reference systems. Two comparisons match both selected imitation coefficients and learning rates; the others compare separately selected procedures. For the fixed teachers and selected procedures, combined weighting improves over RL on two warehouse tasks but shows no statistically resolved gain over quality-only weighting on any of the five tasks. These results distinguish two questions: whether an agent can reproduce a teacher's actions, and whether following those actions improves team return.

Dense pair refinement incurs cubic work even on structurally simple components. We introduce \St, which uses block--cut and SPQR decompositions to confine complete computation to rigid R-skeletons and to reduce an $s$-cycle to $4s^2-3s$ interactions per round. When the induced colored R-configurations are separable and Schurian, the resulting local correspondences agree at their interfaces and compose into a graph isomorphism. Within this class Stitch matches dense 2-FWL, and neither the total graph size nor the decomposition depth is bounded. The class contains every graph without R-skeletons and, under an explicit enumeration premise, every graph whose R-skeletons have at most thirteen vertices. All graphs recorded in our ZINC, QM9, ZINC-full, and PCQM4Mv2 audit meet this size criterion. In exact experiments Stitch preserves every dense distinction across 1,008 long-cycle cases, lowers cumulative interactions by 60.98\% at the largest tested subdivision level, and reproduces all 400 BREC decisions. We also report prediction and runtime results. A counterexample outside the guaranteed class motivates the one-hop Stitch-Plus variant, which repairs it; whether that variant is generally equivalent remains open.

TL;DR: Stitch2-FWL localizes pairwise higher-order refinement to connectivity pieces and stitches their representations through cut vertices and 2-separators, retaining global 3-WL-level graph discrimination without globally dense pair–pivot interactions.

EEG identity recognition requires representations that remain discriminative across changes in recording conditions. We ask whether spatial covariance geometry can provide a useful initial state for learned latent dynamics. GeoTS-EEGNet combines a temporal encoder with a regularized log-covariance branch, fuses their features to initialize a continuous-depth trajectory, and aggregates the resulting states with a gated recurrent unit. Training uses identity classification, domain-aware hard-triplet learning, and trajectory smoothness. We evaluate the model on processed MCD partitions containing 45 identities and three run-based recording groups from PhysioNet EEG109 containing 109 identities. Rank-1 accuracy reaches 99.931% and 100.000% in the two MCD partition directions, and 99.832%, 99.954%, and 99.893% across EEG109 groups. In the EEG109 Group-3 ablation, removing the covariance branch reduces Rank-1 accuracy from 99.893% to 99.207% and the Fisher ratio from 24.84 to 10.24, whereas removing the ODE slightly improves Rank-1 accuracy. These results support the covariance branch more consistently than they support a general benefit from continuous dynamics. The evaluations concern identities enrolled during training and processed partition/group shifts; they do not establish unseen-identity, verified longitudinal-session, or cross-device generalization.

TL;DR: GeoTS-EEGNet uses spatial covariance geometry to improve robust EEG identity recognition across recording shifts.

Distilling forensic teachers into dedicated tokens can make structural, frequency, and region targets easy to decode while the answer still ignores those tokens. We call that pattern \emph{expert bypass}. The useful question is narrower: when decodability is held fixed, does reliance on the teacher content change generalization to unknown generators? TRACER (Token Representation Alignment via Counterfactual Expert Regularization) keeps that comparison available. Learned slots in a causal multimodal decoder match frozen DINO, Fourier, and SAM targets. A content-matched, norm-matched exchange then trains the answer to follow an opposite-label donor, with a same-label donor as the control for generic substitution. On checkpoints whose teacher-target similarity stays inside $[0.928,0.934]$, raising the decision-reliance score from 0.05 to 1.44 lifts held-out generator balanced accuracy from 88.6 to 94.8. On those same generators, exchange without teachers reaches 90.7. Swapping the teacher-predictive subspace of the slots drops held-out accuracy by 4.8 points; a same-rank subspace that predicts the label and is orthogonal to the teacher map drops it by 1.1. The same bypass-then-reliance pattern appears on InternVL3-2B. Teachers and intervention branches are removed at inference. TRACER (9B) reaches 97.9 on eleven public subsets, 3.8 points above the strongest same-data baseline.

Scientific explanations often encode complex entities, interactions, dependencies, and causal relationships that can be difficult for learners to internalize directly. Analogical narratives offer a promising way to make such knowledge more intuitive and memorable, yet large language models often generate stories that are fluent but structurally incomplete, overly literal, mechanically retold, or dependent on superficial metaphorical substitutions. We introduce SPAN (Structure-Preserving Analogical Narratives), a multi-stage framework for transforming scientific text into self-contained fictional narratives while preserving the underlying relational and causal structure.

SPAN decomposes generation into five explicit stages: causally explicit scientific rewriting, causal and constraint-aware knowledge-graph construction, functional role and affordance grounding, coherent causal story-world synthesis, and causally audited narrative realization. The framework is designed so that important events in the target narrative emerge from established fictional properties, constraints, interactions, and state changes rather than from arbitrary narrative convenience.

We evaluate SPAN against direct LLM generation, ParallelPARC-inspired relational generation, local-to-global analogy construction, role-mapping approaches, and structure-constrained prompting. Evaluation separates three complementary dimensions: generic analogical structure, science-aware structural fidelity, and science-blind narrative quality, using pairwise model judgments, benchmark-based validation, and human assessment. Stage-wise ablations further examine the contribution of each intermediate representation. By treating analogy generation as the construction of a coherent fictional world whose behavior mirrors the structure of the source explanation, SPAN aims to move beyond surface metaphorization toward more faithful, interpretable, and narratively effective scientific analogies.

TL;DR: SPAN turns scientific explanations into self-contained stories whose fictional worlds preserve the source mechanism’s relational and causal structure.

LLM unlearning supports privacy protection by removing unwanted knowledge
without full retraining. LLM teams are widely adopted because collaboration
improves answer quality. Despite advances in robustness to adversarial queries,
repeated sampling, and model updates, unlearning under increasingly widespread
team deployment remains underexplored. Our experiments show that intermediate
messages can enable downstream recovery even when the final answer suppresses
the target. We therefore propose Aggregation-Conditioned Unlearning (ACU)
to directly supervise message recoverability. ACU trains a shared proposer–
aggregator policy using native-output scores and fixed-reader reconstructions from
individual messages, pooled proposals, and full trajectories. It prioritizes the most
revealing audit, assigns credit through independent replacements, and constrains
direct and collaborative utility. Experiments span three model families and two
datasets, with recovery analyses across target models, readers, team sizes, and
sampling protocols. On TOFU, ACU reduces full-trajectory recovery ROUGE
from 41.8 to 19.3 relative to native-output training, and fact recovery by 10.9–15.6
percentage points under matched sampling budgets. These results demonstrate ef-
fective collaborative unlearning while preserving retained capabilities.

TL;DR: We uncover a previously underexplored failure mode of LLM unlearning in collaborative systems and develop an effective recovery-aware unlearning method to address it.

Recent studies indicate that large language models (LLMs) encode global attributes about future outputs beyond the next token, also known as planning. 
In this work, we show that LLMs exhibit refusal planning aligned with human safety preferences, even prior to safety alignment.
However, such human-aligned refusal planning is not consistently reflected in the final decoded outputs of LLMs.
We term this misalignment between planning and behavior as silent refusal planning. 
Through the lens of silent refusal planning, we provide a unified and interpretable explanation for a wide range of safety failures, including harmful instructions following, jailbreak vulnerability, over-refusal, and shallow safety alignment.
Building on this insight, we propose Planning-Steered Decoding, a simple yet effective heuristic method that leverages the human-aligned refusal planning in LLMs to steer the decoding process.
Experimental results demonstrate that our method reduces the attack success rate by 40$\sim$70\% while simultaneously reducing over-refusal by up to $\sim$30\%, and maintaining the general capabilities of LLMs. 
Our method generalizes across diverse LLMs and benchmarks with high data efficiency and incurs negligible inference overhead.

TL;DR: LLMs encode human-aligned refusal planning that can remain silent in their outputs, and we leverage this signal to improve safety.

The performance ceiling of an LLM team is constrained not only by individual model capabilities, but also by inter-member error resonance and predictive differences. Although heterogeneous teaming is often observed to be effective in practice, existing approaches lack complementarity metrics that are computable, interpretable, and optimizable, leaving team composition to rely on heuristics. We propose a heterogeneity-driven team selection framework that performs offline profiling to characterize individual capability along with two complementary signals: one captures decorrelation in error patterns to reduce co-failures, while the other measures divergence in predictive behavior to capture strategy diversity. We formulate team selection as a standardized quality--complementarity combinatorial objective and apply an efficient greedy search to select a small team from a candidate pool. Experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms quality-only baselines under controlled candidate pools and team sizes, establishing reusable selection principles for multi-LLM systems.

TL;DR: C²-MAS optimizes LLM team selection by balancing individual quality with error decorrelation and distributional divergence, consistently outperforming quality-only baselines across 13 benchmarks under fixed budgets.

Learned proposals can help explore multimodal, unnormalized Boltzmann targets, but their endpoint densities may be unavailable for statistical correction. We introduce Neural Non-Equilibrium Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (NHMC), which combines learned forward and reverse conditional momentum distributions with reversible, volume-preserving dynamics. Recorded path densities and target energies yield a computable nonequilibrium work for training, importance weighting, and estimation of normalizing constants and free-energy differences, without evaluating the endpoint proposal density. We also introduce a configuration-space round-trip Metropolis–Hastings update: a reverse path takes the current configuration to an intermediate configuration, and a fresh forward path proposes a new configuration from there. We prove that this update is reversible with respect to the target distribution and that, conditional on the intermediate configuration, the update of the auxiliary path record is an independence Metropolis–Hastings step. We derive lower bounds on accepted inter-region probability flow at stationarity, quantifying the effects of conditional path mismatch and dependence between endpoint and intermediate configurations. The path-space KL divergence controls the mismatch term, but high acceptance alone does not ensure transitions between regions. Across analytically tractable many-well targets, lattice $\phi^4$, and two-dimensional compact $U(1)$, $SU(2)$, and $SU(3)$ gauge theories, corrected estimates agree with analytic or independent references. Controlled $\phi^4$ experiments show that sector-probability estimates can remain consistent with reference values while autocorrelation times vary substantially. In compact $U(1)$, NHMC with standard path-space independence Metropolis–Hastings changes topological sectors in the tested regimes where the HMC reference chains remain frozen.

TL;DR: NHMC learns nonequilibrium Hamiltonian transport and corrects it in path space, combining expressive learned dynamics with importance weighting and exact Metropolis correction for multimodal unnormalized targets.

Benchmarking in reinforcement learning is usually relative: algorithms are ranked by returns on environments whose optimal policies are unknown. As a result, distance to optimality is unobserved and empirical conclusions can be entangled with reward design, stochasticity, hyperparameters, and simulator details. We develop a ground-truth-first benchmark view based on converse optimality, where benchmark fixtures carry certified optimal values and policies. The paper unifies deterministic continuous-time generators for sensitivity studies, stochastic native discrete-time generators for oracle-referenced comparison, and new output-feedback extensions for partially observed control. The partial-observation construction distinguishes two cases that ordinary scoreboards conflate: memory-limited nonlinear systems whose hidden state is reconstructible from public innovations, and noisy-sensor LQG systems with irreducible information loss. We also show how non-affine raw actions, finite-covariance non-Gaussian disturbances, and nonsmooth value functions fit the same fixture logic through actuator pullbacks and Clarke-subdifferential certificates. The evidence supports the methodological claim: benchmarks should not only rank policies, but measure their certified remaining gap to an attainable optimum.

TL;DR: We introduce RL benchmarks with analytically certified optimal policies and value functions, enabling direct measurement of distance to optimality.

Existing generative 3D human motion models can generate realistic movements but struggle to meet numerical targets. This limits their use for controlled biomechanical comparisons, which require varying specific movement characteristics to prescribed values while minimizing unintended changes to other properties. We propose NumMotion, a lightweight adaptation framework for precise numerical control of movement characteristics in text-conditioned 3D human motion generation. NumMotion conditions a frozen generator on explicit numerical inputs through a compact adapter. Target fitting matches motion measurements to requested values, while Jacobian regularization encourages proportional responses to changed requests and penalizes unintended changes in other controlled properties. We introduce a benchmark based on NimblePhysics covering seven action categories, with two numerical controls per category, to evaluate simultaneous target success, cross-control interference, and motion quality. We demonstrate that NumMotion meets the requested numerical target in 94% of trials versus 8.8% for baseline MDM.

TL;DR: We propose an adaptation framework for numerical control in human motion generation models.

We introduce SciTrek, a synthetic question-answering dataset for assessing and improving long-context numerical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Existing long-context datasets with inputs beyond 64K tokens either target simple information retrieval or, when they do involve reasoning, rely on artificial contexts, while numerical reasoning remains largely overlooked in both cases. SciTrek addresses these limitations with questions that require numerical operations (e.g., counting, sorting, aggregation, and comparison) over collections of full-text scientific articles. Questions are generated automatically by formulating them as SQL queries over a database of article metadata (titles, authors, and references), and ground-truth answers are obtained by executing these queries. The underlying SQL provides a transparent, verifiable specification of the reasoning each question requires, enabling fine-grained error analysis. Furthermore, the proposed  automated pipeline scales to arbitrary context lengths and dataset sizes with minimal human supervision, supporting contamination-resistant evaluation over time and supplying abundant data for post-training. Extensive experiments show that frontier open-weight and proprietary LLMs struggle even with ostensibly simple questions: the best-performing model achieves only 46.5% exact match at 128K tokens, and performance degrades steadily as contexts grow. Fine-grained analysis reveals systematic weaknesses on citation-related questions and on compound logical conditions, particularly those involving negation. Finally, post-training on SciTrek, particularly with GRPO, can improve performance on other long-context reasoning benchmarks.

TL;DR: A dataset for evaluating and improving long-Context numerical reasoning over scientific articles

Financial nonstationarity creates a deceptively hard inference problem: an extreme return can be evidence of a persistent regime change, a transient distributional shock, or both. Most probabilistic forecasters route these possibilities through the same adaptive representation, leaving persistence and residual shape statistically entangled. We introduce FiSeCast, a persistence-aware forecaster that separates
the two roles by construction. A recurrent context encoder parameterizes context-dependent regime transitions together with regime-specific location, scale, and finite-mixture Student-t emissions. Across time, FiSeCast propagates only the discrete regime posterior; intraregime mixture labels are redrawn conditionally at each step, while observed shocks may still influence future contexts through
the encoder. This is an inductive bias rather than a claim of generic latent-state identifiability. We formalize the resulting persistence allocation, characterize the logarithmic tail order of contemporaneous regime Bayes factors, and derive exact forward likelihood evaluation. In controlled recovery experiments, the factorization reduces shock-induced false switching, and across five financial markets FiSeCast attains the best observed mean LPS and CRPS among the reported methods. The results suggest that explicitly deciding what is allowed to persist can be as important as increasing distributional flexibility

TL;DR: FiSeCast separates persistent regime changes from transient shocks through a persistence-aware probabilistic forecasting model, improving calibration and predictive performance across financial markets.

Changes in joint calibration and actuator response can turn a geometrically plausible grasp into an execution failure. Past interactions provide evidence about these changes, but reusing that evidence requires transferring information about the hand across different objects and contacts. We introduce GraspTTT, a graph-structured test-time training framework for cross-object grasp adaptation. GraspTTT stores execution feedback in global and link-local fast weights, updated through motion and grasp-outcome prediction losses. Local memories exchange information along the hand graph, and each new query reads the adapted state to produce bounded joint corrections. Offline training learns the memory update and readout, while deployment updates only fast weights using interactions with other objects. We evaluate correction feasibility, history transfer, and memory organization through controlled simulation experiments. Within the student’s bounded action space, independently revalidated teacher corrections increase grasp success from 11.46% to 28.75% under standard solver settings, a gain of 17.29 percentage points over uncorrected candidates. This establishes substantial correction potential without changing the wrist pose, execution duration, or force limits. In GraspTTT, finger-specific perturbations produce fast-weight changes 2.77–4.42 times larger in affected links than elsewhere, and memory interventions alter joint commands and grasp outcomes. These experiments connect transferable execution feedback, spatially organized test-time memory, and bounded grasp correction within a common adaptation framework.

LLM role-playing are expected not merely to imitate a character's linguistic style, but to act consistently with the character's experiences, motivations, relationships, and situational constraints. However, existing evaluations often rely on holistic model judgments or constrained question answering, providing limited supervision for complex, open-ended character behavior. We formulate \textbf{Role-Play Decision-Making} as a source-grounded generation task to enhance LLM anthropomorphic abilities and introduce \textsc{RoleTrace}, a dataset and training framework constructed from decisions recorded in novels. Using an iterative decision-mining and evidence-tracing pipeline, \textsc{RoleTrace} identifies decision points, retrieves temporally valid experiences available to each character, and organizes supporting and countervailing factors into character-centric evidence graphs. The dataset contains 1,875 decision instances from 20 narrative corpora and 317 characters, accompanied by 4,086 graph nodes, 7,081 causal edges, and 8,257 chronologically ordered experience events. Each instance pairs a character profile, prior experiences, and current situation with a structured reference reaction spanning thoughts, feelings, actions, and speech, together with source-linked evaluation criteria. We use \textsc{RoleTrace} to evaluate open- and closed-source models and to improve role-playing models through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, providing a fine-grained and auditable framework for moving role-playing agents beyond surface-level persona imitation.

Mobile-use agents are increasingly entrusted with actions over contacts, calendars, messages, files, and other security-sensitive phone state. Yet existing GUI-agent red-teaming settings often assume adversary capabilities that are unavailable to an external phone attacker, such as modifying DOM/XML content, injecting overlays, using accessibility hooks, or changing model internals. We study a lower-capability and more realistic threat model in which the adversary can only send ordinary SMS notification text that the agent observes during task execution. We propose PhoneJack, a black-box slot-bandit optimizer that factorizes notification injections into five functional slots and searches over slot arms using upper-confidence-bound selection. To address sparse binary success feedback, we further introduce PhoneJack-RM, which uses $R_\phi$, a vision-language reward model, to score leave-one-out prompt variants and provide slot-level credit during offline prompt search. We also introduce PhoneJack-Bench, a mobile red-teaming benchmark with 30 offline critical-step tasks and 8 online Android rollout tasks across four mobile-actionable risk categories, evaluated by rule-based action and state checkers. On held-out offline tasks, PhoneJack-RM reaches 85.5% attack success rate, improving over PhoneJack by 19.6 percentage points and over the strongest non-PhoneJack baseline by 36.7 points; prompts optimized by PhoneJack transfer to online rollouts with 44.9% ASR@6. These findings show that ordinary SMS notification text is a realistic and measurable hijack surface, and highlight the need to advance mobile-use agent security through systematic methods such as PhoneJack.

TL;DR: We show that ordinary SMS notification text alone can hijack mobile-use agents, and propose PhoneJack, a reward-guided slot-bandit optimizer, together with PhoneJack-Bench for measuring this threat.

Multimodal generative models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, yet existing benchmarks primarily evaluate general capabilities and narrowly defined safety risks. As a result, they provide limited insight into whether models can proactively recognize and comply with concrete, jurisdiction-specific legal constraints while still satisfying legitimate user requests. We argue that **legal alignment** constitutes a distinct dimension of AI alignment beyond ethical alignment, requiring models not only to avoid unlawful outputs but also to reason about and operate effectively within legally permissible boundaries. To study this problem, we introduce **LawDance**, a benchmark for evaluating legal alignment in image advertising generation. The benchmark assesses three complementary capabilities: **risk awareness**, measuring whether models can identify legal and regulatory risks and refuse non-compliant requests; **safety robustness**, evaluating resistance to jailbreak attacks such as prompt injection; and **boundary sensitivity**, measuring whether models can preserve user utility by fulfilling requests to the greatest extent permitted by law. Our experiments reveal substantial weaknesses in current state-of-the-art models, even under progressively strengthened legal guidance harnesses ranging from general legal instructions to explicit statute-grounded rules. Many models exhibit a polarized behavior pattern: **either breaking the law or refusing the task**, with safeguards that remain fragile under adversarial prompting. At the same time, several models demonstrate an emerging ability to identify compliant alternatives and satisfy user intent without crossing legal boundaries, suggesting that legal alignment requires more than simple refusal-based safety mechanisms. LawDance shows that both unsafe compliance and excessive refusal can constitute alignment failures. More broadly, the benchmark reframes AI safety as a problem of **constrained capability**: not merely determining what models must not do, but enabling capable models to accomplish as much as possible while reliably operating within jurisdiction-specific legal boundaries.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made significant progress in visual reasoning through explicit chain-of-thought (CoT), interleaving visual evidence acquisition with inference over that evidence. Recent work shifts this reasoning process into a continuous latent space, reducing reliance on lengthy textual reasoning traces. In this setting, latent representations are progressively updated to incorporate visual evidence and support inference. However, a unified latent transition couples evidence acquisition and inference within the same state update. Our analyses show that late-stage relative state changes diminish, even though gold-answer-informed state modifications can still reduce answer loss. Controlled analyses further show that local answer-loss gradient directions vary with visual facts and reasoning operations, even when the latent state is held fixed. Motivated by these findings, we introduce Decoupled Perception--Reasoning Adaptation (\method), which learns separate low-rank corrections for evidence acquisition and inference. Perception/reasoning annotations guide their learning and selection while the host parameters remain frozen. At each latent step, a router selects a correction based on the current state, and the corrected state carries information into subsequent reasoning. Across four latent-reasoning hosts and six visual-reasoning benchmarks, \method improves six-benchmark mean accuracy by $1.60$--$5.21$ percentage points over the corresponding hosts. Equal-norm random and sign-reversed projection interventions on M$^3$CoT demonstrate the importance of learned correction directions.

TL;DR: At inference, DePRA steers hidden-state transitions at each step of multimodal latent reasoning by selecting between separately learned perception and reasoning corrections.

Multi-image mathematical reasoning requires a model to identify entities across views, recover numerical and relational facts, and determine which visual evidence is reliable enough to support a solution. Existing multimodal reasoners typically operate directly on image-text representations, making it difficult to control evidence selection or diagnose when visual evidence is incomplete or contradictory. We introduce M2E-X, a two-stage framework that separates evidence construction from downstream reasoning. Stage 1 converts multiple images into an image-backed evidence graph containing grounded entities, OCR and value cues, intra-view relations, and cross-view correspondences. Stage 2 retrieves a sparse proof-oriented subgraph, aligns the selected evidence with the question, and verifies its completeness, semantic consistency, and recoverability before the evidence is exposed to a frozen vision-language reasoner. The framework further supports counterfactual verification and selective abstention when the available evidence cannot be safely released. This formulation turns multi-image mathematical reasoning into a controlled evidence selection and verification problem rather than unconstrained end-to-end generation. We evaluate M2E-X using both proof-level evidence metrics and downstream mathematical reasoning accuracy.

TL;DR: M2E-X converts multi-image math problems into structured evidence graphs, retrieves question-relevant proof subgraphs, verifies their completeness and consistency, and exposes only safe evidence to a frozen vision-language reasoner.

In a network of networks (NoN), such as a production line, an analyst observes one subnetwork, the target subnetwor}. Two observed variables may move together because of an unobserved common cause, a latent cause. A latent cause inside the subnetwork calls for local inspection; one outside, a spillover, calls for tracing it upstream. Existing methods that allow for latent causes report that two variables share a latent cause, but not whether it lies inside the target subnetwork or outside. In the data the two cases look the same, so telling them apart needs an assumption about how the system is built. Supplying that assumption, and working out what it makes possible, is our contribution; the method we build on that assumption is Local Causal Discovery for Networks of Networks (LCDNN). We assume modularity: a latent cause inside acts on a single causal cluster, a group of observed variables reached by the same latent causes from inside, while a spillover reaches across two or more clusters. Once the direct effects among the observed variables are removed, what dependence still crosses clusters can only have come from outside. Under this assumption and conditions we state, the distribution of the observed variables determines the direct effects among them and, for every pair that shares latent causes, its type: whether those causes lie inside the subnetwork (intra-network), outside it (inter-network), or on both sides (mixed). The distribution does not determine the latent causes themselves. Explicit counterexamples show that two of our conditions cannot be dropped. We prove that LCDNN attains this identification, and that from samples it recovers the effects and types correctly with probability approaching one, its estimates of the effects becoming more accurate at the usual rate, under further conditions stated in the paper. LCDNN needs no observations from another subnetwork and no prior knowledge of the clusters; when it can recognize no cluster, it says so instead of guessing. It applies to linear systems with independent, non-Gaussian latent causes and noises, and lets the observed variables affect one another without feedback loops. We evaluate LCDNN on simulated NoNs that satisfy its conditions, where it recovers direct effects with fewer false edges than existing latent-aware methods and recovers clusters and types that compositions of existing methods do not, and on two public systems, a physical light tunnel with a validated causal graph and the causalAssembly manufacturing benchmark, which need not satisfy its conditions; we report where it succeeds and where it fails.

TL;DR: LCDNN is a new method that recovers a target subnetwork’s causal graph from local-only Network-of-Networks data, and determines whether hidden confounding is internal or due to external spillover, with theoretical guarantees.

In a network of networks, such as a production line, each team sees only the variables recorded in its subnetwork, its target variables. An incident may start in a target variable or a hidden source, an unrecorded mechanism of the same or a neighbouring subnetwork, each calling for a different action. Existing root cause analysis (RCA) names only a target variable or a latent state it posits, and normal operation does not reveal which hidden source acts in which directions. We propose Shift Footprint Matching (SFM), a framework for RCA when the source may be hidden.From a labelled context per hidden source, an otherwise normal period in which that source was made more variable, SFM learns its footprint:the fixed set of directions in which it can move the target variables' mean. SFM indicates how far the data can decide: the source, or its coarser type (target, local hidden or external) or route (the subnetwork responsible). Besides one predicted source, it returns those the incident does not rule out, without a coverage guarantee at our sample sizes. We prove that,in a linear system with one mean-shifting source, how footprints overlap decides exactly when the incident's mean shift identifies the source, type or route, and that, for identification, labels matter only for the type and route. On simulated systems and, for hidden sources, a chemical-process benchmark, SFM names the true source more often than adapted RCA methods,though simpler rules on the same footprints sometimes match or exceed it.

TL;DR: SFM is a new method of root cause analysis that can name a source outside what the team records, by learning each source's shift subspace from ordinary operating history, with sharp conditions for source, type and route identification.

Graph neural networks (GNNs) need to exploit improved message passing without surrendering control over predictions already trusted in deployment. We introduce Reference-Tail Trust (RTT), a framework that admits learned updates inside a frozen GNN and certifies the prediction actually served. RTT couples graph-based proposal states with a constrained internal optimizer: each displacement is charged for its worst-case terminal cross-entropy increase through the incumbent's remaining message-passing layers. A trajectory-validated tube and an independent checker enforce per-node probability floors, $p^{\\mathrm{s}}\_{ic} \\ge e^{-H\_{\\mathrm{row}}} p^{\\mathrm{r}}\_{ic}$, and a call-level budget, $\\sum\_{i} w\_{i} D\_{\\infty}(p^{\\mathrm{r}}\_{i} \\Vert p^{\\mathrm{s}}\_{i}) \\le H^{+}$, uniformly over labels. Calls whose adapted outputs pass certification require no separate full incumbent rollout; failed certificates trigger whole-call fallback. We derive the exact probability-floor frontier by water-filling, characterize architecture-constrained efficiency, and establish conditions under which internal propagation exploits evidence unavailable to restricted output correctors. In the reported ogbn-arxiv audit, RTT achieves $6.5 \\times 10^{-3}$ nats of mean gain per call, with a one-sided 95% regression-rate upper bound of 0.95% and a 95% negative-flip upper bound of 0.51% on the uninspected part of the reserved node population. Its mean gain is 61% of a cross-fitted posterior-based frontier estimate and exceeds the strongest matched one-pass corrector by $0.9 \\times 10^{-3}$ nats. Reported experiments span eight proposals, six graph-incumbent families, structural and temporal graph shifts, and molecular prediction, with additional image and tabular evaluations. RTT makes GNN adaptation a budgeted, certifiable inference decision rather than an unconditional model replacement.

Speech is normally given to a language model at its input, where encoder features
occupy context positions the model was never pre-trained to read. Slimducer
attaches at the other end: a 3 M-parameter joint network writes into the language
model’s own frozen output projection, so the model sees only its own vocabulary
indices, beginning at bos, as in pre-training. Nothing else trains — 0.38% of
783.7 M, with the speech encoder and the language model frozen and its 151,936-
way head unchanged — and every model reported here was trained on a single
24GB consumer GPU.
Keeping that head whole is what removing the label axis from the alignment lattice
buys: no T × L × |V| tensor is retained for a backward pass, where predictor-side
transducers must cut their vocabulary to a few thousand. Decoding is framesynchronous,
so bounded audio chunks reproduce whole-utterance decoding —
streaming that an input-side coupling cannot offer at all, having to see the utterance
before the language model attends over it.
The same 3M parameters carry beyond transcription. On LibriSpeech Slimducer is
slightly behind a fully fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 of thirty times its trainable size and
18% to 39% better relative outside that domain; with a 3.4M text-only adapter on
the frozen backbone it translates speech into German at 14.98 BLEU against 12.09
for a cascade of the same backbone, and answers questions about the utterance just
recognised.

TL;DR: Slimducer is a streamable speech LM with 3M traininable parameters.

Contactless heart-rate estimation from millimetre-wave radar remains challenging in naturalistic environments, where weak cardiac motion is obscured by respiration, body movement, and time-varying multipath. These disturbances generate broadband spectral interference and competing frequency peaks, limiting methods that estimate heart rate independently from short radar windows. We present a motion-aware temporal framework for robust heart-rate estimation from continuous in-cabin radar recordings. The framework extracts cardiac-frequency evidence from phase-preserving range–angle–Doppler measurements and integrates information across overlapping observation windows. A long-horizon dynamic-programming tracker exploits physiological continuity to recover coherent heart-rate trajectories from ambiguous spectral observations, while a learned noise-aware representation reduces the influence of motion-corrupted measurements and strengthens cardiac evidence. Unlike conventional regression-based approaches that map individual radar windows directly to heart-rate values, our framework explicitly combines measurement reliability, spectral evidence, and temporal consistency. We evaluate the method on continuous in-cabin radar recordings against synchronised physiological reference measurements using subject-held-out testing, with comparisons to regression-based neural-network baselines. The framework addresses a central limitation of contactless cardiac monitoring: reliable heart-rate estimation when the cardiac component is not the dominant spectral peak.

Diffusion-based visual generative models deliver strong image and video synthesis quality but incur high inference costs because sequential samplers repeatedly evaluate large networks. Caching-based methods reduce inference latency by reusing intermediate computations across adjacent timesteps. However, existing cache controllers rely primarily on local temporal variation and overlook the trajectory-level consequences of cache reuse. We introduce Error-Propagation-Aware Cache (EpaCache), a training-free caching policy that adaptively allocates the reuse budget on timesteps with lower downstream impact. Experiments on image and video synthesis models demonstrate that EpaCache consistently improves the latency--fidelity trade-off over existing caching methods. On FLUX.1-dev, EpaCache outperforms the prior state-of-the-art caching method in both latency and fidelity, reducing inference time from 11.7 s to 11.3 s while improving PSNR from 21.4 to 22.8. On HunyuanVideo, EpaCache achieves a 2.63\times speedup over uncached inference and improves SSIM from 0.891 to 0.905 over the prior state-of-the-art method at matched latency.

AI-generated video detection requires capturing subtle generation artifacts while avoiding the redundancy and computational cost of densely processing RGB frames. We propose an adaptive sparse RGB querying framework that leverages compressed-domain cues to guide both video-level detection and selective RGB evidence acquisition. Specifically, we characterize residual, motion, and coding statistics in the compressed domain to obtain a lightweight global prediction and rank spatiotemporal locations according to their joint rarity. Only a small number of informative RGB tubelets are then decoded and processed by a compact RGB evidence network, whose prediction is combined with the compressed-domain evidence through source-normalized fusion. To further adapt computation to individual videos, we introduce a utility predictor that estimates, from the currently available label-free evidence, whether acquiring additional RGB queries is likely to improve the prediction, enabling adaptive transitions between adjacent query budgets. The entire detector is trained and calibrated solely on the source domain, without target-domain adaptation. Experiments on five public benchmarks comprising 46 generator subsets show that our method achieves an average AP of 92.82\% and AUC of 93.30\%, outperforming the compressed-domain-only detector by 9.94 and 9.61 percentage points, respectively. Despite its strong cross-generator performance, the detector contains only 0.056M active parameters and requires 0.340 GFLOPs per video, demonstrating the effectiveness of compressed-domain cues for accurate and lightweight sparse RGB querying.

TL;DR: We detect AI-generated videos efficiently by using compressed-domain cues to identify informative regions and adaptively query only sparse RGB evidence.

Safety preference training can make a model refuse harmless requests; fit to those comparisons does not certify that behavior. Preference fit, likelihood realization, and behavioral realization must be measured separately: a well-fitted comparison set is no certificate for the behavior it is meant to identify. We audit that identifiability question at a fixed policy, first-order, relative to the defining comparison bank and metric. The Jacobian of the fitted margins — the reference-relative preferred-minus-rejected log-ratio — characterizes what the comparisons constrain; the behavioral gradient outside it quantifies the locally unconstrained component of a named functional. On safety prompts, that functional is the refusal/explanation log-odds of a fixed four-class candidate set, computed without sampling. We use Sign-DPO to vary likelihood realization at comparable held-out accuracy. Across six DPO conditions combining pair semantics with reference checkpoints, chosen-response likelihood shifts reverse sign with pair semantics (descriptive only), while the refusal share rises in every condition, intervals excluding zero. The residual is operational, not just geometric: finite interventions that nearly preserve the defining margins alter sampled generation at 1.5B and 7B, though the format direction's sign reversal does not replicate on an untouched pool. Selectivity is in parameter space: at equal count, random comparison sets can leave more of a target direction free than behavior-relevant ones. Single-step updates at one shared parameter norm of 0.05 reach eight fixed target directions without target-specific tuning. Using established projection and cost formulas, we test that prediction against finite interventions and sampled generation.

TL;DR: Preference fit alone does not certify behavior: we measure residual behavioral freedom and test its operational consequences through finite interventions in trained language models.

When do summaries of route distributions preserve an entropic optimal transport decision? Within a declared endpoint feature family, exact preservation requires representing the full free-energy cost. We quantify the optimal loss when preservation fails, allowing full-reference coefficient tuning and arbitrary conditional routing under separate endpoint and route-information caps. Around an exactly represented operating point at fixed positive temperature, reduced loss is an ordinary transport-weighted projection error, whereas physical loss includes a rank-one correction determined by conditional route information. The additional coefficient vanishes in every endpoint-cost direction exactly when that information profile is represented. A finite construction keeps the true mean unchanged and reverses the optimal ranking of two equally sized feature families. We extend the sharp loss formula to smoothly recomputed summaries of constant rank by projecting the cost derivative relative to the moving representation. In a separate weak-adaptation limit, the first missing cumulant determines a common reduced and physical coefficient. Global localization connects these expansions to closed-family infima, not selected coefficient curves. Controlled checks and two route studies retain accurate simplification and failures of finite-budget extrapolation. The results distinguish approximating a transport objective from preserving the information-constrained decision it supports.

TL;DR: Route summaries can rank oppositely under endpoint approximation and information-constrained physical loss; we characterize the sharp difference and extend it to recomputed features.

Reusable agent skills combine metadata, procedural instructions, and examples in text artifacts such as SKILL.md. Sharing a file does not, by itself, provide a common interface for inspecting its structure or maintaining alternative deployment representations. We present SkCC, a compiler-style system that separates skill normalization and static analysis from target-specific rendering through a typed intermediate representation, SkIR. Four emitters instantiate reusable rendering policies for agent deployment presets; these policies are implementation choices, not established optimal formats. The compiler also performs structural and permission checks and inserts rule-triggered constraint text, without providing runtime enforcement. In historical SkillsBench evaluations, the complete compiled condition has a higher mean reward than the original skill condition, with paired differences of 0.274 on 22 retained Claude Code pairs and 0.1424 on 74 retained Kimi CLI pairs (reported paired-test $p=0.0103$ and $0.0063$). Codex CLI and Gemini CLI results are descriptive, with Gemini using best-of-three selection. Separate audits characterize compilation outcomes and static-rule activation. These results provide evidence for two evaluated end-to-end presets, while leaving component attribution, alternative emitter choices, selection effects, and runtime safety unresolved. SkCC offers an inspectable normalization-and-emission interface for studying these questions rather than a guarantee of universal performance or security.

TL;DR: SkCC separates skill normalization and static analysis from target-specific rendering, with scoped empirical evidence for complete deployment presets rather than universal performance or runtime security guarantees.

Independent sampling gives large language models multiple attempts at a complete solution, but cannot combine correct partial results from different runs. Building on task decomposition and local error correction, we ask when intermediate states can be reused reliably with imperfect checks. We first formalize the single-chain bottleneck under matching subproblem success rates and independence assumptions. We then separate two risks in local reuse: exhausting the attempt budget and returning an incorrect state that passed the check. Uniform bounds on these risks and on continuation from correct states give a lower bound on whole-task success through the product of stage reliability guarantees. For $N$ steps and target failure probability $\delta$, an $O(N\log(N/\delta))$ computation budget suffices when cumulative accepted-state error remains within a fixed fraction of $\delta$ and per-attempt generation and checking costs are bounded. Experiments across eight reasoning models characterize complete-answer retries and two-stage candidate selection. Across four DeepSeek models, second-problem success is 36.2% without first-problem context, 57.2% with its answer, and 58.3% with its reasoning and answer. These measurements compare continuation under different context configurations and include fallback paths; they do not measure whether both subproblems are answered correctly on the same retained path.

A 3D asset admits multiple valid part decompositions, while semantics-aware seg-
mentation should reflect both the desired granularity and the parts a user wants to
extract. Ideally, a practical segmentation model should strive for a simple principle:
what you ask for is what you get. However, realizing this goal is hindered by
two core obstacles: the lack of multi-granularity training data and the absence of
a holistic control mechanism. We propose FLEXPART, a unified framework for
text-controlled 3D mesh segmentation. To establish flexible control, we introduce
a holistic control prompt comprising semantic part names with location and shape
clauses. To support this mechanism, we utilize an automated Vision-Language
Model (VLM) pipeline to construct a large-scale dataset of multi-granularity parti-
tions and their corresponding prompts. Driven by this data, FLEXPART generates a
view-independent part-identity field in native 3D space, directly assigning discrete
part IDs to mesh faces. To compel the model to respect semantic conditions rather
than rely on geometric priors, we train the model using randomized background
dropping. Furthermore, an inference-time VLM planner can automatically com-
plete descriptive clauses from 2D renderings, allowing users to simply name the
desired parts in ordinary words. FLEXPART with planner-completed prompts out-
performs the strongest evaluated baseline by 15% in mIoU, even when that baseline
receives ground-truth guidance. On our held-out FLEXPARTBENCH, FLEXPART
leads at each granularity and improves average mIoU by 22% over the strongest
baseline. With only the requested part names supplied by the user, it also improves
IoU by 35% over the strongest click-driven baseline on selective segmentation

Efficient allocation of inference compute is essential for scaling high-quality image and video generation with diffusion and flow-based models. With feature caching, requests benefit differently from additional full-network evaluations, so redistributing a fixed compute budget can improve overall batch fidelity. Finding the best joint allocation requires balancing the fidelity gains from giving some requests more full steps against the losses from giving others fewer. We introduce SHARE (Shared-budget Allocation across Requests), a budget-allocation layer that learns budget–fidelity responses from offline rollouts of a frozen cache executor, using training requests disjoint from evaluation and targets that capture both PSNR and LPIPS. At inference, a lightweight predictor uses common-prefix features to estimate fidelity at candidate budgets, and dynamic programming jointly assigns integer budgets to maximize regularized predicted fidelity gains under the shared constraint. Each request resumes once from its saved prefix under the assigned budget, with the executor scheduling the remaining full steps and all prefix evaluations included in the exact shared total. Across Wan2.1, FLUX.1-dev, and Qwen-Image, SHARE improves PSNR and SSIM over uniform-budget BAG at all nine evaluated operating points and LPIPS at eight, including a 21.6% LPIPS reduction on FLUX.1-dev at an average budget of 20 full steps. Code will be publicly released.

LLM training is shifting from manual design and annotation to interaction-driven self-evolution. However, existing self-evolution methods face a fundamental dilemma between task diversity and verification reliability: environment-bound methods obtain precise feedback but confine learning to narrow domains, while open-ended self-generation broadens the task space but lacks reliable verification, allowing misleading rewards to pollute the training loop. We identify agent skills as a powerful middle ground to reconcile this tension: each skill ensures deep, verifiable execution in a specific scenario, while an evolving skill library enables broad and continually expanding task diversity. Leveraging this insight, we introduce Skill Self-Play (Skill-SP), a co-evolutionary framework comprising a proposer, a solver, and a dynamic skill controller. Orchestrated via a reinforcement learning loop, these components co-evolve in a continuous self-play loop: the proposer generates challenging tasks conditioned on dynamically sampled skills; the solver explores candidate solutions to push its capability boundaries; and the skill controller collects execution feedback to update and expand the skill library. This interactive co-evolution effectively bridges the gap between structured verification and open-ended exploration. Empirical evaluations on tool-use and reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that Skill-SP, serving as a robust evolution engine, consistently pushes the performance ceiling of competent backbones while catalyzing striking turnarounds for initially misaligned models.

Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions. Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored. We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts. MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes. We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry.
