Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird's-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map. Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 2.60\% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory. MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own trajectories by comparing teacher and student next-token distributions at each visited context. However, standard reverse-KL training treats token-level disagreements alike. Under large mismatch, it strongly suppresses sampled tokens rejected by the teacher while only weakly promoting teacher-preferred alternatives. Moreover, a disagreement may reflect a reasoning error, acceptable student behavior, or incompatible expression and generation conventions; disagreements of similar magnitude can therefore require different training responses. We propose GARD, a geometry-aware objective-routing method that constructs probability-aware effective supports and measures their bidirectional coverage. GARD routes teacher-supported student behavior to reverse KL, reachable teacher alternatives to reverse KL with a teacher-top-K forward-KL correction, and unsupported disagreement to abstention. On five mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-8B as the teacher and Qwen3-1.7B-Base and Qwen3-4B-Base as students, GARD achieves the highest average accuracy and shortest average responses among the trained methods. Relative to vanilla OPD, it improves average Avg@8 by 3.31 and 2.36 percentage points while reducing average response length by 44.9% and 59.7%,
respectively. It also reduces looping and maintains actor entropy close to vanilla OPD. These results support the premise that different disagreements require different distillation objectives.

A core goal of efficient reasoning is to improve the accuracy--efficiency
frontier.
However, jointly improving reasoning accuracy and inference efficiency can be
challenging, as the two objectives can favor different reasoning behaviors.
Independently post-trained models already offer distinct strengths in
accuracy and efficiency. We introduce Lightning Weave, a post-training
framework that extracts and composes these independently learned
capabilities in a single student through on-policy distillation. Each acquired
capability is represented by the policy shift from the model before
post-training to the resulting specialist. Lightning Weave combines aligned log-ratio
shifts at shared student token states and uses Tilted-Target DOPD to convert the
cached signals into a stable learning target. Each anchor pair scores the
cached trajectories once, enabling subsequent student training without serving
multiple live anchor models concurrently. Across
diverse student models and benchmarks in mathematics and code, Lightning Weave
substantially improves upon the base students and achieves a state-of-the-art
accuracy--efficiency frontier. On
Qwen3.5-4B, it raises HMMT 2025 accuracy from 59.2% to 64.0% with 10.7%
fewer response tokens, and LiveCodeBench v5 accuracy from 41.7% to 54.2%
with 9.6% fewer response tokens. Adjusting the relative strengths of the
anchor signals yields a strong empirical accuracy--efficiency
Pareto frontier. These results establish Lightning Weave as a new practical route to
efficient reasoning through capability composition.

Human annotation pipelines train and gate most deployed domain models, yet there is no validated way to decide which reviewers a capable model still needs. We introduce the $\textbf{Annotator Value Scoring Model (AVSM)}$, a five-dimensional behavioral measure of an annotator's contribution, and its self-knowledge reformulation $\textbf{Residual~AVSM}$, and evaluate them on a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system: $541{,}621$ human verification events, 483 reviewers, $1{,}184$ businesses, of which the model's prediction is confirmed unchanged 71% of the time. We make four contributions. $\textbf{(1)}$ We specify and calibrate $\Pik$, a per-transaction estimate of model self-knowledge trained from logs alone: expected calibration error $0.037$, and it predicts human correction far better than the model's raw confidence (AUROC $0.845$ vs. $0.662$), a gap post-hoc calibration of the confidence does not close, establishing self-knowledge as a signal distinct from output confidence. $\textbf{(2)}$ $\Pik$-gated routing is precise: on held-out businesses at a 20% review budget the routed set is 92.5% genuine corrections, and at matched budget confidence-routing misdirects $1.25\times$ as many real corrections into auto-acceptance. $\textbf{(3)}$ Using a simplified but faithful reproduction of the production
model, counterfactual $\textbf{segment}$ ablation shows redundant reviewer groups are causally removable: deleting the rubber-stamp cluster moves confirmation by $-0.31$pp, and pruning to high-value pairs raises correction survival ($98.4\%\!\rightarrow\!99.0\%$). $\textbf{(4)}$ We analyze the behavioral dimension that aims to capture right-first-time expertise and show it conflates expertise with overconfidence unless gated by correction quality, the overconfident cohort scores $\textbf{higher}$ on raw behavior (76.2 vs.\ 70.1), and re specify it accordingly. Underpinning these, we prove an identifiability theorem: no semivalue (Shapley, Banzhaf, Beta-Shapley, leave-one-out) of a utility that reads the data only through consensus-aggregated labels can identify annotator accuracy, and under gatekeeper/quota aggregation the computable value collapses per item to a Shapley-Shubik power index. Consistently, per-pair Shapley on our majority-vote deployment associates with volume ($r{=}0.24$), not quality, while group-level value remains measurable by ablation; the limit and the group-redundancy result replicate on a public Linux-kernel corpus.

Recent single-stage 3D generative models commonly adopt VecSet representations, encoding 3D shapes as unordered sets of latent tokens.
However, compared with two-stage methods that provide explicit positional guidance, these models must implicitly infer token positions throughout denoising, limiting their generation quality.
We observe that, despite the absence of explicit positional conditioning, VecSet tokens retain recoverable spatial correspondences.
Building on this observation, we propose Position Forcing, a position-based self-conditioning framework. During denoising, Position Forcing recovers token positions from the current clean latent estimate, quantizes them at progressively finer resolutions according to the denoising stage, and feeds the resulting positional encodings back into the diffusion Transformer.
This progressively refined positional feedback provides spatial guidance at a granularity appropriate to each denoising stage, guiding shape generation along a coarse-to-fine trajectory and substantially improving generation quality without a separate position generation stage.
Experiments demonstrate that Position Forcing achieves strong performance among single-stage 3D generative methods and outperforms several competitive multi-stage approaches.

TL;DR: Position Forcing improves single-stage 3D generation by recovering token positions from geometry latents and using them as coarse-to-fine spatial self-conditioning during denoising.

Pretrained robot policies have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in complex manipulation tasks.
However, these frozen policies struggle to maintain safety and task performance when faced with unseen scene configurations and dynamic environments.
To address this challenge, we introduce SafeWAM, a safe test-time adaptation framework that dynamically steers base policies through adapt-on-demand planning.
Its key idea is to assess safety and task progress from world-model predictions, guiding both action selection and further exploration.
A learned Risk Monitor anticipates near-term safety risks and selectively activates planning. Forward Simulation then uses the world model to predict how the scene evolves under candidate action sequences. These predictions inform Value Feedback, which evaluates safety and task progress to guide action selection. When no candidate meets both criteria, Dynamic Augmentation progressively expands beyond nominal proposals and repeats simulation and evaluation.
Experiments on VLA-Arena and SafeLIBERO show that SafeWAM increases safe success rate by 21.2--62.0 percentage points over direct execution of the base policy across suites, while also improving task success.
Analysis across planning budgets demonstrates effective test-time scaling in safe task completion.
Its safety and task-performance benefits also extend to real-world settings, where it adapts to varied obstacle configurations, including challenging cluttered scenes.

Self-evolving large language model (LLM) agents often improve by diagnosing observed failures and using these diagnoses to revise their strategies or update their training data. 
This reactive paradigm addresses known weaknesses but leaves latent capability gaps undiscovered until the agent encounters tasks that expose them. 
Can an agent instead use prior experience to anticipate failures on unseen tasks and proactively acquire the capabilities needed to avoid them? 
We introduce **EvoForesight**, a framework driven by failure forecasting for agent self-evolution. 
EvoForesight constructs a dynamic capability graph from task execution outcomes, then combines graph-derived capability statistics with task representations to estimate success probabilities and predictive uncertainty on unseen tasks. 
These forecasts guide the generation of interactive tasks that target anticipated weaknesses. 
After validation in the target environments, the generated tasks are combined with previously observed challenging tasks to update the agent through reinforcement learning. 
Iterating this process enables the agent to translate evidence from past interactions into targeted learning opportunities beyond its observed failures. 
Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show improvements in task performance, learning efficiency, and generalization to out-of-distribution scenes. 
These results support failure forecasting as a means of identifying high-value training tasks and advancing agent self-evolution from post-hoc failure remediation toward proactive, forecast-guided capability acquisition.

TL;DR: We introduce EvoForesight, a proactive self-evolution framework for LLM agents that forecasts failures on unseen tasks via capability graphs and enables targeted task generation and RL updates for improved generalization.

The effectiveness of agent memory ultimately depends on whether the underlying LLM gives each memory in context an appropriate degree of influence over its response. Yet this capability has remained largely overlooked. To assess this capability, we introduce MemCalib, a benchmark grounded in realistic memory-system scenarios for evaluating memory use and advancing optimization algorithms. Results on the MemCalib test set reveal that frontier open- and closed-source models struggle to use memory appropriately. They frequently over-use or under-use memory rather than matching each proposition's actual use to its target level, leading to biased, low-quality responses. Experiments with common post-training algorithms, including group relative policy optimization and on-policy self-distillation, further reveal a clear directional skew: trained models improve in one direction while deteriorating in the other. We therefore propose MemCalib-RL, an ordered bidirectional counterfactual credit-assignment algorithm that separates over- and under-use signals and localizes their credit to response tokens through exact atom ablation. Results across model families and scales (Qwen3-8B, Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) show that MemCalib-RL achieves the best overall performance while better balancing over-use and under-use, with gains generalizing beyond MemCalib in external benchmark evaluation. Further experiments support its design choices and robustness and provide insight into its training dynamics.

High-fidelity 3D scene generation remains a fundamental challenge in computer graphics. Diffusion methods face fundamental challenges when scaling to complex environments with many interacting objects. Conversely, procedural systems can synthesize large-scale scenes with rich geometry, but rely on implicit generative processes that are difficult to control or condition. This gap highlights the need for an explicit representation that can bridge learning-based models and high-quality procedural generation. We propose OmniSceGen, a representation-driven framework that formulates 3D scene generation as predicting a generation-aware parametric representation. Central to our approach is the Structured Parametric Language (SPL), which explicitly captures the parametric states of procedural scene generators and enables fine-grained controllability. To operationalize SPL, we instantiate it with the InfiniGen generator by implementing a bidirectional pipeline that encodes procedural scenes into SPL specifications and decodes SPL back to high-fidelity scenes. Leveraging this engine, we construct a large-scale dataset of 0.93M SPL-annotated scenes paired with text and floor plan, among which 195K have multi-view and panorama images, and train a multi-modal model to synthesize SPL from diverse inputs. Experiments demonstrate that OmniSceGen achieves strong and interpretable control over complex scenes while preserving the visual fidelity and scalability of procedural generation.

Inference-time scaling—spending more compute during prediction—has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving model performance. Yet, contrary to common practice, we show that the benefit of additional inference compute is fundamentally input-dependent and non-monotonic: difficult examples benefit from extended computation, while easy examples saturate quickly and excessive compute can even degrade performance. 

We introduce \textbf{Stress-Adaptive Inference Scaling} (SAIS), a framework that learns \emph{when} and \emph{how much} inference compute to allocate per input. SAIS constructs a lightweight stress representation that captures uncertainty, instability, and cross-trajectory disagreement—signals that indicate whether the current inference state is likely to benefit from additional computation. A learned policy then selectively allocates compute only where it provides value.

Theoretically, we characterize the non-monotonic utility of inference scaling and derive conditions under which adaptive allocation strictly dominates fixed budgets. Empirically, SAIS achieves near high-budget performance with substantially lower compute on both classification and retrieval tasks, outperforming fixed budgets and heuristic routing strategies. Our results establish adaptive inference scaling as a principled alternative to uniform compute allocation.

TL;DR: A lightweight framework that learns to allocate inference compute adaptively based on input-dependent stress signals, achieving near high-budget performance with substantially lower average compute.

Science‑inspired vision models show that explicit propagation dynamics can provide structured and interpretable alternatives to conventional token mixing. Existing formulations, however, typically construct and adapt visual propagation within a particular dynamical family, while visual representations can require substantially different spatial interactions across samples, channels, and network stages. We explore cross‑regime adaptive propagation and introduce TailProp, a hierarchical vision backbone built upon the Tail Propagation Operator (TPO). TPO uses Gaussian and Cauchy stable‑process propagators as complementary bases with rapidly decaying and heavy‑tailed spatial influence, and predicts a content‑conditioned channel‑wise coefficient to adaptively combine them. Because this coefficient is spatially shared, the two responses are fused directly in the DCT domain with a single DCT/IDCT pair, yielding $O(N^{1.5})$ spatial mixing for square feature maps with $N=HW$ and fixed channel width. Across image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, robustness, and cross‑backbone restoration, TailProp consistently outperforms matched propagation baselines; TailProp‑B reaches 84.4% Top‑1 accuracy on ImageNet‑1K, 50.3/44.8 box/mask AP under the 3× Mask R‑CNN schedule, and 50.8% mIoU on ADE20K. Controlled ablations further show that these gains are not explained by single‑basis propagation, an additional same‑family branch, or within‑family adaptive order alone, supporting complementary two‑basis propagation as an effective design principle for visual representation learning.

TL;DR: TailProp adaptively mixes Gaussian and Cauchy propagation in the DCT domain, enabling complementary light- and heavy-tailed global modeling with consistent gains across vision tasks.

Sparse voxel reconstruction offers an efficient representation for high-fidelity 3D modeling, yet its geometry is commonly optimized from local photometric evidence and discrete visibility statistics. This often leads to fragmented surfaces, excessive subdivision, and floating artifacts, particularly in weakly textured or sparsely observed regions. We introduce SurfSVR, a novel sparse voxel reconstruction paradigm that treats 2D surface priors as explicit 3D geometric regularizers. Instead of directly lifting noisy pixel-wise depth predictions, SurfSVR first organizes each image into coherent surface regions by jointly reasoning over appearance, monocular depth, normals and cross-view geometry. Each region is then represented by an adaptively selected planar or quadratic surface model based on fitting reliability and geometric complexity, while cross-model agreement distinguishes reliable geometry from ambiguous predictions. These structured 2D priors are lifted into 3D and integrated throughout the reconstruction pipeline. They guide surface-adaptive voxel subdivision, provide region-level depth and normal supervision during optimization, enhance geometrically reliable sparse-observed surfaces in voxel pruning, and suppress off-surface floaters during post-refinement training. This unified design converts semantic and geometric coherence in image space into persistent structural constraints in 3D. Extensive experiments on 3 public benchmarks demonstrate that SurfSVR consistently improves sparse voxel reconstruction across scenes with substantially different visibility and geometry characteristics, achieving state-of-the-art reconstruction quality. 
Codes and models will be released soon.

Whole-slide image (WSI) analysis presents a supervision mismatch: an agent makes local decisions while navigating a multi-gigapixel slide, yet supervision is often available only as a single slide-level label, with no feedback on individual decisions. Inspired by how pathologists draw on representative prior cases, we ask whether a WSI agent can learn to form and use memory from coarse feedback rather than through weight updates. This requires learning not only what to remember, but also where and when remembered experience should influence local decisions. A natural approach selects candidate experiences by their marginal reduction in counting error. However, we identify a failure mode termed positive-influence collapse: the number of candidates with positive influence falls from 50 after the first memory admission to zero by the tenth, despite many candidates remaining. Coarser supervision also shortens memory-growth trajectories, suggesting that aggregate feedback rapidly loses resolution for distinguishing beneficial local experiences. Motivated by this observation, we introduce \textbf{\ours{}} (\textbf{MeM}ory-\textbf{A}ugmented \textbf{W}SI Agent), which decouples memory construction from memory application. Marginal error reduction serves as a conservative admission signal, calibrated retrieval-space coverage determines where admitted experiences can be trusted, and memory is consulted only for uncertain regions. Extensive experiments show that \ours{} learns a compact and transferable memory from slide-level supervision, reducing mean absolute error by \textbf{57\%} on \dsA{} and by \textbf{37\%} on an external dataset, without region annotations or weight updates. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

Diffusion Transformers deliver state-of-the-art video generation, but their long spatiotemporal sequences make attention the dominant deployment cost. Low-bit attention can address this cost by running both matrix multiplications on low-bit Tensor Cores, but a deployable kernel must be both accurate and fast. Accuracy is limited by outliers: a block's quantization scale is set by its largest entries, leaving every other entry few effective bits. Prior work smooths queries and keys, but value outliers follow no fixed channel or spatiotemporal structure and remain the dominant source of output error. Speed is limited by softmax: the high-precision exponential between those two multiplications becomes the longest pipeline stage on datacenter GPUs. We propose VC-Attention, a training-free low-bit attention kernel that addresses both by pairing Value smoothing with a fused probability Cast. V-Smooth reorders value tokens by lightweight online clustering, so that each hardware block holds values of similar size. It quantizes only the residual left after subtracting the block mean and restores that mean from the row sum the online softmax already maintains. ExpCast-FP8 maps log-domain scores directly to E4M3 probability codes with one fused multiply-add, eliminating the FP32 exponential and the format conversion. We implement VC-Attention at 8 bits on B200 and H200, port it to B300, and run V-Smooth alone at 4 bits on RTX PRO 6000 and RTX 5090. Across Wan2.2, LongCat-Video, HunyuanVideo-1.5, and MiniMax-H3, VC-Attention improves fidelity over SageAttention2 at 8 bits and SageAttention3 at 4 bits, speeds up attention over BF16 FlashAttention-4 by 1.50–1.59× on datacenter Blackwell and Hopper, where the 8-bit FlashAttention-4 it modifies reaches 1.24× on B200, and by 2.51–3.56× on workstation cards, and runs the denoising loop 1.25–1.26× and 1.59–1.64× faster.

TL;DR: Low-bit attention mechanism that is accurate and efficient for video generation

Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as a human-guided co-evolutionary process in which worlds and agents continuously shape one another through interaction. However, scaling this process to increasingly complex real-world settings faces two bottlenecks: (1) Manually constructing large-scale, heterogeneous, and verifiable environments is costly and difficult to scale; and (2) Agent capability is increasingly constrained by the Harness, whose manual iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. We introduce ***Create, Evolve, and Explore***, a recursive self-improvement framework that automates this loop through a Trinity of Creator, Evolver, and Explorer, enabling Agent Harnesses to co-evolve with automatically generated worlds. Within this loop, recurring failure mechanisms across heterogeneous tasks point to shared capability gaps. This finding motivates capability-conditioned Harness families: Harnesses evolve from a shared root of reusable capabilities into branches organized by capability composition rather than task boundaries, enabling each Harness to serve a class of heterogeneous tasks with similar requirements. Finally, we introduce Game2World to evaluate frozen Harnesses on unseen games and in real-world embodied systems. Experiments span 15 task directions and 88 unique seed tasks, ranging from visual perception to embodied interaction, including newly introduced tasks in visual inspection, process control, and construction. Compared with the initial Harness, evolved Harnesses improve mean task success rate by 30-point, with a 40-point gain on real-world open-world place search tasks.

TL;DR: Multimodal Harness RSI through world–Harness co-evolution centered on shared capabilities, enabling reuse and specialization across heterogeneous tasks.

Hallucination is a property of how an answer relates to its source, not of the model that wrote it. We make that observation operational. A small open-weight model that merely reads a generated answer against its source document carries, in its own activations, enough signal to catch hallucinations from any generator, including closed APIs whose internals no detector can access. We extract eighteen mechanistically grounded features from this reader, organized around three failure mechanisms, and train a stacking ensemble across six analyzer architectures from 0.5 to 9 billion parameters. Every analyzer beats the ReDeEP token-level baseline on RAGTruth, winning 35 of 36 analyzer and generator pairings. On the out-of-distribution LLM-AggreFact benchmark, held fully out of training, our best analyzer reaches 73.7 percent balanced accuracy, within 1.3 points of a purpose-trained supervised model despite no exposure to its domains. Two findings surprised us. Removing a standard adversarial NLI corpus improved transfer by 2.8 points, and detection quality sits in a 2.1-point band across an eighteen-fold parameter range. A causal check closes the loop. Ablating the twenty highest-importance attention heads raises the generator's own hallucination rate by 11.3 to 29.2 points, while matched random ablation of equal size stays far behind, at zero and 7.1 points on the two families

TL;DR: A small open weight model can detect hallucinations from any generator, outperforming white box baselines on 35 of 36 pairings, with head ablations confirming it reads circuits whose removal causally increases hallucination

Autonomous field systems must make decisions from incomplete, asynchronous, and unequally reliable observations while accounting for distribution shift and imperfect actuation. We propose a missingness-aware framework that combines random Fourier features, adaptive reliability-weighted kernel mean embeddings, and causal attention to construct context, control, and plan beliefs. Future true-vertical-thickness trajectories are represented as residual corrections to an interpretable geometric backbone, while a conditional variational autoencoder generates action-conditioned scenarios. Predictive uncertainty combines heteroscedastic scale, latent dispersion, model variation, geological compatibility, distributional novelty, and effective evidence, followed by chronological conformal calibration. Candidate plans are evaluated through stochastic executed-action and transition models using Mean--CVaR model predictive control, branch-specific tail allocation, and barrier penalties. Under contractive approximate policy improvement, persistent sampling, dynamics, actuation, approximation, and numerical errors imply convergence to a bounded neighborhood of the ideal policy. In the chronological well-data experiment, geometry-preserving residualization reduces RMSE from \(14.719\) ft to \(8.888\) ft, although residual shift causes severe conformal undercoverage. In counterfactual control simulations, Mean--CVaR MPC provides the strongest observed mean--tail trade-off. Throughout, we distinguish dataset-supported forecasting, simulated control, and architecture-level diagnostics.

Learning-assisted autonomy must reason under incomplete sensing and uncertain actuation without granting an uncalibrated model direct authority over safety-critical actuators. We introduce a modular architecture combining measurement-age-aware multimodal belief construction, candidate-plan-conditioned probabilistic forecasting, executed-action-aware mean--CVaR planning, heterogeneous command supervision, bounded-error safety tightening, and random-feature kernel--Galerkin approximation. The forecaster conditions on \( \xi_t=c_t\Vert\psi_t^{\mathrm{ctrl}}\Vert\pi_t \), which combines a \(64\)-dimensional reliability-aware belief, a \(32\)-dimensional control-context embedding, and an \(8\)-dimensional candidate-plan embedding. Observation masks and measurement ages regulate kernel-mean aggregation and temporal attention. Future scenarios model both trajectory uncertainty and stochastic command realization. Experiments use \(5{,}000\) chronological UAV telemetry records and \(4{,}992\) rolling sequences. Recurrent and kernel models remain strong point-forecasting baselines. The complete belief is less accurate under clean sensing but preserves calibrated coverage and representation stability more effectively under severe missingness and persistent staleness. Kernel--Galerkin experiments further show that low Bellman residual can coincide with severe numerical ill-conditioning. Since the dataset lacks synchronized command, execution, and solver logs, the control experiments are presented as telemetry-grounded counterfactual simulations rather than flight-safety validation.

Autonomous systems must act from incomplete observations while accounting for uncertain futures and imperfect command execution. We propose a three-layer closed-loop framework. Layer I constructs a missingness- and age-aware multimodal belief using modality encoders, random Fourier features, weighted kernel mean embeddings, recurrence, and reliability-biased attention. Layer II generates policy-conditioned scenarios of future targets, executed actions, physical states, trajectory costs, and barrier losses. Layer III combines kernel--Galerkin generalized Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman evaluation, mean--CVaR model predictive control, nested risk propagation, and executed-action-aware CVaR control-barrier constraints. The defining modeling choice is to integrate the conditional execution law \(P_A(da\mid\chi,u)\) in both value evaluation and safety analysis rather than assuming \(A_t=u_t\). Common random numbers, constrained policy improvement, safe backtracking, and command--execution residual learning support stable comparison and online actuator adaptation. Experiments on traffic, groundwater, and UAV benchmarks evaluate forecasting, calibration, belief robustness, random-feature sensitivity, and 4,600 counterfactual candidate-risk evaluations. Controlled Monte Carlo studies further compare six controllers and actuator gain--delay stress. These experiments provide pre-deployment methodological evidence; they do not establish causal command effects, field-calibrated actuation, or operational safety.

Can a sequential system detect an approaching regime transition before it becomes visible in the observations themselves? We study this question as an information problem and derive an information-theoretic limitation for any detector whose stopping rule is measurable with respect to the observed data. Specifically, we show that the cumulative divergence $I_{T1}=\sum_{s=1}^{T1} KL(P_s^{(1)} || P^{(0)})$ accumulated during a latent build-up interval determines the information available for pre-transition detection: when $I_{T1}\leq\log(1/\delta)$, the probability of firing before the transition is bounded for every reactive detector satisfying a false-alarm constraint $\delta$. For the Gaussian linear-drift model, we derive the corresponding cumulative information in closed form and show that it grows cubically with build-up duration. We then develop a non-parametric detector based on temporal score channels and a learned representation trained using transition-endpoint supervision. Under an explicit hypothesis-class richness and optimisation assumption, the learned representation is guaranteed to be at least as informative as the best feasible linear projection. Experiments on a controlled latent-regime system and two real-data domains examine the relationship between cumulative information, detector behavior, representation, and event prevalence. The synthetic experiments show systematic dependence of lead-time and coverage on signal strength and build-up duration, while the real-data evaluations expose substantial false-alarm challenges under low event prevalence. Together, the results establish cumulative information as a fundamental constraint on reactive pre-transition detection and provide a framework for studying how available information is converted into early-warning decisions.

TL;DR: We show that pre-transition detection is fundamentally limited by accumulated information, and develop a causal multi-channel detector and learned representation to test when early warning is possible.

As language models scale, their final-answer performance often changes, but
accuracy alone does not characterize changes in the text trajectories they
generate while solving a problem. We introduce Reasoning-Trajectory
Measurement (RTM), a measurement framework for analyzing observ-
able properties of generated reasoning trajectories across model scales.
RTM specifies a set of trajectory-level observables and a protocol for test-
ing whether their scaling behavior is consistent with smooth variation or
localized change. We further describe the Reasoning Transition In-
dex (RTI) as a future aggregate summary of validated trajectory mea-
surements; it is not treated as a direct measurement of latent reasoning
mechanisms.
As an initial controlled study, we evaluate Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on matched GSM8K prompts and decoding settings.
We measure trajectory length, line structure, explicit step markers, lexical-
marker rates, and descriptive answer accuracy. The two models differ in
several observable text statistics, including generated length and explicit
step-marker use. However, the two-scale pilot does not test for a disconti-
nuity, identify a critical scale, or establish a general reasoning transition.
Our contribution is therefore a transparent measurement protocol and re-
producible pilot for future multi-scale studies of how generated reasoning
trajectories vary with model capacity.

TL;DR: A controlled measurement protocol and pilot study for analyzing how observable reasoning-trajectory statistics vary across language-model scales.

Learning-based control can fail when observations are incomplete, predictions depend on candidate actions, and commands are not delivered as intended. We present a belief-to-action framework with three components: a reliability-aware multimodal belief using availability, measurement age, source quality, random Fourier features (RFF), a cumulative kernel mean embedding (KME), and temporal attention; an action-conditioned probabilistic predictor that separates commanded from executed actions; and a risk-sensitive controller combining Mean--CVaR model predictive control with tightened CVaR control-barrier constraints. We prove model-conditional feasibility transfer under bounded barrier-loss error and show that approximate safe policy iteration converges to a $2\bar\varepsilon/(1-\gamma)$ neighborhood under persistent error. On a geographically held-out property-crime panel with 315 area--year examples, simple low-variance predictors outperform higher-capacity proxies under 30\% missingness, and an uncalibrated nominal 80\% interval covers only 41.9\% of outcomes. In a separate 3,000-rollout semi-synthetic control study, executed-action-aware CVaR--CBF control achieves the lowest upper-tail loss, while Mean--CVaR MPC achieves the lowest mean loss and observed violation probability. Observational and simulation claims are separated explicitly. The intended use is auditable place-level service allocation, not person-level prediction or enforcement.

Existing memory-augmented LLM agents store past experience exclusively in prompt space, as textual summaries or retrieved passages, while keeping model parameters frozen throughout a rollout. Such agents can \emph{look up} what they have seen but cannot \emph{learn from} it: their policy is unchanged by experience, and any information dropped from the context is permanently lost. We introduce \texttt{TMEM}, a self-evolving parametric memory framework in which the agent not only compresses history into explicit memory but also absorbs distilled supervision into fast LoRA weights $\Delta_t$ via lightweight online updates, genuinely altering its future behavior within a single episode. We formalize this as an agentic decision process with fast-weight rollout dynamics: actions are sampled from $\pi_{\theta_0+\Delta_t}$, while extraction actions produce supervision that updates $\Delta_t$ for subsequent decisions. This view makes the extraction policy directly optimizable by RL: training $\theta_0$ improves not only task actions but also the quality of the data used for online LoRA adaptation. We further propose SVD-based initialization of the LoRA subspace to improve adaptation quality under a limited online update budget. Experiments on LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, multi-objective search, and CL-Bench show that \texttt{TMEM} outperforms summary-based and retrieval-based baselines across different model scales.

The rapid evolution of text-to-image (T2I) generation models has effectively solved the foundational challenge of raw pixel synthesis, shifting the community's focus toward fulfilling increasingly intricate user requests. While recent agentic image generation workflows enhance static inference with advanced capabilities like external knowledge retrieval and iterative reasoning, they mostly operate in isolated silos with fixed ``one-size-fits-all" topologies. This inevitably leads to severe compute-mismatch, where simple queries are forced through computationally heavy pipelines. To bridge this gap, we present **GenRouter**, the first unified workflow routing framework for agentic image generation. We first formulate **GenCanvas**, standardizing diverse agentic pipelines into a universal set of foundational primitives and executable templates. Operating over this unified space, GenRouter adaptively routes heterogeneous prompts to their optimal workflows via (***i***) **demand profiling**, (***ii***) **experience matching**, and (***iii***) **Pareto filtering**. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate that GenRouter achieves superior visual alignment while reducing execution costs by over $95$% and latency by $65$% compared to heavyweight static pipelines. Furthermore, the system continuously self-evolves via accumulated experience, enabling robust zero-shot generalization that boosts performance and halves computational overhead.

Bayesian inference for unknown drift in scalar additive-noise SDEs relies on the Girsanov likelihood, which admits an exact Gaussian posterior on any discretized mesh. We characterize the spectral geometry of this posterior in closed form: under simultaneous diagonalizability of the prior covariance and observation weights, the posterior contracts selectively as the noise level $ \sigma \to 0 $, concentrating in a growing set of low-frequency modes whose count $N_\rho(\sigma)$ obeys the predicted continuum scaling law $N_\rho(\sigma) \asymp \sigma^{-2/(2\nu+1)}$. We test this prediction not by fitting a single exponent, but by tracking how the fitted exponent changes as the discretization $n$ grows from $16$ to $256$: it converges from $-1.27$ toward the continuum value $-1/2$, with a finite-size extrapolation landing within $1.2$ standard errors of it. This spectral geometry has a concrete computational consequence: the preconditioned Crank--Nicolson (pCN) sampler, run at a single fixed step size, suffers severe acceptance collapse as $\sigma$ decreases, with $74%$ of chains freezing entirely in our small-noise regime. An independent pilot-search experiment further shows that the step size required to maintain workable acceptance shrinks sharply with $N_\rho(\sigma)$. We also test the natural hypothesis that a closed-form mode-wise mismatch ratio explains this degradation mode-by-mode; the resulting correlation is statistically indistinguishable from zero and disagrees in sign between estimators. We report this negative result rather than omit it, since the paper's central claims do not depend on it. Together, these results provide an exact and empirically supported account of a concrete small-noise computational obstruction for function-space MCMC, while making explicit what remains mechanistically unexplained.

TL;DR: We characterize how pCN sampling degrades as an SDE posterior concentrates in the small-noise regime, linking sampler behavior to the growth of informative posterior modes.

We study learning-based autonomy under heterogeneous, delayed, and missing observations. The proposed three-stage framework first maps modality-wise values, availability masks, and measurement ages to a reliability-aware belief using random Fourier features (RFFs), a contribution-weighted cumulative kernel mean embedding (CW-CKME), adaptive forgetting, and reliability-biased temporal attention. The belief and candidate actions then condition probabilistic state and trajectory predictors. Finally, an executed-action model supports Mean--CVaR and branch-CVaR model predictive control (MPC), kernel--Galerkin value approximation, online actuator adaptation, and a tightened CVaR control-barrier-function (CBF) shield.

Experiments on drip and tomato irrigation data cover random, block, and modality-level missingness. On drip, direct and modality-specific features outperform cumulative kernel representations; Quantile GBDR obtains the lowest forecasting RMSE, $0.672$. On tomato, CW-CKME gives the highest normalized belief score, while a sparse-GP approximation obtains the lowest RMSE and predictive-error CVaR$_{0.95}$, $0.981$ and $1.711$. Nominal $90\%$ quantile intervals achieve empirical coverage of $0.599$ on drip and $0.884$ on tomato, exposing substantial dataset-dependent miscalibration. In a five-seed synthetic control study, Mean MPC has the lowest observed mean and tail costs. Adaptive CVaR--CBF reduces actuator-gain estimation error by about $35\%$ relative to the fixed-model shield, while all evaluated controllers remain within the simulated safety band. The results support gated fusion of recent, modality-specific, cumulative, and attended beliefs rather than unconditional kernel accumulation. Under contraction and uniformly bounded approximation error, approximate policy evaluation converges to a quantified neighborhood of the ideal value function.

Autonomous irrigation must act safely despite incomplete sensing, uncertain dynamics, and imperfect water delivery. We introduce a three-layer architecture that connects missingness-aware perception, probabilistic prediction, and risk-aware actuation. The perception layer combines modality-specific encoders, random Fourier features (RFFs), reliability- and age-weighted kernel mean embeddings (KMEs), and temporal attention to construct a compact field belief. The prediction layer conditions soil-moisture and evapotranspiration forecasts on a structured triad comprising field belief, current control context, and planned actuation. The decision layer uses executed-action-aware scenario generation, mean--conditional-value-at-risk (CVaR) model predictive control (MPC), kernel--Galerkin value approximation, and a two-sided control-barrier-function (CBF) safety filter with margins for model, actuator, sampling, approximation, and numerical errors. Experiments use a 3,000-record tomato dataset and a 3,780-record drip-control dataset. Because the datasets are not time-synchronized, perception forecasting is evaluated directly, whereas cross-dataset control and plan conditioning is treated as a proxy stress test rather than causal evidence. The results show that missingness can alter latent beliefs and actions before average forecast error changes substantially, kernel attention is more stable than Euclidean pooling, actuator and implementation errors materially affect safety, and persistent errors imply convergence to a quantified neighborhood rather than exact optimality.

Inference-time verification can improve the reliability of large language model
(LLM) outputs, but it also increases inference cost. A central open question is
therefore not only whether additional verification helps, but when its expected
benefit justifies its cost. We formulate Adaptive Verification Scaling (AVS), a
framework that treats verification effort as an input-dependent budget allocation
problem. In the general formulation, a policy selects a verification budget from
pre-verification uncertainty and disagreement signals, with the goal of improving
the accuracy–cost trade-off relative to uniform verification.
We report a diagnostic GSM8K pilot of a restricted two-action instantiation using
Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. The current self-verifier requests repair
for all 100 evaluated examples, causing the procedure to collapse to a fixed three-
call pipeline. Although its accuracy point estimate exceeds that of a matched
fixed-budget baseline (9.0% versus 6.0%), the paired bootstrap confidence inter-
val includes zero and no computation is saved. Thus, the pilot does not validate
adaptive verification scaling; instead, it identifies calibrated pre-verification sig-
nals as the central requirement for a complete evaluation of the framework.

TL;DR: We diagnose when inference-time repair helps LLM reasoning and show that useful repair alone does not guarantee selective compute allocation.

Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide transferable forecasting capabilities across diverse domains, but their deployment is often constrained by computational cost. A frozen TSFM may nevertheless reveal transferable behavior beyond its forecast values: it can change its forecast for the same absolute future target when its fixed-length context advances by one step. We formulate predictive revision distillation to transfer these cross-origin responses to compact students. Since forecast changes need not be task-relevant, we propose Revision Geometry (RG), which relates calibrated teacher revisions to outcome-conditioned corrections using training data. Their time-frequency correspondences define a response geometry for measuring student-teacher revision discrepancies, while task-compatible gradient coordination integrates auxiliary guidance with supervised training. RG requires no teacher hidden states and leaves the deployed student's inference graph unchanged. Across eight TSFMs, thirteen datasets, and ten students, comprising 1,040 evaluation cells with three seeds each, RG reduces mean pinball loss by 12.35% relative to task-only training and is best in 928 cells. On a matched panel, direct predictive-revision matching outperforms output matching, and RG achieves a further 8.86% reduction over direct predictive-revision matching. Gains over task-only persist at longer horizons and in interval quality. Revision–correction coherence yields teacher rankings distinct from forecast accuracy and is positively associated with RG's gains over direct predictive-revision matching. These findings support predictive revisions as a useful distillation object alongside forecast values.

Autonomous irrigation must transform incomplete multimodal observations into reliable predictions and physically executed actions. We introduce a three-layer framework that connects missingness-aware belief construction, belief-conditioned probabilistic prediction, and risk-aware control under actuator uncertainty. The belief layer combines observation masks, measurement age, modality-specific random Fourier features, reliability-weighted kernel memory, and temporal attention. The prediction layer compares classical baselines with GRU--Gaussian and conditional variational models conditioned on observation and control context. The control layer evaluates mean--CVaR MPC, branch-tail allocation, and executed-action-aware CVaR--CBF control under finite scenario sampling and command--execution mismatch. Experiments use controlled corruption of irrigation records, five-seed neural prediction simulations, and 120 matched closed-loop controller episodes. Reliability-aware beliefs improve pump-label macro-$F_1$ under structured outages but do not uniformly improve forecasting or calibration. Quantile GBDR gives the lowest pooled trajectory RMSE, while the perception--control CVAE is the strongest neural point forecaster. No predictor attains nominal 90\% coverage. Executed-action-aware CVaR--CBF gives the lowest aggregate simulated cost, tail risk, and violation rate, but increases switching and action mismatch. Persistent model and actuator errors produce nonzero convergence neighborhoods. The results support modular evaluation across belief, prediction, risk, control, and execution spaces, while remaining distinct from field-certified irrigation safety.

When intervention targets are uncertain, learning causal relationships and
identifying directly perturbed variables become a joint task.
We develop an exact mixed-integer program based on optimized parent-set scores (PS-MIP) for joint graph and intervention-target estimation in
linear Gaussian structural equation models under stochastic hard interventions.
The method can incorporate candidate-edge restrictions and partial target
knowledge when available. For each random variable, PS-MIP evaluates candidate sets
of direct causes, or parent sets, by optimizing
the likelihood parameters and compatible target patterns, retaining both the
score and a minimizing target pattern. A global mixed-integer program then
selects parent sets subject to acyclicity. Under stated conditions, this
reduction preserves the joint objective and reconstructs the graph, targets,
and likelihood parameters. On synthetic data, PS-MIP achieves favorable
false-discovery--true-discovery trade-offs relative to several benchmark algorithms for causal discovery with unknown intervention targets, along with strong intervention-target recovery in denser settings. An exploratory study
on real data from a controlled physical system further demonstrates recovery
beyond simulation.

TL;DR: We introduce PS-MIP, a mixed-integer optimization method for jointly learning causal graphs and unknown intervention targets, with favorable synthetic results against competing methods.

Humanities-oriented publications contain rich visual materials whose scholarly meaning is jointly conveyed by images, captions, and body text. Despite extensive digitization, complex page layouts leave these resources visually accessible yet computationally locked. Existing document parsers recover page structure but not image--text semantic association, while general-purpose vision-language models lack reliable document-level evidence alignment and guarantees of verbatim extraction. We therefore formulate image-centric multimodal information extraction and introduce CHIME-Bench, where each target image, its caption, directly related body text, and provenance are organized into a traceable Image-Centric Multimodal Context Unit (ICMCU). The benchmark comprises 30 publications, 5,508 pages, and 6,239 human-verified ICMCUs, supporting both component-level and end-to-end evaluation. We further provide a reproducible reference framework combining document parsing, page-level joint vision-language reasoning, and deterministic validation. Evaluations of direct PDF processing, per-image alignment, and page-level joint reasoning show that structured processing substantially improves complete ICMCU recovery (58.64\% $F_1$ for the best configuration), while body-text association remains a major bottleneck. CHIME-Bench thus establishes a standardized, traceable foundation for document understanding, knowledge-base construction, and multimodal model training.

Autonomous systems must forecast and act under asynchronous multimodal observations, informative missingness, stale measurements, transition mismatch, and imperfect actuation. We propose a unified perception--control--planning framework that encodes modality values together with availability and measurement age, maps modality-specific representations through random Fourier features (RFFs), forms contribution-weighted cumulative kernel mean embeddings (KMEs), and applies reliability-biased temporal attention to obtain a belief state. The belief and executed-action history condition Gaussian recurrent and conditional variational predictors. The control layer combines executed-action-averaged dynamics, Kernel--Galerkin value approximation, Mean--CVaR model predictive control (MPC), branch-dependent tail allocation, and CVaR control-barrier filtering with an explicit error ledger. Controlled simulations show that the proposed belief reduces latent and forecast RMSE by approximately 7.9\% and 8.4\% over last-value propagation and reduces policy regret by 23.3\%. Under narrow-bound adversarial stress, Mean MPC attains the lowest empirical CVaR and violation rate, demonstrating that risk labels alone do not guarantee robust behavior when scenario tails are undersampled, projections are myopic, or margins are transferred between incompatible spaces. We establish convex-fusion stability, belief-to-control and forecast error transfer, CVaR tightening under bounded loss error, and convergence of approximate safe policy iteration to a quantified neighborhood rather than exact optimality.

Large language models are increasingly deployed as advisors whose stated objective is not perfectly aligned with the user's: recommender systems optimize for engagement, sales assistants for purchases, and negotiation agents for favorable concessions. Whether such advisors remain truthful when honesty conflicts with their own payoff is a core alignment-evaluation question. This paper turns the canonical Crawford-Sobel cheap-talk model into a pre-specified benchmark for measuring LLM honesty under preference misalignment. Classical cheap-talk theory predicts neither full revelation nor complete silence, but coarse monotone partition communication, with fewer informative intervals as preference conflict increases. A sender observes a state $\omega\in[0,1]$, wants the receiver's action close to $\omega+b$, and sends one costless message to a receiver whose ideal action is $\omega$. To keep the study defensible and easy to complete, the confirmatory design uses $5$ bias levels, $3$ prompt frames, one pre-specified low-temperature decoding setting, $200$ states per treatment cell, and a pre-registered $4$-model run requiring $12{,}000$ sender calls, which we then extend to eight models, five prompt frames, and $39{,}569$ logged sender calls. The positive-bias grid is $b\in\{0.01,0.04,0.08,0.12\}$, for which the exact most-informative Crawford-Sobel partition sizes are $7$, $4$, $3$, and $2$. Under a $20$-bin discretization, the corresponding oracle normalized mutual-information values are $0.5294$, $0.3268$, $0.2205$, and $0.1829$. Running the full design on eight models spanning two capability tiers - the four pre-registered instruction-tuned models (GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B) and four reasoning models added afterwards (GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Kimi-K3), for $39{,}569$ logged sender calls in total - we find that all of them over-reveal relative to the most-informative cheap-talk equilibrium by a factor of $1.8$ to $4.5\times$: pooled over models excluding Llama-3.3-70B, whose format-violation rate excludes it from pooled statistics, normalized mutual information stays at $0.82$-$0.96$ where the oracle prescribes $0.18$-$0.53$. Informativeness declines with bias as predicted ($\widehat\beta=-1.71$, $t=-7.50$) but never approaches the strategic optimum; rather than coarse partitions, models exhibit near-full revelation with a constant upward offset that tracks their bias (linear exaggeration). Payoff-maximizing versus honesty framing has negligible effect. A structural hint separates capability from propensity: told the equilibrium partition size, reasoning models state a correct Crawford-Sobel cell in $0.20$-$0.99$ of messages while the non-reasoning tier never exceeds $0.005$, and one model overrides a deliberately infeasible hint to state the true partition instead. The strategic capability is therefore present and goes unexercised unless it is asked for, which locates the failure in propensity rather than in competence. A decoder ablation shows the finding is recoverable only when the receiver reads the sender's stated number: an embedding-only decoder mis-reads the same data as near-babbling.

TL;DR: Given a private state and a misaligned payoff, LLMs over-reveal instead of playing the coarse cheap-talk equilibrium; told the equilibrium partition, reasoning models can produce it, so the failure is propensity rather than capability.

Learning to control networked mobility systems requires more than accurate forecasting: a controller must represent spatial coupling, propagate predictive uncertainty, and coordinate interacting decision makers under operational constraints. We formulate this problem as graph-coupled stochastic optimal control and develop a modular architecture combining an RKHS value representation, a physics-informed neural approximation of the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation, a conditional variational autoencoder for scenario generation, and a mean-field coordination layer. The RKHS component yields an explicit kernel-gradient feedback law, while the neural residual increases approximation capacity. Conditional trajectories support prediction-interval calibration and tail-risk evaluation, and the mean-field approximation replaces all-to-all interaction with dependence on an aggregate state distribution. Prototype studies on UAV sensor data and UTD19 traffic measurements evaluate obstacle classification, one-step forecasting, multimodal probabilistic prediction, and simplified closed-loop stabilization. In the quick-run traffic study, attention pooling obtains the lowest mean RMSE among ten variants, but every variant has zero F1 at the default event threshold. The results support component-level feasibility while identifying calibration, repeated-seed evaluation, graph quality, and end-to-end closed-loop validation as necessary next steps.

Most coding-agent benchmarks are static: an agent receives a complete task de-
scription up front and is judged only by its final code. Real coding assistance is
interactive, with users clarifying goals, adding constraints, and correcting mistakes
over multiple turns. We introduce SWE-Together, a multi-turn benchmark recon-
structed from real user–agent coding sessions. To make real interactions verifiable,
we curate 109 repository-level tasks from 11,260 recorded sessions, selecting ses-
sions with recoverable repository states, clear user goals, and observable outcomes.
To replay these interactions across agents, we build a reactive LLM-based user
simulator that preserves the original users’ intents and provides feedback when
the coding agent’s progress requires it. To evaluate agents as collaborators, we
measure both final repository correctness and the number of corrective feedback
turns required during the interaction. Experiments with frontier coding agents show
that stronger agents generally achieve higher final success rates while requiring
fewer interventions, suggesting an improved user experience.

TL;DR: SWE-Together turns 109 real user–agent coding sessions into replayable multi-turn tasks, where an LLM user simulator re-issues the original feedback as the agent works, scoring both final correctness and how much user correction the agent needs.

Incorporating rich task-relevant context, such as domain knowledge and external observations, is a key capability yet remains challenging for Bayesian optimisation (BO). Recently, practitioners have started to use large language models (LLMs) to generate and execute BO programs through coding harnesses. In such emerging practices, the posterior belief is shaped not only by Bayesian inference but also by LLM-generated model and data artefacts, offering a flexible route for task context to enter BO as executable code. To study whether and how LLMs can be harnessed to compile diverse contextual signals for BO, we formulate LLM-compiled BO as generalised-context decision making. We propose HarBO, a BO-specialised harness that compiles generalised context into the core artefacts of standard BO through a validated multi-stage workflow. Our theory analyses the regret under imperfect compilation and the effect of adding new context. Across synthetic functions and real-world benchmarks, we find that LLM harnesses can effectively compile context into standard BO, achieving competitive performance with specialised LLM-embedding-based and direct LLM-in-the-loop BO methods. General coding harnesses can be effective in familiar domains such as hyperparameter optimisation, but fall short in unfamiliar, context-rich domains. Together, these results establish LLM harnesses as a promising, but not automatically reliable, route for making rich task context usable in BO.

TL;DR: LLMs can compile task-relevant context into Bayesian optimisation through coding harnesses, while HarBO provides a specialised staged harness that makes this compilation more reliable.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show strong potential in visual mathematical reasoning, yet remain bottlenecked by inaccurate visual perception---most failures originate from perceptual errors rather than reasoning deficiencies.
Compounding this, individual models exhibit \textit{perceptual stubbornness}: they cling to initial observations with extreme overconfidence, failing to self-correct even when provided with ground-truth judgements.
To address this, we propose Conflict-Guided Multi-Agent Collaboration (CGMAC), which structures observations from heterogeneous agents into a shared perceptual playbook---a dynamically maintained list of fine-grained visual facts.
A Conflict Localization mechanism categorizes each entry as consistent, complementary, or conflicting, while a Convergence Assessment module governs iteration.
Critically, reflection is conflict-triggered: agents perform targeted rechecks only on conflicting entries, enabling efficient perception correction within a single additional round.
This strategy allows heterogeneous agents to expose each other's visual blind spots and converge on accurate perceptual grounding.
On MathVision, Gemini2.5Pro and GPT-5 achieve gains of +3.0\% and +10.2\% respectively, with secondary reflection applied to only 10\% of instances---demonstrating that this training-free approach delivers edge-case gains for frontier models while preserving inference efficiency.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for everyday assistance, yet existing benchmarks poorly reflect the requests users actually make in practice. Unlike standardized questions, everyday tasks are often open-ended, casually specified, and context-dependent: users may omit requirements that must be inferred from their background, goals, and task context. We introduce xDailyBench, a benchmark of 248 expert-curated tasks spanning 51 scenarios. The tasks are grounded in requests that users have actually completed or genuinely intended to accomplish with AI tools, with relevant user background and task context incorporated when necessary to preserve implicit needs. Each task is paired with a fine-grained rubric for reference-free evaluation, with rubric criteria further annotated by an five-dimensional capability taxonomy for diagnostic analysis. We evaluate multiple frontier models in a unified agentic setting. The best models achieve overall scores of about 75.6\%, respectively, leaving substantial room for improvement. Further analysis shows that failures concentrate in grounding, reasoning, and accuracy rather than surface presentation. XdailyBench reveals a persistent gap between benchmark competence and the ability to reliably satisfy everyday user needs. Our data is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/status/Xdaily-2B1D.

TL;DR: We introduce xDailyBench, a benchmark evaluating LLMs on realistic everyday tasks requiring contextual understanding and inference of implicit user needs. Experiments reveal substantial gaps in models' ability to satisfy everyday requirements.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) without human-annotated data, often referred to as “zero RL”, has emerged as a powerful paradigm for eliciting chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. However, due to computational constraints, existing studies are largely restricted to small models, leaving the training dynamics and emergent capabilities at a large scale unexplored.
To meaningfully explore this frontier, we aim to elicit high-quality reasoning behaviors from the model.
However, we find that naive scaling often suffers from poor readability, token redundancy, and a lack of adaptive reasoning depth. To address these challenges, we present a stable and efficient training pipeline, incorporating algorithmic and system optimizations such as clipped importance sampling, training-inference ratio correction, and mixed-precision control. 
Our experiments offer three key findings that validate the bitter lesson of scaling: (1) scaling to 1T parameters significantly enhances sample efficiency and performance ceilings; (2) the training process progresses sequentially through an initial discovery phase followed by a sharpening phase; and (3) the model spontaneously develops advanced cognitive behaviors, including anthropomorphism, structured formatting, self-verification, parallel reasoning, and context anxiety, rendering hand-crafted heuristics redundant. Evaluated on seven challenging mathematical benchmarks, Ring-2.5-1T-Zero achieves competitive performance. Additionally, to assess CoT quality beyond final-answer correctness, we propose a structured evaluation framework across three dimensions: comprehensibility, reproducibility, and efficiency, under which our model demonstrates clear advantages in producing structured and concise reasoning traces.

TL;DR: We scale zero reinforcement learning to a 1T-parameter model through a stable multi-stage training pipeline, achieving strong mathematical reasoning while enabling controllable reasoning budgets and concise, structured reasoning traces.

Adaptive training becomes scientifically useful when its effect can be connected to the model that is evaluated. We introduce ACTA, a diagnostic protocol that makes this connection explicit through controller measurements, applied actions, effective optimizer updates, and selected-model exposure. In a 75-run matched speech-text distillation study, ACTA reveals that acoustic-only, aligned-text, and shuffled-text systems return identical predictions and probabilities in all 15 seeds under global validation-best selection: their selected models come from the shared acoustic stage. Final-epoch evaluation instead compares the completed schedules and yields different endpoint contrasts. Paired endpoint probes show that repaired controller weights produce resolved shared-trunk gradient and update changes in all 15 probed seeds, while the deployed controller remains unresolved in three seeds. Historical interventions trace the deployed failure to insufficient resolution at the MMD observation scale, and MELD reproduces the same measurement/action signature. Thus ACTA converts an opaque endpoint comparison into an interpretable sequence of checks, separating mechanism exposure, optimizer engagement, and predictive inference.

Training a model needs parameter updates through iteration. The number of parameters keeps growing. The update process looks more and more like solving a high-dimensional complex dynamical system. This poses challenges for compute and for understanding. Physics often uses a macroscopic view to replace microscopic computation. In recent years, a bridge has opened from Newtonian mechanics to the Boltzmann equation and then to fluid equations. This bridge links the microscopic and macroscopic worlds. We build on this idea. We propose a new view. We treat the saved parameters as particles. We treat the model structure as space. One update then becomes one large-scale particle motion. We can then extrapolate the parameter update with physics methods. This explores a possible replacement for gradient updates. We organize six methods in a hierarchy. They are trajectory prediction, second-order analysis, surface reconstruction, field theory, Hamiltonian dynamics, and kinetic theory. We test them on classification, segmentation, and translation tasks. Our results show two sides. At the parameter level, some predictors come close to the truth. The early freeze method scores 0.4292 against a truth of 0.4561. The late BGK method scores 0.5781 against a truth of 0.5734. The weight variance also follows a first-order relaxation. At the function level, the framework fails. We put the predicted parameters back into the model. The accuracy then drops to random chance, around one percent. We locate two root causes. First, the extrapolation time depends on the training stage. No single predictor works across all stages. Second, the reverse mapping breaks the channel order inside the convolution kernels. Low parameter error therefore does not mean good function. A kinetic diagnosis adds one more point. The conservation laws, the Gaussian ground state, and universality are all missing in the weights. A strict derivation of the weight fluid equation is therefore not possible for now. This paper does not offer a ready-to-use predictor. It proposes and tests a new idea. It explores the idea in a systematic way. It locates the current boundary of the idea. We hope this points the way for future work.

TL;DR: We treat a model's parameters as computable physical particles and other physical quantities, model their changes across iterations with mathematical and physical laws, and thereby derive the parameter update rule without any training.

Linear probes are the standard way to ask what a representation encodes, but the properties they target come from annotation, so the ground truth is noisy and its structure is outside the experimenter’s control. We instead build a generative world model in which the factor of interest is written into the data by hand, which lets us ask which parts of a factor survive an encoder–decoder’s latent bottleneck. Utterances are synthesized so that a latent affect state modulates pitch, energy, rate and spectral tilt across speakers of differing expressiveness; a nonstationary label process calibrated to asset dynamics supplies task labels and serves only as a measurement instrument. At matched latent dimension we compare a matrix latent that keeps twelve temporal frames, as neural audio codecs keep a sequence of latent vectors, with a vector latent that pools them into one global code. Three findings. First, the pooled bottleneck’s reconstruction error is essentially unchanged (0.257 to 0.254) across a 16°ø increase in budget and stays within 0.011 of the within-utterance share of the input variance, which we measure directly; the matrix configuration goes below that bound and improves with capacity. Second, on a structured factor most of the layout gap follows from averaging rather than from training: pooling a trained matrix latent after the fact leaves slope R2 0.06, unchanged under tiling. What training adds above that baseline grows log-linearly in channel width, and an ablation shows it is carried diffusely rather than by particular channels. A scalar factor separates the layouts by 0.02, but a ridge probe on the raw log-mel input reaches only 0.74 on that target, so there was little room for it to; the trajectory gap is 0.43 under a convolutional trunk and four to ten times smaller under a transformer that mixes frames before the bottleneck. Third, the ordering holds on 21,900 real podcast clips for contour components measured from the encoder’s own input, which tests information preservation rather than recovery of affect. Across five frozen encoders the loss to pooling ranges over 0.15 to 0.77 and follows neither trunk class nor parameter count, so which encoders are sensitive remains open.

TL;DR: Pooling over an audio bottleneck’s temporal axis discards within-utterance structure, regardless of the factor being represented, and this loss cannot be detected by the scalar probes commonly used in this literature.

Reinforcement learning with GRPO now drives the reasoning ability of language models, yet its
training curves are still predicted by fitting saturating functions whose constants carry no
mechanism. We instead derive a reduced-order model (ROM) of GRPO training from the GRPO update rule. Treating
the expected reward as a scalar order parameter, we reduce clipped, momentum-driven stochastic
ascent to a two-dimensional stochastically forced damped oscillator whose coefficients are derived
from the learning rate, momentum, sampling lag, clip gate, KL weight, and group size. Its mean
trajectories form a closed-form family of equations that covers monotone
saturation, overshoot, and damped oscillation. The derivation explains why most design choices
change training efficiency but not the performance ceiling: optimizer hyperparameters set only the
oscillator's rates, while the ceiling is a fixed point that moves only with the reward, the KL
weight, and the group size. It also shows that policy staleness and clipping add damping rather
than removing it. Across three language models from 1.5B to 7B parameters, trained on
mathematical and code reasoning at two group sizes each, the closed form fits evaluation reward
with $r^2$ between $0.96$ and $1.00$, matches the ScaleRL sigmoid on monotone curves, and captures
non-monotone curves it cannot. A single pole pair fits all components of a structured, multi-component
reward at little loss of fit, a setting that empirical scaling fits leave open, and the per-component fits explain out-of-distribution performance: runs transfer when correctness rises, not when total reward rises through formatting. We also report where the model fails: KL relaxes more slowly than the reward, and the fitted pole sum is smaller than momentum alone predicts.

TL;DR: Science of GRPO Training

Two representations can encode identical task-relevant information yet collapse under distribution shift in entirely different ways, and no standard diagnostic can tell them apart before deployment. We introduce $M_{\mathrm{stab}}(\phi;\mathcal{T})$, a post-hoc, computable measure of how robustly a fixed, frozen representation preserves task information under an anticipated transformation class $\mathcal{T}$, requiring no retraining, no multiple environments, and no labeled target data. We prove three results built on a corrected foundation: a $\sqrt{M_{\mathrm{stab}}}$ generalization bound relating Bayes-risk degradation to $M_{\mathrm{stab}}$, derived via Pinsker's inequality after showing the natural Fano-based argument used in prior attempts is invalid, and certified order-tight by a matching lower-bound example; an exact characterization showing $M_{\mathrm{stab}} = 0$ if and only if the posterior $p(Y\mid\phi(X))$ is $\mathcal{T}$-invariant, with Bayes-prediction agreement following as a strictly weaker corollary; and a total-variation shift-mismatch bound guaranteeing graceful, not catastrophic, degradation when the anticipated and deployed shift families differ. We validate this last, most practically consequential result twice. A stratified, confound-controlled feature-space study, spanning three backbones, two datasets, and 54 representation conditions, shows $M_{\mathrm{stab}}$ on an anticipated shift predicts degradation under a disjoint, unseen deployment shift (partial rank $r = 0.65$, $p = 5\times10^{-5}$, positive in all six strata), decisively outperforming mutual-information and CKA baselines under an identical test. A corroborating real-pixel-corruption study across supervised, contrastive, and self-supervised objectives confirms the same direction under genuine corruptions, reported with the statistical caveats its smaller model count demands. Together, theory and evidence establish $M_{\mathrm{stab}}$ as a rigorous, deployment-ready tool for selecting robust representations sight unseen.

TL;DR: We introduce a tight, post-hoc diagnostic for representation robustness under distribution shift, with corrected information-theoretic guarantees and validation across 100+ representations under synthetic and real shifts.

General-purpose robot agents must learn from experience, transfer their knowledge to new tasks, and act efficiently during physical execution. Code as Policies (CaP)
methods provide flexibility by generating and repairing robot programs after a
task arrives. However, runtime coding is slow and often encodes task-specific
coordinates and recovery decisions, limiting generalization and transfer. Although
recent self-improving CaP methods use experience from past programs, they
still rely on runtime code generation, and their ambiguous play-time objectives
may lead to experiences that are not applicable to downstream tasks. In this
paper, we address the evolution-to-execution problem by moving coding to the
evolution stage, while using more flexible and efficient function calls within
a Reasoning-and-Acting (ReAct) loop at runtime. To this end, we introduce
RACAP, an agentic framework that evolves typed policy application programming
interfaces (Policy APIs), a ReAct agent harness, and experience memory before
deployment. During evolution, we adopt a two-phase strategy that combines
capability curriculum learning with autonomous self-evolution, enabling the
system to learn and evolve gradually and steadily. During this process, the Policy
APIs are optimized for generalizability and steerability. The ReAct agent maintains
task-objective-driven working memory and experience-based long-term memory,
enabling it to handle long-horizon tasks. At runtime, it uses visual observations
and perceptual feedback to call Policy APIs, adapt its strategy, and respond
promptly to changes in physical state. Experiments demonstrate the generalization,
transferability, and efficiency of RACaP. On LIBERO, RACaP achieves 54.4%
in-domain success, transfers zero-shot to LIBERO-PRO with 45.0% success,
and solves 46.0% of long-horizon tasks on LIBERO-Long, compared with at
most 4.0% for CaP baselines. On LIBERO-PRO, RACaP achieves 2.5× the
success rate of CaP baselines while providing a 1.9× speedup in median policy
time. For more efficient on-robot edge deployment, we use rejection-sampled
fine-tuning to distill the ReAct agent’s decision traces from GPT-5.6 into a compact
Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct model. The distilled model achieves a 13.2× per-decision
inference speedup and reduces repeated physical calls from 16 to 4. These results
show that separating reusable code from runtime decisions enables continued
evolution, effective transfer, and efficient long-horizon control.

Interactive 3D head generation requires coordinated speaking and listening motion that responds to an evolving conversation.
