Existing generators use incoming observations as context but keep their parameters fixed, leaving conversational patterns unused as a learning signal. We introduce **EvolvingAvatar**, a causal generator that uses test-time training to adapt to user face video and dyadic audio during interaction. Its *dyadic context prediction* objective provides a self-supervised learning signal from audiovisual context without target motion labels at test time. Persistent fast weights accumulate these updates within each conversation to guide motion generation, while transient jaw adaptation responds to current audiovisual context. Predicted speech activity controls how persistent adaptation guides motion. We also introduce **InterHead-Bench**, a unified 455.95-hour benchmark built from single-view and dual-view conversation videos. Experiments show improved conversational motion statistics over strong baselines. On the hardest out-of-distribution split, generation improves as conversations unfold, reducing mismatch with recorded user--avatar expression statistics by up to 11.1% from the first interval. *We will publicly release our source code and data after the review process.*

TL;DR: EvolvingAvatar learns as conversations unfold, using self-supervised test-time training to adapt 3D head motion for both speaking and listening.

Floorplan reconstruction from 3D scans for applications such as area measurement requires not only recovering room structure but also accurately locating walls and corners.
Existing learning-based methods can recover structure, which however, will incur substantial localization errors.
We present Joinery, a metrically faithful method that inherits the geometric precision of classical fitting by reformulating floorplan reconstruction as learning which walls join.
Specifically, we fit walls directly to the point cloud and predict their pairwise adjacency with a transformer that integrates wall geometry with the surrounding point-cloud evidence.
The predicted adjacency then guides the assembly of walls into rooms, and corners are located by intersecting the fitted wall lines.
To assess metric fidelity, we also introduce an evaluation protocol that reports geometric errors in real-world units alongside recovery performance at the corner, room, and scene levels.
On Structured3D and SpatialLM, Joinery improves structure recovery at all three levels and achieves mean corner localization errors of $8.2\mathrm{mm}$ and $11.2\mathrm{mm}$, respectively, compared with $49.7$--$76.2\mathrm{mm}$ for the five baselines.
Evaluation on HouseLayout3D further shows that the synthetic-trained adjacency prediction model generalizes to real scans.

Extractive rationalization models enhance neural network transparency by using a dual-stage architecture where a generator selects human-interpretable predictive fragments (rationales) for a predictor. Despite their inherent accountability, recent findings reveal that these frameworks are critically vulnerable to tailored backdoor attacks, which exploit the generator’s discrete selection mechanism to bind malicious shortcuts while maintaining clean performance. Conventional defenses, such as heuristic purification or standard adversarial training, often fall short; they simultaneously degrade gold rationale quality and fail to dismantle these advanced spurious correlations. To address this deadlock, we propose InvRation, an end-to-end framework designed to induce invariant rationale representations against diverse backdoor and shortcut manipulations. Drawing inspiration from continuous transformation, we bypass the optimization bottlenecks of discrete text space by constructing a continuous latent perturbation manifold. Active Manifold Adversarial Mining (MAM) is then employed to explore and extract worst-case perturbations that maximize classification risk and rationale drift. Furthermore, to prevent representation collapse, we introduce a Rationale Feature-Consistent Contrastive Mechanism (RF-CCM), aligning latent representations of clean and perturbed rationale views within the generator. Extensive evaluations across five NLP benchmarks demonstrate that InvRation substantially suppresses the Attack Success Rate (ASR) from over 98\% to below 8\%, effectively neutralizing backdoor shortcuts while simultaneously preserving or boosting task accuracy and gold rationale faithful.

Foundation-model agents increasingly improve through repeated verifier-guided updates on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and tool-augmented web tasks. Yet endpoint rewards constrain final outcomes rather than the internal computation along sampled trajectories. Local deviations can therefore accumulate over long executions and destabilize policy optimization. We formalize this path dependence as discrete holonomy in hidden-state transport. We prove a local-to-finite control chain: local transport residuals telescope into full-path Jacobian disagreement; transported curvature accumulates into the relative holonomy characterized by this disagreement; and the disagreement controls finite endpoint error. This connection motivates Path-Jacobian RLVR, which directly regularizes transport disagreement between same-prompt rollouts using efficient shared-probe vector-Jacobian products. Experiments across mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive decision-making settings show that Path-Jacobian RLVR generally outperforms the PPO baseline across multiple models and tasks. Ablations over Jacobian estimator budgets and model architectures further demonstrate improved training stability and the generality of the gains across both discrete and continuous trajectory models.

TL;DR: Semantically equivalent reasoning paths diverge because of holonomy, we bound it with curvature and fix it with a regularizer.

Latent moderators that read a model's own activations are far cheaper than guard models, but nearly all score a single layer. We argue depth is a signal. Projecting last-token states onto per-layer LDA harm directions yields a trajectory whose shape separates harmful from benign prompts: harmful trajectories drift upward, and benign ones fluctuate. We call this Harmfulness Propagation Dynamics (HPD) and show analytically that depth-aggregated drift estimation achieves signal-to-noise scaling $L^{3/2}$, unlike terminal-layer readout (Proposition~1). We introduce HERALD (**H**armful **E**ncoding **R**ecognition via **A**ctivation **L**ayer **D**ynamics), which extracts seven shape descriptors from the trajectory and classifies them with a 289-parameter MLP, storing one $d$-dimensional direction per layer ($262$\,KB for $L=32$) with no extra forward pass. Across eight benchmarks and four backbones, HERALD improves over the strongest latent baseline by $2.8$-$4.6$ F1, reaches $89.3$ average F1 on OLMo2-7B, and outperforms all guard models on adversarial jailbreak detection ($98.4$ vs. $96.9$ F1 on WildJailbreak). However, HERALD V2 achieves $90.1$ average F1. We report a matched-supervision protocol alongside in-domain results and release per-instance trajectories for interpretability that single-layer detectors cannot provide.

TL;DR: HERALD detects harmful prompts by tracking their upward drift across layers via per-layer LDA directions, then classifies seven trajectory shape features with a 289-parameter head, no extra forward pass, just 262 KB storage.

Most high-quality open language-model checkpoints are dense autoregressive (AR) models, whereas strong diffusion language model (dLLM) checkpoints remain scarce. We address the upcycling task of converting a pretrained dense AR model into a fine-grained sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) diffusion language model, which simultaneously reuses dense pretraining, changes the training objective to block denoising, and expands each dense feed-forward network into a grid of routed FFN-slice experts. Expert-choice (EC) routing fixes expert-side capacity and is substantially faster than token-choice (TC) routing in our training stack, but it also exposes structure-specific failures in fine-grained upcycling. First, all upcycled variants are initialized from the same dense FFN, making early router learning poorly conditioned. Second, EC balances experts but does not guarantee that each token receives a complete slice-wise FFN path. Third, soft routing regularizers do not fully determine the hard routing pattern used at inference. We propose \ours{}, an EC-based upcycling recipe with delayed router re-initialization, a slice-structured routing objective, and inference-time coverage repair. On Qwen3-4B upcycled to a 
-expert diffusion MoE, \ours{} reaches a  downstream average across MMLU, GSM8K, MATH, and HumanEval, exceeding vanilla EC by 
 and a TC baseline by  while running on top of the EC dispatcher; exact-one slice coverage rises from  to and zero-coverage events drop from  to .

Language-model systems increasingly consume generated trajectories through parsers, monitors, verifiers, and local editors, making explicit intermediate state part of the interface between a model and downstream computation. We study whether this machine-addressable trajectory state can be controlled independently of final-answer behavior using instruction duplication: repeating only a procedural instruction, without retraining, decoding changes, or model-internal interventions such as activation steering. Across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, moving from one to two instruction copies raises deterministic completion of all eight requested trajectory states from 90.22% to 93.17%, eliminating 30.2% of the formal failures remaining after one copy, while aggregate answer accuracy remains exactly 60.21%. A complete 2 × 2 × 2 placement factorial shows strong saturation and placement dependence rather than additive gains, with a trailing duplicate producing the strongest tested effect. Human audit shows that many machine-detected transitions are perceptual ties, indicating that human-semantic and controller-operational equivalence need not coincide. This distinction becomes operational in Answer Engineering, a deterministic trajectory editor: in a 1,000-case SSNHL reproduction, adding the same trailing duplicate raises the controller-equipped endpoint from 84.2% to 97.1%. Duplication also increases premature commitment and weakens a nearby contrastive branch, showing that it is a control parameter rather than a monotone improvement. Together, these results show that instruction copy count and placement can serve as simple black-box controls over the explicit trajectory state exposed by language models to downstream systems.

TL;DR: Repeating a procedural instruction changes machine-addressable LLM trajectory state without changing aggregate answer accuracy; in a deterministic trajectory editor, it raises the controller-equipped endpoint from 84.2% to 97.1%.

High-fidelity electromagnetic (EM) simulations are indispensable for the design of microwave and wave devices, yet repeated full-wave evaluations over high-dimensional design spaces are often computationally prohibitive. While neural surrogates can amortize this cost, learning high-dimensional EM response mappings remains difficult under limited simulation budgets due to strong and heterogeneous parameter couplings. In this work, we introduce low-rank tensor function representations as a principled surrogate modeling paradigm for EM problems and provide a systematic study of representative low-rank formats, including Tucker-style low-rank tensor function representation (LRTFR) as well as neural functional tensor-train (TT) and tensor-ring (TR) baselines. Building on these insights, we propose a pairwise low-rank tensor network (PLRNet) that uses learnable pairwise interaction factors over compact coordinate-wise embeddings. Experiments on representative EM surrogate tasks demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a more favorable overall trade-off between accuracy, robustness, and parameter efficiency, with stable optimization in high-dimensional regimes.

TL;DR: We introduce low-rank tensor function representations as a unified paradigm for electromagnetic surrogate modeling and, guided by a systematic study of representative formats, propose PLRNet for heterogeneous parameter interactions.

We propose TA-PGD-ILSR, a modular first-order framework that combines monotone gradient descent, event-triggered perturbations, impulsive lower-level-set restarts, and anytime-valid local stopping. The impulsive level-set restart (ILSR) operator approximately solves the target-level equation $f(z)=f(x)-\Delta_L$ using a damped minimum-norm correction based only on function values and gradients. Candidate restarts are committed only after verified objective decrease; unsuccessful trials are rolled back without modifying the incumbent or persistent optimizer state. Under trajectory-wise smoothness, reachable strict-saddle geometry, and a uniform conditional PGD escape condition, we establish finite high-probability termination at an approximate second-order stationary point or within a declared strongly convex basin, together with explicit gradient-oracle accounting. A separate lower-level accessibility result bounds the failure probability and number of accepted ILSR transitions from relevant nonglobal local minima. After independent verification of basin entry, a recursive confidence sequence provides an anytime-valid stopping certificate for the local stochastic phase. Controlled analytic benchmarks show that gradient descent initialized at a stationary strict maximum remains trapped, whereas TA-PGD and ILSR escape and reach positive-curvature minima. A unified reproducibility pipeline generates the software environment, run-level results, trajectories, figures, and manuscript tables.

Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) are common chronic gastrointestinal disorders in which treatment response can vary substantially between patients and over time. This makes the selection of an effective treatment difficult, particularly when symptoms change across repeated visits. A digital twin can represent the changing patient state and estimate how that state may respond to a candidate treatment. However, we did not identify a public longitudinal patient-level treatment-response dataset for GERD or IBS that supports direct evaluation of this type of model. In this study, we therefore develop a literature-calibrated simulation and propose GutTwin, a neural state-space digital twin that combines a recurrent patient-state encoder, treatment-specific prediction heads, and split-conformal uncertainty calibration. The simulated cohort contains 2,000 patients with GERD, IBS, or both and 24,000 monthly patient-visit records. We compare GutTwin with linear, multilayer perceptron, recurrent, and independent treatment-arm baselines using patient-grouped cross-validation. The recurrent models reduce next-visit prediction error relative to the flat baselines, with GutTwin reducing root mean squared error by about 5% for GERD and 6% for IBS compared with ridge regression. The counterfactual analysis gives a different result, where the simpler T-learner achieves lower error than GutTwin. Conformal coverage remains close to the 80%, 90%, and 95% nominal targets on both conditions. These findings show that longitudinal state modeling can improve short-term prediction, while additional model complexity does not automatically improve counterfactual estimation. The study provides a transparent simulation-based evaluation protocol that can later be tested using real longitudinal GERD or IBS data.

TL;DR: GutTwin combines recurrent patient-state modeling with treatment-specific heads and conformal uncertainty; sequence models improve next-visit prediction, while a simple T-learner performs better for counterfactual estimation.

Physics-inspired objectives are frequently proposed for generative video
models, yet it is often unclear whether a proposed latent regularizer has
the intended representational effect before it is evaluated in a complete
video-generation system. We study this preliminary question at the level of
latent temporal dynamics.
We formulate PhyS-Diffusion, a physics-inspired latent-video modeling
framework containing a second-order latent-dynamics regularizer, interaction-
aware attention, and optional surrogate-energy guidance. These components
are surrogate constraints: they encourage selected properties of latent
trajectories, but do not recover a physical simulator or guarantee physical
correctness.
Our empirical evidence deliberately isolates the second-order regularizer.
We train matched small latent video autoencoders on procedurally gener-
ated videos of bouncing discs. Across five matched independent trials, the
regularizer reduces mean held-out latent acceleration energy from 0.027831
to 0.001564. This change entails a small reconstruction cost: mean re-
construction MSE increases from 0.012846 to 0.013078. Thus, the exper-
iment establishes a smoothness–reconstruction trade-off in the evaluated
representation-learning setting.
The evidence is narrow by design. It does not evaluate a pretrained video
diffusion backbone, interaction-aware attention, surrogate-energy guidance,
physical-consistency benchmarks, or real-world physical validity. We there-
fore position this work as a reproducible mechanism diagnostic rather than
evidence that the complete framework improves video generation or physical
consistency.

TL;DR: A controlled five-seed diagnostic shows that second-order latent regularization smooths latent video trajectories at a small reconstruction cost, without claiming improved physical video generation.

Agent harnesses have become a key paradigm for enabling large language models to solve long-horizon tasks through planning, tool use, and repeated interaction with dynamic environments. However, existing data-refinement methods, largely developed for multi-agent systems with relatively fixed interaction patterns, struggle to adapt to heterogeneous tasks and stochastic environmental feedback. This mismatch creates a fundamental tension between improving refinement efficiency and preserving information essential for downstream task execution. We introduce TidyLoop, which reformulates harness data refinement as a long-horizon reinforcement-learning task to strengthen a reusable loop-level refinement skill through adaptive primitive selection and execution feedback. To learn adaptive refinement without relying on explicit refinement supervision, we develop a paired-trajectory reinforcement-learning objective that turns long-horizon execution outcomes into comparable refinement feedback across diverse tasks. To capture the delayed and trajectory-dependent consequences of refinement, we further learn latent refinement dynamics and optimize the policy through long-horizon imagined rollouts, enabling the refinement skill to anticipate downstream effects beyond immediate context reduction. Extensive experiments show that TidyLoop achieves more efficient long-horizon refinement without sacrificing task performance, supporting loop-level refinement skill learning as an effective alternative to fixed refinement strategies.

Safe reinforcement learning methods typically rely on transient penalties while assuming stationary environment dynamics. We show this creates *replay*: when penalties decay, reintroducing the same stimulus re-triggers delayed harm because the environment responds identically. We introduce the *Replay Suppression Diagnostic (RSD)*, a policy-frozen evaluation protocol that isolates environment-side mechanisms within an explicit reset-and-freeze construction, and prove that under this construction, stationary observable dynamics make replay unavoidable. We propose *Regret-Aware Persistence Deformation (RAPD)*, a mechanism, not a policy-optimization algorithm, that equips a mediator with bounded, dual-timescale transition memory: fast-decaying *traces* and slow-integrating *scars* that deform the transition kernel with provable distortion and odds-contraction bounds. Across four controlled domains (MovieLens-25M recommendation, Safety Gym control, Reddit cascades, and graph diffusion up to $10^5$ nodes), results are mixed and metric-dependent: cumulative replay harm (AUC-R) improves in every domain, sometimes substantially, but peak-harm suppression (RAG) is weak or absent in two of the four, and the domain with the strongest effect carries the largest utility cost. A controlled ablation causally isolates the mechanism, and a targeted follow-up experiment resolves an anomalous baseline result on graph diffusion rather than leaving it unexplained. We report these results, including their limits, honestly, and treat RAPD as a concrete existence proof that mediator-side memory can address a failure mode policy-side memory structurally cannot under a full reset, rather than as a deployment-ready system.

TL;DR: A policy-frozen diagnostic exposes replay as a structural failure of stationary dynamics, and RAPD suppresses it by giving the environment bounded persistent memory.

Can AI systems be aligned to human values? The popularization of large language models (LLMs) and multi-modal foundation models has seen a rise harms spanning from toxic speech and hallucinations to AI agents executing unauthorized actions. Within the field of AI safety, these harmful instances are often framed as “the alignment problem,” of models being “misaligned” with human values. Researchers have responded by pursuing applied and theoretical AI “value alignment” efforts, often without specifying what they mean by human values. How does the field of AI value alignment conceive of human values? How are these conceptions of values technically operationalized and evaluated? What does the emergent theory of value from this field signify for the future of AI?

We annotated 94 AI value alignment research papers to discern their implicit theory of values in AI. The majority do not define values, relying heavily on “preferences” as a stand-in that runs the risk of reducing complex, culturally situated concepts down to binary choices. As researchers dispense with using human annotators for model training and evaluation, turning instead to synthetic data and LLM-as-a-judge approaches to aligning and evaluating models, we identify the potential to close off alternative methods for contesting and enacting values in foundation models. In making AI value alignment’s philosophical commitments explicit, we seek to bring greater specificity and under-explored perspectives into the debate on whether and how AI can address human values.

TL;DR: A critical review of influential alignment literature to reveal the lack of coherent view of human values in the field.

arge language models (LLMs) can produce multi-step chain-of-thought (CoT)
responses, yet analyses of reasoning commonly focus on generated tokens or final
answers rather than the temporal organization of internal activations. We study
activation trajectories extracted from generated reasoning traces and ask whether
low-dimensional coordinate systems support predictable held-out transitions.
We introduce Reasoning Genome, a representation-learning framework
that encodes intermediate hidden states into 128-dimensional coordinates
with reconstruction and transition regularization. We evaluate the frame-
work on GSM8K and StrategyQA using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct,
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, and TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, across
three matched random seeds. All representations use trajectory-level splits,
training-only standardization, and the same held-out linear one-step transition pro-
tocol. Reasoning Genome yields lower standardized transition error than PCA,
random projection, and raw hidden-state baselines in all six model–task condi-
tions. However, a matched-capacity MLP autoencoder obtains lower error in every
condition, and all methods yield negative held-out R2. Cross-model alignment di-
agnostics yield held-out linear CKA values of 0.665 between the two Qwen scales
and 0.651 between Qwen2.5-0.5B and TinyLlama.
The study provides a controlled diagnostic for comparing activation coordinates.
It does not support the claims that Reasoning Genome is the most predictive rep-
resentation, that its coordinates are universal across models, or that they directly
encode semantic reasoning operations.

TL;DR: We provide a controlled diagnostic for testing whether low-dimensional coordinates of LLM activation trajectories support held-out transition prediction.

Quantum computing calibration depends on interpreting experimental data, and calibration plots provide the most universal human-readable representation for this task, yet no systematic evaluation exists of how well vision-language models (VLMs) interpret them. We introduce QCalEval, the first VLM benchmark for quantum calibration plots: 243 samples across 87 scenario types from 22 experiment families, spanning superconducting qubits and neutral atoms, evaluated on six question types in both zero-shot and in-context learning settings. The best general-purpose zero-shot model reaches a mean score of 72.3, and many open weight models degrade under multi-image in-context learning, whereas frontier closed models improve substantially. A supervised fine-tuning ablation at the 9-billion-parameter scale shows that SFT improves zero-shot performance but cannot close the multimodal in-context learning gap. As a reference case study, we release our model, an open-weight model based on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B that reaches 74.7 zero-shot average score.

TL;DR: QCalEval evaluates vision-language models on quantum calibration plots and releases a trained open-weight reference model for this task.

As agents move from research prototypes to deployed tools, their capability increasingly depends on model-external execution infrastructure, commonly termed the agent harness. Changing this harness while holding model weights fixed can substantially alter task performance. Current agent evaluations typically report downstream performance under a chosen harness, leaving a model's ability to develop the harness itself comparatively underexplored. We introduce HarnessDev, a benchmark that shifts the unit of evaluation from task outputs to runnable infrastructure. HarnessDev covers two stages. In Creation, the agent starts from a minimal seed and a small number of cases, then builds a complete execution system. In Evolution, it starts from its own created harness and iteratively revises it using downstream execution feedback, with the goal of improving benchmark performance. We then evaluate each constructed harness on capability—task success on held-out benchmarks, and efficiency—execution-token cost. The reported Creation results cover six creator LLMs, four domains, and five downstream benchmarks totaling 2,207 unique downstream instances, with hidden evaluation tasks withheld from development. We find that generated harnesses remain substantially behind mature human-engineered references on code and on search and research, while matching or exceeding the selected references on writing and machine-learning experimentation, with large variation in execution cost. Evolution produces some performance gains, but they are unstable and transfer only partially to held-out tasks. Experiments with a fixed runtime model further show that the gains depend strongly on the model executing the harness, indicating limited transfer across models.

Self-consistency (SC) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by aggregating multiple sampled answers, but it treats sampled reasoning traces primarily through their final-answer agreement. This leaves open whether structural properties of intermediate reasoning, such as equation consistency, numerical coherence, and completeness, provide additional information about answer reliability.

We study this question using Structure-Validated Self-Consistency (SC-SV), a lightweight framework that extracts structure-derived scores from model-generated reasoning traces. The score uses symbolic usability, equation consistency, numerical coherence, final-answer stability, and reasoning completeness, without model retraining, task-specific labels, or an external learned verifier.

Across six matched model-seed conditions on MathBench-X-Synth, a controlled symbolic reasoning benchmark, the structure-derived score predicts final-answer correctness substantially better than an answer-agreement-based self-consistency score (mean AUROC $0.8826$ versus $0.7244$). However, using the score in our current top-ranked-trace aggregation rule does not improve final-answer accuracy over standard SC. These results show that reliable trace ranking and reliable answer aggregation are distinct inference-time objectives. We position lightweight structural signals as promising tools for selective prediction, abstention, and adaptive verification, while identifying the design of an effective aggregation rule as an open problem.

TL;DR: Structure-derived signals predict whether LLM mathematical answers are correct better than self-consistency agreement, but do not automatically improve answer aggregation.

Representations learned from operational telemetry often fail to transfer across systems because observation-level similarity is not the same as operational similarity. A memory-pressure episode in one stack can look unlike the same condition in another, while two visually similar metric windows can react very differently to the same corrective action. This paper studies a different training relation: two pre-intervention states are treated as response-equivalent when the same known intervention produces sufficiently similar measured post-intervention responses. We formulate each training episode as multimodal pre-action telemetry, an intervention identifier, a measured response vector, and a system/domain label. The proposed model combines modality-specific temporal encoders, gated fusion, action-conditioned response prediction, a response-equivalence contrastive objective, and a domain-adversarial regularizer. The design is intended to preserve action-relevant semantics while reducing platform-specific shortcuts. Evaluation is defined a priori around whole-system leave-one-domain-out transfer using public microservice telemetry and a separately instrumented live test bed. The central comparison is against observation-based time-series representation learning, response prediction without response-equivalence, and domain alignment without response-equivalence; action and response shuffling serve as negative controls. No causal-identification claim is made. The paper instead asks a falsifiable representation-learning question: does grouping states by what actually happens after the same intervention produce embeddings that transfer better to an unseen system? Numerical results are intentionally withheld from this pre-registration-style draft until the authors complete the real-data runs described in the experimental protocol.

TL;DR: We learn cross-system telemetry representations by treating two states as equivalent when the same intervention produces a similar measured response, and test whether this relation improves transfer to unseen systems.

Lighthouse Attention proposed a symmetric hierarchical pooling and gradient-free selection mechanism that accelerates long-context pre-training by 1.4–1.7× end-to-end while recovering dense-attention quality after a brief SDPA resume phase. Despite these gains, three structural rigidities limit its potential: (i) a fixed per-layer top-k budget that ignores head-to-head variance in selection entropy; (ii) independent scoring across pyramid levels, discarding the strong prior that coarse-level selections should bias fine-level routing; (iii) no mechanism to carry selection state across transformer layers, even though empirical evidence shows that important tokens tend to recur across depth. We address all three limitations in Pharos, a drop-in augmentation to Lighthouse Attention built around four coordinated mechanisms: Depth-Sounding Budget Allocation (DBA) redistributes the global k budget across heads proportional to per-head selection entropy; Range Light Cross-Level Guidance (RCG) injects upsampled coarse selection scores as a learned additive bias into fine-level logits before top-k; Tidal Momentum Selection (TMS) maintains an exponential moving average of selection logits across layers, creating a persistent prior over globally important tokens; and Fog Gate Confidence Fallback (FCF) dynamically widens the attention beam for low-confidence heads via a learned binary threshold. We prove that DBA strictly tightens the selection-recall bound of Lighthouse Attention under any non-uniform head-entropy profile, and that TMS provably reduces cross-layer selection variance. All four mechanisms are implemented as a drop-in wrapper over the existing selection interface with no asymptotic overhead.

TL;DR: Pharos augments Lighthouse Attention with four mechanisms—adaptive budget allocation, cross-level guidance, tidal momentum, and uncertainty-aware fallback—improving long-context LLM pre-training efficiency.

Distributed LLM serving separates two placement problems that are usually solved by different, disconnected mechanisms: which replica should handle a request (routing), and which physical page should hold a given key-value (KV) block once it arrives (intra-node paging). PagedAttention solved the second problem within one node; consistent-hash request routers solve the first across a cluster. Neither reaches the boundary between them: the decision of which node in the cluster should own a given KV block, made without a centralized index. We propose Buoy, a synthesis rather than a new primitive: weighted consistent hashing over content-addressed block identities already computed by existing prefix caches, protected from power-law prefix popularity by a bounded-load cap whose overflow is resolved by rendezvous hashing across a small replica set, composed with unmodified intra-node paging via an explicit two-level chain-affinity split. A coordination service is scoped to cluster-membership metadata only, bounding its write load to membership-change events rather than to the request or block rate. We give the placement algorithm, the two structural guarantees that follow directly from existing theorems (bounded remap cost on scale events, bounded worst-case load), and a comparison against PagedAttention, DualMap, and LEAD along complexity axes.

TL;DR: Buoy unifies KV-cache placement across distributed LLM clusters using bounded-load consistent hashing over content-addressed block identities, eliminating the need for a centralized placement index.

Watermarking enables the attribution of text generated by large language models, but most existing methods determine watermark placement from local token statistics. Local uncertainty alone may be insufficient in knowledge-intensive generation, where entities, relations, dates, and identifiers are semantically constrained. We introduce WorldMark, a generation-time interface that retrieves semantic and episodic knowledge, converts the retrieved content into a token-position-dependent saliency score, and modulates the strength of an existing host watermark through Asymmetric Knowledge Modulation. WorldMark requires no backbone retraining and preserves the original detector. We evaluate WorldMark on OPT-1.3B, LLaMA-3-8B, and Mistral-7B across C4, TriviaQA, and NaturalQuestions. The main evaluation uses the C4 and OPT-1.3B setting, while the remaining configurations are used to examine transfer across model architectures and knowledge-intensive datasets. On the primary C4 evaluation, WorldMark improves the three reproduced MorphMark variants by an average of 0.0296 in robust TPR at 1\% FPR and 0.0108 in robust F1. The average perplexity decreases by 0.0312 under the reported evaluation protocol. A scaled evaluation with 500 samples per configuration covers seven logits-based, sampling-based, and hybrid watermark hosts. Component ablations show that retrieved context alone is insufficient and that the gains depend on semantically aligned saliency estimation and asymmetric modulation.

TL;DR: WorldMark adapts LLM watermark strength via world‑knowledge memory and asymmetric modulation, improving robustness without retraining or extra detector parameters.

Chest X-rays can be acquired from different directions, and acquisition view is often treated as a technical nuisance that should be removed from learned representations. We study this assumption for anteroposterior (AP) and posteroanterior (PA) chest radiographs and find it difficult to justify. Modern visual representations encode the acquisition view with near-perfect accuracy, close to 0.99 AUROC, this signal remains strongly decodable throughout the encoder, and clinical information itself predicts the view. Directly suppressing acquisition reduces its predictability but also degrades clinical performance, and a systematic evaluation of five broad families of correction strategies, spanning invariance penalties, subspace projection, counterfactual generation, and domain-alignment methods, shows the same pattern: each is matched or beaten by a random or shuffled control, so acquisition cannot be treated as a cleanly removable nuisance. We propose JEPA-Acq, an acquisition-conditioned joint-embedding predictive model that instead learns how a latent representation changes between real same-patient AP and PA studies. The model uses bidirectional latent prediction conditioned on the target view and the time between studies, while a clinical classification head keeps the representation useful for diagnosis throughout training. Across two independent ten-seed evaluations, seven baseline methods, and four hospital datasets, JEPA-Acq gives the strongest validated cross-view transfer in the benchmark while retaining competitive clinical performance. These findings suggest a broader principle for robust representation learning: when a nuisance factor is strong and clinically entangled, modeling its structured effect can be more appropriate than enforcing blind invariance.

TL;DR: We show that AP/PA acquisition is a clinically entangled representation factor that is better modeled through acquisition-conditioned latent prediction than blindly removed.

Visual design generation requires detailed organization over textual content, graphical elements and spatial layout, while users typically provide only concise, high-level requests. Prompt enhancement (PE) bridges this gap by transforming user requests into detailed textual conditions for image generation. In this work, we represent the enhanced prompt as explicit layers corresponding to individual visual components, and study how to optimize this structured PE using downstream visual feedback. We identify a feedback granularity mismatch under conventional sequence-level optimization: structured prompts may contain dozens of layers and thousands of tokens, whereas generation errors are often localized to only a few layers. Broadcasting a single rollout-level advantage to the entire prompt therefore results in coarse credit assignment. To address this issue, we propose LAPE, a Layer-Aware Prompt Enhancement framework that grounds visual defects to corresponding prompt layers and applies layer-localized advantage corrections. The same defect-to-layer grounding principle further enables test-time refinement by selectively revising defective layers for image regeneration. To evaluate the effectiveness of LAPE, we additionally introduce a comprehensive benchmark containing 600 concise user requests across 150 fine-grained task types. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over baselines and strong generation performance.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has become a standard paradigm for enhancing the capability of large reasoning models. RLVR typically samples responses independently and optimizes the policy using rewards from final answers. This paradigm has two limitations. First, independently sampled responses often contain similar intermediate reasoning steps, causing redundant exploration and wasted computation. Second, sparse final-answer rewards make it hard to identify useful steps. Tree-based methods partly address this problem by sharing prefixes and comparing branches from the same prefix to provide fine-grained signals. However, branches that reach similar reasoning states after diverging still explore independently, causing redundant exploration. Moreover, isolated local comparisons can lead to high variance in advantage estimation. To address this challenge, we propose GraphPO (Graph-based Policy Optimization), an RL framework that represents rollouts as a directed acyclic graph, with generated reasoning segments as edges and semantic states summarized from reasoning paths as nodes. GraphPO virtually groups semantically similar states, shares downstream outcome evidence while preserving original generation contexts, and reallocates redundant expansion budgets to other frontier states. Its dual-group advantage compares incoming paths for efficiency and outgoing steps for correctness, deriving process supervision from outcome rewards. Our theoretical analysis shows that GraphPO can reduce centered-advantage variance and favor shorter correct paths. Experiments across reasoning and agentic search benchmarks show that GraphPO outperforms chain- and tree-based baselines with the same token budget or number of trajectories. Our code is at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GraphPO.

Safety in large language models is typically produced through opaque optimization and evaluated only after training, leaving its internal representation poorly understood. We introduce **MSREP** (Modular Safety Representation Extraction and Prediction), a framework for identifying and validating low-dimensional safety representations in language model residual streams through causal intervention and differentiable $L_0$ gating. Across nine controlled backbones spanning 350M to 13B parameters and four architectures, we find that safety information is highly concentrated, with fewer than 5\% of representation dimensions sufficient to capture refusal behavior. These findings generalize to a 30-model evaluation pool spanning diverse architectures and scales: representation quality improves predictably with model scale, transfers across architectures with 0.68-0.86 self-consistency (0.57-0.79 behavioral validation), and supports safety-aware pruning that preserves alignment substantially better than magnitude-based pruning at 20\% sparsity ($\Delta S=-0.03$ vs. $-0.18$). Together, these results show that safety is not uniformly distributed throughout model representations but instead exhibits a compact, scalable, and partially transferable structure that can be exploited for safety analysis, prediction, and compression.

TL;DR: Safety in language models is mediated by low-dimensional, transferable subspaces that can be extracted, predicted across scale, and preserved during compression.

Language-model answers can be fluent yet incorrect, and a single generation often provides limited evidence about their reliability. We study whether known semantic relations between answers to controlled variants of the same problem provide a useful test-time reliability signal. We formulate these relations as semantic unit tests: an answer should remain unchanged under an answer-preserving rewording and should change predictably under a mechanically specified numerical intervention. Given a problem and a frozen language model, SUT-R queries the original problem and two controlled variants, then measures whether the resulting answers satisfy the corresponding metamorphic relations. The resulting test-pass score requires no learned verifier, token probabilities, or chain-of-thought annotations. On a held-out controlled arithmetic benchmark, the score predicts original-answer failures more accurately than disagreement among three cost-matched self-consistency samples (AUROC 0.9661 versus 0.7279). It also identifies low-risk subsets, with error risk 0.0083 at 50% coverage and 0.0119% at 70% coverage. The same signal does not, however, yield a statistically reliable improvement in fixed-cost answer aggregation: the current mapped-back three-call rule matches random transformed-query selection. A small real-task stress test likewise does not demonstrate transfer beyond the controlled setting. Thus, semantic unit tests are an interpretable controlled reliability diagnostic, while reliability estimation and final-answer selection remain distinct objectives.

TL;DR: Training-free semantic tests reliably flag errors in controlled arithmetic, but do not yet improve aggregation or transfer to natural tasks.

Artificial Intelligence Virtual Cells (AIVCs) are envisioned as scientific agents that simulate cellular responses, explain underlying mechanisms, and support hypothesis-driven discovery. Existing AIVC benchmarks, however, operate primarily at the simulation layer, motivating complementary evaluation of how models interpret experimental evidence and formulate biological hypotheses. We introduce OmniVCBench, a figure-centric, source-traceable benchmark for the interpretation component of an AIVC. It contains 6,077 curated single- and multi-subfigure question--answer pairs derived from figures and experimental contexts in the scientific literature. Guided by Bloom's taxonomy, we instantiate interpretation-layer counterparts of the AIVC Predict--Explain--Discover agenda through three scientific reasoning tasks. These comprise L1 evidence-conditioned inference, L2 mechanistic explanation, and L3 evidence-grounded hypothesis proposal. We further introduce AIVC-Judge, a task-conditioned MLLM-as-a-judge framework with category-specific, reference-aware rubrics for evaluating open-ended responses. A complementary Model-Derived Hard-Negative Mining (MDHNM) strategy converts plausible errors observed during model inference into MCQ distractors for lower-cost evaluation. Within the evaluated heterogeneous model pool, MCQ accuracy correlates positively with AIVC-Judge scores, providing a complementary view of performance alongside open-response evaluation. Evaluating both proprietary and open-weight multimodal models shows that even the best proprietary model reaches only 3.28 out of 5.00 under AIVC-Judge. Supervised fine-tuning and retrieval-augmented generation on the auxiliary OmniVCTrain corpus provide modest, configuration-dependent gains. Together, OmniVCBench combines source-aligned cellular figures, interpretation-role organization around Predict--Explain--Discover, and paired open-response and controlled MCQ evaluation. It provides a source-traceable resource for assessing evidence-grounded reasoning in candidate AIVC interpretation components. Code and data demo are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OmniVCBench.

Tool-augmented LLM agents face a fundamental context-management challenge as tasks involve increasingly complex tool interactions. A key source is an \emph{execution-granularity mismatch}: locally deterministic tool workflows may require multiple tool operations, while task-level reasoning often only needs their composed result. Exposing intermediate observations and value transfers as separate model-visible steps inflates context and forces the model to manage low-level procedural dataflow in the main reasoning trace. We propose HyperTool, a unified executable MCP(Model Context Protocol)-style tool interface that enables models to organize multi-step tool operations while controlling the granularity at which intermediate computations and observations are exposed to the main trajectory. The model composes existing tools with program logic within code blocks, completing locally deterministic tool operations within a single execution unit while keeping intermediate states in the local execution context. Only processed results are returned to the main trajectory when task-level reasoning is required, thereby enabling proactive context management. To train models to use this interface, we synthesize HyperTool-format trajectories from cross-tool compositional tasks and verify them in real MCP environments. Experiments demonstrate that, with only simple supervised fine-tuning, Qwen3 8B and 32B achieve average score of 50.90 and 56.45 on MCP-Universe, respectively, substantially outperforming the base models and other baselines. Their performance surpasses or matches that of much larger open- and closed-source models (e.g., GLM-5.1), demonstrating strong gains in multi-step tool use.

Sequential recommendation is dominated by two-tower models that encode each item into one vector, summarize the user's history into a query, and match the two by inner product. Item encoders have grown richer, from item-identifier embeddings to large language models, yet the item vector remains a single representation computed independently of who is asking. Relevance, however, depends on the user–item pair, and a static vector cannot express which aspects of an item matter to a given user. Here we show that the item representation itself can depend on the querying user. PRISM decomposes each candidate over a shared frozen sparse dictionary and adds a behavior-derived perturbation to the routing logits before top-K selection, so that different users activate different atom supports for the same item. Setting the perturbation gain to zero recovers the non-personalized encoder exactly. On four public datasets and one industrial dataset, PRISM outperforms identifier-based, content-based, and large-language-model-based recommenders and a target-dependent ranker on most metrics, and ablations trace the gain to which atoms are selected rather than how they are weighted. Item-side quantities are precomputed, so PRISM deploys as an exact post-retrieval scorer. Personalizing the representation thus complements personalizing the query, and the exposed atom support makes each recommendation inspectable.

TL;DR: PRISM personalizes an item’s sparse representation by conditioning top-K atom selection on user behavior, yielding stronger sequential recommendation than fixed item embeddings and fixed-support personalization.

Standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning of small language models (SLMs) trains exclusively on extractive domain summaries — teaching a model what the domain says, but not how to reason about it. This paper introduces the Enriched Fine-Tuning Pipeline with LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation (EFTP-J): a novel integrated framework that couples enriched multi-trace training data with a hardware-portable semantic evaluation protocol. The training pipeline synthesises four complementary trace types from raw PDF corpora without any teacher model: (1) extractive knowledge summaries, (2) Chain-of-Thought (CoT) decomposition traces, (3) Knowledge Graph (KG) concept-linking traversal traces, and (4) self-critique traces in which the model evaluates a draft answer against a four-criterion rubric and refines it. The evaluation pipeline employs an LLM-as-a-Judge protocol with a deterministic rule-based fallback that operates on any hardware — eliminating the GPU dependency of prior judge implementations. Applied to TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0 on a ten-document academic corpus (136 content chunks, 349 enriched training samples), EFTP-J is evaluated alongside six baseline augmentation strategies in a seven-way empirical comparison. The EFTP-J trained model (FT-v2) achieves a perfect LLM-judge score of 1.00 on structured methodological questions, and 0.75 on recommendation synthesis tasks on CPU hardware — demonstrating that reasoning capability baked into model weights at training time produces qualitatively superior outputs on structured question types compared to extraction-only fine-tuning. The dual-mode judge (LLM + rule-based fallback) successfully evaluates all 42 answer–question pairs without failure, resolving the JSON-generation fragility that prevents pure LLM judges from operating reliably on sub-2B parameter models. Together, EFTP-J constitutes the first published framework to jointly address the training-data reasoning gap and the evaluation robustness gap for small language model deployment.

Physiological regulation from wearable and multimodal sensing is a partially observed decision problem: measurements are asynchronous and quality dependent, missingness can be informative, future responses are heterogeneous, and a commanded intervention may differ from the intervention actually delivered. We introduce LDA-ANS, a learning-driven autonomy framework that connects three stages. First, modality-specific encoders, random Fourier features, a reliability-weighted kernel mean memory, and measurement-age-aware attention construct a finite-dimensional probabilistic belief from incomplete observations. Second, a context--control--plan triad identifies the current operating context, predicts action-conditioned physiological trajectories, and estimates the longer-horizon risk and feasibility of candidate plans. Third, an executed-action model is integrated with mean--CVaR model predictive control, branch-dependent tail allocation, an uncertainty-tightened CVaR control-barrier filter, and regularized kernel--Galerkin policy evaluation. We prove stability of the triad under belief perturbations, validity of CVaR tightening under bounded loss error, recursive model-relative feasibility under a robustly feasible baseline, and convergence of approximate safe policy iteration to an explicit error neighborhood. The empirical study separates observational prediction from control evidence. Participant-grouped evaluation on a 21-participant physiological dataset produced 140 leakage-audited transitions; the best classical predictor differed by endpoint, with Random Forest for heart rate, Ridge for mean arterial pressure, and Extra Trees for cardiac output. Structured missingness and architectural ablations quantify the roles of kernel memory, random features, attention, measurement age, and information quality. Synthetic closed-loop experiments evaluate nominal, delayed, non-response, sign-reversal, transition-shift, and compound failures. Adversarial tests show that lower mean loss need not imply safety, that fallback availability does not imply fallback invariance, and that persistent model, actuation, sampling, approximation, and numerical errors yield convergence to a neighborhood rather than exact optimality. The framework is intended for retrospective modeling, digital-twin stress testing, and supervised advisory evaluation, not unrestricted autonomous physiological actuation.

Understanding cellular responses to genetic and chemical perturbations is central to studying gene function and designing interventions. Recent perturbation models predict transcriptional responses, while risk-controlling calibration provides guarantees for selected interventions. These advances leave an important research question open: do stronger statistical guarantees improve experiment selection? To address this question, we establish a theoretical separation between statistical validity and experimental utility: tighter bounds can halve expected utility while remaining valid on every draw. The underlying mechanism is that controlling a set's average failure rate does not ensure that adding interventions improves outcomes. Theoretically, we develop finite-population guarantees and a loss decomposition that distinguishes useful choices excluded by certification from suboptimal selections within the certified set. Empirically, retrospective genetic and chemical screens show that selection objectives and available information shape experimental utility. Estimated-utility selection outperforms lower-bound maximization in all 18 exploratory chemical-screen settings with equally weighted successes and failures, and a locked test on eight additional cell lines confirms the mean gain. We further show, through a frozen pathway evaluation, that a pretrained perturbation model improves over a generic ranking but provides no additional benefit to the tested rule when measurements from a related cell line are available. These expression-surrogate results suggest evaluating perturbation models by predictive performance, statistical certification, and the utility of selected interventions, while accounting for the biological information already available. We open-source our code and evaluation protocols to enhance reproducibility in the research community.

Artificial neural networks (ANNs) achieve strong performance but at the cost of extreme parameter density. In contrast, biological networks operate with sparse, highly organized structures in which dendrites play a central role in information integration. We introduce the Dendritic Topological Network Model (DTNM), a generative framework that embeds dendritic-inspired connectivity principles into sparse artificial networks. Unlike conventional random initialization, DTNM defines connectivity through parametric distributions of dendrites, receptive fields, and synapses, providing explicit control over modularity, hierarchy, and degree heterogeneity. This parametric flexibility allows DTNM to produce diverse network topologies, from clustered modular architectures to hierarchical, hub-dominated structures, whose geometry can be characterized and optimized with network-science metrics. Across image classification benchmarks, DTNM consistently outperforms data-agnostic sparse initialization baselines at extreme sparsity (99%), in both static and dynamic sparse training regimes. When integrated into state-of-the-art dynamic sparse training frameworks and applied to Transformer architectures for machine translation, DTNM likewise outperforms the other evaluated methods. Crucially, in cross-task parameter-transfer evaluations with no target-task hyperparameter tuning, fixed DTNM configurations still outperform the evaluated data-agnostic baselines. We further introduce a data-informed extension, iDTNM, that incorporates input-correlation statistics into the same dendritic structure and narrows the performance gap with data-informed sparse initialization methods. These results show that bio-inspired network topology can provide a transferable structural prior for scalable and sparse models.

Federated RLHF keeps preference data on clients, but the resulting model updates can still reveal information about those preferences. We identify three leakage channels from an honest-but-curious server: membership inference against uploaded reward models, gradient-based recovery of individual preference directions, and inference of a client's local domain under non-IID training. Membership AUC reaches $0.94$ for the LoRA reward model, while a single gradient reveals the preference direction with near-perfect accuracy in the absence of sufficient noise. Under a non-IID split, the inferred topic distribution reaches a rank correlation of $0.90$ with the client's actual topic mix. Differential privacy reduces these leakage channels at a measurable utility cost: at $\varepsilon{\approx}2.4$, personalized preference accuracy decreases from $0.90$ to $0.71$. The same qualitative leakage is observed across reward models of different model scales, indicating that the issue is tied to the federated reward-model training pipeline rather than a particular model size.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as mobile assistants, where a key challenge is leveraging personal information scattered across multiple applications (apps) to complete user instructions. However, due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks, their capabilities remain poorly understood. To address this gap, we introduce SPIEval, a human-curated benchmark grounded in five cognitive capabilities (i.e., reasoning, disambiguation, integration, preference inference, and multi-intent decomposition). SPIEval comprises 250 tasks spanning 4,335 personal records distributed across 10 apps and supports multi-turn interaction through 21 tools. Analysis shows that the benchmark exhibits diverse scenarios, challenging tasks, scattered information, controllable environments, and verifiable outcomes. We evaluate nine representative LLMs and find substantial room for improvement. The best-performing model, GPT-5.5 (xhigh), achieves only 57.3\% accuracy, while the weakest achieves just 16.4\%. Further analysis reveals that 79\% of failures stem from inaccurate information localization, as LLMs often commit to plausible but incorrect information instead of continuing retrieval for verification. We also find that fewer than 2\% of retrieval actions employ advanced search methods and observe substantial variation in search efficiency across models. These findings expose fundamental limitations of current LLM-based mobile assistants and motivate future research in this direction.

Large language models make weight storage and memory traffic major inference costs, motivating low-precision formats that represent each weight with only a few bits. Such formats use a scale to map floating-point values into a small codebook; NVFP4 improves local range utilization by letting every 16 E2M1 weights share an E4M3 block scale. Choosing that scale is difficult in GPTQ because quantizing one column updates those that follow, so evaluating a block independently can misestimate its final reconstruction error. Large models pose a second challenge: full-precision weights, calibration activations, and second-order state cannot all remain on one accelerator, while assigning complete layers to devices leaves each time-consuming layer solve serial. We introduce \emph{Schur Replay}, a scale-selection algorithm that reproduces the GPTQ updates caused by each block scale and scores the resulting block error after accounting for compensation from unquantized columns. Separately, our execution infrastructure keeps only the active layer resident, tiers activations across device, host, and disk, retires full-precision layers after export, and distributes independent output rows across tensor-parallel ranks. Together, the algorithm and framework attain $99.35\%$ and $100.84\%$ question-weighted recovery from BF16 across seven benchmarks on Qwen3.5-397B-A17B and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct. On the 397B model, the infrastructure reduces per-layer calibration time by $15.17\times$ over ModelOpt and $23.14\times$ over LLM Compressor, with lower memory used per GPU.

TL;DR: Schur Replay combines recurrence-aware scale selection with memory-bounded distributed GPTQ, enabling NVFP4 quantization of 70B–397B LLMs with near-BF16 accuracy and substantially lower calibration time and memory.

Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has been increasingly used for brain classification, yet existing methods primarily focus on temporal dynamics at the local and inter-regional levels, overlooking the complementary temporal, spatial, and spectral characteristics of brain dynamics across local, inter-regional, and whole-brain levels. To address this limitation, we propose a temporal-spatial-frequency attention fusion network (TSF-AFNet) for fMRI-based classification. The proposed method jointly models intra-regional activity, inter-regional connectivity, and global interactions via a triple-attention mechanism, which adaptively emphasizes salient spatial regions, informative temporal windows, and discriminative frequency components, yielding fused and interpretable representations for accurate classification. Experiments on large-sample fMRI dataset including 519 schizophrenia patients and 602 healthy controls demonstrate that TSF-AFNet achieves an accuracy of 83.89\%, outperforming methods based on regional time courses, inter-regional functional connectivity, dynamic functional connectivity, and state-of-the-art fusion approaches. Furthermore, our method identified abnormal spatial regions, including the frontal cortex, hippocampus, and thalamus, altered low-frequency global components, markedly changed connectivity windows, and critical fused connectivity patterns associated with schizophrenia. In summary, TSF-AFNet is an effective and interpretable fusion method for fMRI-based classification while enabling meaningful biomarker discovery.

Generating a playable visual novel requires coordinating narrative text, branching interaction logic, and audiovisual assets. We present IF-Line, a structured production system that connects narrative authoring to executable visual-novel graphs for Godot. Versioned narrative and media artifacts, content-hash anchoring, and explicit dependencies support deterministic compilation, failure localization, and selective regeneration. Character states extracted from generated chapter dialogue condition both interactive roleplay and subsequent chapter writing. Successful repairs can inform generation policies through paired acceptance checks with bounded score regression and explicit human approval. We evaluate the system through complementary reading, expert, and repair studies. In a blinded, LLM-judged reading panel anchored on 15 successful IF-Line outputs, with two disclosed InfiPlot case substitutions, IF-Line ranks first or tied on five of six retained reading-experience items. A separate ten-expert study gives IF-Line the highest descriptive composite score, with different rankings on individual dimensions. In a controlled study of 54 synthetic Chinese stories, a method-blind LLM judge classifies 89/108 attempts from a separate localization--planning--patch method as clean repairs, compared with 50/108 for full-output revision, at higher generation-token usage. Two policy-acceptance records show higher mean style and coherence scores and lower aggregate token usage relative to their recorded baselines; identical proposed policy content, unavailable baseline revision identifiers, and observed null-control variation limit causal interpretation.

Context engines that index a repository and return files to a coding agent report large gains over lexical baselines, but those gains are rarely decomposed: how much comes from a learned reranker that would help any candidate pool, how much from the engine’s own candidate generation, and how much from choices selected on evaluation data? We answer this for one open-source engine, Delphi, using a protocol that records case-level development exposure, builds component-matched conventional retrievers from the same embedding model with Delphi’s own rerankers and query expansion, varies candidate generation and learned reranking factorially, and performs branch-level ablations on a fresh never-scored draw. Across three SWE-bench Verified draws unseen by development, Delphi’s advantage over the full conventional stack lies primarily in its candidate pool: before learned reranking, Delphi candidates lead by +0.19 to +0.28 MRR, while the shared rerankers recover most of the weaker conventional pool’s MRR deficit but cannot recover missing recall. A fresh branch-level ablation attributes most of the candidate-pool advantage to chunking, indexing, and fusion implementation, followed by vector-heavy weighting; the four structural branches contribute jointly, but no individual branch is necessary. On a repository-disjoint commit-to-files set, the pattern reverses: Delphi’s candidate pool has lower recall and the rerankers add little to either system. Matched output contracts also turn an apparent hosted-engine lead on documentation retrieval into a statistically unresolved comparison, while re-indexing reveals substantial ranking instability across fresh installations. Finally, a preregistered executable SWE-bench pilot finds no resolved repair-rate effect from retrieval seeds at its current sample size and audits the context actually delivered to the agent. We release code, per-case artifacts, agent trajectories, sequential analyses, and a case-level exposure ledger.

TL;DR: Context-engine gains on SWE-bench mostly come from strong reranking plus better chunking, indexing, and weighting—not any single structural retrieval branch—and the effect reverses on commit-to-files queries.

LLM-driven software engineering agents have become a central testbed for real-
world language-model capability, yet their training remains limited by the avail-
ability of high-quality SWE tasks. Existing synthetic data methods typically create
tasks through fixed mutation or bug-injection procedures, making the resulting dis-
tributions largely independent of the agent’s own weaknesses and training progress.
We introduce SOCRATIC-SWE, a closed-loop self-evolution framework that reuses
the agent’s historical solving traces as a source of training signal. Rather than
treating traces only as evidence for reward computation, SOCRATIC-SWE distills
them into structured agent skills that summarize recurring failures and effective
repair patterns. These skills then guide the generation of targeted repair tasks in
real repositories. Candidate tasks are checked through execution-based validation
and scored with a solver-gradient alignment reward, so that the retained tasks are
both verifiable and useful for improving the Solver. The updated Solver produces
new traces, enabling the task curriculum to adapt over successive rounds. Across
SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Lite, SWE-bench Pro, and Terminal-Bench
2.0, SOCRATIC-SWE consistently improves over self-evolving baselines under
the same compute budget, reaching 50.40% on SWE-bench Verified after three
iterations, 3.40 percentage points above SSR. These results suggest that solving
traces can serve as a scalable substrate for self-evolving SWE agents.

Improving robot policies on new tasks without collecting additional expert demonstrations remains a central challenge in robot learning. World action models (WAMs) use broad video priors to jointly predict future videos and actions, offering a potential source of supervision for adapting to new tasks. However, generated videos may fail to depict task completion, and even visually successful videos may be paired with inconsistent actions that lead to execution failure. We propose EVO-WAM, a framework that adapts WAMs to unseen tasks by learning from their own generated video-action trajectories, without executing candidate actions in an external environment. First, we augment WAM training with state prediction and anchored multi-frame context to enable complete autoregressive rollouts without external execution feedback. Second, we identify reliable training experience by selecting task-completing prefixes with a vision-language model and verifying their video-action consistency with an inverse dynamics model. Third, we iteratively train the WAM on verified prefixes and generate new rollouts with the updated model. On seven unseen RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, EVO-WAM increases average success rates from 26.9% to 68.0% for Cosmos3 and from 28.5% to 46.4% for DreamZero, reaching approximately 2.5× and 1.6× their initial success rates. On three unseen long-horizon composite tasks in the real world, it improves Cosmos3's average success rate from 20.0% to 76.7%, a gain of 56.7 percentage points. A demo video and interactive case studies are available in the supplementary material and on our anonymous project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/supplementary-13803/index.html.

TL;DR: EVO-WAM improves world action models on unseen tasks by learning from self-generated trajectories verified for task completion and video-action consistency, without additional expert demonstrations or external execution feedback.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over enterprise corpora must ingest heterogeneous documents—PDF reports, scanned agreements, spreadsheets, presentation
decks, and word-processed text—yet most chunking pipelines apply a single static
strategy and the choice is made by hand. We present a document-aware chunking
framework: a zero-cost structural profiler (DocProfiler) and a rule-based router
(StrategyRouter) route each document to one of six chunking strategies, deploying a section-aware semantic strategy with fragment absorption (SAG) as a safe
default and isolating presentation decks page-by-page, with every strategy gated
behind experimental evidence. Two findings anchor the contribution. First, a
font-aware heading-recovery step at the parser, not the chunker, is a precondition
for heading-aware chunking: without it, a heading-grouped strategy degenerates to
the semantic baseline. Second, with heading structure restored, SAG shows a small
positive point estimate over a fixed semantic baseline on 12 enterprise documents
across four formats (overall 0.970 versus 0.968) that is not statistically significant
at N=12 (bootstrap 95% CIs fully overlap), with no regression. We report honestly
that the router’s aggregate gain over the best fixed default is small (+0.001) because
that default is already strong; the router’s value is avoiding type-specific failures.
A large-table splitting fix eliminated a 100% over-limit failure. Under a matched
dense retriever, our strategies are competitive with a published fixed-window baseline (Qchunk); on the enterprise documents themselves, routing reduces the mean
section gold-set size by 6.8% but does not measurably move dense Recall@k,
bounding the retrieval payoff to the downstream system. Document-aware routing
is orthogonal to query-aware adaptation and composes with it.

Traffic autonomy requires a closed loop linking uncertain perception, multimodal prediction, planning, control, and physical execution. We propose a learning-driven autonomy framework built around a context--control--plan triad. Context-perception is formed from modality-specific encoders, explicit missingness and measurement age, random Fourier features (RFF), a contribution-weighted kernel mean embedding (KME), and reliability-biased temporal attention. Control-perception summarizes commanded and executed actions and their mismatch, while plan-perception represents candidate interventions. A triad-conditioned conditional variational autoencoder predicts multimodal futures. Mean--CVaR model predictive control supplies a nominal action, and an executed-action-aware CVaR control-barrier-function filter modifies that action when adverse-tail safety is inadequate. Branch-dependent CVaR prevents rare hazardous modes from being diluted by common benign predictions. RFF bases also support a regularized Galerkin approximation of the generalized HJB residual. Under contraction and bounded persistent error, approximate safe policy iteration converges to a quantified neighborhood of the optimal safe value. Experiments using 8,760 hourly traffic records, an audit of 1,048,575 UTD19 detector records, and a stylized rare-event control simulation provide proof-of-concept evidence. The complete belief is more robust than Euclidean and last-state pooling under added missingness, while CVaR-based filters remove collisions in the tested simulation. The empirical results are deliberately scoped: aggregate data support belief and forecasting analysis, whereas control, planning, actuation, and neural sequence models remain simulation or surrogate evaluations.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for clinical decision support, yet existing benchmarks rely on expert-constructed cases or retrospective records and fail to capture real-world diagnostic processes, particularly the evolving reasoning and decision-making under uncertainty. We introduce the PULmonary Sequential Assessment of Reasoning (PULSAR), a benchmark of 188 real-world, multi-institutional longitudinal diagnostic trajectories reconstructed from medical records and expert case discussions at three tertiary hospitals. Records from each patient were consolidated into a unified longitudinal case and then structured into a standardized clinical reasoning framework through iterative consultation with senior attending physicians, covering the full diagnostic workflow from initial presentation to diagnosis, treatment, and patient outcomes. Three attending pulmonologists, each with over ten years of medical training and at least five years of independent clinical practice, independently annotated the cases. During annotation, physicians were restricted to the information available at the corresponding stage. For S2--S3 annotation, they could access only S1; for S5--S6 annotation, they could access S1 and S4. Later-stage evidence, the final diagnosis, treatment, and patient outcome were hidden until the corresponding earlier-stage annotations had been completed. Two senior attending pulmonologists, each with more than ten years of independent clinical practice, reviewed and adjudicated disputed annotations. Pulmonology trainees assisted with standardized data verification under specialist supervision. PULSAR emphasizes high-difficulty cases that challenge even pulmonology trainees. With expert-curated reference reasoning, we find that while state-of-the-art LLMs perform strongly given sufficient information, they struggle under realistic, multimodal, longitudinal settings, failing to plan appropriate diagnostic pathways, missing critical tests, and overlooking high-risk conditions, which mcould lead to suboptimal clinical decisions if used without appropriate clinician oversight. PULSAR provides a high-fidelity testbed for evaluating LLMs in real-world clinical decision-making.

TL;DR: PULSAR is a high-fidelity benchmark comprising 188 real-world respiratory cases for evaluating longitudinal diagnostic planning and decision-making under uncertainty.

Agents that persistently modify memory, skills,
prompts, or configuration can differ from the
versions that were evaluated. This position paper argues that
safety analysis for such agents should separate three
causal questions. *Certification* compares the update rules that 
generate future versions. *Gating* compares a proposed persistent update, or
a consequential downstream action, with a feasible safer alternative.
*Debugging* searches for recorded updates whose rollback prevents
recurrence when the same declared scenario is rerun.
The questions differ in intervention, comparator, horizon, and
identification problem. Common causes can shape both updates and outcomes, so logged
associations may not identify their effects. 

In this paper, we argue that safety analysis for self-improving agents requires causal inference.
To make our position constructive, we work through candidate designs
for all three questions, with a persistent-memory gate developed in
greatest detail. These derivations are deliberately partial: they show
how causal reasoning exposes the relevant comparator, graph, assumptions,
evidence, and failure conditions. A concrete implementation must derive
its graph and evidence requirements from the architecture of the agent
it governs.

TL;DR: Safety analysis for self-improving agents is a causal problem, not a prediction problem. Certification, gating, and debugging each need their own causal inference tools and assumptions.

Multi-modal planning is promising for autonomous driving by representing multiple plausible behaviors in ambiguous and long-tail scenarios. Existing methods mainly focus on improving trajectory multi-modality, enhancing trajectory representations, or reshaping the candidate distribution.
