We introduce SpatialChain, a dataset of 28,350 training and 899 test examples pairing spatially-oriented GQA questions with scene-graph-grounded reasoning chains, retained only when the generated answer matches the symbolic ground truth, and an evaluation protocol that scores a model's reasoning chain against the symbolic scene graph independently of its final answer. We define a shortcut as a correct answer whose chain is not grounded in the relations the question requires, and validate the measure against 198 human-annotated items. Applied to nine thinking-enabled VLMs, the protocol surfaces findings invisible to accuracy: (i) four of nine models achieve ≥79% accuracy while exhibiting shortcut rates of 39% or more, and the shortcuts take two forms, restatement of the question and decorative description, that accuracy conflates; (ii) chain quality predicts correctness within seven of nine models but not across models, and multi-hop questions are no harder than single-hop ones, indicating that the bottleneck is perceiving individual relations rather than composing them; (iii) SFT on SpatialChain improves Qwen3-VL-8B by +6.2 pp in-domain and lowers its shortcut rate to 22%, while amplifying yes-bias and specializing output style at the expense of external benchmarks. Data, generation scripts, and evaluation code are released at an anonymized repository.

TL;DR: SpatialChain pairs 28K spatial VQA questions with scene-graph-grounded reasoning chains and a human-validated judge, showing that high-accuracy VLMs often answer correctly by restating the question or describing the scene, not by spatial reasoning.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often estimates advantages from only a few responses per prompt, making local reward statistics noisy. We introduce Empirical Bayes Policy Optimization (EBPO), a critic-free method that uses running population moments to balance within-prompt reward differences and between-prompt comparisons. Gaussian and Beta–Binomial constructions provide closed-form weighting rules with constant-size historical state. We derive the exact batch-normalized estimator: the shared historical mean cancels, while the estimated weight controls both the between-prompt contribution and the normalization scale. This characterization connects local and global reward normalization and identifies when saturated response groups receive nonzero advantages. Population-risk identities further motivate the weighting rules and establish their oracle equivalence under matched Beta moments. With four responses per prompt, topic-ordered EBPO-BB achieves math macro-average Pass@1 scores of 65.69% and 62.45% on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B. On Qwen3-8B, Gaussian and Beta EBPO outperform the best tested fixed weight by 1.45 and 2.76 percentage points, respectively; the Gaussian variance proxy also exceeds a noise-corrected alternative by 2.81 points. Additional coding, ordering, group-size, and training-dynamics studies characterize the method’s operating regimes.

TL;DR: EBPO uses empirical-Bayes statistics to balance within-prompt and between-prompt reward signals, with an exact normalization analysis and improved small-group reasoning performance.

How much of sparsity allocation can be determined before checkpoint-specific allocation analysis begins? We show that inference-time propagation reveals a widespread architectural ordering in Transformer blocks: deviations introduced earlier generally receive greater block-to-logit downstream exposure than deviations introduced later. Across 25 of 26 evaluated checkpoints, this ordering identifies block position as an informative architecture-available allocation signal and establishes a directional architectural prior for sparsity allocation.
We operationalize this direction through Position default, a principled sparsity-adaptive architectural allocation that requires no checkpoint-specific allocation measurement, candidate evaluation, or allocation search. Across five LLaMA-family checkpoints, Position default captures 91.5% to 100% of the perplexity gain obtained through checkpoint-specific refinement while substantially improving downstream task performance over Uniform. Controlled non-sequential pruning and allocation-reversal experiments establish that the identified direction is performance relevant rather than an artifact of sparse-prefix mask construction or nonuniformity alone.
Together, these results show that a substantial fraction of sparsity-allocation value is available before checkpoint-specific allocation analysis begins. They motivate an allocation-reference hierarchy that separates architectural value from checkpoint-specific refinement and support a position-first, not position-only, approach to sparsity allocation.

Knowing how much a causal predictor could improve need not reveal the gain of the repair actually learned. We quantify this gap in a scalar Gaussian causal experiment with known intervention geometry: auxiliary data identify effect magnitude up to bounded contamination, while diagnostics identify direction. The target is the squared-loss gain of the realized trained repair relative to a fitted reference. Jointly optimizing the learner and assessor under uniform learning MSE $\eta$ avoids the trivial solution of making no repair. At the usual $1/k$ learning scale, every feasible learner incurs a $k^{-2}$ assessment floor, even when oracle potential is estimable at a faster rate. In the magnitude-rich regime, we characterize a sharp leading-log frontier: the assessment exponent is $\min\{\ell_k,2k\eta_k/U\}$ to first relative order, where $\ell_k=\log(1/(k^2E_k))$ and $E_k$ is auxiliary precision. A diagnostic-abstention rule attains this exponent with unknown nuisance parameters. We also bound the critical allowance window and transfer the frontier to adaptive sampling by exact Gaussian simulation. Finite-grid experiments distinguish sign-tail suppression from total MSE and expose conservative finite-budget behavior. The result isolates how the assessment target changes information requirements in this experiment; it is not a general causal identifiability claim.

TL;DR: We characterize a sharp leading-log trade-off between learning accuracy and assessing a causal repair's realized gain in a scalar Gaussian model.

Large language models offer a promising approach to customs tariff classification, but reliable fine-grained classification requires access to large and evolving tariff nomenclatures. While retrieval can provide this information at inference time, it remains unclear how retrieval strategy affects classification performance relative to the capability of the underlying model. We systematically evaluate four retrieval strategies across eight LLMs and 900 classification tasks spanning the 10-digit HTSUS and EU TARIC nomenclatures. We find that retrieval strategy is a major determinant of performance: effective retrieval narrows gaps between model tiers, and weaker models with appropriate retrieval can outperform stronger models with less effective retrieval. Hierarchical guidance particularly benefits weaker models, whereas stronger models perform comparably with simpler, more efficient heading-level retrieval. Retrieval from the applicable nomenclature also substantially reduces invalid-code generation compared with parametric inference and open-web search. As an exploratory extension, augmenting hierarchical retrieval with web search provides complementary classification information but can reduce nomenclature adherence for some models. Overall, tariff classification performance depends not only on model capability, but critically on how tariff information is retrieved and presented.

TL;DR: Retrieval strategy matters as much as model capability in LLM-based tariff classification: effective retrieval can enable weaker models to outperform stronger ones, while the optimal retrieval structure depends on model capability.

Transformer architectural modifications frequently measure a statistic on internal
representations, observe that it is large, remove it architecturally, and report an improvement. Interpreting that sequence requires evaluating whether the statistic exceeds its noise floor, whether it survives a geometric null, and whether the training
gain requires the specific direction removed. We formulate these requirements as
three reusable checks and apply them to self-attention removal, which deletes the
component of an attention head’s output aligned with its own value vector. Across
twelve pretrained models (6,784 head rows, 124M to 6.9B parameters), an earlier-
position causal null accounts for 48% to 63% of the head-value cosine alignment,
with no monotone scale trend. Under grouped-query attention, this alignment is
specific to each head’s own key–value group and reverses across groups (+0.24 to
+0.27 within-group,−0.11 to−0.19 across-group). Split-half reliability demonstrates that the per-head intervention effect is resolvable in GPT-2 ($r_{\Delta} = 0.80$)
but attenuated in Pythia-160M (0.42) and Pythia-410M (0.53), whereas structural
self-cosine reliability is near-perfect in all three ($r_{stat} > 0.99$); which statistic predicts its own intervention is model-dependent. In a pre-registered 3-arm by 8-seed
paired factorial at $4.0 \times 10^8$ tokens per run (399 900 672 tokens), a matched arbitrary rank-one direction does not differ from baseline (+0.0011 nats, p = 0.197),
while self-directed removal lowers validation loss (−0.0029 nats, Holm-corrected
p = 0.0023) and outperforms the matched arbitrary control directly (−0.0040
nats, p = 0.0018). The training benefit is specific to the direction removed at
50.9M scale, but a large cosine alignment alone does not establish redundancy in
frozen models.

TL;DR: Self-value alignment in attention heads is partly background geometry; only self-directed removal, not a fixed arbitrary direction, lowers validation loss, motivating reliability, null-model, and direction-control checks.

AI agents increasingly operate as persistent, interacting populations, not as single models answering one prompt. In this setting, safety failures can spread through memory, tools, peers, and institutions long after the triggering event. We study this regime with AgentWorld, a long-horizon experimental environment. Eight parallel worlds of ten LLM agents run from identical initial conditions: seven homogeneous single-model worlds and one mixed-model world. The study spans more than 850,000 LLM calls and roughly 50 billion tokens. After operational state had accumulated, we introduced three controlled probes. Each tested whether a running world could contain untrusted
instructions, verify an unsupported public claim before acting, and preserve privacy after an announced memory exposure. No world satisfied all criteria across all probes. The dominant failure was not non-recognition. Agents recognized threats, yet they still stored hostile payloads, repeated unsupported claims, inspected exposed private memories, or acted on retained content up to 46 hours later. Harmful and illegitimate content crossed the boundaries deployed systems rely on: memory, action, publication, communication, and governance. Longer operation revealed further system-level failures. These included public conformity despite private disagreement, recurring tool-use errors after days and thousands of actions, harmful economic dynamics, and collective objectives outside the intended scope. Model-level
safety does not compose into system-level resilience. Individually safe agents form persistent systems with qualitatively different failure modes. Safety evaluation should require evidence that deployed agent systems can contain, recover from, and learn from adversarial stress over time.

TL;DR: Persistent multi-agent AI systems can turn isolated safety failures into long-lived system-level   failures through memory, tools, peer interaction, and governance, requiring long-horizon stress testing   beyond single-agent benchmarks.

Citizen-science repositories now contain billions of species occurrence records from around the world, but these observations cluster heavily in human-accessible areas. Existing models use a small fraction of these records and are not evaluated for extrapolation from these observed areas to remote areas where camera traps and acoustic recorders are often deployed. We scale relative occurrence species distribution models to use all this data, training a multimodal implicit neural representation network called OCELOT that fuses spatial coordinates with satellite foundation embeddings on two orders of magnitude more observations than previous work: 2 billion GBIF records across 100,000 taxa. Scaling to this regime requires co-designing the data pipeline, taxonomic representation, loss formulation, and model architecture: spatiotemporal thinning and sub-linear cell sampling correct for spatial redundancy and observer bias, while an additive taxonomic readout shares representations across species, genera, and families to improve predictions for rare taxa. To evaluate performance in remote areas, we benchmark geographic extrapolation using the NDCG metric on spatial block holdouts up to 600 km. Satellite foundation embeddings improve extrapolation by 51% over coordinate-only models and outperform classical bioclimatic rasters. The resulting model also sets a new standard on established interpolation benchmarks, demonstrating that optimizing for geographic extrapolation does not compromise in-distribution accuracy.

Long-context models are sold on window length. Decoder suites that test that length—RULER, NoLiMa, AbstentionBench (unrun on SUPERCTX)—show saturation and weak abstention. SUPERCTX is a sealed-corpus detector, not a longer window. It emits a recomputation-checkable presence certificate, or a detector-layer empty set with a model-free 3×10^{-5} false-alarm backstop (rule of three on 0/100,002 nulls) over a declared synthetic 50,811-entry corpus, and only when absence is bound to an exhaustive scan or a zero-false-dismissal index. Face-narrowing reachability is 11.2% of entries; a face-narrowing empty set is not certified absence. The generation layer has no abstain path: after a detector reject it still emitted identifier-shaped answers at 1.000 (600/600) under an alternative protocol.

On that synthetic registry, needle retrieval@1 was 1.000 (n=300) against 0.000–0.003 for vanilla RAG and 0.000 for ColBERTv2 (doc_maxlen=180) and BGE-M3. Giving RAG the same regex anchor SUPERCTX extracts lifts needle@1 to 1.000, so the retrieval gap is a handle-access gap, not a ranking win. We do not headline an abstention gap: a powered RAG empty-set sweep on the nonexistent-anchor protocol was not run, and ColBERTv2/BGE-M3 were not scored on that protocol (recorded skip). The operational absence number is the model-free 3×10^{-5} backstop, not a parametric GPD pin. A live demo is at [research.com.ai](https://research.com.ai).

Project demo: **[research.com.ai](https://research.com.ai)**

TL;DR: Agents get a context-native memory upgrade with proof-carrying recall, certified negatives, and verifiable abstention—measuring 1.000 needle retrieval and 0.940 joint success on the paper's bank-layout protocol without replacing the decoder.

Over the lifetime of a patient, personal health tracking and healthcare services accumulate enormous amounts of multimodal data. However, fully utilizing the informational potential of these trajectories, representing them in a compact way for easy access by machine learning and data analysis methods, as well as exploiting their potential for personalized predictions is still a critical challenge.
Established artificial intelligence (AI) approaches often fail to capture the complex dynamics of these multimodal longitudinal clinical data over time as well as their natural uncertainty. They are either limited to categorical data or few modalities, lacking generative and forecasting capabilities, or not fully reflecting the temporal irregularity of real-world health data. We present a task-agnostic generative transformer model that can represent and extend sequences of patient states, incorporating all available information and modalities of a patient's lifetime. It can natively process structured and unstructured clinical records, measurements, waveforms, imaging, as well as categorical events. We also introduce a bidirectional time integration as well as a variational latent space to model the inherent uncertainty of patient journeys. Our model is the first in its domain that provides both full multimodal support and generative inference. We show that it produces highly informative and predictive sequences of patient state embeddings over time and that it can be used for zero-shot forecasting future developments for an individual, estimating risks, and simulating counterfactual clinical interventions. For training and evaluation, we merge all available MIMIC data to obtain more than 559M clinical events from 299,000 patients. Overall, we introduce a scalable foundational patient state encoder and prediction engine that can serve as a backbone for a broad variety of downstream models, predictive systems, and highly individualized medical treatments.

TL;DR: We introduce a novel variational transformer model as a holistic patient state encoder and prediction engine for lifetime patient trajectories, the first multimodal yet generative model in its field.

Group Relative Policy Optimisation (GRPO) enhances large language models by estimating advantages across a group of sampled trajectories. However, mapping these trajectory-level advantages to policy updates requires aggregating token-level importance ratios within each sequence. A fixed aggregation mechanism limits the algorithm's adaptability across tasks and training stages. We propose \textbf{HolderPO}, a generalised policy optimisation framework unifying token-level ratio aggregation via the Holder mean. By modulating its order $p$, our framework provides continuous control over gradient concentration and variance bounds. Theoretically, positive orders concentrate gradient weight toward high-ratio tokens, whereas decreasing $p$ monotonically tightens an upper bound on the policy-gradient variance under the stated assumptions. These complementary effects motivate a dynamic annealing algorithm that progressively decreases $p$ during training. Empirical signal-density diagnostics characterise the availability of successful rollout feedback on AIME24 and MATH500, complementing their different static-$p$ preferences. Evaluations compare static and dynamic orders across mathematical and agentic benchmarks. Our approach achieves an average accuracy of $55.2\%$ across five mathematical benchmarks on Qwen2.5-Math-7B and a $95.3\%$ success rate on ALFWorld.

Adversarial attacks are fundamental tools for evaluating the robustness of deep neural networks. Minimum-norm attacks seek the smallest perturbation that reaches the adversarial region, but the underlying optimization is highly nonconvex and further complicated by box constraints and norm-dependent structure. As a result, different trajectories may converge to stationary points with substantially different distortions, making the estimated minimum norm sensitive to the region explored. Motivated by the fact that first-order Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) stationarity is necessary but not sufficient for global optimality, we propose Adaptive Proximal Sequential Quadratic Programming (APSQP), a unified inner-outer framework that couples reliable local refinement with KKT-guided exploration of the decision boundary. The inner layer employs a box-aware proximal SQP scheme for which we establish convergence of the first-order KKT residual under fixed smoothing and proximal parameters and the stated regularity conditions; this analysis further motivates the practical adaptive parameter rules used in APSQP. The outer layer reuses previously identified boundary geometry to guide successive restarts toward alternative stationary regions. APSQP supports minimum-norm $\ell_1$, $\ell_2$, and $\ell_\infty$ attacks within a common optimization framework and extends to an approximate $\ell_0$ attack. Experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10, including adversarially robust models, show that APSQP consistently finds lower-distortion adversarial examples than strong minimum-norm baselines while maintaining high attack success rates.

Diffusion-based driving planners capture diverse behaviors but can generate unsafe trajectories under distribution shift. We propose BridgeGuard, a safety-constrained diffusion planning method that progressively strengthens a constraint term during denoising to drive intermediate trajectories toward a scene-dependent safety domain. Corrections operate in a low-dimensional curve space, promoting geometric coherence. A learned module, DistanceFieldNet, predicts a time-dependent distance field from bird's-eye-view features. Value and spatial-gradient supervision at queries sampled beyond expert trajectories teaches this field about both safe and unsafe regions. The learned field supplies the constraint term through safety injection while the pretrained perception backbone and planner remain frozen. We further establish sufficient conditions for terminal safety in an idealized continuous-time bridge. On Bench2Drive, BridgeGuard improves driving score/success rate from 87.99/74.99% to 90.88/76.36% for BridgeDrive and from 80.79/58.18% to 90.46/74.09% for $\text{DiffusionDrive}^{\text{geo}}$, demonstrating cross-model generalization.

TL;DR: BridgeGuard introduces an explicit Safety Drift mechanism that enforces safety constraints during reverse diffusion, enabling more robust diffusion-based trajectory generation for end-to-end autonomous driving.

Agent benchmarks typically evaluate post-trained models through end-to-end interaction, although the abilities that support agent behavior begin to devolop during pre-training. Can we evaluate base models' agentic potential before behavior alignment? To address this, we introduce PreAgent, a framework that evaluates agentic potential directly in base models, without requiring tool-protocol alignment or full environment interaction. Specifically, PreAgent extracts eight atomic capabilities from the complete agent execution lifecycle that are natively supported by base models. Accordingly, we extract verifiable decision nodes from recorded agent trajectories, and leverage causal contexts and execution feedback to construct conditional-likelihood preference and constrained generation tasks for each atomic capability. Additionally, We extend the evaluation to 32K and 256K context bins and group decisions within each task to measure long-context decision performance and joint correctness across steps. Extensive experiments show that PreAgent achieve a mean Spearman rank correlation exceeding 0.9 with post-SFT performance across different checkpoints of the same model, while also demonstrating strong predictive power in cross-model evaluations. These results highlight that PreAgent effectively assesses base-model agentic potential, providing a direct signal to guide mid-training optimization.

TL;DR: PreAgent evaluates base-model agentic potential before behavior alignment through eight atomic capabilities, with long-context and trajectory-level extensions.

Mid-training equips pretrained large language models with specialized and reasoning capabilities, but the returns of this stage are bounded since additional serial compute yields little further downstream improvement and can even degrade some capabilities, which places a practical ceiling on how much compute mid-training absorbs. We revisit how this compute should be allocated to a single run or multiple similar optimizations. We find that branches forked from a shared checkpoint under controlled recipe reaches measurably different regions of parameter space, and establish a form of compatible diversity that extending one run cannot supply. Therefore, we introduce Trajectory Soup, which distributes a mid-training budget over several independent branches, and consolidates strongest checkpoints selected on validation through intra- and inter-trajectory averaging into a single model. A local bias and variance analysis separates the two averaging levels, showing that inter-trajectory averaging removes residual error beyond the reach of temporal averaging, while checkpoint selection carries a bias that bounds how many checkpoints are worth merging. Across model scales, learning-rate schedules, token budgets, and trajectory counts, Trajectory Soup improves aggregate downstream performance over the strongest single-trajectory average under matched budgets and keeps improving as budgets expand, with the advantage preserved after an identical post-training pipeline. These results position trajectory allocation and merging as a practical way to extend the compute-scaling frontier of mid-training beyond serial saturation.

Unified multimodal models combine visual understanding and generation in one system. Most current methods use discrete autoregressive language modeling with continuous visual generation or depend on discrete masked diffusion. Recent studies indicate that pretrained continuous representations can serve as effective generative targets for both vision and language, offering a conceptually unified alternative. This prompts the question of whether direct modeling in continuous spaces can provide a strong foundation for unified multimodal modeling. To address this, we introduce JUICE, which models frozen pretrained image and text representations with a single flow matching Transformer, MM-RiT. MM-RiT connects modalities using bidirectional joint attention and modality-specific noise schedules. Joint denoising lets the model exchange cross-modal context under uncertainty, while conditional tasks provide boundary guidance. Flexible assignment of observed and noisy streams supports image generation, captioning, visual question answering, and joint generation within a unified interface. To study JUICE's design principles, we systematically study generative frameworks, training mixtures, and representation spaces during multimodal pretraining. Our findings are: (i) JUICE delivers strong image generation and matches autoregressive baselines in semantic caption alignment; (ii) combining joint and conditional denoising balances generation and captioning in a single model; and (iii) representation spaces show task- and scale-dependent trade-offs. Based on these findings, we scale JUICE from 179 million to 2.1 billion trainable parameters, achieving competitive image generation results and comparable visual understanding results without LLM initialization. The SigLIP2 variant achieves 0.86 GenEval and 66.15 VQAv2 at $224\times224$ resolution. On multi-solution mazes, coupled image-text sampling resolves cross-modal mode mismatch and matches the joint success of the strongest sequential cascade, without requiring a fixed generation order. These results demonstrate that pretrained continuous representation spaces offer a promising foundation for unified multimodal modeling.

TL;DR: JUICE unifies visual understanding and generation by jointly modeling pretrained continuous image and text representations with a single flow matching Transformer.

Memory-efficient optimization is critical for training increasingly large language models (LLMs). A popular strategy involves gradient low-rank projection, storing only the projected optimizer states, with GaLore being a representative example. However, a significant drawback of many such methods is their lack of convergence guarantees, as various low-rank projection approaches introduce inherent biases at each step relative to the original optimization algorithms even after taking expectation over stochastic sampling, which contribute to performance gaps compared to full-parameter training. Aiming to tackle this problem, this paper investigates the layerwise sampling technique for debiasing low-rank projection mechanisms. In particular, an instantiation of the paradigm gives rise to a novel and step-wise unbiased low-rank optimization method named GaLore Unbiased with Muon (GUM). We theoretically prove that GUM matches the convergence guarantees of the base Muon algorithm while preserving the memory efficiency of low-rank techniques. Empirical experiments on LLM fine-tuning and pretraining also demonstrate non-trivial improvements over GaLore and even better performance than full-parameter training. This improvement is shown to stem from a more uniform distribution of knowledge inside models, with further evidence supporting a specific practical guideline for memory budget scaling: keeping a moderate GaLore rank 
 and scaling up the number of randomly activated full-rank layers.

As large language models are increasingly used as evaluators (LLM-as-a-Judge), selecting reliable judges has attracted growing attention. Current practice often evaluates judges by average accuracy, but high accuracy can mask reliability limitations across domains, response perturbations, and adversarial manipulation. We introduce JudgeExam, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-as-a-Judge reliability on real model responses. JudgeExam contains 1,100 seed examples covering multiple-choice, short-answer, and process-oriented questions across multiple domains. For each seed, we construct four controlled variants: Equivalent Answer, Near-miss Flip, Attack Invariant, and Judge Hacking. Building on this design, we propose Robust Correct Decision Rate (RCD) and Manipulation-Resistant Robust Correct Decision Rate (MRCD). Both metrics measure joint correctness within a response family: RCD assesses robustness under non-adversarial transformations, while MRCD additionally assesses reliability under manipulation. Experiments with 13 judge models reveal substantial differences in reliability across question types and domains. The benefits of prompt refinement, model-side thinking, and chain-of-thought (CoT) also vary across models, producing different reliability--cost trade-offs; some configurations even increase cost while reducing reliability. These results show that selecting reliable LLM judges requires considering task type and domain, inference cost, and model reasoning configurations, rather than relying solely on average accuracy.

Deep learning can read microsatellite-instability (MSI)
status directly from H&E whole-slide images, and pathology
foundation models (FMs) report AUROCs above 0.94. Because a
patient can contribute several slides, evaluation protocol matters.
We benchmark MSI-H versus MSS under patient-grouped
pipelines on TCGA-COAD and TCGA-STAD across encoder and
MIL-head panels. The central controlled TCGA-COAD experiment
fixes 581 feature-covered slides from 240 patients, H-Optimus-1
features, CLAM-SB, five seeds, eight folds and training settings
while changing only the split generator. Slide-random splitting
raises five-seed slide-level AUROC from 0.9429 to 0.9608 and
AUPRC from 0.8701 to 0.9225; patient-grouped folds have zero
patient overlap, whereas slide-random folds expose 90.98% of
validation slides to a training patient. Prediction-backed CONCH
probes reproduce the same direction in COAD and STAD, and a
harmonized 486-slide STAD Virchow2→Prism2 probe does
likewise. The unsupported Prism2 COAD row is not reported.
These internal results quantify split-induced optimism but are not
external clinical validation.

Coding agents need to establish that a program satisfies a specification and that the specification captures the requested behavior. We study how expert diagnosis of verification failures can become reusable guidance for this work. Our approach combines executable language definitions in K with a kit of procedures for constructing specifications, repairing proofs, and auditing their adequacy. A human-guided development campaign on HumanEval, a benchmark of 164 Python programming tasks, achieves a 164/164 success rate with the semantics and the kit, measured by final AI audit Pass verdicts after two targeted repairs. To examine whether auditing detects problems that successful proofs leave unresolved, we construct 12 author-reviewed pairs of clean and defective packages. Every package passes its K proofs, and completed audits identify all defects and accept all clean packages. We then use KleverBench to test specification and proof construction for 31 programs with changed operator meanings. Comparisons with complete acceptance rules and equally long generic advice yield mixed results across two model and budget settings, motivating further work on selecting useful guidance within resource limits. Human-reviewed Optimism proofs establish expected pause reverts for six operations within declared input bounds under London semantics with unbounded gas. We report progress, difficulties, and lessons toward agents that deliver programs with checkable correctness arguments.

TL;DR: We study expert-curated verification guidance through matched controls, adequacy audits, and scoped EVM proofs.

We present Paxar, a planning-before-rendering autoregressive framework for long-form audiovisual generation.
Paxar first constructs a compact but informative audiovisual plan, then renders full-resolution audio-video under its guidance, autoregressive in both stages for efficiency.
We find that an informative plan must combine multiple representations, each providing essential information.
We introduce Asymmetric Encoding to compress them into a compact token sequence while avoiding conflicts.
The planner generates this compact plan with larger temporal strides for long-range coordination.
The renderer uses smaller strides to synthesize full-resolution video and audio, guided only by the plan and neighboring history.
Decoupling these stages allows the planner to be trained on more data for better coordination and enables low-cost plan exploration and editing before rendering.
On multi-shot benchmarks spanning 12 to 30 seconds, Paxar substantially outperforms autoregressive and two-stage baselines in overall score, while matching or slightly exceeding bidirectional baselines.
It also exhibits less quality degradation as video duration increases.
Paxar also extends naturally to image-conditioned generation, audio-guided generation, and video-to-video editing.

Scaling Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) to large populations is challenging because the joint state-action space grows rapidly with the number of agents, making coordinated policy learning increasingly difficult. Transformer-based sequence models have become a strong MARL paradigm for modeling cross-agent dependencies, but single-sequence agent modeling remains difficult to scale due to quadratic attention cost and autoregressive decoding latency. Motivated by multi-scale organization in natural and social systems, we propose the \textbf{Hierarchical Multi-Agent Transformer (H-MAT)}. H-MAT organizes real agents into a flexible multi-tier hierarchy with higher-level virtual nodes, factorizing coordination across local groups rather than modeling all agents as a single sequence. Within this hierarchy, masked intra-group encoders summarize local interactions into bottom-up reports, while top-down decoders generate instructions that guide lower-level decision making. We analyze H-MAT from three perspectives: local deviation from a reference global-attention representation, the role of value-relevant top-down instructions in conditioning local policies, and the sub-quadratic attention complexity of the hierarchy. Experiments on NEOM and MAgent with up to $N=1024$ agents show that H-MAT achieves state-of-the-art performance with substantially reduced computational overhead. Ablations show that H-MAT benefits from report-instruction routing, shallow topology, robust grouping, attention, and weight sharing, without sacrificing small-scale performance.

Neural models are often trained to learn relations between objects, such as ordering or grouping them into classes. These models are usually evaluated by how accurately they classify new pairs of objects.

Accuracy shows whether individual answers are correct, but not whether they are consistent with each other. Each relation has rules that hold across pairs. For example, ordering must be transitive (if $a$ precedes $b$ and $b$ precedes $c$, then $a$ precedes $c$) and must never place $a$ both before and after $b$. Similarly, equivalence relation must be reflexive, symmetric and transitive. A model can be highly accurate and still break these rules, or follow them while disagreeing with the target relation. Ablation studies have a similar gap. Randomizing a model's weights is often assumed to remove what it learned, but whether the randomized model still produces consistent answers is not usually verified.

We propose an evaluation protocol that reports accuracy together with the rules each relation should satisfy. For each rule, we compute how often random, independent answers would satisfy it at the same rate of positive predictions. This tells us how much consistency the model shows beyond chance. We also compare weight randomization with controls whose behavior is known in advance, such as returning a fresh random answer on every call. We test the protocol on small encoder–comparator models trained on synthetic ordering and equivalence tasks over 200 objects. Training and evaluation pairs are kept separate, and results are replicated across three worlds and three training seeds. Our experiments show that similar accuracy does not imply similar relational structure, and weight randomization does not guarantee its removal.

TL;DR: Evaluating relational learning requires more than pairwise accuracy: algebraic consistency and carefully designed controls reveal relational structure that can persist even after model weights are randomized.

Long chain-of-thought reasoning makes large language models more capable, but it also gives harmful intent a place to hide: a dangerous premise introduced in an intermediate step can propagate through the rest of the trajectory, where outcome-level safety training rarely reaches. We present PRISM, a process-level risk-aware tree search framework that enforces safety during inference. PRISM first scores each query along four risk dimensions and maps the aggregate risk to search depth, width, exploration, pruning threshold, and risk penalty, so benign queries retain large budgets while risky ones are searched conservatively. Inside a risk-aware Monte Carlo tree search, a SafeUCT rule penalizes path risk, dangerous nodes trigger subtree pruning, and a four-dimensional joint process reward evaluates utility, harmfulness, coherence, and faithfulness online; a lightweight value model replaces most full rollouts, and the final trajectory is selected from a safety--utility Pareto front. On HarmBench, StrongReject, and XSTest with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PRISM reduces attack success rate by 31.0 and 46.3 percentage points over the base model and lowers over-refusal rate to 7.2%, while utility on AlpacaEval 2.0 and GSM8K remains close to the base model, giving the highest safety--utility score (0.755) among safety-tuned and inference-time baselines.

TL;DR: PRISM improves the safety of large language model reasoning by using risk-aware Monte Carlo Tree Search to evaluate, prune, and select reasoning trajectories at the process level while preserving utility on benign tasks.

Deep research reports answering the same query may develop different evidence, explanations, and conclusions. Evaluating these reports requires assessing both the quality of individual analyses and their relative contributions to the task. We introduce a benchmark that combines task-specific pointwise audits with guideline-based pairwise comparisons to address these complementary questions. Pointwise audits assess how well each report meets individual requirements, while pairwise comparisons weigh substantive differences in evidence, analysis, and presentation. Passage-linked report representations locate these differences, and selective evidence verification checks consequential claims to inform the judgments. The benchmark comprises 40 Chinese and English tasks from three existing benchmarks, 280 reports from seven research systems, 1,099 human-reviewed evaluation criteria, and blinded human preferences on 80 report pairs. Evaluation across the seven systems reveals distinct strengths in responsiveness, evidence, insight, and readability. The combined evaluator achieves 86.25% agreement with human preferences and Cohen's $\kappa = 0.746$. Together, the report collection, reviewed criteria, and human annotations provide a common resource for comparing deep research systems and studying automated report evaluation.

TL;DR: A benchmark combining pointwise audits and route-aware pairwise comparisons to evaluate deep research reports against human preferences.

Once a model has learned a task, can its computation change without changing its behaviour? We study recurrent--attention hybrids in which recurrent state and retrieval can support the same answer. After accuracy has converged, penalising retrieval shifts causal reliance to recurrence while endpoint behaviour is preserved. This is learned reorganisation rather than output shrinkage: unpriced controls do not drift, inference-time attenuation to the same retrieval share collapses accuracy, and a no-penalty availability intervention produces the same rerouting. The governing condition is substitutability. A route-only capability screen fixed before steering separates complete handover from failure (19.77M parameters: 3/3 vs. 0/3; MNIST/CIFAR-10: 8/8 vs. 0/8), and non-additive fusion shows capability is necessary but not sufficient. After successful handover the retrieval route can be deleted at no accuracy cost, replacing context-growing retrieval state with constant-size recurrent state. On TinyStories, where copying has no recurrent substitute, pricing yields stable partial transfer but retrieval never becomes deletable. Behavioural convergence therefore need not fix causal implementation: even after a task is learned, the computation supporting it can remain steerable.

TL;DR: After a recurrent-attention hybrid has learned a task, penalising retrieval shifts its causal reliance onto recurrence without changing accuracy. When the two routes can substitute for each other, the retrieval route can then be deleted at no cost.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enables large language models to access external knowledge during inference, but its reliance on external knowledge bases also introduces new attack surfaces. Existing data extraction attacks against RAG systems mainly follow two approaches: prompt injection attacks, whose effectiveness heavily depends on the generator's instruction-following capability, and backdoor-based attacks that induce the generator to directly reproduce or paraphrase retrieved documents. However, existing backdoor-based attacks still struggle to simultaneously achieve high extraction fidelity and attack stealthiness. In this paper, we propose RAGLeak, a supply-chain privacy backdoor attack against RAG systems whose key idea is to decouple information leakage from direct textual exposure. RAGLeak implants a trigger-controlled reversible context obfuscation behavior into the generator, causing it to output an encoded representation of the retrieved private documents when triggered. An auxiliary LLM then recovers the original content using the encoding rule, enabling high-fidelity data recovery while reducing direct textual overlap between the leaked output and the original documents. We evaluate RAGLeak across three model families and three application domains. RAGLeak achieves an ASR of up to $100\%$ while causing only limited impact on benign model utility. Moreover, under representative detection-based defenses, its ASR decreases by at most $10$ percentage points, while the implanted backdoor remains effective after downstream clean fine-tuning. Furthermore, RAGLeak generalizes across generator models of different scales and model versions. Our results reveal an underexplored supply-chain privacy risk in RAG systems. The source code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAGLeak-4B67.

TL;DR: We reveal a supply-chain privacy risk in RAG systems and propose RAGLEAK, a reversible backdoor attack that enables high-fidelity document extraction while reducing direct textual exposure.

Modular models aim to decouple capability development from foundation model training, allowing capabilities to be independently developed, shared, and composed through lightweight adapters while leveraging a common foundation model. This paradigm enables many capabilities to be served from a single model rather than maintaining separate models for each task. Realizing this vision requires an inference architecture that supports efficient capability composition and adapter switching while introducing minimal overhead relative to the shared base model. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) provides a natural building block for modular models, enabling independently trained adapters to be selected and composed over a shared backbone. However, LoRA adapters modify the key and value projections in the self-attention mechanism. As a result, the KV cache stores adapter-specific representations, which can prevent subsequent adapters from being safely activated on the same context, a phenomenon we refer to as KV-cache contamination. We show that KV-cache contamination consistently degrades performance across adaptation targets, contamination levels, and adapter ranks, reaching up to 28.5 percentage points in the most severe settings, increasing as more context is cached under prior adapters. To mitigate this issue, we introduce Shadow Residual (SR), a transformer decoder architecture that decouples adapter-specific computation from the cached attention state. SR maintains capability-specific information in a parallel residual stream while the KV cache is written exclusively by the base model. This enables arbitrary adapter transitions within a single generation without rebuilding cached states or incurring additional KV-memory overhead. Across diverse tasks, domains, context lengths, and model scales (3B-30B parameters), SR recovers 85.2\% of the performance gain achieved by LoRA while eliminating KV-cache contamination. Beyond quality, SR enables efficient multi-adapter execution, reducing time-to-completion by up to $10.34\times$ on ReAct-style agent workloads. These results establish Shadow Residual as an an effective architectural primitive and efficient capability composition.

The scaling laws for recommender systems have been increasingly validated, where MetaFormer-based architectures consistently benefit from increased model depth, hidden dimensionality, and user behavior sequence length.
However, whether representation capacity scales proportionally with parameter growth remains unexplored.
Recent analyses of deep ranking backbones show that the effective rank of token representations follows a damped oscillatory trajectory across layers, failing to increase consistently with depth and even degrading in deeper layers.
\newtext{We analyze fixed-backbone rank dynamics through a bound on head-wise token mixing and local spectral bounds for the per-token feed-forward network. We further characterize covariance transfer under shared local Jacobians at matched dimensions and covariance spectral effective-rank retention through end-to-end conditioning, motivating the initial token space as a design target.}
Guided by this analysis, we propose **RankUp**, an architecture that enlarges and diversifies the initial token space through randomized permutation splitting over sparse features, a multi-embedding paradigm, global token integration, and crossed pretrained embedding tokens.
RankUp has been fully deployed in large-scale production across three advertising scenarios of a large advertising platform, yielding GMV improvements of 3.41\%, 4.81\% and 2.12\%, respectively.

CueMind

TL;DR: a sentence that is short

Learning reliable surrogates for geodynamics requires modeling strongly coupled physical fields across heterogeneous spatial and temporal scales. We introduce GeoSim, a benchmark of high-fidelity two-dimensional mantle-plume simulations generated with I2VIS, spanning variations in plume temperature and lithospheric thickness and providing six coupled physical fields over full simulation trajectories. Evaluation of representative neural operators reveals a pronounced field-wise difficulty gap: models that accurately predict scalar fields can still incur substantially larger errors on velocity, while strong short-window performance does not necessarily translate into stable autonomous rollout. Motivated by these observations, we introduce MFGNO, a Multi-Field Graph Neural Operator that jointly represents the coupled physical fields and incorporates field-difference information into graph message passing. On GeoSim-Plume1, MFGNO reduces the horizontal and vertical velocity errors by 91.9% and 91.5%, respectively, relative to the best external baseline for each component, while exhibiting trade-offs on scalar fields. Controlled ablations show that the velocity gain is associated with the joint multi-field design as a whole, whereas the additional contribution of explicit difference inputs is not established at the present scale. Long-horizon experiments further show that the short-window velocity advantage persists within the temporal range represented during training but does not yield stable extrapolation far beyond it. Together, GeoSim and MFGNO provide a benchmark and empirical framework for studying multi-field representation, field-wise failure modes, and long-horizon stability in learned geodynamics surrogates.

Embodied multi-agent collaboration enables agents to tackle complex, long-horizon tasks by leveraging complementary capabilities and parallel execution in shared environments. Realizing this potential requires agents to effectively translate communicated information into appropriate actions. However, coordination-related information may already be available in an agent's interaction history but remain underutilized when making subsequent decisions. We refer to this failure mode as the *communication-to-action gap*. To bridge this gap, we introduce *actionable coordination beliefs* (ACoB), where each agent maintains a belief that guides its actions and is continuously refined based on the outcomes of those actions. We incorporate actionable coordination beliefs into the MINDcraft framework through three components: (1) a freshness-aware belief that integrates task context, local observations, interaction history, and execution outcomes; (2) a hierarchical belief-to-action reasoning module that performs coordination-level and action-level reasoning to determine the agent's next action; and (3) an execution and revision module that updates and refines the belief based on the outcomes of executed actions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ACoB can enhance performance, suggesting that our proposed method can effectively bridge the communication-to-action gap and enable agents to make better use of communicated information for subsequent actions.

TL;DR: ACoB bridges the communication-to-action gap in embodied multi-agent collaboration by maintaining and refining actionable beliefs that convert communicated information into effective decisions.

Flow-matching world-action models (WAMs) excel at continuous control but rely predominantly on offline imitation, as their deterministic formulation lacks analytical transition likelihoods required for online reinforcement learning. We introduce WAM-R1, a systematic effort to explore the R1-style reinforcement learning post-training paradigm for incentivizing action reasoning in world-action models. By formulating action generation via Euler-Maruyama stochastic differential equations, WAM-R1 derives exact closed-form Gaussian transition probabilities without Monte Carlo approximations. Furthermore, a hybrid-window sampling schedule confines exploratory deliberation strictly to early generation steps before switching to deterministic ODE integration, eliminating physical execution chatter and bounding policy ratio variance. This formulation provides a unified, modular interface compatible with both actor-critic and critic-free policy objectives under dual drift and anchor guardrails. Across LIBERO and RoboCasa, WAM-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance within 10 to 20 online updates from converged imitation baselines. Crucially, with only 50\% demonstrations, it breaks imitation limits and surpasses competitive baselines trained on full demonstration coverage. Code: \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/WAM-R1-RL-Post-Training-7461}.

TL;DR: WAM-R1 enables online RL post-training for flow-matching world-action models via hybrid-window SDEs, outperforming full-data baselines with only 50% demonstrations on LIBERO and RoboCasa.

Generative video world models can now synthesize increasingly open-ended environments that agents can navigate and interact with in simple ways. Yet open-ended generation does not imply full interaction: as a generated world expands, newly created content through navigation should also expand what the agent can act upon, and as the agent changes the world, those changes should become persistent parts of the environment rather than transient visual effects. We characterize these two requirements as Open-World Interactivity, where newly generated or encountered entities are dynamically incorporated into the actionable world, and Persistent State, where interaction outcomes are committed to the world state and continue to influence subsequent observations and interactions. We present ONEIRA, an interactive video world model that closes the loop between generation and interaction through an explicit, extensible world state continuously managed by a coding agent. Given the current observation and an action or high-level goal, the agent reads the world state, grounds the relevant entities, plans the interaction, and writes its outcome back into a world state table. When exploration reveals new objects, the agent dynamically incorporates them from generated observations, allowing the interaction space to expand with the generated world. Meanwhile, previously induced state changes are carried across video segments, making the consequences of interaction persistent parts of subsequent world evolution. The updated world state is rendered along the camera action trajectory into a coarse conditioning video, from which a video generator fills in the appearance, motion, and interaction details not explicitly represented in the state. Experiments show that ONEIRA enables direct and logically consistent interaction with newly generated objects during open-world exploration, while preserving the effects of prior interactions consistently over long horizons.

Multi-task optimization must reconcile gradients that differ in scale and direction while reflecting user priorities over the tasks. Existing methods commonly optimize an aggregate objective or infer a compromise from gradient geometry, leaving the allocation of first-order progress implicit. We introduce Gradient Profile Matching (GPM), a direct interface that converts positive task priorities into requested normalized directional derivatives. Exact GPM realizes every feasible profile through a minimum-norm pseudoinverse construction, with an explicit residual otherwise. Our theoretical guarantees apply to feasible requests under this exact construction. First, under a direct gradient step, it gives strict common first-order descent for every positive profile with nonzero task gradients, including nonuniform profiles. Second, priority ratios directly specify relative normalized local progress. Third, it preserves its direction when identical full-model gradient constraints with matching priorities are added or removed and under positive loss rescaling. To study practical behavior, we apply EMA and spectral Tikhonov regularization before Adam, trading exact instantaneous matching for a smoother, more stable gradient signal that Adam may further transform. On NYUv2 and QM9, changing the requested profile produces corresponding endpoint redistribution toward the prioritized tasks; the experiments measure this endpoint effect rather than exact per-step matching or common descent. GPM therefore provides an explicit and interpretable mechanism for controlling local progress in multi-task learning.

TL;DR: GPM provides explicit local control over multi-task progress, with common-descent and exact duplicate-stability guarantees and experiments demonstrating priority-driven endpoint redistribution.

Self-evolving LLM agents solve long-horizon tasks through sequences of actions, where an early
mistake can alter the state encountered at every subsequent step. A critic can provide intermediate
feedback to detect and correct such errors. As the actor learns from experience, however, its
behavior and failure patterns change, potentially leaving a fixed critic misaligned. We introduce
NPAC, a Non-Parametric Actor-Critic framework that maintains separate actor and critic memories
while keeping both LLMs frozen. The actor memory stores reusable skills distilled from successful
trajectories and refined through replay-validated updates, while the critic memory stores recurring
failure modes together with their trigger and outcome statistics. At the start of each task, the
critic uses task relevance and these statistics to retrieve failure modes that refine a task-specific
rubric. It audits the unfolding trajectory against this rubric using its own inspection and
verification tools. Feedback can be requested by the actor or initiated by the critic upon detecting
a rubric-relevant deviation. During learning, the two memories are updated independently after each
task, enabling both actor behavior and critic feedback to adapt through accumulated experience.
Experiments on GAIA, ALFWorld, and BFCL-v4 show consistent improvements over representative baselines.
On ALFWorld with Qwen3-32B, NPAC raises the mean held-out success rate from 52.0\% to 82.3\% across three seeds.

Pretrained visual models can recover shape and track motion, but these predictions do not specify a robot body that can accommodate the observed action. We study how to turn visual observations into mechanical design specifications. We propose $\mathrm{M}^{3}$ VGT a mesh-constrained morphology-motion co-design framework. Given a mesh and a video, the framework generates a modular body of extensible struts and converts predicted image observations into mesh-guided spatial trajectories. These trajectories guide body layout and actuator stroke allocation under geometric and mechanical constraints. Feedback-controlled simulations with torso support evaluate cat, horse, and dog inputs. Compared with shape-only designs using fixed strokes, co-design reduces the trajectory adjustment required by rod-length limits by 22.7-55.8% and improves tracking. It retains at least 95.6% of the baseline shape F1 with identical node and strut counts. These results show that designing body geometry and actuator travel around observed motion produces mechanisms better matched to the actions they are meant to perform.

TL;DR: We use observed motion as a functional design signal to synthesize robot bodies that preserve a target shape while better accommodating the intended action.

Despite rapid advances in Code Agents, their misuse can produce bloated and disorganized code that harms readability, extensibility, and robustness, highlighting the need to evaluate their refactoring capabilities. Code smells provide a structured lens for such evaluation, but real-world refactoring cases are poorly suited for systematic smell-level analysis due to highly imbalanced smell distributions and the frequent entanglement of refactoring with bug fixes.

To this end, we introduce \textbf{SmellBench}, a benchmark that organizes refactoring tasks by code smell for fine-grained evaluation of code agents. SmellBench creates diverse refactoring tasks by introducing code smells into real-world open-source projects, with each task undergoing multi-stage verification and human review. SmellBench contains 294 cases derived from 7 real-world repositories, covering 7 representative code smell types, 3 difficulty levels, and 2 instruction settings. We evaluate refactoring performance from three complementary aspects: functional correctness, localization accuracy, and refactoring quality. Experiments across multiple code agents and frontier large language models reveal substantial room for improvement: even the SOTA model achieves only 50.34\% in smell elimination. Further analysis shows that current agents often focus on local code changes and struggle with cross-file reasoning, limiting their ability to perform comprehensive refactoring.

State-of-the-art self-supervised algorithms provide really strong weight initialization that can be easily transferred to downstream tasks such as image classification. However, when the downstream task's domain shifts from the self-supervised database used to pretrain the models, these models tend to produce sub-optimal results. Ideally, we would like to pretrain a new model on our new image domain, but we may lack enough samples to train DINO-like models. To address these issues, we propose SegBYOL, designed as a self-supervised method to improve semantic segmentation on unnatural image databases. SegBYOL is a two-step method that first uses a small labelled set of images and a calibration algorithm to generate pseudo-labels for all our unlabelled images. It then learns strong features oriented towards segmentation by applying the BYOL loss between pixels of the last feature maps. Doing so allows it to learn pixel-wise features instead of image-level features, which seem less suited to segmentation tasks. Another benefit of this is that the loss is computed between more samples, simulating larger batches. The last feature maps also go through a decoder network predicting the pseudo-labels obtained in the first step. To evaluate our method, we benchmarked it against the original BYOL, the DINOv3 unsupervised algorithm, and the state-of-the-art DINOv3 trained on LVD-1689M. On three different datasets of microscopic and sonar images, we obtained a systematic improvement of the macro-F1 score of at least +1\% over every competitor.

Multi-view fundus imaging provides complementary evidence for diabetic retinopathy (DR) grading, yet existing methods face three interrelated challenges: visual-only models lack explicit access to clinical knowledge of disease severity, the diagnostic value of each view varies across patients and representation levels, and conventional classifiers largely ignore the ordinal relationships among DR grades. We propose TPDOM-DR, a unified framework that jointly models clinical semantics, dual-level view reliability, and ordinal expert fusion. First, a Description-weighted Text Prototype module (DTP) learns to aggregate multiple grade-specific clinical descriptions and uses residual prompts to construct task-adaptive semantic prototypes. Second, a Dual-level Reliability Interaction module (DRI) estimates view reliability separately from global semantic and local structural features and couples them through global–local interaction. Third, an Ordinal Expert Routing module (OER) normalizes the output scales of three heterogeneous diagnostic experts and dynamically combines them while imposing ordinal constraints in both the representation and prediction spaces. Trained only on the four-view MFIDDR dataset, TPDOM-DR achieves 87.08% accuracy and 96.96% AUC, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 3.07 and 1.38 percentage points, respectively. Without fine-tuning, it also outperforms all evaluated baselines on three external single-view datasets, supporting its cross-dataset transferability.

TL;DR: TPDOM-DR combines clinical text prototypes, dual-level view reliability, and ordinal expert routing to improve diabetic retinopathy grading and cross-dataset transfer.

Alterations in cortical shape are a key hallmark of many neurodevelopmental disorders yet detecting them remains difficult due to the fact that every human brain forms differently. What this means is that ‘normative’ development should be defined relative to each individual's starting brain geometry, and that 
measuring longitudinal change generates far more reliable biomarkers of disease than the standard approach of cross-sectional comparison to a population average. Nevertheless, measuring this growth reliably requires overcoming the limitations of standard registration frameworks, which fail to handle the rapid, complex deformations of early brain expansion. Here, we propose a recurrent CNN optimised with a spatiotemporally adaptive biomechanical loss derived from ground-truth weekly growth estimates. Evaluated on  longitudinal fetal and preterm MRI; our approach yields smooth, biomechanically realistic transformations that reproduce true regional cortical growth more than three times more accurately than classical and learning-based image registration baselines (median surface-area error 7\% vs. 26\%), and improve segmentation overlap by nearly 7 Dice points (79.7 vs. 73.0).

Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon tasks through task decomposition and heterogeneous model collaboration. However, effective orchestration in long-horizon settings requires continual adaptation to evolving execution states and runtime-harness constraints, while sparse and delayed supervision makes it difficult to attribute outcomes and accumulate reliable experience. We introduce MoMA (Mixture of Models and Agents), a recursive self-evolving orchestration model that continuously improves multi-agent collaboration through the joint evolution of model capability knowledge and orchestration policy. MoMA generates state-adaptive workflows by jointly determining subtasks, models, tools, contexts, and dependency structures. From execution trajectories, a state-aware Wiki optimizer extracts, verifies, and refines conditional model capability knowledge through evidence attribution, active verification, and update gating. MoMA then combines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with Wiki-privileged on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), to integrate task outcomes, workflow feedback, and capability-aware supervision, progressively internalizing validated capability knowledge into the orchestration policy. The updated policy induces new execution trajectories that provide further evidence for capability refinement, forming a recursive cycle of knowledge evolution and policy improvement. Across coding, information retrieval, and complex reasoning tasks, MoMA achieves the highest average performance among the evaluated orchestration methods, while its evolving workflow structures and model allocation patterns demonstrate the progressive emergence of more selective and task-adaptive orchestration strategies.

TL;DR: We propose MoMA, a recursive self-evolving orchestration model trained to continually learns task-adaptive multi-model collaboration strategies for long-horizon tasks.

Physics-Informed Machine Learning (PIML) arises as a way to incorporate physics knowledge in automatic learning processes. The most popular model of this domain may be PINN (Physics-Informed Neural Network), a network using a composite loss function including physics dynamics and constraints in addition to learning errors on observations. This methodology has good results on benchmark problems, but shows limits when the problem to solve becomes more complex. On simpler problems, choices on the constitution of the network is essential to find a good estimation of the dynamic system behavior. More recently, DeepONet structure has showed good results on benchmark dynamical problems, but is constructed to output a single dynamical variable. The goal of the models proposed in this study, is to adapt and segment the neural network structure to target learning on simpler parts of the problem. Four structures are proposed to be evaluated on a complex dynamical system, building thermodynamics. A simplification of the dynamical system is proposed as a system of three Ordinary Differential Equations (ODE), involving three target dynamical variables. Results of The Multi-DeepONet adaptation, as well as Multi-Head and Multi-Branch DeepONet, showed a real gain of performance, compared to standard PINNs and non-physics-informed models.

Personalization remains a critical challenge in driving recommendation systems, as human drivers exhibit heterogeneous driving behaviors, influenced by short-term intentions and shaped by long-term habits. To achieve personalization, memory-augmented agents emerge as a promising paradigm that can infer short-term intentions from immediate observations while capturing long-term habits from accumulated memories. However, existing agent workflows typically organize memories as loose structures, failing to identify consistent long-term habits from memory relationships. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes GraphMem, a graph-structured memory-augmented agent workflow for personalized driving recommendations. The contributions are threefold. First, unlike loosely organized memory architectures, GraphMem leverages a novel graph representation to reveal memory relationships, which enables more accurate, efficient retrieval of relevant historical driving experiences, leading to structured evidence for personalized driving recommendations. Second, GraphMem integrates differential privacy into memory representations, thereby providing theoretical privacy guarantees for graph topology. Third, GraphMem optimizes graph construction hyperparameters using Bayesian optimization to balance driver privacy and memory utility, thereby enhancing the utility-privacy trade-off. Experimental results demonstrate that GraphMem outperforms several state-of-the-art methods in retrieval while effectively supporting downstream decision-making. Ablation studies further isolate the contributions of graph structure, privacy mechanisms, and Bayesian optimization schemes. Overall, the study advances personalized driving recommendation systems through privacy-preserving graph-structured memory representation.

Production guardrails for large language models are dominated by the LLM-as-a-judge pattern: a second generative model reads the first model's output and writes a verdict. The pattern is accurate and explainable, but architecturally incompatible with interactive serving SLAs: in production deployments, an evaluation turn adds upwards of 1,500 ms of latency, generates over 1,500 additional tokens, consumes critical accelerator KV-cache, and imports autoregressive long-tail latency jitter into system p99s. We ask whether factual verdicts can be read from internal model representations rather than generated. We formalize representation-as-a-judge: a framework that probes the transformer residual stream at serving time via a non-blocking forward hook to emit scalar factuality scores. We establish the theoretical condition under which probing adds zero critical-path compute latency (requiring probe retirement within the execution shadow of downstream layers) and show a 31B parameter model satisfies this with three orders of magnitude of slack. Sweeping probe depth across intermediate blocks on Gemma 4 31B demonstrates that factual separability is non-monotone: linear discrimination rises from an ROC-AUC of 0.420 at layer 8 to a peak ROC-AUC of 0.628 (SNR 1.898) at layer 20 before decaying near the unembedding head, confirming that factual consistency forms in the deep semantic manifold prior to vocabulary projection collapse. We also prove that centered two-class cosine separation is identically 2 for any binary data, explaining a common metric degeneracy. Operating at an empirical cost ratio of c_FN / c_FP ≈ 6.87 (tau = 0.873), our probe incurs <0.85 ms overhead (~1,700x faster) with zero critical-path token cost. Rather than an autonomous verdict engine, we position representation probing as an ultra-fast screening stage that filters benign traffic, reserving expensive generative judges exclusively for asynchronous audit on flagged subsets.

TL;DR: Probing intermediate residual stream activations at layer 20 screens LLM hallucinations with sub-millisecond latency and zero token overhead.

Code agents locate and combine evidence distributed across repository
files before they can edit code reliably. Although post-training teaches tool
use and search workflows, the underlying model's ability to relate definitions,
usages, and behavioral constraints is also shaped by the repository contexts
seen during pretraining. Existing repository-level pretraining commonly
orders files and cuts the resulting sequence at the context limit. For
repositories spanning multiple contexts, however, a good global order does not
determine which related files remain jointly visible. We study this
under-specified composition decision and introduce \emph{ChunkTopo}. ChunkTopo
constructs a repository dependency graph, selects disjoint file groups that fit the token capacity while reducing dependency cuts, orders files and groups
prerequisite-first, and assembles the ordered groups into training contexts.
Comparisons hold the file manifest, per-file exposure, model architecture,
language-modeling objective, context length, and training budget fixed.
Against a strong repository-topological baseline, ChunkTopo improves
SWE-Agentless file-localization F1 from 9.31 to 13.36 on Qwen2.5-7B with 32K
contexts; the gain persists at 14B (33.66 to 35.59) and with an 8K training
context (11.37 to 14.93). These results show that repository-context
composition can strengthen cross-file evidence localization, a foundation
capability used by downstream code agents.

TL;DR: By replacing standard topological sorting with graph-partitioned "dependency-dense" contexts during continued pretraining, we minimize severed file dependencies, unlocking zero-overhead gains on SWE-bench and long-context benchmarks for code agents.

Tests generated from a short programming ticket may miss requirements that the ticket
leaves unstated. We evaluate whether giving the test generator an explicit specification
improves the code repaired from its tests. The comparison holds the code drafts,
tester, and test count fixed. The baseline is instructed to probe invalid inputs and
edge cases; the grounded condition also receives the specification as a list of rules.
A separate, hidden gold suite assesses final correctness.
On specification-completeness tasks, grounding improves final correctness by 38
percentage points on each of three Claude tiers and by 36 points on held-out tasks
(task-level sign test over 18 tasks, $p=0.002$). Much of the detection benefit remains
when the specification is supplied as ordinary prose: this condition detects 27 of
30 bugs, versus 30 with a rule list. Coverage planning without the specification
detects 2. Increasing the ungrounded test budget does not close the difference, and
full-pipeline evaluations with GPT-5.3 Codex and Gemini 3.5 Flash also show improved
final correctness. On behavioural tasks, grounded tests have a 0% false-alarm rate;
the baseline rejects correct code on 33% of checks.
For these defects, supplying the relevant requirements was more effective than
generating additional ungrounded tests. No advantage was observed on well-specified
algorithmic tasks. Missing or incorrect specification rules remain a source of
undetected bugs and misleading test expectations.

TL;DR: Giving test-generating LLMs explicit specifications improves code correctness and reduces false alarms more than generating additional ungrounded tests on specification-completeness tasks.

Adapting general-purpose LLMs into a reliable healthcare assistant requires more than injecting domain knowledge. High-quality expert supervision is scarce and expensive to scale, while different forms of domain knowledge should be incorporated according to how they are used. We present RESPIRA (Rule-guided Expert Supervision for Parametric Internalization and Retrieval-Augmented Adaptation), a healthcare domain adaptation framework addressing these two challenges.
First, RESPIRA follows the principle that expert knowledge should be codified before it is scaled, extracting recurring interpretation and recommendation patterns from expert cases, formalizing them into reusable rules, and using these rules to guide controlled supervision scaling.
Second, RESPIRA follows the principle that domain knowledge should be organized according to how it is used, internalizing reusable behavioral and reasoning knowledge into model parameters while retaining document-grounded and update-sensitive factual knowledge in an external retrieval repository for on-demand access.
We instantiate RESPIRA in the case of sleep-respiratory care and develop RespiraLM-32B, evaluating it on three representative healthcare tasks: Report Interpretation, Personalized Health Advice, and Domain Chat. Across these tasks, RespiraLM-32B demonstrates stronger task-specific domain alignment than a broad range of open-source LLMs, while remaining competitive with proprietary frontier LLMs. In particular, on Domain Chat, RespiraLM-32B outperforms both open-source and proprietary general-purpose LLMs across the reported automatic metrics. These results show that rule-guided supervision scaling and selective knowledge organization proposed in RESPIRA can effectively transform a general-purpose LLM into an effective and specialized healthcare assistant.

TL;DR: RESPIRA adapts general-purpose LLMs to healthcare by combining rule-guided expert supervision scaling with selective knowledge internalization and retrieval-augmented adaptation.

The few deep scanpath models spanning search and free viewing predict where the eye goes but not why. Deep Guided Viewer (DGV), inspired by Guided Search, is a scanpath model based on a drift-diffusion race, in which candidate locations drift noisily toward a threshold and the first to cross it wins the next fixation. The race selects fixations on a fused top-down/bottom-up priority map from frozen vision models, with inhibition of return and an evidence bound on stopping. The full model fits sixteen parameters for target-present and target-absent search and twelve for free viewing. Eleven of the sixteen form nine factors with psychological readings. The accuracy cost is small. DGV reaches $94$--$98$ %of a leave-one-observer-out human ceiling on MultiMatch and $80$--$93$ %  on ScanMatch across four datasets, at most $0.076$ MultiMatch  below models trained end to end. Unlike them, DGV shows why each of its fixations is made: its top-down and bottom-up shares, the inhibition that discourages revisits and the rule that ends the trial. Only the evidence bound is recovered, from a group of images or even a single target-present one, and it carries most of the difference between target-present and target-absent search.
