To our knowledge, DGV is the first model coupling deep front-ends with psychologically named parameters across search and free viewing, and the first deep scanpath model to test its parameters for recovery.

TL;DR: A training-free, interpretable scanpath model unifies visual search and free viewing at 96–98% of the human ceiling, with sixteen psychological parameters whose identifiability is measured before they are interpreted.

Multivariate time series imputation remains challenging, especially under non-uniform missingness where observational completeness varies drastically across time periods and sensors.
Recent methods typically segment multivariate time series into patches and aggregate information across them without explicitly accounting for observational completeness. 
Consequently, dense self-attention can propagate information inferred from severely incomplete patches alongside those supported by more complete observations, degrading imputation accuracy.
In this paper, we propose RAMoE, a reliability-aware global mixture-of-experts framework with knowledge retrieval, which aims to improve multivariate time series imputation by limiting the influence of unreliable information while effectively exploiting reliable information.
To do this, RAMoE uses specialized experts to capture heterogeneous temporal patterns and computes reliability scores by combining routing probabilities with source-patch observational completeness.
To share expert knowledge across patches, RAMoE restructures the conventional route-compute-combine pipeline into extraction-consolidation-retrieval:
experts extract temporal prototypes from individual patches and consolidate them into a variable-specific knowledge pool. Reliability scores then bias attention toward more reliable prototypes during reconstruction.
Experiments on seven datasets show that RAMoE outperforms the compared baselines, with a 15.2\% relative reduction in average MSE across datasets over T1, the strongest baseline overall.
The code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/RAMoE-0960/}.

Indirect prompt injection in LLM agents is usually summarized by aggregate attack success rate, but this hides whether the same benign user tasks remain vulnerable when the attacker changes objectives. We ask whether task susceptibility is persistent: can risk estimated from previously observed malicious goals predict failures under a held-out goal? We introduce CASPER, a leave-one-malicious-goal-out measurement protocol that estimates a task-level susceptibility profile from observed goals and evaluates the frozen ranking on an unseen attacker objective. Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent, spanning GPT, Llama, and Qwen models, we observe consistent cross-goal persistence. In four primary settings, median Spearman correlations range from 0.602 to 0.682, all 74 evaluable held-out goals have positive association, and task-identity permutation tests reach the resolution floor of 10,000 permutations. This structure is not determined by aggregate attack success rate. Qwen3.6-27B retains a predictive task ranking at only 9.4\% ASR, while a MiniMax-M3 condition with 53.1\% ASR and substantial outcome variation shows little cross-goal alignment. Near floor and ceiling conditions can instead make the ranking statistically unidentifiable. Finally, historical task risk improves held-out failure coverage over random allocation under limited defense budgets. These results show that prompt-injection vulnerability can contain a persistent task-specific component across attacker objectives, and that measuring this structure provides information that aggregate ASR alone does not capture.

TL;DR: Prompt-injection vulnerability shows persistent but conditional task-level structure across unseen malicious goals, providing a useful signal for security prioritization.

Runtime safety shielding can keep a multi-agent system within physical constraints while still altering the behavioral cues produced by a learned policy. We study this proposal-to-execution mismatch as shield-induced intention distortion. IntentShield addresses the mismatch with a lexicographic execution procedure. Temporal safety is certified first, reward-competitive safe actions are retained next, and semantic fidelity is used only to rank the remaining candidates. Certified safety is therefore never exchanged for legibility. We evaluate the method in two cooperative particle environments with private goals using ten paired seeds, a matched reward-aware shield, mechanism ablations, noise-shift tests, and a leave-one-seed-out temporal observer drawn from a different model family. Relative to the matched reward-aware shield, IntentShield reduces in-distribution Jensen-Shannon proposal-to-execution distortion by $14.7%$ in Crossing and $16.7%$ in Bottleneck, while true-goal evidence loss decreases by $16.2%$ and $15.0%$. Mean hard-violation rates do not increase. Cross-fitted temporal observers recognize private goals above chance and independently reproduce lower semantic distortion in both in-distribution tasks. The effect also remains under a goal-oblivious ablation, whereas crossing under noise shift is inconclusive for the independent observer. These results support safety-compatible semantic repair in the evaluated settings, but they do not establish universal observer invariance or deployment-level safety.

TL;DR: Safety-first, reward-competitive runtime repair is shown to reduce proposal-to-execution distortion of private-goal evidence in two controlled MARL environments without increasing mean hard-violation rates.

Every day, people continuously infer situational context and adjust the way they understand and remember the world. Context, signaled by the prefrontal cortex, is known to modulate working memory and episodic memory, but the algorithmic understanding of this modulation remains limited. Here, we train a recurrent neural network (RNN), augmented with an episodic memory buffer, to infer context using Bayesian inference as it continuously makes predictions of upcoming scenes while watching naturalistic movies. When the inferred context modulates the RNN’s recurrent connectivity (the basis of working memory) in a low-rank manner, the model’s activity patterns best match neural responses in human participants who watched the same movies during fMRI. Context also modulates episodic memory retrieval, such that the model retrieves memories based on not only content similarity but also context similarity. This is implemented as a key-value system with self-attention, designed to explicitly encode context and retrieve context-congruent memories. The resulting model not only better resembles human brain representations but also learns to retrieve human-like memories much faster than a model without context modulation. Together, our findings suggest a computational mechanism by which context modulates information maintenance and long-term memory retrieval in naturalistic environments.

TL;DR: A brain-inspired architecture for context-dependent memory maintenance and retrieval

We study pixel-level localization of \moire{} patterns in digital photographs.
The task predicts a spatial artifact map beyond image-level detection. We
construct approximately 21,500 synthetic image--target pairs and develop two
architectures. \modeldual{} adapts an existing spatial--frequency demoireing
network to dense prediction, while \modeltriple{} adds a stationary wavelet
branch for localized frequency information. The three domains are combined
using Triple Dynamic Fusion with SimAM attention and a residual connection.
Both models are trained on the synthetic pairs under a common $L_2$ objective.
The triple-domain model reduces the best reported error from 0.0177 to 0.0143,
an improvement of approximately 19\%, and exhibits a smoother validation curve.
The predicted maps localize the artifact at pixel granularity, which is a
prerequisite for selective restoration and downstream quality assessment.

HiLiftAeroML is, to our knowledge, the first open high-fidelity computational fluid dynamics dataset dedicated to high-lift aircraft aerodynamics. It contains 1,800 simulations spanning 180 variants of the NASA Common Research Model high-lift configuration and ten angles of attack from $4^\circ$ to $22^\circ$. Each case was generated with a GPU-accelerated explicit wall-modeled large-eddy simulation approach on solution-adapted grids of 300--500 million cells, covering attached, separated, and post-stall flow conditions. Comparisons with wind-tunnel measurements for reference landing configurations show good agreement in integrated loads and sectional pressures, with grid adaptation substantially improving drag and pitching-moment predictions. The CC-BY-4.0 release includes geometries, time-averaged surface and volume fields, integrated loads, validation material, and deterministic benchmark splits. Initial GeoTransolver and Transolver baselines, evaluated on the complete native surface and volume support of every held-out case rather than on a sampled subset, reconstruct the fields well for several interpolation and held-out-geometry tests, while high-angle separated flow, limited-data training, and out-of-distribution flow-regime shifts remain substantially harder. The dataset and baselines provide a common resource for developing and assessing data-driven models for realistic high-lift aerodynamics.

TL;DR: HiLiftAeroML provides 1,800 high-fidelity simulations of high-lift aircraft aerodynamics and neural-operator benchmarks, showing strong interpolation and unseen-geometry prediction but challenges under data scarcity and flow-regime shifts.

Small molecule drugs often bind to proteins through unexpected rearrangements of protein pockets. These cryptic rearrangements are challenging to predict intuitively. Here we ask: Can protein conformation generators recover these cryptic binding pockets at the atomic scale? We introduce CrypticAtoms, a benchmark curated from 21 pairs of apo (unbound) and holo (bound) structures spanning 17 different proteins of diverse functionality. We evaluated conformational generators by scoring the heavy atoms of pocket residues that move between the apo and holo structures, thereby creating the chemical environment for small molecule binding. Accurate atomistic recovery of cryptic pockets requires that the generated pocket is more similar to the holo structure than the apo structure. Although AI-based methods show higher performance than non-AI controls, no method recovers more than 14 of 21 pairs, with just seven of those within 1 Å of the holo structure. Two of the 21 holo pockets remain unrecovered by every evaluated pipeline. Redocking the reference ligand to the generated pocket provides a complementary assessment of the sampled atomic environment, critical to structure-based drug design. Strikingly, most methods fail to reach a docking score commensurate with the reference holo conformation. Additionally, diversity metrics distinguish methods that concentrate their predictions near a particular conformation from those that explore the conformational landscape broadly. CrypticAtoms sets a standard for sampling cryptic pocket conformations at the atomic scale, and it demonstrates that the field has more work to do to accurately predict cryptic pockets.

TL;DR: An atomic-scale benchmark of cryptic protein pockets reveals strengths and gaps in current AI-based samplers’ ability to recover ligand-compatible geometry and diverse pocket states.

What is the geometry of a visual percept?
The most widely used protocols for decomposing neural network representations into interpretable parts treat concepts as isolated directions,
yet recent work shows that concepts are often realized as geometric structures in low dimensional regions of activation space. We turn to the literature of Structured sparsity to close this gap, and show that block sparsity, which groups directions into blocks, is the prior matched to a generative model in which a representation is a sparse sum of low-dimensional manifolds---the modern, learned form of a classical idea in visual neuroscience, where a visual feature is carried by a coordinated group of neurons rather than a single tuned one. We implement three variants of block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) and, through a minimum-description-length analysis, show that all three describe activations more compactly than direction-based featurizers, with the recovered concepts typically two- to four-dimensional.
We then use BSFs to (i) recontextualize prior work, showing that curve detectors in InceptionV1 actually read from a single continuous curve manifold, (ii) discover novel manifolds including shadows and lighting in DINOv3, and (iii) support interpretable control of image generation in diffusion models (SDXL) via manifold steering.

TL;DR: SAEs shatter concept manifolds into directions; block sparsity is the matched prior, and BSFs recover low-dimensional manifolds across vision models.

Cross-modal adversarial attacks—simultaneously perturbing image and text inputs—are often assumed to be strictly more dangerous than single-modality attacks. This paper challenges that assumption through a systematic study of adversarial synergy across eleven vision-language models (VLMs) spanning five architectural paradigms: dual-encoder (CLIP, SigLIP), ITM fusion (BLIP), unified
embedding-decoder (LLaVA), cross-attention bridge (BLIP-2, Qwen-VL), and unified transformer (Emu3, Janus-Pro, JanusFlow). A synergy metric measures whether joint cross-modal attacks exceed the sum of individual modality attacks, with a balance factor penalizing imbalanced contributions. The key finding overturns a natural assumption: deeper cross-modal fusion does not produce greater vulnerability. The earliest-fusion model (Emu3, shared embedding from layer one) is actually the most robust (synergy S = 0.125), while certain dual-encoder variants (SigLIP) show superadditive vulnerability (Sraw > 1). Architecture choice itself provides inherent robustness: unified transformers with shared embeddings create gradient competition (subadditive interference), while frozen-encoder architectures (Janus) eliminate cross-modal synergy by design. These findings directly inform the design of secure multimodal systems: shared-embedding or frozen-encoder designs are preferable when cross-modal attackrobustness is critical. The same architecture category can also produce opposite synergy patterns (Emu3 Sraw = 0.319 vs. Janus Sraw = 1.000), revealing that sub-architectural mechanisms dominate over macro-level categories. The proposed gradient channel framework explains these patterns theoretically and yields qualitative predictions for untested architectures.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have approached image segmentation by reasoning about visual content and predicting target locations. Their generated responses contain reasoning traces and localization proposals that can serve as working memory when revisiting the same image and query. Our exploration reveals that MLLMs benefit from using this self-generated working memory as context, leading to enhanced reasoning segmentation. Motivated by this finding, we seek to strengthen the backbone model's reasoning segmentation capabilities by distilling the guidance gained from revisiting prior attempts, enabling it to benefit with or without working memory at inference time. To this end, we propose Reasoning Segmenter with Working Memory (SWiM), a working-memory distillation framework for reasoning segmentation. Specifically, SWiM selects rollouts based on segmentation quality to construct working memory and uses the memory-conditioned model as a teacher. The teacher provides token-level distributional supervision along student-generated trajectories, while the student receives only the original image and query. Joint optimization of on-policy self-distillation and outcome-based reinforcement learning combines working-memory guidance with direct feedback on segmentation quality. Extensive experiments on reasoning segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that SWiM achieves state-of-the-art performance, validating the effectiveness of working-memory distillation. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SWiM-0310.

Deep learning models are used to forecast traffic accident risk, but their robustness to adversarial attacks remains underexplored. Such attacks could cause high-risk regions to be predicted as low-risk, potentially leading to missed warnings. Existing attack methods for images and continuous-valued traffic forecasting do not directly apply to accident records, which contain many zeros and take discrete, non-negative values. We propose Adversarial Attack and Defense for Traffic Accident Prediction Models (AAD-TAPM). Its attack method selects a small set of spatial nodes using historical accident risk and model saliency, then draws replacement accident-risk values from a distribution fitted to historical records. For defense, we retrain the forecasting model on these adversarial samples. When 10% of nodes are perturbed, our attack yields lower Recall@K and MAP than adapted PGD- and MIM-based methods on the NYC and Chicago datasets. On the NYC dataset, our defense yields lower RMSE than conventional adversarial training and Mixup under five PGD-based attacks.

Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) tend to entangle target evidence with background context, and existing background-suppression methods typically rely on task-specific architectures or introduce additional parameters and inference cost. To alleviate this, we propose RDCNet, a general background-suppression framework built on Reconfigurable Differential Convolution (RDC), which enhances the network with paired positive and negative branches during training while introducing no additional deployment overhead at inference. Specifically, during training, the two branches are optimized to be functionally complementary: the positive branch learns target-oriented responses while the negative branch learns context responses to be suppressed, and their responses are combined through a pre-coupled differential operator before shared normalization and activation, so that target evidence is enhanced while background activations are canceled. Besides, a spatial complementary loss penalizes co-activation of the two branches at the same locations, requiring no pixel-level foreground masks or extra annotations. During inference, the compatible branch convolutions are algebraically fused into a single standard convolution, so the deployed network exactly recovers the baseline topology, parameter count, and FLOPs. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, MS-COCO, and PASCAL VOC show that RDCNet consistently improves on top of VGG, ResNet, ResNeXt, and YOLO backbones. RDC-VGG16 improves top-1 accuracy by 1.80, 3.32, and 3.89 percentage points on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1K, respectively. RDC-ResNet50 reaches 78.60% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K (+2.61 points), while RDC improves CIFAR-100 accuracy by 1.26, 4.97, and 3.07 points on ResNet50, ResNet56, and ResNeXt-29, respectively. For detection, RDC-YOLOv5s improves mAP@0.5 by 3.0 and 4.1 points on MS-COCO and PASCAL VOC, respectively, without increasing the deployed parameter count.

TL;DR: RDCNet trains CNNs with paired positive (target) and negative (context) branches that are algebraically fused into the original single-branch network after training, achieving background suppression with zero additional inference cost.

Autonomous scientific discovery requires learning systems that can choose experiments, observe their outcomes, and use those observations to decide what to test next. In conventional small-molecule discovery, however, synthesis and experimental testing limit each design cycle to a relatively small and local set of compounds, making rapid exploration of large chemical spaces difficult. Most molecular machine-learning methods are therefore developed and evaluated on static datasets that abstract away this experimental loop. We introduce ATLAS, a real-world active-learning environment for small-molecule discovery connecting a synthesizable space $>10^8$ molecules to automated nanoscale synthesis, direct-to-biology screening, and higher-fidelity follow-up assays. ATLAS supports model-selected batches of $10^3$–$10^4$ compounds on 2-3 week experimental cycles, increasing the breadth of each design cycle by orders of magnitude while providing a closed loop between model decisions and experimental feedback. We demonstrate this environment in evaluating two distinct models and policies, targeted at hit discovery and expansion, and at multi-parameter hit optimization.

TL;DR: ATLAS is a real-world closed-loop active-learning environment for drug discovery, linking >10⁸ synthesizable molecules to experiments and enabling agents to improve hit discovery and potency-selectivity optimization.

Automatic differentiation has enabled rapid progress on continuous-variable mechanical design problems, but gradient-based optimization still struggles with optimization involving discrete variables. The standard approach is to optimize using a continuous relaxation of the choices, then commit to a discrete design at the end. Why this procedure selects unfavorable basins is poorly understood. Here, we introduce a practical design problem inspired by origami, where automatic differentiation is used to design shapes with a target functional behavior. Each origami sheet has a fixed geometry, and a bilevel optimization framework tunes which one of four discrete hinge types to place at each fold. Baseline gradient-based design settles into basins with a large discretization gap: relaxed optimization solves 94% of runs, but the final, discrete solutions succeed only half the time. We find that the gap can be relieved with a surprisingly simple modification. An initialization prior uniformly biased toward the stiff, flat hinge option boosts the final solve rate from 53% to 74%. Applying the prior adds no additional compute and leaves the optimization process unchanged. Compared to the baseline, sheets produced with the prior have greater geometric compatibility and mechanical stiffness. Thus, a simple intervention can move the search to a new loss basin that has physically interpretable signatures and soft solutions more robust to discretization. Though the prior's effect is robust, its identity is fragile. We test other priors with similar characteristics, including one that matches ours at over 90% of the hinges, and they all fail to reproduce the gap-narrowing effect. Our work raises two new questions: when does a discrete design problem have favorable basins accessible via initialization priors, and how can the most effective priors be found?

When a neural network predicts a physical system accurately, has it learned the governing physical law, and if so, does the network's internal computation actually use that law throughout its domain of validity? To answer these questions, we develop a mechanistic interpretability framework that uses counterfactual perturbations over physical variables and a coverage-aware causal-consistency measure to test whether model behavior satisfies the relationships and invariances prescribed by a specified physical law, whether this consistency can be localized to an internal circuit, and whether law-relevant variables are accessible within that circuit and contribute causally to that consistency. We illustrate the framework on a MoCap-to-Radar spatio-temporal transformer model, evaluating whether it learns to simulate the Doppler law, \(f_{d}=\frac{2v^\mathrm{rad}}{\lambda}\), from motion-capture and radar data in which neither \(f_{d}\) nor \(v^{\mathrm{rad}}\) is directly provided. We show that the model's consistency with the law, including the expected radial velocity dependence and tangential velocity invariance, can be causally attributed to a small circuit composed mainly of temporal attention heads, with \(v^{\mathrm{rad}}\) becoming accessible after temporal attention and then contributing causally to the consistency.

TL;DR: We develop an interpretability framework that enables physics-grounded counterfactuals to test whether a physical law is used. On a radar-synthesis transformer, we localize its consistency with the Doppler law and analyze the mechanism supporting it.

Emotion recognition in natural language plays an important role in affective computing and human--computer interaction, yet the co-occurrence structure among emotion categories remains underexplored by existing discriminative models, and how to encode such structure into interpretable latent representations remains an open problem. To address this, we first analyze GoEmotions using Non-negative Matrix Factorization, revealing interpretable emotion modules supported by visualization and community analysis. Building on these findings, we propose an NMF-guided Sparse Variational Autoencoder (NMF-SVAE) for structured emotion representation learning. Each latent dimension is anchored to a data-driven emotion module through a frozen NMF-initialized decoder, while an $\ell_1$ sparsity constraint and an alignment objective encourage selective and interpretable latent activations. Unlike prior structured VAEs that rely on fixed psychological dimensions such as Valence-Arousal-Dominance, NMF-SVAE derives its latent structure directly from data, allowing emotion modules to adapt to fine-grained category distributions. The pretrained encoder is integrated into a RoBERTa-Large classifier via head-wise gated fusion, enabling structured affective knowledge to transfer to new label spaces without retraining the NMF-SVAE encoder. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of NMF-SVAE, which achieves the best F1 on five datasets and the best Recall on six.

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard recipe for improving the reasoning ability of large language models, but its training time is dominated by generating long reasoning rollouts. Serving rollouts in low precision offers a direct speedup, yet low-precision RL training often plateaus below its BF16 counterpart due to an amplified training–inference mismatch: the trainer and rollout engine can assign different probabilities to the same tokens even under identical weights, making nominally on-policy training effectively off-policy. In this paper, we revisit the clipped objective under this mismatch and identify a fundamental failure mode. The mismatch not only mis-scales the importance weight but also displaces the clipping gate that enforces the trust region, silently excluding tokens that should contribute to learning, and existing importance-sampling corrections repair the weight but cannot restore the excluded tokens. We therefore propose Factorized Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (FISPO), which rebuilds the objective under the distribution that actually generates the rollouts: it replaces the keep-or-discard gate with a saturating factorized importance weight on every token, bounding the policy ratio against optimization drift and the mismatch ratio against engine noise. Under FP8 and MXFP8 rollouts, FISPO recovers the reward and accuracy of the BF16 reference across four mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

TL;DR: Low-precision rollouts amplify the training–inference mismatch, which displaces the clipping gate of PPO-style objectives. FISPO rebuilds the gate and bounds a factorized importance weight, recovering BF16 accuracy at FP8 rollout speed.

Analyzing classroom teaching behavior provides teachers with data-driven feedback for optimizing instructional design, yet existing recognition research mostly analyzes teachers or students in isolation, relies on a single modality, and fuses multi-source data with naive strategies. We present CIBNet, a multimodal fusion network that recognizes seven categories of classroom interactive behavior from synchronized video and audio. The visual branch, CIBNet-V, couples a spatial reconstruction unit that suppresses redundant
background with a temporal focus unit that highlights key frames. The audio branch, CIBNet-A, encodes log-Mel spectrograms and their dynamic derivatives with a multi-scale attention module. A multi-level modal fusion strategy then routes complementary evidence between the two modalities through gated bidirectional cross-attention units at four depths, guarded by a joint unimodal-constrained loss against
evidence degradation. We also construct MMCIB, a multimodal classroom interactive behavior dataset of 1,509 samples. CIBNet achieves 0.915 accuracy on MMCIB, out performing the video-only (0.839) and audio-only (0.736) branches and all baselines.

TL;DR: It presents CIBNet, a multimodal fusion network that recognizes automatically categories of classroom interactive behavior from synchronized video and audio.

Traditional sleep-staging methods primarily pursue higher accuracy through increasingly capable models, applying the same model to every EEG epoch regardless of difficulty. Such uniform deployment expends computation on epochs that a smaller model could handle reliably, motivating cascades in which a primary classifier accepts its reliable predictions and defers the remainder to a more capable model. In this paper, we study the first stage of such a cascade: maximizing the coverage of fixed primary predictions subject to a prescribed accepted-risk target. We propose COVER (COVerage-oriented Error Ranking), which integrates two key innovations: (i) auxiliary-informed primary-error learning, which replaces maximum softmax probability (MSP) with a learned error score while preserving the primary labels, and (ii) fixed-scale scorer refinement, which builds on this score to directly maximize coverage under an empirical accepted-risk constraint rather than error-prediction accuracy over all epochs. We evaluate COVER on Sleep-EDF-20 at a 5% accepted-risk target, with subjects held out from all fitting and selection. Auxiliary-informed error learning raises mean subject coverage from 31.5% for MSP to 48.8% at similar subject-equal risk. At equal acceptance volume, with MSP accepting the same number of epochs as the learned scorer in each subject (20,639 in total), errors fall from 1,467 to 867. Fixed-scale refinement then adds 1.7 percentage points of coverage over its initialization in nested development, and COVER attains the highest mean coverage among eight evaluated scorers, 50.4% at 4.5% subject-equal risk, above the selective-ranking baseline SELE (49.3%) and the probability-fusion comparator DuoF (43.6%). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to combine auxiliary-informed primary-error learning with fixed-scale coverage refinement for selective sleep staging, offering a basis for reliability-aware allocation of computation in cascaded sleep staging.

TL;DR: COVER learns where a fixed sleep-staging classifier errs from primary and auxiliary outputs, then refines this score to maximize coverage under an accepted-risk target, raising subject coverage from 31.5% (MSP) to 50.4% on Sleep-EDF-20.

World models can be studied as experimental systems with response laws of
their own. We introduce MultiEcho, a framework for estimating these laws
through controlled counterfactual interventions, delimiting their applicability,
and separately testing their physical correspondence. Across nine simulated
physical systems and seven frozen model configurations, three-reference
estimators predict complete intervention responses and recover intervention
parameters. Estimator selection uses discovery data only; frozen fits are
evaluated on validation and confirmation contexts. The experiments distinguish
response predictability, intervention readability and physical accuracy.
Responses can be locally describable yet poorly match physical effects
in the same target coordinates. Event-window, visibility and camera interventions
reveal conditional applicability, and paired generator configurations show reduced
readability under a scene prompt with stronger guidance. Magnitude sweeps expose
small image errors alongside large relative effect errors. An exact-reset
material experiment separates registered visible-response success from fixed-readout
failure on material-dependent futures at matched positions and velocities.
Exact finite-scale identities resolve odd and even response errors; first-order
remainder bounds specify when refined calibration converges. MultiEcho provides
an experimental basis for studying learned-world laws independently of, and in
relation to, physical laws.

TL;DR: MultiEcho uses controlled counterfactual experiments to characterize learned worlds’ own response laws, where they hold, and how they correspond to physical reality.

Clinical CT and UHRCT cannot resolve individual trabeculae, whereas synchrotron radiation microCT (SR$\mu$CT) provides 3.2~$\mu$m high-resolution references but is not applicable for in vivo imaging. The two domains differ by $31.25\times$ in resolution, are only coarsely paired, and have drastically different data volumes. Moreover, clinical UHRCT suffers from severe partial volume effects, strong noise, and beam hardening/scatter artifacts, while SR$\mu$CT is nearly free of these. Existing super-resolution networks and pretrained-prior methods (GLEAN/StyleGAN2, Stable SR/LDM) underperform because they target pixel generation---diverse details and SSIM/PSNR---and do not explicitly model these physical differences. This indicates that $32\times$ super-resolution via pixel generation is intrinsically ill-posed. We propose a paradigm shift from pixel generation to topological inference: deterministically predicting invariant microstructures from macro-scale low-resolution inputs, evaluated by morphological parameters. We realize this paradigm via structural dual super-resolution, coupling forward physical degradation (micro-to-macro) with inverse structural inference (macro-to-micro) through structural duality constraints. The method is an end-to-end, few-shot, compact structural dual network (SDN), comprising a bidirectional modeling network for forward degradation and inverse reconstruction, a pyramid structural consistency discriminator, and four structural duality constraints. On the test set, SDN achieves morphological parameters largely consistent with SR$\mu$CT across six metrics, enabling clinical UHRCT (e.g. BV/TV 0.3793  228\% error, Tb.Th 357.2$\mu$m 4793\% error) with micro-imaging-level morphological quantification (BV/TV 0.1156 vs 0.1163, Tb.Th 7.3$\mu$m vs 10$\mu$m), with SSIM reaching 0.8. Trained on 3.2 $\mu$m SSRF data, the model generalizes well to 3.25 $\mu$m isotropic BSRF data from an independent source, validating cross-source generalization and confirming that the designed network achieves trustworthy structural inference rather than pixel generation.

Reusable skills help coding agents complete recurring work more consistently, but retaining task history can preserve a successful strategy after the conditions that justified it have changed. We study Skill-Template-Induced Context Collapse (STICC) as a skill-conditioned form of context contamination in which repeated skill invocation and persistent write-back cause previously valid strategies to override contradictory current-task evidence. To study this problem, we construct controlled sequences of related but non-identical coding tasks, in which early tasks establish a recurring repair strategy and later strategy-reversal tasks require the agent to abandon it. We independently vary repeated skill injection and context persistence in a prespecified $2 \times 2$ factorial design. The completed evaluation covers 40 controlled tasks across four task families, 13 counter-pattern tasks, and three counter-pattern placement regimes, totaling 3,840 episodes. In the prespecified primary experiment, retaining history increases failure much more when the skill is present than when it is absent, yielding a +25.0 percentage-point interaction. This pattern appears across task families and task orders. Blind matched-history attribution links 16 of 24 Skill + Persistent failures to historical override, and removing the implicated spans lowers counter-pattern failure from 66.7% to 44.4%. A complementary seven-task experiment reduces failures from 6/7 under Persistent Context to 0/7 under Scoped Cleanup. These results support stale-history removal as a mitigation principle, while human review shows that the current automatic gate cannot reliably trigger such cleanup by itself.

TL;DR: Stale histories from repeated reusable-skill invocation can override current-task evidence in coding agents, while removing the implicated history substantially reduces context-collapse failures.

Training-free token merging reduces the cost of pretrained Vision Transformers
(ViTs), but sequence-wide matching creates quadratic candidate sets and
globally indexed merge plans that add planning and execution overhead. We
introduce Structured Token Merging (STM), which co-designs merge selection and
execution through bounded window-local groups. STM orders patch tokens along a
Hilbert curve; within each window, it chooses the token with the lowest
class (CLS) token-to-key compatibility as
the destination and scores every other token only against that destination. A
global top-$r$ over all window-local candidates then allocates the fixed merge
budget adaptively across the image. This converts candidate construction from
quadratic to linear and yields conflict-free, bounded reduction groups. These
structured groups enable a fused window-granular kernel that combines weighted
merging with residual addition and LayerNorm while writing the compacted
sequence directly, avoiding separate global gather--scatter and normalization
passes. STM also propagates an effective token-size state used by both weighted
aggregation and proportional attention. Under aggressive repeated merging,
STM applies an order-preserving nonlinear companding rule that controls the
concentration of this state across layers. STM achieves up to a $1.91\times$
model-forward throughput speedup over the unmerged ViT-L/16 backbone at
$384\times384$. Across COCO retrieval, SigLIP2 zero-shot recognition, and
YOLOS object detection, STM retains task performance without retraining,
spanning retrieval, classification, and detection settings.

The growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs) drive interest in low-latency edge inference, where quantization is essential. 
While weight-only quantization is widely used on mobile devices, maximizing NPU integer compute efficiency necessitates quantizing activations as well. Achieving this is challenging, as dynamic scaling handles heavy-tailed distributions at the cost of runtime latency, whereas traditional static quantization suffers from severe accuracy loss. To resolve this dilemma, we present FIRON, a fully static, integer-only quantization framework co-designed with an NPU backend for efficient and accurate end-to-end LLM inference.  FIRON jointly learns offline-foldable rotations and static quantization scales, and allocates INT16 to the heavy-tailed SwiGLU output, so that inference requires neither online rotations nor runtime scale estimation. On the systems side, our NPU backend keeps the entire Transformer block in integer arithmetic on the NPU: a scale-aware radix-256 decomposition maps INT16 activations onto native low-bit matrix engines, and a fused, layout-aware execution path leaves no standalone conversion pass. Across four Qwen3 and Llama-3.2 models, FIRON outperforms state-of-the-art quantization methods while staying near-lossless with an average perplexity gap of about 1.0 on WikiText-2 and C4 and an average accuracy drop of 0.8 percentage points on six zero-shot tasks relative to BF16. On a Qualcomm Snapdragon SM8750 NPU, it achieves 1.75--3.00$\times$ prefill and 2.59--3.73$\times$ decode speedups over FP16 NPU execution and 7.93--18.78$\times$ prefill speedups over CPU, and 1.14--12.53$\times$ and 2.10--5.24$\times$ the energy efficiency of CPU and floating-point NPU baselines across prefill and decode.

Contrastive Language Image Pre-training (CLIP), which allows visual features to be compared with text describing normal and abnormal states, enable using category names as identifiers to construct text prompts. However, for visual anomaly detection these identifiers may be unavailable or confidential. This paper provides a novel Privacy-aware Prompting CLIP (PP-CLIP) framework that replaces explicit category-name inputs with image-conditioned latent prompts while retaining normal/abnormal text cues. A learnable prior branch supplies context to a frozen visual encoder, and an output-level fusion produces condition text to be embedded on the image. PP-CLIP is trained on a public Visual Anomaly (VisA) dataset and evaluated across industrial and medical benchmarks without target-domain adaptation. Experiments show that PP-CLIP achieves competitive performance compared with five counterpart methods and reaches average image-level and pixel-level AUROCs of 94.2% and 94.1% on five industrial targets. Results vary by dataset and metric, but all demonstrate that PP-CLIP can retain useful detection and localization can be retained without category-name inputs.

Serving a large language model (LLM) across a fleet of deployments requires several weight-precision operating points. Multi-precision formats serve them all from one stream whose prefixes are valid lower-precision codes, instead of storing multiple copies. We present StagQ, a multi-precision weight format whose main stream is a 2-bit group-wise affine base followed by a configurable number of 1-bit refinement planes on a dyadic step schedule. Every supported precision is a readable prefix, decoded by an affine map derived from metadata shared across all precisions, with no per-weight lookup. A sparse side record, filled both before and after the grid is fitted, holds out the few weights the grid serves worst. We report two configurations of the encoder. At two bits the cheaper one leads the strongest multi-precision baseline on Llama-3.1-8B, Phi-4 and OLMo-2-7B by 3.1 to 6.8 MMLU points, at a slightly lower logical rate. At three bits it leads on Llama-3.1-8B, leads on Phi-4 at a higher rate, and ties on OLMo-2-7B. At four bits it ties on all three, at a higher rate. In a batch-one matrix–vector product on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, timed on synthetic weights, our kernel is faster than the two baseline kernels in most shape–precision cases.

TL;DR: A multi-precision weight format in which every precision is a directly readable prefix that can be efficiently decoded by the same affine map; it beats the strongest multi-precision baseline at two and three bits, usually at a lower rate.

ESG events propagate through directed heterogeneous financial networks in a stepwise manner, with the core task of situation awareness being to deduce the complete evolutionary trajectory across micro, meso, and macro levels from an initial sparse excitation. Existing graph neural networks typically overlook the inherent delays in directed propagation, while conventional propagation models rely predominantly on homogeneous mixing assumptions, exhibiting notable deficiencies in characterizing gradual node responses. This paper proposes the Directed Information Propagation Graph Neural Network (DIPGNN), which systematically addresses the above challenges from three dimensions. In the spatial dimension, cross-correlation vectors within the pre-event window are employed as edge embeddings, embedding steady-state propagation delays as structural priors into the graph. In the state dimension, the classical three-state formulation is extended to six states, with early-exposed and late-exposed states introduced to distinguish "signal reception" from "expectation adjustment," and a defunct state is incorporated to mark nodes that exit the propagation chain due to liquidity depletion. In the evolutionary dimension, a contrastive "excitation–inhibition" driving force replaces the fixed propagation rate, with the transition matrix dynamically generated at each time step from node latent states and global situational context via a lightweight MLP, enabling environment-adaptive non-homogeneous propagation. The model simultaneously outputs microscopic expectation indices, mesoscopic propagation matrices, and macroscopic diffusion indices. On two real-world datasets, DIPGNN reduces macro-level errors by over 19\% relative to the optimal baseline, achieves average early warning of high-risk states by 4.1 days, identifies liquidity-depleted nodes 3.2 days in advance with a false positive rate below 7\%, and ablation experiments validate the synergistic necessity of each core design component.

TL;DR: This paper proposes DIPGNN, which integrates directed heterogeneous financial graphs, six-state propagation dynamics, and excitation-inhibition-driven non-homogeneous transitions to trace ESG shock evolution across micro, meso, and macro levels.

Reproducing a physics paper is one way to examine an AI system's ability to solve scientific problems. Turning its theory into numerical calculations requires a sequence of reasoning, and mishandling any step can still yield a convincing figure. Existing benchmarks give the solver the full paper, leaving the target results exposed. A figure match alone, therefore, does not guarantee that the reasoning behind it was right. Thus, we propose a protocol for auditing whether a paper was faithfully reproduced. A physicist selects one figure from each of 60 papers. We mask the target figures and provide conditions to reproduce them. An automated evaluator checks each run against criteria drawn from physics practice. To see whether problem-solving ability improves, we also rerun each task with the governing equations and symbol definitions. Only 10.8 % of runs passed all criteria. With the equations and symbol definitions, the solver identified the correct physical model more often. Yet most runs still failed to reproduce the target figure. Also, repeated attempts with feedback corrected implementation errors but not these failures. Pass rates, furthermore, fell as a paper's theory became more abstract. The physicist then reviewed both failing and passing runs and found that the solver introduced shortcut methods the paper never states, which the automated evaluator missed. The weakness lies in the reasoning that turns a theory into a calculation. Evaluating an AI system means asking not only whether its result looks right but also whether the reasoning behind it is sound. Looking right is not being right.

TL;DR: We audit the reasoning behind an LLM solver's reproduction of a physics paper, not just whether the result matches. Looking right is not being right.

Empirical studies in asset pricing indicate that the impact of market events on asset prices propagates along the correlation structure in a discontinuous, pulse-like decaying manner—information intensity diminishes exponentially with graph distance, and the propagation speed shifts dynamically with market regimes. However, existing graph neural networks model information as continuous, smooth diffusion over graphs, which not only contradicts the above empirical regularities but also introduces redundant per-time-step updates during event-sparse intervals. This paper proposes the Event-driven Spiking Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (ESHGNN), a framework for temporal graph modeling tasks involving multiple relation types and sparse event inputs, with asset pricing as the primary validation scenario. Specifically, the multiple inter-asset correlations are decomposed into three orthogonal dimensions—fundamentals, tail risk, and attention—whose dominance is adaptively modulated by macro-state-driven coordination weights. Node dynamics are constructed using leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons, where both the time constant and the firing threshold are sensitive to market volatility and exhibit an antagonistic synergy that maintains a bounded signal-to-noise ratio in high-volatility regimes. A state-adaptive graph convolution reweights node structural centrality via spike activation levels, enabling event-driven influence redistribution. Theoretical analysis establishes the model's permutation equivariance, bounded membrane potential, and exponential decay of information diffusion. In empirical evaluations covering complete bull-bear cycles of the CSI-300 and S&P-500, the proposed method achieves predictive accuracy and portfolio returns significantly superior to baselines, with effective update steps accounting for only 18.7% and a 5.5× speedup over the optimal dynamic baseline.

TL;DR: This paper proposes ESHGNN, which decomposes asset relations into fundamental, tail-risk, and attention channels, models event shocks as LIF-driven spiking propagation, and enables state-adaptive influence reallocation for asset pricing.

Interactive text-to-SQL systems often fail after syntax and schema checks have succeeded: the query counts the wrong entity, applies the wrong time basis, or silently multiplies rows across one-to-many joins. We introduce evidence-bound query contracts , a versioned interface that links result-changing decisions to visible evidence and compiles supported decisions into finite SQL obligations. Admission is three-valued---pass, fail, or unknown---and later turns modify the contract through explicit patches rather than unconstrained regeneration.
We evaluate the idea at three levels. First, an audit of saved interactive runs shows that static validity is a weak proxy for task success: two 20-task pilots produce 12 and 15 statically valid candidates, but only 5 and 1 evaluator matches. Second, on 34 controlled SQL variants, the checker rejects all seven targeted, result-changing counterexamples, accepts all six supported correct controls, and returns unknown on 21 variants outside its analyzed subset. A 36-database multiplicity sweep further isolates the need to aggregate two one-to-many sources before joining. Third, a post-hoc 43-task shared-tool stress test reveals the cost of narrow coverage: the revised hard gate completes 0 tasks, versus 4 and 5 in reused reference and soft-contract runs, and rejects 12 of 13 diagnostically matching submission attempts. On the constructed supported cases, finite checks make no observed admission error; on broader SQL, hard gating is useful only when checker coverage is measured and expanded. Risk--coverage, contract readiness, and update preservation should therefore be reported alongside end-to-end accuracy for interactive text-to-SQL systems.

TL;DR: Evidence-bound query contracts turn justified user decisions into versioned SQL checks. They catch targeted semantic errors, but a 43-task stress test shows narrow hard gates reject 12/13 evaluator-matching candidates.

Dynamic scene reconstruction with 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) is constrained on edge hardware by offline Structure-from-Motion (COLMAP) preprocessing and the high memory and computational cost of 4D Gaussian optimization. We present C2C4DGS (Camera-to-Canvas 4D Gaussian Splatting), an edge-efficient, SfM-free stereo 4DGS framework enabling complete Camera-to-Canvas execution on embedded devices with stationary dual-camera rigs. By replacing offline SfM point-cloud generation with a hardware-calibrated stereo epipolar prior and compressing spatiotemporal dynamics using a compact 4D multiresolution hash grid with Degree-1 Spherical Harmonics, C2C4DGS substantially reduces memory use while eliminating offline SfM overhead. On a server GPU, it reduces end-to-end processing time from 158 to 23.4 minutes, achieving a $6.8\times$ speedup from raw video to rendered output. The framework also supports monocular configurations for compatibility with standard benchmarks and enables complete on-device training and rendering on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano with 8 GB physical memory through NVMe-backed virtual memory paging. Under identical conditions, existing 4DGS baselines immediately encounter out-of-memory failures, whereas C2C4DGS achieves stable, OOM-free end-to-end execution on the edge platform.

TL;DR: We introduce a lightweight, dual-mode 4D Gaussian Splatting framework optimized for dynamic neural rendering on both high-performance server GPUs and memory-constrained embedded edge hardware.

Chinese firms now supply open-weight models, cloud regions, network equipment, and platforms across Southeast Asia, yet the region's AI rules do not look Chinese. We ask whether governance travels with AI artifacts and answer with an audit built so that it can also detect transfer. The audit separates a low-friction capacity channel from a high-friction institutional channel, distinguishes an exporter's outreach operating from its succeeding, and codes adoption on six indicators (statutory-text lineage, regulator form, standards anchoring, governance-club membership, official discourse, and embedded de facto governance) under an explicit codebook. We apply it to four corridor states (Singapore, Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines) and to Cambodia as a most-likely-transfer counter-case, against capacity documented in 48 engagements across nine Southeast-Asian states and a release of Singapore's national model built on a Chinese open-weight base. The finding is component-wise. Although China's governance outreach is under way, no corridor state has adopted an algorithm-filing regime, a security-ministry AI content regulator, or a "core socialist values" content mandate; under the baseline rule, the only full Chinese-model codes in the 30-cell matrix belong to Cambodia and rest on an instrument that predates China's October 2023 governance-export push; and sovereignty and localization appear as congruent local design, with Vietnam's AI law (December 2025), the region's first standalone binding AI statute, taking a risk-based form. We extend the audit to the artifact layer by tracing licences and use policies along base-to-derivative lineages of Southeast-Asian open-weight models. Because an audit instrument must itself be audited, we report agreement with an independent second coder, re-code the matrix under a permissive rule that counts untraceable congruence as adoption, and release the codebook, per-cell evidence, and dataset. We close with a dated 2028 prediction, leading indicators, and a re-run protocol.

TL;DR: Chinese AI capacity spans Southeast Asia's stack, yet no corridor state has adopted China's content-control governance model; a reliability-tested, multi-layer audit shows where transfer is absent and where it is at most partial.

Activation checkpointing removes most resident intermediate states, but it must retain the full-sequence hidden states between recomputed blocks. These interfaces can become the remaining batch-dependent activation bottleneck. Compressing a broader set of tensors saves bytes, but also exposes more backward operators to approximation. We instead ask where approximation has the highest memory leverage and the smallest optimization surface. This leads to Residual-Corrected Checkpoint Activation Compression (ResCAC), which compresses only checkpoint interfaces and stores each as a packed row-wise 4-bit approximation plus a packed 4-bit correction of its residual. This design leaves parameters, optimizer states, and intra-block recomputation unchanged. The motivating ablation is decisive: compared with plain 4-bit interface compression, residual correction reduces trajectory error by 99.08% and validation degradation by 98.97%, while changing peak-memory saving by only 0.13 percentage points. Across three 1,000-step Qwen2.5-0.5B runs, ResCAC reduces peak memory by 18.24% at 1.058× checkpoint runtime, with a mean validation-loss difference of +0.000012. Under a shared 8-bit-optimizer protocol, it increases the largest sustained feasible batch by 52.5% at 1.5B parameters and 69.9% at 3B. These results support a bounded principle for checkpointed decoder-only language models: concentrate approximation
at recomputation interfaces, then explicitly correct the error that would otherwise accumulate.

TL;DR: ResCAC reduces the memory cost of activation checkpointing by compressing retained checkpoint interfaces with low-bit quantization and correcting reconstruction errors with a compact residual.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) often learn high-frequency components more slowly than low-frequency ones, while evaluating PDE residuals with automatic differentiation (AD) can require costly coordinate-derivative graphs, particularly for higher-order and high-dimensional problems. We introduce KAW-PINN, an explicit spectral physics-informed model that combines finite trigonometric maps with a non-tensor compositional structure motivated by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation. The spectral maps expose frequency content and enable analytical coordinate differentiation through closed-form trigonometric derivatives and chain-rule composition, while standard backpropagation is retained for parameter optimization. For multiple physical fields, KAW-PINN shares coordinate-wise spectral primitives and learns output-conditioned mixtures before output-specific decoding. In 1D Poisson tests, combinations of the finite harmonic dictionary accurately approximate tested off-grid frequencies, while an out-of-range case exposes the finite-support limit. For a 2D Poisson problem on a perforated domain, analytical differentiation maintains the accuracy of an isomorphic AD implementation while reducing training time by 57.2% and peak allocated memory by 53.0%. For a manufactured 10D incompressible Stokes problem, KAW-PINN attains a joint relative $L_2$ error of 0.03668 under parameter-matched comparisons, compared with 0.34777 for a multilayer-perceptron PINN (MLP-PINN) and 0.23227 for a Fourier-feature PINN (FF-PINN); ablations identify output-conditioned aggregation as the main source of the multi-field improvement. These results support explicit spectral structure as a unified design for high-frequency representation, efficient PDE differentiation, and high-dimensional multi-field composition.

TL;DR: KAW-PINN combines explicit spectral Kolmogorov-Arnold structure with analytical coordinate derivatives to improve high-frequency PDE representation, reduce residual-evaluation cost, and support high-dimensional multi-field learning.

Feedforward reconstruction of dynamic driving scenes requires integrating observations across multiple views and time steps into a coherent 3D representation. PointForward established state-of-the-art feedforward driving reconstruction by lifting image observations into sparse 3D queries, demonstrating the effectiveness of point-aligned scene representations. However, these queries are largely processed independently, limiting information exchange across space and time, while direct global attention among tens of thousands of point queries is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we present $\textbf{PointForward V2}$, which advances point-aligned representation to point-aligned interaction. Our key idea is to mediate query interaction through compact, scene-structured registers. For the static background, frame-wise Static Scene Registers compress point information, communicate across frames, and propagate the aggregated context back to the queries. For each dynamic instance, queries from different frames are aligned in an object-centric canonical space and interact through instance-specific Dynamic Instance Registers. We further employ 4D positional encoding that combines aligned spatial coordinates with original timestamps, enabling spatially aligned yet temporally distinguishable interactions. In this way, PointForward V2 enables scalable spatio-temporal reasoning directly among lifted 3D queries without dense global attention. Experiments on Waymo, nuScenes, and Argoverse 2 demonstrate state-of-the-art reconstruction performance across large-scale driving benchmarks.

Knowledge distillation trains a student network to imitate a trained teacher, and later methods let the student also learn from the teacher's internal activations. A deployed classifier, however, is usually frozen, so its internal features stay fixed and only the final layer that turns them into class predictions can be replaced. That layer is trained once with the rest of the network and never revisited, so nothing measures how much useful information in the features it ignores. This paper introduces such a measure, the readout gap, defined as the extra test accuracy a better final layer reaches while the rest of the network stays unchanged. To estimate it, the network becomes its own teacher, and signals distilled from it, such as its output scores, confidence and activations, train a small, inexpensive classifier that replaces the final layer. Ten combinations of these signals are compared on six benchmark datasets and 11 network families. The gap is positive for 46 of the 47 network-dataset pairs and never negative. It grows as the original layer weakens and peaks in binarized networks, where even that layer's weights take only two values. Almost all of it comes from the network's own signals, so it reflects information the original layer ignores, not a benefit of extra models or rescaled scores. Hence one configuration chosen only on other datasets improves 39 of the 47 pairs at little extra cost, so the readout gap should be measured on any frozen classifier before the decision to retrain it.

TL;DR: We measure the readout gap, the accuracy a frozen representation supports beyond its own decision layer, by pointing knowledge distillation back at its own teacher so the model that improves is the one distilled from.

How can we verify whose music contributed to an AI-generated output?
This paper demonstrates how input-based attribution can provide verifiable evidence of which audio sources were used in a generation and whether they shaped the output. To do so, we condition the generation solely on audio without any text input, then trace the inputs behind each output, and establish their musical effect. In prompt adherence tests and controlled input swaps, the stems generated by our generator, Euterpe, follow the prompt audio in timbre and the context audio in harmony. Yet these outputs may still reproduce training data not supplied as inputs. We therefore audit memorization with our musical version identification model, Argus, and find few reproductions outside the input records. On human-judged cases within the flagged pool, it achieves higher precision and recall than the other tested memorization detectors. The two evaluations suggest that input records and output analysis provide complementary evidence for attribution, on which rights-holder reporting and compensation can draw as the AI music economy takes shape.

Audio examples are available at https://iclr2027.github.io/

Position encoding provides multimodal language models with structural information about text and visual inputs. A central challenge is to distinguish visual entities and preserve their local geometry without conflating these relations with text sequence positions. 
We propose \emph{\textbf{G}auge-\textbf{I}nvariant \textbf{R}elation \textbf{F}ields} (\textbf{GIRF}) for cross-modal position encoding. GIRF constructs cross-modal rotary phases from a relation field that explicitly separates local text order, visual entity identity, and within-entity spatiotemporal geometry, while retaining the base positional encoding for text--text and vision--vision attention. This separation distinguishes which visual entity a token belongs to from where it lies within that entity. The relation field is invariant to shifts in text-segment and image-grid coordinate origins, while preserving entity order and local visual structure. To address the decreasing separation between bounded entity coordinates in long multi-image sequences, GIRF introduces a resolution gate that progressively incorporates relative image-origin phases into text-to-vision attention. This correction supplements the relation field with inter-image positional information and remains invariant to a common shift of image origins. The gate and its reference images are determined entirely by the causal input structure, without target-image annotations or answer-dependent routing. Together, these components encode complementary aspects of cross-modal position through rotary phases, leaving content projections and attention normalization unchanged.

Simple remedies for a failed document parse—switching parsers, resampling the page, adding margins, or suppressing ruling lines—can recover missing content while corrupting facts that were already correct. Aggregate accuracy hides this trade-off. We cast intervention selection as paired, action-specific prediction of quality gain, newly introduced damage, and execution cost. Our framework, Evidence-Preserving Interventions (EPI), enumerates candidate actions offline, selects at most one action from the original input and base parse, and uses a post-action gate to accept the candidate or roll back to the base output. The gate family also supports finite-sample calibration of conditional source-group damage. We evaluate EPI with deployed parsing services and a 200-source controlled geometry matrix containing 3,600 successful action calls. On 150 source-disjoint test groups, the frozen EPI gate gains 0.0530 diagnostic loss (paired bootstrap 95% interval [0.0435, 0.0626]) at an extra-call fraction of 0.538 and records zero harmful active groups among 68 observed active test groups. The corresponding one-sided 95% exact upper limit is 0.0431, so this is an empirical zero-event result rather
than a zero-risk claim. The eight-group calibration split cannot satisfy the protocol’s minimum of 30 active groups and therefore returns the base policy by design. These results support selective intervention under controlled raster perturbations; formal calibration and transfer to public documents remain open.

TL;DR: EPI learns which document-parsing intervention to run and whether to roll it back by modeling gain, new damage, and cost; it improves diagnostic loss by 0.0530 at a 0.538 extra-call fraction, with 0/68 harmful active test groups observed.

In a mixed-reality assisted surgical environment, surgeons need to interact naturally with virtual environments and robotic systems while maintaining sterile operations. However, complex surgical scenes, cluttered visual backgrounds, and the limited informativeness of unimodal inputs make reliable interaction-intent recognition difficult and the cost of collecting and annotating medical interaction data is high, making it difficult to obtain large-scale training data. How to fully utilize the complementary information between images and text under limited sample conditions to achieve stable and scalable multimodal intent understanding is a key issue in mixed reality surgical interaction. To address these challenges, we propose \textbf{QueryBind}, a CLIP-based method for few-shot multimodal intent understanding that jointly models instance-level text and gesture images.We introduce a Cross-modal Binding Fusion (CBF) module to integrate textual semantics and gesture-based visual cues. Through lightweight modality adaptation, multiplicative interaction, cross-modal discrepancy modeling, and constrained residual fusion, CBF captures the agreement, discrepancy, and complementarity between the two modalities, producing a unified and discriminative multimodal representation. To improve prototype-based classification under limited supervision, QueryBind regularizes the prototype geometry during episodic training and refines the support prototypes according to query--prototype compatibility at inference time. This refinement requires neither gradient updates nor encoder adaptation.

TL;DR: A multimodal intent recognition framework MTFusion for small sample mixed reality surgical interaction
