Serving a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model pays for expert precision twice: the resident footprint pays for every expert the router can reach, while each batch-one decode step pays only for the experts it selects. These are two different rate functionals over the same per-expert widths, yet published per-expert MoE allocators constrain only the first. We call the difference the store–read gap; in the released BitsMoE checkpoint, 2.54 bits per weight (bpw) of storage become 7.50 bpw of decode traffic. We propose DuoRate, which stores once and reads per workload. Offline, it stores one uniform tier of a prefix-readable weight stream and bakes a distortion tensor. Online, it profiles a workload's own prefill without labels and solves a Lagrangian rate–distortion allocation under the decode functional; routing frequency provably cancels from every per-expert decision, and the solve costs one dot product per expert and a bisection. A deployment therefore keeps a single artifact that prefill reads at the stored rate and decode reads at the workload's own rate. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, DuoRate reading 2.3 bpw exceeds every 2-bit-class baseline by 6.3 to 47.0 points of average accuracy, and at 2.9 bpw it matches 4-bit formats that read 1.4–1.7 bpw more. The advantage is largest under long decoding: on GSM8K, DuoRate at 2.9 bpw matches or exceeds every 4-bit format and trails BF16 by only 0.25 points, and at 2.6 bpw it still matches or exceeds the 4.5-bit NF4 and FP4. Against controls in its own format, the allocation alone is worth 0.07–0.11 bpw of read rate. Code will be released upon publication.

TL;DR: MoE serving pays for expert precision twice: once in storage, once per decode step. DuoRate stores one tier and reads a per-workload prefix chosen by label-free rate–distortion allocation, matching 4-bit accuracy at 2.9 bpw read.

Dynamic graph anomaly detection (DGAD) flags abnormal edges in evolving networks, such as network intrusions and online fraud. Existing detectors either learn what an anomaly is from real graphs or encode it in fixed rules. However, simple anomaly signals change meaning across graphs: the same signal ranks anomalies above normal edges on some graphs and below them on others. A new graph also has no labels, so a frozen detector must infer from its unlabeled context which evidence to trust. We propose StreamPFN, a prior-fitted detector trained only on synthetic event streams. First, a synthetic prior generates normal processes, labeled anomalies, benign patterns that resemble them and varied recording conventions, and lets some attacks begin in the unlabeled prefix of a stream. Then, a graph-agnostic encoding describes each edge by its relations to recent edges and by relative time scales, so one transformer can score graphs it has never seen. Finally, a parameter-free gate compares an edge with the prefix when an attack dominates its recent history. On fourteen datasets, StreamPFN has the highest zero-shot AUROC on every dataset. On the seven datasets with real anomalies it averages 85.6%, compared with 59.9% for the best published baseline. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/StreamPFN-DE6D/.

TL;DR: A detector trained only on synthetic event streams and applied frozen, zero-shot, beats detectors trained on real graphs on recorded anomalies; injection benchmarks mainly measure knowledge of the injection procedure.

Training with exact conservation projection can make an autoregressive PDE surrogate depend on that projection at inference. The projected objective leaves the raw invariant component undetermined; without projection, this component can affect later conserving predictions. We cross output coordinates, training projection and inference projection in an eight-cell design. In a 30-seed FNO Advection study, the three-way interaction in conserving RMSE is $0.22974$ [$0.19644$, $0.26345$] and exceeds the prespecified material threshold in 9/12 resolution--horizon cells. An independent 30-seed shallow-water FNO study finds material interactions in 6/8 cells. Training and inference credits nearly cancel in the bundled comparison. A same-checkpoint input intervention shows that changes along the invariant input direction affect conserving predictions. The native-grid U-Net result remains unresolved. Projection changes need rollout evaluation even when one-step conserving error is unchanged.

TL;DR: Training and inference projection interact in autoregressive FNO rollouts; an eight-cell design separates this dependence from output-coordinate effects.

A key challenge in scaling multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) to hundreds of agents is the credit assignment under the curse of dimensionality. Existing credit assignment methods either fail to scale to large populations or provide only heuristic guidance without formal guarantees. To address this gap, we propose Shapley Mean-Field Q Value (SMFQV), a theoretical framework for large-scale credit assignment. We prove that SMFQV admits a decomposition into the expectation of an individual contribution plus coalition-weighted action advantage, with an approximation error that shrinks with the number of agents, which formally justifies why the mean-field approximation becomes essentially free at scale. We further establish the existence of a mean-field equilibrium (MFE) and show that any MFE constitutes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium of the finite-population game, with $\varepsilon$ vanishing as the population grows. For practical estimation, we analyze the generalization error of the Shapley Mean-Field Approximate Marginal Contribution (SMFAMC) estimator and establish a bias–variance decomposition with a $K^{-1/2}$ convergence rate. From an algorithmic perspective, we develop two policy gradient methods: SMF-MADDPG and SMF-MAPPO. Experiments on team-reward symmetric against scenarios with up to 288 agents demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve surprising performance and remain remarkably robust as the number of agents grows. Code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SMFMARL-5888}.

Evaluating claim admission in shared agent memory is challenging because repeated claims may be mistaken for independent evidence. An agent may copy or paraphrase a retrieved belief, while admitting a false claim exposes subsequent agents to it. To study this problem, we introduce the Correlated Promotion Benchmark (CPB), which evaluates whether candidate claims should be admitted to shared memory.CPB-Static constructs a frozen test split from publicly annotated sources with fixed gold actions. CPB-Live runs multi-agent teams over a shared store, records all writes and retrievals, and tracks source lineage defined by each scenario. A separate consumer answers from the store alone. We evaluate eight admission policies across four agent families. Our results show that policies which deduplicate sources reject many true claims alongside false ones, whereas policies preserving answer coverage admit nearly as many false claims as unrestricted sharing. A rule gating on declared source type lowers false adoption to 0.06–0.09 in this scenario mix, with correctness of 0.58–0.65. Its protection fails when a reworded false copy is typed authoritative. Given one uncontested false memory and no external evidence, consumers assert it in 0.97–0.99 of probes. CPB separates dependence from truth and shows how admission decisions affect later answers under controlled, synthetic conditions. Code is available at \url{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/iclr_2027-3194}.

Effective rule retrieval must recognize not only what a clause is about, but when it applies. Cross-encoder rerankers model fine-grained query–clause interactions, yet introduce candidate-specific computation at retrieval time. We introduce RuleDistill, a framework for transferring condition-sensitive ranking into a single-vector retriever. Its central idea is to distill not only a document preference, but how that preference changes when an applicability condition changes. RuleDistill constructs controlled query–clause quadruples, selects teacher-supported preference reversals through bidirectional filtering, and learns their mixed four-score contrast. This contrast removes additive query and document offsets and directly supervises the interaction between changes in their embeddings. Integrated with listwise distillation, directional supervision, and representation preservation, the framework couples boundary discrimination with retention of ordinary retrieval quality. Experiments span five English and Chinese rule-retrieval sources and a bilingual executable rule collection. On 240 held-out-template development pairs, RuleDistill improves joint boundary accuracy over matched independent-margin regression by 3.75, 7.08, and 2.50 percentage points for models trained on OR-ShARC, DAPR-ConditionalQA, and SLARD, respectively, while meeting fixed retrieval-retention criteria. The resulting model requires one query encoding, one stored vector per clause, and no online reranker. RuleDistill thus brings interaction-based supervision into the simplicity of single-vector retrieval.

TL;DR: RuleDistill distills condition-sensitive preference reversals from a cross-encoder into a single-vector retriever through controlled query–clause quadruples, enabling applicability-aware rule retrieval without online reranking.

Embodied agent systems increasingly use a hierarchical architecture: a high-level vision-language model (VLM) planner selects semantic subgoals, and a low-level vision-language-action (VLA) policy generates action chunks. To reduce onboard compute and power use, a local GPU pool is often used to serve both models for a robot fleet. Each robot requires planner calls to select subgoals and policy calls throughout subgoal execution. Planner delay can postpone the next subgoal and policy delay can slow action updates, but their effect on task success changes as the task progresses. Contact-rich manipulation, for instance, is timing-critical because a delayed update can cause failure, whereas free-space motion often tolerates the same delay. Existing embodied serving systems set fixed service-level objectives (SLOs) for planner latency and policy update rate, sized for timing-critical phases. However, applying these SLOs in delay-tolerant phases wastes GPU capacity and limits how many robots the pool can serve.

We introduce Tempo, a phase-aware serving system that schedules work according to its predicted effect on task success rather than fixed SLOs. At runtime, Tempo estimates each robot's current execution phase and scores every candidate planner and policy decision by its predicted task-success loss, using phase profiles calibrated once per policy and task suite. This common currency enables phase multiplexing: because robots reach timing-critical phases at different times, Tempo shifts GPU capacity from robots in delay-tolerant phases to robots for which additional service prevents the most loss. We evaluate Tempo on LIBERO, CALVIN, and SimplerEnv with three VLA policies, serving up to 128 concurrent robots on eight GPUs. At 128 robots, Tempo outperforms the strongest baseline on every benchmark, improving task success by 34.4--44.6 percentage points.

Temporal Knowledge Graph (TKG) representation learning captures structural dependencies and temporal evolution for event prediction. A tool-using agent can complement representation-based predictions by assessing historical support for competing candidates and using reliable feedback to guide further learning. This integration presents two challenges. First, historical events exhibit heterogeneous relevance across relation queries. Second, context-dependent prediction feedback may not provide transferable supervision. To address these challenges, we propose an $\mathbf{A}$gent-enhanced $\mathbf{T}$emporal Knowledge Graph $\mathbf{R}$epresentation learning framework with hierarchical $\mathbf{M}$emory ($\mathbf{ATRM}$). Specifically, hierarchical TKG memory organizes the historical TKG into interaction, configuration, and regularity memory at increasing levels of abstraction. A conflict-aware tool-use mechanism combines candidate-specific historical support with representation-based scores to refine relation rankings. We further introduce cross-snapshot LLM-guided process distillation, which employs an offline LLM to select relation-confusion anchors from historical prediction traces. Anchors validated on later graph snapshots provide context-conditioned ranking constraints for further TKG representation learning, with no LLM calls required during inference. Comprehensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that ATRM achieves average relative improvements of 4.42%, 7.26%, 4.99%, and 1.19% over the runner-up in MRR, Hits@1, Hits@3, and Hits@10, respectively.

Sparse LiDAR regions of interest (RoIs) mix a few target returns with background and neighboring objects. Aligning a pooled descriptor with object references can therefore regularize context as well as the target. We propose ShapeSieve, which selects local evidence before privileged alignment. A shared encoder represents proposal-relative points and bird's-eye-view statistics; separate targetness and class-compatibility scores define an evidence distribution. The selected representation is aligned with observed training objects and refines the native RoI feature through a gated residual update. References are used only during training, and inference requires a single LiDAR scan. On Waymo, the complete multi-class detector achieves 74.61% Vehicle Level 2 AP and 74.28% APH. With track references fixed, selected alignment improves Level 2 AP by 0.56 percentage points over uniform alignment and AP beyond 50 m by 1.37 points. KITTI experiments also separate the complete multi-class model from a Car-only variant with alignment disabled. The deployed query path adds 0.34 million parameters and 8 ms to a 195 ms host on an RTX 3090. These results support selecting the representation on which privileged supervision acts.

TL;DR: ShapeSieve selects target-relevant LiDAR evidence before training-only reference alignment and uses the same evidence for gated RoI refinement.

Fixed-horizon action anticipation is usually specified by a nominal horizon
and a sampling grid. Together, they specify the intended decision time and
sampled feature positions, but not the latest raw observation that can
influence the reported score. We call the latter the effective temporal
information boundary. It can change through three implementation choices:
Support, Dependency, and Readout (S/D/R).

Our formal result establishes that, even with a fixed nominal horizon and
sampling grid, the effective information boundary cannot in general be
recovered without S, D, and R. Once the contract is specified, compliance
reduces to reachability.
This gives an exact characterization and a linear-time static checker: exact
annotations recover the structural verdict, while conservative annotations
provide a sound compliance certificate.

The distinction is measurable in controlled experiments. On EK100, changing
only the evaluated state of the same checkpoint and forward pass changes Verb
Top-1 by $+6.57\pm0.29$ points (95\% t-CI $[6.21,6.93]$), while direct
target-action overlap remains zero. This is a counterfactual readout of our controlled GRU,
not a re-evaluation of a published system's official score. Prefix-preserving
interventions confirm that the exposed models use post-cutoff features. On
AFFT's released causal GPT-2 future predictor, removing only the temporal mask
changes the logits on $99.9\%$ of validation samples but produces no Top-1
action flips. A controlled Transformer trained
on the same grid provides a complementary non-recurrent probe: zeroing
post-cutoff inputs changes $59.7\%$ of Top-1 predictions when the horizon
readout can attend to them, versus exactly $0.0\%$ under a causal mask, across
five seeds in a controlled probe on pre-extracted features. Support is illustrated with a
released RU-LSTM flow configuration whose audited support extends $0.05$\,s
beyond the nominal boundary under the reconstructed preprocessing alignment.
A seven-family audit shows which temporal contracts can be fully reconstructed,
only partially certified, or still require source-level inspection.

TL;DR: A fixed anticipation horizon does not uniquely determine a model's effective temporal information boundary; we formalize the missing Support/Dependency/Readout contract and provide a static checker with controlled and released-model evidence.

Reinforcement learning has emerged as a promising approach for improving LLM agents on long-horizon search tasks, where agents make numerous intermediate decisions to reach the desired outcome. These steps vary in importance: some are critical, decisively influencing subsequent progress and even task success, while others are trivial, with little impact on what follows. However, existing RL methods fail to distinguish critical steps from trivial ones. This can bias policy learning, causing agents to over-reinforce inconsequential steps while under-learning from those that critically shape future outcomes,  resulting in suboptimal policies with redundant tool use.
To address this issue, we introduce CAPO, a criticality-aware agentic RL framework that measures the criticality of each step through its counterfactual influence on future outcomes, and uses this measure to adapt the learning emphasis across steps. Through a probing analysis, we observe that agent hidden representations encode such counterfactual influence, enabling us to develop a lightweight criticality probe. For critical steps identified by the probe, we estimate their step-level rewards by comparing alternative branches from the same prefix, while upweighting them in policy optimization. For trivial steps, we downweight their contributions to policy optimization, reducing the reinforcement of low-impact behaviors.
By learning more from critical steps and less from trivial ones, our framework improves the effectiveness and efficiency of long horizon agent learning. Experiments across four challenging benchmarks show that our method improves task success by 7.2% over the strongest baseline, while reducing redundant tool use by 15.2%.

Agentic capabilities have become a central dimension of large language models (LLMs), enabling their application to complex real-world tasks. However, existing agentic evaluations are typically designed around multi-turn interaction and dynamic execution, making it difficult to directly assess the agentic capabilities of pretrained base models. To address this gap, we introduce SWE-BaseBench, a benchmark derived from SWE-Bench Pro for evaluating pretrained base models. SWE-BaseBench focuses on three representative capabilities that are central to real coding-agent workflows:  repository localization, tool call, and reflection.For each capability, we extract representative scenarios from real-world coding-agent trajectories and transform them into static tasks suitable for evaluating pretrained models, thereby enabling evaluation without executing the full agent interaction.We then systematically evaluated 11 recently released open-weight base models. Our results reveal substantial variation across capability dimensions, highlighting the distinct strengths and limitations of each model. More importantly, model performance rankings on SWE-BaseBench exhibit a strong rank correlation with the performance of their corresponding post-trained models on SWE-Bench Pro. These findings indicate that SWE-BaseBench can serve as an informative early-stage evaluation signal for diagnosing and systematically comparing base-model capabilities during LLM development. More broadly, its construction paradigm provides a reusable methodological framework for deriving base-model-compatible evaluations of agentic capabilities from real-world agent workflows.

TL;DR: SWE-BaseBench reconstructs real coding-agent decision contexts as static tasks to evaluate the coding-agent potential of base models before post-training.

Test-time adaptation (TTA) methods for time-series forecasting update a deployed model, or a small adapter around it, from incoming ground truth. However, the label for an H-step forecast does not exist until H steps after the forecast is made, and real data pipelines add further delay before it can be used. We build a leakage-free evaluation harness in which the label of forecast origin s becomes available for updates only at step s+d with d ≥ H, and we enforce this rule inside the released code of four recent TTA methods (TAFAS, COSA, PETSA and DynaTTA), run on their own backbones and checkpoints across five standard benchmarks (ETTm1, ETTh2, Weather, Electricity and Traffic). As reference points we add two closed-form correctors: a bank of recursive least squares (RLS) filters combined by a per-coordinate median, with no tunable hyperparameters and a cost of 56 microseconds per step on the 7-channel streams, and an ELF-style linear corrector. Under causal delayed labels the picture is asymmetric, and we report it as such. On ETTm1 every audited method genuinely adapts, yet the RLS bank still beats three of the four at a small fraction of their cost; only DynaTTA beats the bank, only at the minimum causal delay, and at roughly 2,500 times the per-update cost; the ELF-style corrector beats all four. On the other four datasets, the largest statistically significant improvement any published method achieves over its own frozen checkpoint is half a percent, on all four at least one published method is significantly worse than the frozen model at the minimum causal delay, and on drift-heavy ETTh2 longer label delays make every adapter that separates from the frozen model, ours included, significantly harmful. We also show that next-step (leaky) updates inflate the apparent gains of simple adapters by up to 110 percent, and that the backbone training recipe moves frozen online error by up to a factor of 25, more than any adaptation effect we measure. We release the harness, the integration patches and all cached runs.

TL;DR: Under causal, delayed label release enforced in four published TTA methods' own code, closed-form correctors match or beat them on four of five benchmarks at a fraction of the cost; leaky updates and backbone recipes move error more than adaptation.

Video-language models with full-history softmax attention accumulate a growing video key-value cache, making sustained processing of unbounded streams costly. We present LinearMem, a vision-language architecture that decouples video-memory updates from language modeling. Its video branch replaces the video cache with fixed-size Gated DeltaNet (GDN) states, while its language branch retains standard softmax attention over language tokens. An exact decomposition of teacher attention motivates a learned per-layer, per-head gate that combines video-memory reads with language self-attention through convex fusion. Attention-operator distillation trains the memory and its readouts, followed by fusion training and joint adaptation to teacher logits. For fixed model dimensions and bounded input chunks, ingesting $n$ video tokens requires $O(n)$ total time and $O(1)$ video-state storage; querying the stored video memory costs $O(1)$ with respect to $n$. Single-layer measurements confirm the predicted scaling. Distilled from Qwen2.5-VL-7B on captioning sequences without question-answering (QA) fine-tuning, LinearMem retains 80.0--94.3\% of teacher accuracy across five QA benchmarks and 95.4--115.7\% of teacher METEOR on two captioning benchmarks. Memory probes further show that action and needle information can remain decodable even when language answering deteriorates. These results establish an efficient video-memory interface while identifying a gap between information stored in recurrent memory and its use in language generation.
We publicly release the code and trained model weights.

TL;DR: LinearMem decouples video memory from language modeling through distilled linear attention memory module, enabling video-stream processing in linear time with constant video-memory usage.

Mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation faces two practical difficulties: sparse annotations and domain shifts caused by scanners, centers, and acquisition protocols. MedSAM provides a strong semantic prior when labels are limited, whereas conventional task models adapt readily to source data but may encode anatomical structure together with domain-dependent appearance. We propose SynFoM, which couples MedSAM with an anatomy-style disentanglement branch. Instead of the neural mutual-information estimator used in MI-SegNet, SynFoM minimizes a Wasserstein dependence objective between the joint anatomy-style distribution and the product of its marginals. A gradient-penalized 1-Lipschitz critic supplies the discrepancy signal, while image reconstruction preserves complementary information across the two representations. On six public prostate-MRI domains, SynFoM reaches 87.88% average Dice, compared with 86.89% for SynFoC, and reduces HD95 from 14.51 to 7.60. On four liver-CT datasets, average Dice increases from 84.94% to 86.71% and average HD95 decreases from 30.26 to 20.70; Dice reaches 90.29% on the unseen 3D-IRCADb-01 dataset. The clearest gains are in boundary localization.

TL;DR: SynFoM couples MedSAM with an anatomy-style disentangled model and minimizes Wasserstein dependence between anatomy and style representations for robust mixed-domain semi-supervised medical image segmentation.

A single observation can admit several plausible futures, making uncertainty
an essential part of world modelling. However, quantum generative models
remain underexplored for this task. We introduce Quantum-JEPA, a latent-action
JEPA framework that learns distributions of future representations using a
conditional quantum Born prior. Circuit measurements generate binary latent
actions, which a shared predictor maps to alternative future representations.
We train the quantum prior through the quality and diversity of these
predictions using a sampled energy objective. On constructed datasets with
multimodal futures, our model learns distinct continuations for the same observation.
The entangled prior learns correlations between latent-action bits that
support coordinated futures across multiple agents.
With correlated classical and quantum prior implementations, our sampled learning
mechanism improves prediction validity and distributional fidelity over the
evaluated variational baselines. Within this framework, the quantum
prior combines competitive predictive performance with a compact
parameterization under finite-shot training with readout noise.
Unlike prior work only focusing on simulation, we also verify the feasibility
of inference with trained priors on a real QPU.
These results establish a
trainable quantum component for JEPA future prediction and a basis for
exploring quantum-enhanced world models at larger scales.

TL;DR: Quantum-JEPA uses a conditional quantum Born prior to learn latent actions for multimodal future prediction in JEPA world models.

Topology Adaptive Graph Convolutional Networks define convolution in the vertex domain. As, it uses fixed-size learnable filters that adapt to the graph topology. TAGCN have accuracy limitations when higher filter size than two is opted. In this paper, we have proposed TAGII, an extension of TAGCN which simply extends vanilla TAGCN by adding a teleport probability in the convolution formula. The teleport term has been drawn from the Personalized PageRank scheme of APPNP. The same idea was later adopted as the initial residual in GCNII. At every step of message passing, it mixes a controllable fraction of the original node features and preserves local feature identity and reduces over-smoothing. It keeps the multi-hop power of the original topology-adaptive filters. TAGII needs no spectral approximation. The additional computational overhead is almost negligible. Experiments conducted on standard node classification datasets clearly demonstrate improved performance over the baseline TAGCN. It has also shown competitive performance when compared with recent deep graph convolutional models.

Agent memory is essential for personalized e-commerce agents to reuse
user preferences and constraints across interactions. However, existing
benchmarks primarily evaluate downstream responses or task outcomes,
making it difficult to isolate the quality of the memory itself. We
introduce \textbf{QMemBench}, a benchmark for directly evaluating
\emph{query-conditioned agent memory} in personalized e-commerce. Built
from de-identified real-world order histories and queries from a
large-scale instant-retail platform, the benchmark evaluates whether a
memory system serves information that is both historically supported and
relevant to the current query. Each instance is paired with a
query-specific target memory, enabling multi-level evaluation at the
parameter, semantic, slot, and preference-dimension levels. Experiments
across five agent memory systems and reference baselines reveal
substantial differences across systems, evaluation levels, and
preference dimensions. We further validate the benchmark in a real-world
production setting using an independently developed production-side
memory evaluation protocol. Together, these results establish
\textbf{QMemBench} as a direct and practically grounded
evaluation framework for agent memory in personalized e-commerce.

Model scaling and generational advances improve overall medical capability, but the gains remain uneven. Capability gaps narrow as base models evolve, while deficits in specialized knowledge and deeper capabilities persist. Medical post-training therefore remains necessary, with the objective shifting from broadly adding medical data to injecting valuable new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Therefore, we introduce Cross-Document Aggregation for Medical Knowledge Injection (CAMKI). First, CAMKI aggregates hierarchical content from multiple medical sources into an extensible and interpretable medical knowledge space with traceable and enumerable combinations, enabling efficient discovery of potentially valuable knowledge from source materials. Second, it provides a configurable knowledge-tree mining pipeline in which mining conditions and traversal topologies control evidence organization, sample generation, and verification. Third, CAMKI provides a medical knowledge injection framework that enables base models to acquire source-supported knowledge through post-training. The full CAMKI pipeline improves model performance across a range of medical benchmarks.

TL;DR: CAMKI builds a traceable knowledge tree from medical sources, mines verified training examples, and injects source-supported knowledge into base models improving performance across medical benchmarks.

Recovering a digital microstructure satisfying targetted physico-chemical properties is an ill-posed inverse problem. The structure to property mapping is inherently many-to-one, and multiple parameter sets can satisfy the same target descriptors. A useful generative model for this setting must therefore sample the equivalence class of valid solutions rather than recover a single reference. this requirement renders standard evaluation protocols, such as pixel parity and parameter parity, inadequate. We introduce a classifier free guided diffusion model, conditioned via FiLM and cross attention on scalar physico chemical descriptors and on the two-point autocorrelation profile, that generates diverse 2D projections of porous catalyst support microstructures from target properties alone. A companion regression network, trained on the diverse outputs of the diffusion model, extracts underlying aggregation parameters from any generated microstructure. To assess physical consistency without collapsing generative diversity, we adopt a round-trip evaluation protocol. Generated microstructures are inverted to parameters, simulated again by a reference physical model, and compared to the original targets at the level of physico chemical descriptors. Trained on 30,000 synthetic microstructures generated via a parametric COX point process, the pipeline produces microstructures with simulated again descriptors matching the targets, including cases where retrieved parameters differ from the reference set. It is the expected signature of a well behaved generative model in a many-to-one inverse setting. This framework provides a physically consistent AI driven alternative to traditional optimization for microstructure design.

TL;DR: A property-guided diffusion model generates digital multi-scale porous microstructures matching target morphological properties and recovers their underlying aggregation parameters, solving the inverse materials-design problem.

Concept bottleneck models make their decisions interpretable and intervenable by predicting human-understandable concepts. However, under concept substitution tests, removed concepts are still predicted as present, and substituted-in concepts go undetected. As a result, the explanations and interventions these models offer point to dataset priors rather than the actual evidence in the image. We trace this failure to two gaps. First, pooling collapses the whole image into one global vector from which all concepts are read. Second, both the training signal and the decision rule are tuned for class discrimination rather than for deciding whether a concept exists. We further find, counterintuitively, that in a scan of concept readout heads, frozen random queries outperform every pooled head tested. Leveraging this insight, we introduce Spatially Grounded and Existence-Calibrated Concept Bottleneck Models (SEC-CBM). On the readout side, each concept reads evidence from a local region of the image with weights given by its own frozen text query. On the decision side, existence calibration adjusts both the training signal and the decision thresholds, so that concept scores again reflect what is actually present in the image. Experiments show that SEC-CBM simultaneously improves over the strongest prior method in both directions of the substitution test while achieving comparable classification accuracy.

TL;DR: We trace the two-sided failure of concept bottleneck models under attribute substitution to two distinct gaps and close both, yielding the first CBM to outperform the strongest baseline in both directions at negligible accuracy cost.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models trained on large-scale human demonstrations achieve strong performance in general-purpose robot control. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training can further improve such policies from environment feedback, yet updating the entire model is costly, and this cost is paid in full regardless of whether that many parameters are actually needed. We ask whether parameter-efficient RL post-training can match full-parameter RL. We keep the supervised backbone frozen and learn a compact set of low-rank residuals that exactly preserve the supervised policy at initialization and are conditionally composed according to the current representation. Under matched experimental conditions, a single policy post-trained this way across many tasks matches full-parameter RL while updating only a small fraction of the model's parameters. Controlled comparisons show that the initialization and the conditional composition, rather than the number of trainable parameters, determine adaptation quality. We further find that the parameter-efficient policy and full-parameter RL follow different learning paths and that RL does not reorganize the routing by task, yet the parameter-efficient policy still reaches comparable performance, which supports parameter efficiency as a practical direction for scaling multi-task robot learning.

TL;DR: Multi-task RL post-training of VLAs does not need full-parameter updates: routed, zero-initialized low-rank residuals match full RL with 32x fewer trainable parameters , making parameter-efficient RL a practical way to scale VLA post-training.

Consumer-grade wearable devices continuously capture physiological and behavioural signals, offering opportunities for health prediction at scale, yet downstream health labels are often scarce. This motivates self-supervised learning (SSL) in wearable time series, which can leverage large amounts of unlabeled wearable data. Minute-level heart rate and step count are commonly available from consumer wearables, yet it remains unclear whether these two signals alone can support self-supervised representation learning for multi-day health prediction. Many existing approaches predominantly rely on raw sensor signals or proprietary collections of derived features, limiting their accessibility, reproducibility, and applicability to general wearable cohorts. To fill this gap, we introduce PaceMAE, a lightweight $\sim$0.4M parameter day-level masked autoencoder that augments signal reconstruction with auxiliary prediction of patch-level statistics.  Using 2.2 million person-days of Fitbit recordings from the All of Us Research Program, we pretrain on heart rate and step count and aggregate daily representations across seven-day windows for downstream prediction. We evaluate PaceMAE on five demographic and clinical tasks. Relative to reconstruction-only pretraining, PaceMAE increases ER-visit AUROC from 0.60 to 0.65 and reduces age mean absolute error from 10.18 to 8.80 years (13.6\% improvement). It achieves better test performance than an aggregate-feature XGBoost baseline on all five tasks and a supervised baseline on four. In a frozen-encoder comparison, it yields higher point estimates than general-purpose time series foundation model MOMENT on four tasks, including approximately 0.10 higher AUROC for both clinical outcomes. Together, these results show that self-supervised learning at scale from only minute-level heart rate and step count can yield informative representations for a range of downstream health-related prediction tasks, enabling a more accessible approach to wearable-based health prediction.

When does predicting layer-skipping decisions one step ahead pay? We measure a predictive FFN router, PRESAGE, against dense decoding, the same checkpoint routed in-layer, and fixed layer placements on three 7–9B backbones, under eager, device-side and compiled execution. Its eager gain over in-layer routing (1.09–1.17×) is entirely the removal of one host synchronisation per layer: once gates stay on the device, the two decision locations are within 2%. Against dense, compiled skipping wins only on a bandwidth-bound RTX 3090 at batch 1 (1.10–1.21×, of which 1.05–1.15× is skipping and the rest its kernels) and loses on an H100 (0.83–0.90×). One point, Llama skip-4, clears pre-specified stability, quality and speed gates, with or without prediction (quality on GSM8K test against the adapted parent, after an audit found 863/1,000 training problems verbatim in the fine-tuning corpus); the threshold controller collapses at lower keeps. A fixed profile band matches predictive quality on Llama and Gemma, and statically pruning Llama's band matches it at comparable speed (1.09× against 1.11× dense) with no router at all; per-token selection beats the band only on Qwen, where it still fails the quality gate against its adapted parent.

TL;DR: A measurement study of predictive layer skipping: the eager gain over in-layer routing is host-synchronisation removal, device-side paths agree within 2%, and the one point that clears pre-specified gates does so with or without prediction.

Predicting marine debris transport in complex coastal waters is challenging and typically requires hydrodynamic simulation followed by particle tracking. We incorporate tidal periodicity and wind information into Multi-Marginal Flow Matching (MMFM) to learn tide- and wind-driven transport dynamics from particle trajectories, without direct velocity-field supervision or prescribed tidal harmonic constants.
Reference debris trajectories are generated through Lagrangian particle tracking using currents simulated by a two-dimensional hydrodynamic model driven by realistic tidal and wind forcing over 1980–2023, while accounting for wind effects on debris motion. We focus on an interior region with reduced influence from coastal boundaries and topographic variability. Four configurations are compared: no explicit tidal or wind information, temporal features at the M2 (the principal lunar semidiurnal tide)  frequency, features at multiple major tidal frequencies, and these features combined with wind-vector inputs. Evaluation includes trajectory RMSE, spatial error distributions, and agreement between the learned and reference debris transport velocity fields.
Expanding the tidal features beyond M2 and subsequently adding wind inputs improves trajectory prediction across the evaluation years. Velocity-field analysis under a representative flow regime shows a corresponding overall reduction in transport velocity errors. However, localized error increases during a strong wind-change event indicate that wind inputs do not uniformly improve the learned transport velocity field.
The resulting surrogate predicts continuous marine debris trajectories from specified release times and locations by integrating a learned transport velocity field, without requiring a new hydrodynamic simulation at inference. This provides a basis for reducing the computational burden of repeated transport predictions and generating large trajectory ensembles for probabilistic forecasting that accounts for uncertainties in release conditions and forcing inputs.

Diffusion Transformers tie compute to resolution: the token count is the pixel count over a fixed patch size, and the usual knobs degrade the whole image at once. We decouple generation resolution from sequence length by generating each image as a non-overlapping mosaic of latent patches drawn from two spatial scales under an exact token budget. A multi-scale VAE exposes a latent pyramid and decodes from an incomplete mixed-scale patch set; a quadtree selector meets the budget exactly, every refinement costing three tokens; and a scale-aware DiT denoises the resulting variable-length sequence. Which layout the denoiser needs turns out to be a question of what it was trained on. The usual recipe selects each training image's layout from that image, a pairing no sampling-time source can reproduce, and under it a self-generated two-step preview trails a stored real-image layout by 0.7–0.9 FID at $512^2$. Fine-tuning instead on layouts of other training images of the same class closes that gap to within 0.08 FID, and a layout-only study on that denoiser separates what a layout must be from what it need not: a layout of another class, a fixed radial prior, one fixed partition and a smooth random field all match or beat the preview's FID, and the smooth random field matches its sFID at $K=640$, while a white-noise field loses 0.6 FID and the fixed partition loses sFID. Test-time semantic or sample alignment is therefore unnecessary after independent-layout training at $512^2$; a coherent per-sample layout suffices, and the preview is one such source. With only the class label at sampling time, the simplest configuration — one 25-step pass under a per-sample smooth random layout, no preview, no scorer — brings DiT-XL/2 at $512^2$ to 2.92 FID / 6.05 sFID in less time than a dense model given the same extra training and run at 10 steps (4.85 / 6.29), and to 2.68 / 5.45 at 59% of its 25-step latency (3.08 / 4.49); with the preview, 3.05 / 5.94 and 2.88 / 5.54. Every latency, FLOP and memory figure is measured.

TL;DR: Diffusion Transformers on exact-budget mixed-scale token mosaics: after independent-layout training, a single pass under a per-sample smooth random layout (no preview, no scorer) matches dense FID at 59% of the latency at 512²; all costs measured.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning enables large language models to adapt to downstream tasks with a small number of task-specific parameters. Quantum-inspired unitary parameterizations offer compact representations of update directions, enabling methods such as Quantum-PEFT (Q-PEFT) to further reduce adapter parameters. However, Q-PEFT performance depends on interacting structural and training choices, yet evaluating each configuration requires costly GPU fine-tuning. This makes effective use of limited validation feedback essential for joint configuration optimization. We propose QPU-PEFT, a feedback-driven framework for budgeted Q-PEFT configuration selection. At each iteration, QPU-PEFT refits a quadratic surrogate from validation feedback, formulating its acquisition objective as a QUBO and an equivalent Ising Hamiltonian, which are used to retrieve the next configuration for GPU evaluation. We also develop a support-and-stability gate to accept QPU proposals after evaluation and otherwise invoke deterministic classical retrieval. We evaluate proposals on real QPUs. On TianYan-176, the gate accepts a hardware proposal, which differs from the deterministic classical route and satisfies a protocol-level 0.5-point BLEU/ROUGE-L non-inferiority criterion over three paired Qwen2.5-1.5B/E2E retraining seeds not used during selection; TianYan-287 separately invokes deterministic fallback. In single-seed offline replay on Qwen2.5-0.5B, Refitted Ridge-LCB reduces five-seed-mean regret by 39.8% relative to structured GP-EI and remains significantly better than RF-EI, TPE, and random search. On GPT-2/E2E-NLG, five paired full-budget retrainings show gains of 2.638 BLEU and 1.339 ROUGE-L over a learning-rate- and parameter-matched control. Finally, our separate resource-constrained selection reduces validation loss with 33.4% fewer trainable parameters and 52.4% less training time.

Predicting missing links in bipartite networks is a fundamental problem with applications ranging from recommendation systems to scientific and knowledge networks. Recent methods have been developed primarily for large-scale industrial recommendation, where massive interaction data and learned representations enable sophisticated predictive models. However, how these approaches generalize to bipartite networks with diverse structural characteristics and application contexts remains less systematically understood. This motivates training-free, topology-driven approaches that directly exploit the structural information of bipartite networks. In this work, we propose \textit{Network Shape Automata} (NSA), a training-free framework for side-conditioned bipartite link prediction that combines memory-based collaborative filtering with the local-community principles of Cannistraci-Hebb (CH) theory. NSA adapts CH-based structural similarity to the bipartite setting through a topology-aware denominator, integrating topological evidence from both node sets. We evaluate NSA on 13 real-world bipartite networks spanning diverse domains and compare it with conventional memory-based methods, advanced model-based approaches, and direct CH-based link prediction. Experiments demonstrate consistently strong performance across diverse networks and metrics. We further examine NSA's explainability through explanation removal tests. The results demonstrate that NSA provides an effective and transparent approach to side-conditioned bipartite link prediction, with the necessary neighbors identified by NSA providing structurally meaningful evidence for individual predictions.

Black-box hallucination detection typically relies on sampling-consistency methods that query a model repeatedly and score disagreement among its answers. This paradigm fails when a model is confidently and consistently wrong, a failure we term stubborn hallucination. We prove that repeated samples from a stubborn instance are distributionally identical to those from a faithful instance, leaving sampling consistency detectors have zero KL divergence between the two hypotheses and detection power bounded by the false-positive rate. We therefore cast hallucination detection as a Chernoff sequential hypothesis test and propose Chernoff Active Testing (CHAT, which probes beyond passive resampling. CHAT adaptively selects the most informative probe from seven semantic strategies (e.g., reverse querying, false-assertion injection), maps each response to a three-valued label via a text-only judge, accumulates a log-likelihood ratio, and stops once a Wald boundary is crossed. The probe menu and accumulated ratio carry the core detection signal, while the sequential selector acts as a budget optimizer, reducing query cost by 16.0% at matched accuracy. Across five benchmarks, CHAT achieves the highest average AUROC among 14 detectors, with gains concentrated on stubbornness-rich settings. On Stubborn-Bench, our new graded stubborn-hallucination benchmark, CHAT detects 9.9% of stubborn errors at a 5% false-positive rate, versus 0.4% for the strongest passive baseline, while using fewer target-model queries than the strongest baseline on average.

Oil-and-gas AI is commonly evaluated with general reasoning, document extraction, and retrieval metrics that do not measure whether a system can perform industry work. Across classification, extraction, and retrieval, the same failure recurs: a capable general model or apparently strong generic score does not supply the operative distinctions, output requirements, and verification logic that practitioners need. Subject-matter expertise must therefore become part of the evaluated system rather than remain informal context outside it.
We introduce StrataBench, a public evaluation framework for measuring how SME-created tooling changes three operational capabilities: Classify, Extract, and Define. These capabilities organize evaluation across land and title, regulatory and legal, drilling and completions, production, operations, engineering, safety/HSE, and accounting and finance; they do not imply that one implementation transfers among them. We instantiate the framework only for land and title. The evaluation constructs and interventions precede the corpus: land SMEs developed the operative-act guide and extraction contract through larger customer-data studies, while the petroleum representation follows an independently assembled glossary, curriculum, tokenizer, and textbook-tuning pipeline. We then reproduce those tests on releasable synthetic evidence rather than expose protected records. StrataBench Land v1 contains 526 synthetic land packets with 2,074 documents and 628 lease-like instruments across 12 producing states. Public legal and regulatory sources inform 24 packet recipes and 53 original builders; no customer documents, copyrighted form-book text, or certification questions enter the corpus.
Experiments show that SME tooling repairs a different failure in each capability. On 66 instruments, the complete operative-act guide raises fixed-panel accuracy by 0.085 over the closed vocabulary alone (95% CI [0.045, 0.130]). On 628 lease-like instruments, the Extract panel comprises 125,600 matched decisions over the ten fields shared by five models and four conditions. The SME-defined field contract raises accuracy from 0.033–0.424 to 0.855–0.881 without rule prose, while rules without that contract remain inconsistent. Royalty under that contract reaches 0.860–0.890 (Wilson 95% CI approximately [0.83, 0.91]). For Define, we build a petroleum representation stack because generic encoders do not preserve the field’s lexicon and contextual distinctions. The resulting encoder reaches 0.814 recall@3 on 43 domain abbreviations and 0.60 hard-negative accuracy, versus 0.023 and 0.30–0.40 for general encoders, while remaining within 2.8 points of the best general encoder on equation-card retrieval. These results demonstrate that operational readiness depends on the expert tools surrounding and shaping a model, not its general benchmark score alone.
StrataBench contributes the SME-authored guides, contracts, checks, domain representation, corpus generators, and disaggregated scorecards as a reproducible public layer grounded in, but kept legally separate from, private enterprise validation.

TL;DR: StrataBench shows that executable expert tooling substantially improves AI performance on oil-and-gas land-and-title classification, extraction, and retrieval, even when the underlying model and evidence remain fixed.

Multi-modal agents have made significant progress in interacting with open worlds. However, their ability to self-evolve remains limited. Supervised fine-tuning enables imitation but not active experience organization, while outcome-based reinforcement learning promotes exploration yet underuses intermediate trajectory information. To address these limitations, we propose EvolvingBrain, which uses an adaptive skill system as the brain for agent self-evolution, consisting of two components: Stratified Skill Self-Evolution and State-Aware Adaptive Execution. Stratified Skill Self-Evolution: extracts procedural patterns and Problematic Patterns from model-specific trajectories, summarizes experience by generating Skills, and evolves through multiple interactions with the open world, ultimately forming a Stratified Skill Architecture consisting of Domain, Plan, and Action/Trap Skills, which provides the agent with a multi-granularity knowledge repository and a novel evolution approach. State-Aware Adaptive Execution: summarizes long-horizon interactions into Structured Abstractive Memory and uses it to guide the State-Aware Skill Fusion Strategy, enabling the agent to utilize knowledge according to its current state.
Experiments on VAB-Minecraft and DiscoveryWorld demonstrate that EvolvingBrain improves success rates on open-world tasks and exhibits generalization capabilities.

TL;DR: EvolvingBrain enables multimodal agents to self-evolve in open-world by organizing interaction experience into hierarchical skills and adaptively applying them according to the current state.

Symbolic Machine Learning boasts interpretability by design, as it induces hypotheses that are human-readable and directly verifiable. Yet scaling such systems to large and noisy learning tasks remains a long-standing obstacle. This paper proposes GenFastLAS, a hybrid approach that combines the interpretability of symbolic learning with the efficient search space exploration of Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs). In GenFastLAS, an EA explores the feature space of a learning task, while FastLAS, a state-of-the-art symbolic learning system, induces interpretable solutions over the EA-informed feature space. We evaluate GenFastLAS on Machine Learning benchmarks, including an application to a real-world music genre classification problem. Our experimental results show that GenFastLAS outperforms FastLAS and is on par with neural baselines. This demonstrates that GenFastLAS can cope with larger feature sets than FastLAS, while providing the same interpretability and optimality guarantees on the solution it learns over the identified feature subset.

Heterogeneous spacecraft and satellite testbed environment expose similar operational functions through different telemetry names, units, packet layouts, sampling rates, and software interfaces, which makes direct raw-channel transfer unreliable. We investigate an alternative representation: transferable cyber-physical command-response mechanisms that connect commands and operational context to subsystem state, resource use, and physical effects. We introduce and train a Cyber-Physical Mechanism Network (CPMN), a temporal machine-learning model that combines semantic-role state encoding with command history, operational mode, software context, and role-availability masks to produce behavioral-consistency evidence rather than relying only on statistical rarity or known attack signatures. The evaluation contains two evidence layers. On real CuCD-ID v3 noise set, an XGBoost robustness baseline reaches 0.6891 accuracy and 0.6967 macro-F1 at 40 boosting rounds, with no additional measured gain through 150 rounds. CPMN reaches source/collision AUPRC 0.8354, mean matched-pair separation 0.1151, false-consistency rate 0.4250, and target AUPRC 0.8411 with transfer degradation -0.0057. Ablation raises collision AUPRC from 0.5000 to 0.8224 when command history is introduced, while replay and timing interventions remain the main failure cases. Under the evaluated conditions, command-response representations conditioned on action and context retain useful behavioral evidence even when the raw observation schema changes.

TL;DR: The model learns what should happen after a spacecraft command and flags when the observed behavior does not match, even across spacecraft with different telemetry formats.

Large Language Model (LLM) agents now take part in organizational work, where many authors record decisions across documents over months. Because a revised decision arrives as a new document rather than an edit, answering a question requires knowing which version held at a given time. However, most memory systems compress the record at write time. By distilling each document into facts, notes or graph edges, these methods fix what can be answered before any question is asked. To address this, we propose Mem++, a non-destructive memory framework shifting from write-time distillation to read-time selection. Mem++ stores every document whole with its date and author, and it calls no generative model at write time. At read time, it retrieves only documents dated up to the time a question asks about and fuses lexical and semantic rankings. Unlike systems that overwrite older versions, Mem++ keeps them and leaves the choice to the answering model. Evaluations on the organizational benchmark OrgMemBench demonstrate that Mem++ surpasses the strongest memory system baseline by 8.0 to 13.1 points across two answering models. With gpt-4.1-mini, it also achieves the best overall score, 2.6 points above RAG. In addition, Mem++ achieves the best average LLM-judge score on LoCoMo and ranks second on LongMemEval-S, behind only its entity-graph variant. Code will be released upon publication.

TL;DR: Mem++ achieves the best average LLM-judge score on LoCoMo and ranks second on LongMemEval-S, behind only its entity-graph variant.

Before taking action, humans and animals constantly simulate hypothetical actions: What if we did it differently instead? Modern learning systems for robot action execution, however, mostly test the effects of actions only post hoc, by trial and error, which is costly, slow, and sometimes unsafe. We suggest a neuro-inspired architecture that provides a pre-action counterfactual critique mechanism to the robot policy, based on computational models of interaction between the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus during mental simulation. A learned world model generates short imagined rollouts for the proposed action as well as sampled counterfactual alternatives, which are organized into a structured replay buffer by a hippocampal-inspired module, and then evaluated by a prefrontal-inspired arbiter, which signals to accept/revise the proposed action through a calibrated signal before execution. On a simulated six-task manipulation suite, ICC-Net outperforms strong model-based baselines by 12-20 percentage points in terms of the mean task success rate, more than 30% fewer occurrences of unsafe actions, and attaining a fixed performance level with approximately 40% fewer interactions with the environment. All the results of these experiments in this paper are generated from a numerical simulation of the proposed architecture and baselines, not from actual robot testing or GPU-scale training; for this reason, this paper reports these results as a feasibility study and provides a detailed description of what is required for empirical validation.

Ontologies represent knowledge as directed graphs where pairs of unweighted edges do not represent the same semantic distance between the concepts they connect. This distinction is especially important for over 1200 biological ontologies in the BioPortal repository. These ontologies have been curated by scientists and clinicians whose deep understanding of the material is used to create well-organized high-quality content. The ontologies in BioPortal serve as an increasingly important resource for scientific discovery. Existing learning approaches aiming to accelerate scientific discovery operate on ontology topology or learn continuous representations of the hierarchical relations in these ontologies. We introduce a different approach. We have developed deterministic algorithms that embed an ontology into the vertices of a Boolean n-cube by recursively applying ontology-aware bisections. Each bisection is a structural cut of the ontology and adds a dimension to a binary identifier for each node in the ontology. The resulting binary addresses retain explicit provenance for each recursive cut decision without requiring representation learning. Ancestor-aware cuts expose hierarchical structure through bitwise containment tests, i.e. AND operations. The popcount of the XOR of two addresses determines the Hamming distance between the concepts. We present our best refinement of this basic algorithm. This includes a depth-dependent coordinate weighting, and we show that it is an effective heuristic for accommodating the nonuniform semantic distance distinctions made at different levels of the hierarchy while preserving binary concept labels. On the ancestor-descendant prediction benchmark of Bai et al. (2021), the addresses reach 0.913 mAP on WN18RR and 0.871 on the biological knowledge graph GO21 with no representation learning, exceeding ConE (0.895), order embeddings (0.889), and Poincaré embeddings (0.810) on WN18RR, and exceeding ConE on GO21 in all three of their evaluation settings, including 0.827 versus 0.693 when all test pairs are inferred. We prove that the resulting addresses induce positive semi-definite kernels. As node features for a standard graph convolutional network, the same addresses improve accuracy over degree and depth features on an ontology-internal classification task on all five evaluated biomedical ontologies. Every address, including addresses never assigned to a concept, decodes to a coherent set of named ontology concepts, and the addresses predict protein subcellular localization, a label drawn from a different namespace of the ontology.

TL;DR: We introduce a deterministic, training-free Boolean embedding of biological ontologies that preserves hierarchical structure and outperforms learned ConE embeddings on established ancestor-descendant reasoning benchmarks.

Claims that visual representations are semantic have traditionally been verified via readout tasks such as linear classification, retrieval, segmentation, or qualitative localization. These readouts establish that semantic information can be accessed, but they do not reveal how that information is organized, how robust the representation is to non-semantic change, or what can be learned about the structure of semantics from contextual cues. We transform published representation claims into model-specific and falsifiable behavioral predictions and assess them via controlled, fine-grained manipulations of natural images. We use DINO and I-JEPA as primary case studies from published papers. For the DINO contract, we use the self-supervised DINO ViT-S/16 model and the architecture-matched supervised DeiT-S/16 model. Using these, we demonstrate that semantic accessibility and intervention-consistent organization exhibit very different depth trends. Layers with probe accuracies differing by two percentage points can have ordering rates that differ by up to 19.0 percentage points, and the model that is better organized according to the CLS readout shows the reverse ordering as depth increases. We show that semantic organization depends on the readout used. At the final layer, the edited-region patch-token readout yields no reliable difference between the models; yet mean-pooling favors supervised DeiT by 11.0--13.0 percentage points, while DINO leads by 30.9--35.1 percentage points at the CLS readout. We also show that ordering degrades consistently as JPEG corruption increases, although DINO preserves the desired relation under more severe corruption than DeiT. For the I-JEPA contract, correct visible context yields matched-target preference rates of 0.628--0.666; recomputing the prediction from different-species context reduces these rates to 0.474--0.536. We therefore conclude that semantic accessibility, sensitivity, nuisance stability, organization, and contextual prediction are separate properties of the representations. As such, evaluation of a representation as ``semantic'' should specify the property claimed, the corresponding behavioral prediction, the readout, the nuisance reference, the severity level, and other relevant factors.

Clinical time-series prediction relies on interactions among physiological variables, yet these interactions must be learned from measurements collected at different times. Once missing entries are filled, a newly observed value can become indistinguishable from an older value carried forward, obscuring the observation context needed to interpret cross-variable dependencies. Meanwhile, these dependencies can change during a patient’s stay, making a fixed graph insufficient to represent their evolution. The central challenge is therefore to learn how variables interact over time while retaining when the underlying evidence was actually observed. To bridge this gap, we introduce MEDIC, which combines observation context with evolving graph structure. MEDIC discovers shared graph anchors without outcome labels and refines their temporal path for prediction, retaining elapsed time and measurement freshness. On the MIMIC-IV dataset and the eICU dataset, selective graph exchange improves AUROC over fully connected exchange by 2.72 and 2.49 percentage points in matched controls. The learned anchors also share edges across folds and change more smoothly than graphs with shuffled time order. These findings support a way to connect irregular clinical records with evolving dependencies that can be inspected alongside patient predictions across a stay.

TL;DR: We introduce MEDIC, a graph learning framework for patient assessment that captures changing relationships among clinical variables while accounting for irregular measurement times.

Autism spectrum Disorder classification from resting state FMRI on ABIDE-I depends
strongly on the brain parcellation used, and the atlas-selection optimal strategy for combining atlases remains underexplored.Two problems compound this. First, the majority of the existing multi-atlas studies each propose a single fusion mechanism. Second, the prevailing protocols k-fold or single random splits place same-site subjects in both training and test partitions, allowing models to exploit site-specific signals.We fix the cohort (N = 795 ABIDE-I subjects with usable data across AAL-116, Craddock-200 and Dosenbach-161; 372 ASD / 423 TD, 20 sites) and the evaluation protocol, and vary only the combination strategy across four architectures: a joint graph transformer over pooled multi-atlas subject graphs, a learned cross-atlas attention fusion head over frozen per-atlas encoders, a fixed-weight prediction-level deep ensemble, and a stacked ensemble of nine classical base learners. Varying only the fusion stage, Macro-F1 increases monotonically as fusion is deferred (0.619 ± 0.012 early, 0.670 ± 0.033 intermediate, 0.704 ± 0.018 late; endpoints separated at p = 0.0001 under a conservative unpaired test), in a way confirming the prediction.Under leave-one-site-out evaluation with site-disjoint threshold calibration, mean performance falls modestly (0.677 ± 0.078) while across-site dispersion is four times across-fold dispersion, harmonization outweighs every architectural choice we varied, and leave-one-view-out studies yields a view ordering that disagrees in direction with the in-distribution one.

Federated fine-tuning of vision-language models must balance two competing objectives: personalization to each client's local data and generalization to classes never seen during training. Existing federated adapter methods resolve this tension with a single fixed scalar weight that linearly combines a globally shared representation with a locally personalized one, hand-tuned once per dataset and left unchanged across every client and every round. We show that this design is not merely under-tuned but structurally blind to three things a federated deployment cannot avoid: heterogeneous personalization need across clients, the unreliability of a personalized adapter early in training, and the fact that optimal reliance on personalization shifts as training progresses. We term this the static fusion problem and show it produces a consistent failure mode performance peaks early and degrades steadily afterward regardless of which fixed weight is chosen. We propose Dynamic Gamma, a framework that replaces the fixed weight with two complementary signal-driven mechanisms: one derives the fusion weight from the model's own predictive confidence at zero added parameter cost; the other combines each client's label distribution with a live measure of representational divergence between the global and personalized branches, mediated by three lightweight parameters learned jointly with the model. Across three datasets under non-IID federated fine-tuning, Dynamic Gamma matches fixed-weight performance to within at most 0.7pp in final H-Mean while reducing mean post-peak degradation from 3.46pp to 1.67pp, a 52% relative reduction. DG-L reaches zero post-peak decay on EuroSAT and requires no per-dataset weight search. Analysis of the learned parameters reveals an emergent curriculum: the model autonomously shifts its reliance from a distributional signal to a representational one as training progresses, with the same directional shift appearing across all three datasets. We argue that a fusion mechanism combining global and personalized knowledge deserves the same scrutiny as the components it combines, and show that this scrutiny is inexpensive to add.

TL;DR: Dynamic Gamma replaces fixed global-local fusion weights in federated vision-language personalization with adaptive signal-driven weighting, reducing post-peak degradation while preserving final performance.

Standard fine-tuning adapts language models by updating their weights while keeping the computation topology fixed. We introduce T-Tuning, a complementary paradigm that adapts how existing model modules are composed and reused. We reinterpret an N-layer Transformer as N recurrent steps over a bank of N reusable blocks, with the original layer sequence corresponding to a single canonical trajectory in a larger topology space. T-Tuning explores this space along two dimensions: T-Top2 expands computation width by optionally activating an additional block at each step, while T-Loop expands depth through selective feedback connections that reuse earlier blocks. Lightweight routers control these topological choices, enabling either parameter-efficient adaptation with a frozen backbone or joint optimization with standard fine-tuning. On medical knowledge and mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3-4B, router-only T-Tuning outperforms LoRA, while joint topology-and-weight adaptation further improves over full fine-tuning with only 0.02% additional parameters. These results show that computation topology is a promising adaptation space complementary to model weights, enabling language models to improve not only what their modules compute, but also how those modules are composed.

TL;DR: T-Tuning adapts language models by optimizing how existing layers are routed, reused, and composed, providing a topology-space alternative complementary to conventional weight fine-tuning.

A representation that predicts well on its own can be a poor memory for later use. For history compressed before new context arrives, we compare standalone and contextual training under matched writer inputs, storage capacity, and final reader access. The same frozen codes can reverse their predictive ranking when context becomes available. Conditional Gaussian geometry quantifies the regret of a selected standalone-optimal store, and a finite-loss decomposition separates storage and reader error. In a controlled nonlinear task, contextual training reduces mean squared error by 64% across five fitted pipelines; the gap persists with larger stores, more data, and stronger readers. A known compact state can match learned storage, while hiding its coordinates separates state adequacy from the difficulty of learning that state. In hourly weather forecasting, contextual memories have worse standalone accuracy yet comparable or lower forecast error after the current hour arrives. In retrospective clinical prediction, contextual training again helps learned stores, while simple physiological states achieve lower risk. Memory should be selected for the prediction problem it will serve.

TL;DR: A memory that predicts well on its own can preserve the wrong information for later use; training storage for future contextual prediction can reverse which limited representation is best.

We examine 22 LLM-coded manuscript features against original review outcomes for 4,000 ICLR submissions from 2023-2026. Year- and area-adjusted analyses find 18 pooled feature-rating associations and six feature-level linear year interactions after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Three trends, including baseline count, additional validation, and efficiency reporting, pass a common-support screen and score-scale and 2023-2025 checks. Baseline count provides the strongest evidence: its D-versus-A slope remains negative and BH-supported after adjustment for the other 21 features, while validation and efficiency trends are specification-sensitive. On 20 human-reference papers from 2026, the exact downstream five-call labels match human reference labels on 406/440 items (92.3%), with limited rare-category coverage. Subscores, acceptance, and rating dispersion provide complementary outcomes, but no selected secondary-outcome trend survives multiplicity correction. A constructive non-identification result explains why unmatched calibration snapshots cannot separate latent prevalence, annotation error, and reviewer association. The contribution is a reproducible evidence hierarchy for longitudinal manuscript-review associations under measurement and process shift.

Evaluating whether large language models (LLMs) can recover execution-relevant program structure, rather than only produce code that passes tests, remains an open problem. Existing code benchmarks emphasize test-passing outputs, from standalone programming tasks (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench) to repository repair (SWE-Bench); this is useful, but offers limited diagnostic signal about which program semantics a model can recover from source. We introduce TraceEval, to our knowledge the first execution-verified, multi-language benchmark for code semantic reasoning: recovering a program’s runtime call structure from source code. Unlike prior call-graph benchmarks that rely on static-tool output or hand-annotated ground truth, every positive edge in TraceEval is mechanically witnessed by validation execution, eliminating annotator disagreement and label noise for observed behavior. TraceEval consists of (i) 10,583 real-world programs (2,129 test, 8,454 train) extracted from 1,600+ open-source repositories across Python, JavaScript, and Java via an LLM-assisted harness-generation pipeline with tracer validation; and (ii) a reproducible pipeline that converts any open-source repository into new verified benchmark instances. We evaluate 12 LLMs at zero-shot on the held-out test split. The strongest model, Claude-Opus-5, reaches an average F1 of 74.6% across the three languages. To demonstrate the train split’s utility as a supervision substrate, we fine-tune the Qwen2.5-Coder family on it: lifts of up to +55.6 F1 bring tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-32B to 71.2%, within 3.4 F1 of zero-shot Claude-Opus-5. We release the benchmark, construction pipeline, dynamic tracers, and evaluation scripts.

TL;DR: TraceEval benchmarks LLM reasoning about runtime call structure using execution-verified programs.

In quantitative investing, return prediction supports various tasks, including stock selection, portfolio optimization, and risk management. 
Quantitative factors, such as valuation, quality, and growth, capture various characteristics of stocks.
Textual data, like news and earnings transcripts, has attracted growing attention, driven by recent advances in large language models (LLMs).
This paper examines effective and practical ways to leverage multimodal factors and newsflow for return prediction and stock selection.
First, we introduce a fusion learning framework to learn a unified representation from factors and newsflow representations generated by an LLM.
Within this framework, we compare three methods of different architectural complexities: representation combination, representation summation, and attentive representations.
Next, building on the limitation of fusion learning observed in empirical comparison, we explore a mixture model that adaptively combines predictions made by single modalities and their fusion.
To mitigate the training instability of the mixture model, we introduce a decoupled training approach with theoretical insights.
Finally, our experiments on real investment universes reveal:
(1) Within fusion learning, the representation combination method, despite its relatively low architectural complexity, generally outperforms other fusion methods.
The relative performance of fusion methods varies across investment universes, suggesting variation in the predictive relevance of data, particularly news.
(2) The mixture model appears relatively stable across universes and portfolios, delivering comparable or superior performance.
Its enhanced adaptability can be beneficial in settings where the predictive relevance of factors and news is likely more variable.
(3) Fine-tuning the LLM during the training of these multimodal models does not consistently benefit performance; its impact varies across universes, potentially reflecting differences in market efficiency and data characteristics.

Physical discovery frequently begins with measurements that are spatially information-rich yet dynamically incomplete: a 2D passive tracer, projected column density, or an intensity field, rather than the full state variables appearing in first-principles equations. This raises two questions: \emph{*which patterns in an observation are interesting enough to become physical questions?*} and \emph{*how can information in observations be used efficiently rather than compressed into degenerate summaries?*} The first is traditionally called insight; the second is acute in information-rich physical data. Inefficient information use blinds observations to relevant structure and limits how competing theories can be tested. We propose the Morphological Representation Hypothesis (MRH): self-supervised learning (SSL) organizes the spatial and multiscale information in an observable into a physically meaningful representation that preserves physically relevant organization.
