In the Keller--Segel model, the learned embedding exhibits equation-space correspondence; in magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) turbulence, learned morphological neighborhoods exhibit lower average distances in dimensionless physical diagnostic space than density-matched or random neighborhoods. These results illustrate how learned morphological coordinates can organize physical information and support subsequent quantitative analysis and the formulation of physical questions.

TL;DR: Can morphology reflects the physics

Vulnerability-detection benchmarks score the verdict an agent reaches, not the evidence it gathered. A model that recalls a CVE from pretraining therefore scores the same as one that traced the data flow. We study a task where this difference matters, deciding whether a commit introduces a vulnerability. Instead of scoring the verdict, we score whether the agent retrieved the code its conclusion depends on. We present VulContextBench, a benchmark of 111 vulnerability-introducing commits (VICs) across 83 repositories, 63 CWEs, and five languages. Existing datasets label such commits by tracing a fix back through the version history, which often points to the wrong commit. We therefore audit every case by hand against an explicit four-criterion definition of a VIC, so the benchmark does not inherit that label noise. Each case is annotated with gold context, 464 code blocks in total, each tagged by its role in the evidence for the vulnerability. We evaluate seven frontier models with precision, recall and F1 at three granularities (file, block, and line), scored separately on the context an agent viewed while exploring and on the context it finally declared as evidence. The gap between the two is the main finding. Every model opens most of the gold context while exploring, but reports only part of it as evidence. At the level of code blocks, the share of the gold context a model reports is 37 to 73 percentage points below the share it viewed. Qwen3-Coder-Next views 86.3% of the lines in annotated code blocks but cites only 12.9% in its final report. GPT-5.5, which cites the most, views 73% and reports 36%. These results highlight a gap between finding relevant code and selecting it for the final report, which verdict-level benchmarks cannot reveal.

TL;DR: VulContextBench shows that coding agents retrieve most vulnerability evidence but omit much of it from their final reports.

Vision-language robots increasingly use natural language grounded in visual and sensor observations, yet evaluation practices typically assess perception, language reasoning, and action modules as if they were standalone. High scores in individual assessments do not guarantee robust system behavior, as high end-to-end performance emerges from interactions between modules. This paper introduces CROSS-VLR, a structured system-level evaluation methodology that treats these components as an interconnected system and emphasizes task-driven evaluation to trace behavior across module interactions. The methodology is retrospectively instantiated across diverse platforms and domains, including assistive navigation, industrial welding, and educational robotics. By organizing established interface-level measures around information transfer and relating them to end-to-end outcomes, CROSS-VLR supports traceable and comparable evaluation across applications. This work presents system-level evaluation as a complement to component-level and end-to-end measures for developing reliable and interpretable vision-language robotic systems.

TL;DR: CROSS-VLR is a cross-domain framework for analyzing vision-language robot performance by tracing how information and failures propagate across perception, reasoning, and action interfaces.

Feature perturbation is a common strategy for single-source domain generalization (SSDG), but it is usually judged by its final task performance rather than by the representation changes it induces. We explore a different perspective: can feature perturbations be compared through a small set of measurable descriptors that describe how a representation moves? We introduce a four-dimensional representation-space descriptor, comprising feature displacement $D_F$, relational displacement $D_R$, a task-region ratio $\Theta_{\mathrm{Task}}$, and subspace deviation $\Theta_{\mathrm{Subspace}}$. We use this space as an empirical analysis lens for several existing perturbation mechanisms rather than as a presumed universal geometry. Across two object-detection settings with style and weather shifts, we observe recurring differences in the geometric profiles of perturbations and a concentration of relatively stronger OOD-performing configurations in a bounded region of the descriptor space. These observations do not establish a universal optimum, but they suggest a concrete direction for future study: whether SSDG performance may be associated with reproducible regions of representation space that can be identified without target-domain access. As a case study, we introduce Dual-Invariant Spectral Perturbation (DISP), a non-learned Fourier-phase perturbation with explicit controls over phase magnitude $\rho$, channel coupling $\kappa$, and frequency support $\mathcal{M}$. We establish energy preservation and relational invariance at full channel coupling, and empirically examine how the controls alter the proposed descriptors. DISP obtains strong OOD performance in the reported experiments, but the main purpose of the method is illustrative: it shows how explicit perturbation controls can be studied through a representation-space description. We hope this viewpoint can contribute to more interpretable, controllable, and ultimately testable approaches to feature perturbation in SSDG.

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of supporting scientific workflows, but their capabilities across diverse research activities remain difficult to assess systematically. Existing benchmarks often focus on selected scientific capabilities or task types, limiting a comprehensive characterization of scientific agents’ strengths and weaknesses in realistic research workflows. We introduce SCI-AGENT-EXAM, a workflow-oriented benchmark comprising 120 expert-curated tasks across 11 scientific fields and 7 research task types defined by the \textsc{Scientific Workflow Task Taxonomy (SWTT)}. Each task requires both executable artifacts (e.g., code and scripts) and textual artifacts (e.g., reports and explanations). To evaluate the heterogeneous task outputs, we develop a hybrid evaluation protocol combining deterministic programmatic verification for executable artifacts with a calibrated, expert-validated LLM-based judge for textual artifacts. Beyond outcome assessment, we analyze progress and solution stability along execution trajectories to characterize how agents reach their final results. Evaluation of 10 LLM agents reveals uneven capability profiles across scientific task types. For example, while the top agent leads on every task type, the margins are highly type-dependent—cross-agent spread ranges from ~27 points on Tool Orchestration to ~54 points on Literature Synthesis. Trajectory analysis further shows that higher-scoring agents tend to use fewer execution steps and exhibit fewer regression and recovery steps.

TL;DR: Sci-Agent-Exam benchmarks scientific agents on 120 real-world tasks across 11 domains, evaluating both executable artifacts and scientific outputs to reveal a substantial gap between execution correctness and scientific quality.

Repeated storm-surge simulations are needed for coastal risk assessment and scenario analysis, motivating learned surrogates for computationally expensive hydrodynamic models. Learning such surrogates from gridded atmospheric forcing and hydrodynamic response requires capturing how the response depends on both forcing history and spatial interactions. Fourier neural operators (FNOs) provide a global representation of spatial interactions, but standard configurations encode temporal snapshots through channel stacking without a dedicated temporal encoder, while their spectral layers operate over the entire spatial domain. We propose HL-STFNO, a Hybrid-Lift Short-Time Fourier Neural Operator, that combines explicit temporal encoding with localized spectral processing. A hybrid lifting module augments a pointwise projection with a gated temporal transformer branch to encode forcing histories. Within each operator layer, a spatially windowed Fourier branch complements global spectral processing by learning local spectral interactions. Given gridded wind and pressure histories, HL-STFNO directly predicts a sequence of site-specific storm-surge responses simulated by the Advanced Circulation (ADCIRC) model. Experiments demonstrate improved predictive accuracy over several neural-network and neural-operator baselines.  Evaluations across four coastal stations and atmospheric forcing datasets generated by five different climate models further support the effectiveness of the architecture across varied coastal settings and forcing conditions.  These results support combining temporal lifting with local spectral processing for storm-surge surrogate modeling.

Performance scaling increasingly relies on heterogeneous integration, where chiplets communicate through dense die-to-die (D2D) interconnects, whose high-frequency coupling directly affects link performance. Machine-learning surrogates have demonstrated potential to replace slow full-wave electromagnetic simulation in D2D design. However, progress is bottlenecked by data: simulation cost grows super-linearly with conductor count, making large datasets of complete multi-conductor structures prohibitively expensive to produce. In this paper, we introduce OpenInterconnect, an open dataset and model-agnostic benchmark built from reusable two-line, four-port primitives that keep full-wave simulation tractable and compose into larger multiport structures. OpenInterconnect contains approximately 14,500 silicon-interposer microstrip and multilayer coplanar-waveguide (CPW) geometries with complex S-parameters at 601 frequencies from DC to 60 GHz. Across classical regressors, boosted trees, MLPs, and graph neural networks (GNNs), the best models reduce error by 82–99% relative to a mean predictor when trained on OpenInterconnect. Single-line targets are predicted accurately by nearly every model family, reaching 0.026 dB insertion-loss mean absolute error (MAE), while multilayer coupling separates the families, with GNNs strongest at 2.575–2.592 dB MAE over a response range extending to approximately −147 dB. Composed into 83 unseen 32-line CPW structures, primitive predictions estimate near- and far-end crosstalk (NEXT and FEXT), the unwanted interference coupled onto a signal line at the source and receiver ends of the link, within 1.40 and 1.15 dB MAE. Used as a NEXT/FEXT screen, the surrogate correctly flags 100% of failing link designs at an estimated 5.2 × 10^5 speedup over full-wave simulation. These results show that primitive-level learning and composition enable reliable, rapid screening of large D2D interconnect design spaces.

TL;DR: OpenInterconnect is a benchmark and open dataset of Die-to-Die interconnects paired with full-wave simulated S-parameters for training electromagnetic surrogate models.

In real-world AI perception systems, such as intelligent transportation, visual data must maintain verifiable provenance and integrity even after lossy transcoding. However, these two security requirements inherently conflict: deep watermarks optimized to survive benign compression often fail to detect localized malicious edits, whereas classical semi-fragile authenticators are typically destroyed by routine video re-encoding. To reconcile this origin-integrity conflict, we propose BiMark, a dual-band watermarking framework that achieves both tasks simultaneously using a single shared encoder. BiMark strategically disentangles the payloads by embedding a robust camera identity in a low-pass background residual and a fragile content tag in a high-pass foreground residual. We rigorously evaluate our framework under inter-frame codec constraints and localized overwrites. By defining strict safety boundaries across varied threat models ranging from independent pixel overwrites to content-aware inpainting and white-box attacks, we provide a transparent assessment of the system’s defensive capabilities. Our findings show that BiMark reliably preserves camera identity through standard compression pipelines while remaining sensitive enough to detect malicious tampering at a strictly controlled false alarm rate, establishing a principled baseline for verifiable visual data in adversarial environments.

The Sliced Wasserstein and Generalized Sliced Wasserstein distances make optimal transport scalable by comparing one-dimensional pushforwards of distributions, but the observational rule they use is typically fixed globally or adapted from the distributions being compared. In several settings however, the appropriate discrepancy may be externally indexed such that the same pair of distributions is compared under a different state or task. We introduce Controlled Generalised Sliced Wasserstein (CGSW), a family of distances, in which an exogenous control, fixed independently of the distributions, parametrizes precisely how the one-dimensional Wasserstein costs are aggregated, ensuring suitability to the task at hand while also being computationally feasible. We further generalize using the Anchored CGSW (ACGSW) distances which interpolate between the SW and CGSW distance, and hence recover the SW distance as a special case. Various theoretical properties of these distances are proved, including but not limited to well-definedness, Kantorovich grounding, pseudometric and quotient-metric structure for CGSW, metricity and weak-topology equivalence for ACGSW under appropriate conditions, consistency of empirical estimators, an explicit finite-sample W1 rate, and sorting-based sliced-OT complexity . Our autoencoder-based distribution matching experiments show that geometry-matched controls improve adherence to prescribed spiral, half-moon and asymmetric gaussian latent structures relative to SW and GSW baselines across several distributional criteria. These results establish exogenous control as a principled mechanism for making sliced optimal transport responsive to externally fixed comparison structure without adapting the comparison rule to each evaluated pair.

TL;DR: CGSW is an OT framework in which exogenous control changes observation geometry used to compare distributions, while retaining metric, topological, statistical, and computational guarantees through an anchored construction.

Leukemia diagnosis starts with an accumulation of evidences from individual white blood cells (WBC) morphologies across peripheral blood smears (PBS), requiring a hematologist to laboriously review each cell manually. We present Hematology Agent with Learned Oversight (HALO), a modular agentic pipeline that takes PBS image tiles as input, analyzes available cells and their morphology, generates a leukemia impression when diagnostic evidence is sufficient, otherwise flags the case for human review. A YOLOv11 detector localizes and classifies cells within the PBS tiles, DinoBloom-based probes predicts their morphology, and the per-patient evidence is aggregated deterministically into cell differential, blast burden and guideline-based flags which a random forest classifier utilize to predict a leukemia subtype for the patient. A reflection agent then inspects the evidence and may choose to proceed for report generation with the findings, re-aggregate the collected evidence at a higher confidence threshold or escalate the case, but never sets the leukemia subtype. Output reports combine the resulting quantities with a fine tuned language model interpretation under validators that link all reported values to the detected cells. Under patient-grouped 5-fold cross validation on the LLD dataset, with every module trained per fold and all results computed from the predicted detections, HALO reaches 84.8% end-to-end accuracy with reflection and 87\% patient subtyping accuracy and separates acute from chronic leukemia in 45 out of 46 patients. Every report passed validation with no absent values, but 29% of sections written without finetuning the language model stated a diagnosis, which is strictly forbidden by the prompt.

TL;DR: An agentic pipeline that generates verified, patient-level leukemia impressions from peripheral blood smear, and utilizes a reflection mechanism to flag cases where evidence is insufficient

Data assimilation (DA) combines observations and model forecasts to estimate the system state. 
We introduce CRPS-Var, a variational DA framework that leverages a stochastically forced forward model representing a conditional distribution over physically plausible future states. This allows DA to be reinterpreted as a search problem: identifying the forcing whose forecast best agrees with observations. Concretely, we implement our forward model as a generative model trained with the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), a strictly proper scoring rule widely used in probabilistic state-of-the-art AI weather models. 
We find that CRPS-Var is particularly effective in the presence of sparse or noisy observations. That is, we obtain meaningful analysis increments from observation densities as low as 0.01\%, corresponding to a handful of measurements. Beyond robustness to sparse and noisy observations, the approach naturally yields state-dependent analyses without requiring difficult, explicit background-error covariance estimation. We evaluate CRPS-Var on several nonlinear dynamical systems, including Euler, shear flow, and shallow-water equations. We compare against both variational algorithms as well as state-of-the-art AI approaches based on diffusion and flow models. CRPS-Var outperforms all of these in the noisy and sparse setting, while remaining competitive at higher observation densities. Finally, we show that the resulting analyses remain stable over long autoregressive rollouts.

TL;DR: We introduce a data assimilation method that leverages learned probabilistic forecast models trained with a continuous ranked probability score to infer system states from noisy and extremely sparse  observations.

Neural operators approximate solution operators of partial differential equations at a fraction of the cost of numerical solvers. Efficient grid-based architectures such as the Fourier neural operator (FNO) assume uniform rectangular grids, whereas engineering simulations use large, irregular, and locally refined meshes. We introduce L-SplineFNO, a memory-efficient conditional neural operator that couples an FNO backbone with a sparse, learnable tensor-product B-spline transfer between unstructured meshes and a latent Cartesian grid. It incorporates global design and operating parameters through feature-wise linear modulation. A local normalised scatter avoids the geometry-dependent solve of analytic spline transformation while preserving compact support, partition of unity, and spline smoothness by construction. Across six three-dimensional engineering benchmarks, L-SplineFNO achieves strong predictive accuracy while requiring substantially less memory and compute than the compared unstructured operators, scaling to 26.6 million nodes in training and 46 million in inference on a single A100 GPU. It further supports zero-shot super-resolution and efficient closed-form spatial derivatives, and enables deployment on a 29.2-million-node fusion tokamak model.

TL;DR: L-SplineFNO makes the mesh-to-grid transfer in Fourier Neural Operators a learnable, structure-preserving B-spline mapping, allowing for conditional modelling across irregular engineering meshes faster and more accurately.

CryptoWavelets is an innovative neural framework for image encryption, based on an autoencoder architecture trained to simulate structured, mathematically invertible transformations, such as wavelets, in a non-directly invertible latent space. In detail, the core of the model consists of an encoder trained to simulate biorthogonal wavelet transforms, which projects images into a high-dimensional latent space, where visual information is compressed, encrypted, and rendered devoid of direct interpretability. This space serves as an encrypted domain, inaccessible without the trained decoder, whose weights represent an indispensable neural private key for reconstructing the original content. Unlike traditional methods, security does not depend on the computational complexity of a function, but rather on the architectural invertibility and the secrecy of the model parameters. The experiments conducted on the high-resolution DIV2K dataset demonstrate that CryptoWavelets is capable of achieving secure visual encoding with minimal distortion and strong resistance to unauthorized decoding attempts, offering an effective compromise between perceptual quality and cryptographic robustness.

TL;DR: CryptoWavelets encrypts images by mapping them into a hidden neural latent space, recoverable only through the trained decoder.

Legal systems are increasingly implemented through software, yet scalable methods for translating legal texts into accurate symbolic representations remain underdeveloped. We study this problem through tax law, where forms and filing instructions define large computational structures composed of arithmetic, branching, recursion, and tabular reasoning. We introduce a neuro-symbolic framework for the automatic formalization of tax forms and tax-form instructions into executable symbolic programs. Our approach is based on two forms of correspondence between law and logic: structural correspondence, which aligns legal and symbolic components such as cells and schedules, and denotational correspondence, which requires each symbolic component to preserve the meaning of its legal counterpart. We combine large language model synthesis with cell-level verification and an agentic repair loop that iteratively localizes and corrects errors using benchmark tax returns. Evaluated on 30 tax forms from TaxCalcBench and OpenTaxSolver, the framework achieves 100% agreement with benchmark outputs at the cell level. Rather than measuring a single generation pass, this result reflects the performance of the complete neuro-symbolic formalization system. Our work provides both a practical approach to large-scale legal auto-formalization and a foundation for evaluating correspondence between legal texts and executable symbolic representations.

TL;DR: A neurosymbolic formalization system for large-scale legal auto-formalization.

A feasible plan does not by itself authorize execution. When a task contract requires clarification among distinct executable goals, a language model that omits a feasible alternative creates false uniqueness: the planner verifies the proposed goal, and the system executes without authorization. We study this failure in two finite domains, object carrying and resource workflows, using program-generated references hidden from runtime. On 128 frozen carrying test worlds, three-sample candidate unions from Qwen and Gemma are format-valid yet yield 16/35 and 15/33 unauthorized executions. A semantic-completeness audit removes these errors but lowers correct executions from 19 to 6 and from 18 to 5 of 31 unique-goal worlds, whereas a complete-catalog control reaches 26/31. In paired interventions whose carrying prompts contained conflicting output-format instructions, adding a feasible competitor raises carrying errors by 26.6 and 21.9 percentage points (significant after four-way correction at the primary budget), and the errors persist under full checking. In workflows, neither the unions nor the catalog executes at the primary budget; full checking reveals errors for Qwen but not Gemma. For a Qwen interface that passed a development gate, predicate candidates avoid the observed list errors and, under full checking, correctly execute all 64 base test worlds per domain. Reliability evaluations should therefore report candidate coverage, errors, correct autonomy, and checking cost together.

TL;DR: A verified plan need not authorize execution: LLM candidate lists omit executable alternatives, causing false-uniqueness errors; a completeness audit removes them at a large autonomy cost, and a qualified predicate interface avoids both.

Acoustic control of fluid droplets beyond the Rayleigh regime is governed by the coupled effects of fluid inertia, gravity, interfacial tension, and spatially varying acoustic forces, resulting in nonlinear and strongly state-dependent droplet dynamics. Prior numerical and theoretical studies developed an Eulerian multiphysics formulation based on the incompressible Navier--Stokes equations with gravitational, interfacial, and acoustic body forces, and showed that finite-size effects can substantially alter the levitation response. In particular, the critical acoustic energy increases from $3.5$ to $5.1$ and $16.2,\mathrm{J,m^{-3}}$ for droplet diameters of $0.9$, $1.0$, and $1.2,\mathrm{mm}$, respectively, while partial cancellation between opposing acoustic-force regions leads to non-monotonic suspension behavior. Selective suspension has also been demonstrated, with a $1.8,\mathrm{mm}$ droplet suspended while a $1.3,\mathrm{mm}$ droplet settles at $E_{\mathrm{ac}}=12,\mathrm{J,m^{-3}}$. These results establish the complexity of the underlying dynamics, but existing approaches primarily characterize the response to prescribed acoustic conditions rather than learning how the actuation should change as the droplet evolves. In this work, we address this gap by formulating acoustic levitation as a physics-grounded sequential decision-making problem and learning an adaptive control policy through reinforcement learning. The evolving droplet state is used as the observation, acoustic excitation defines the action, and the multiphysics model provides the transition dynamics of the environment. The policy is trained to maximize long-horizon levitation performance while simultaneously maintaining the target position, avoiding settling, and limiting unnecessary acoustic actuation. This enables the controller to continuously adjust the excitation according to the instantaneous droplet state rather than operating at a fixed acoustic condition. We evaluate the learned policy across different droplet sizes, initial positions, and acoustic operating regimes, including conditions outside the training distribution, and examine levitation stability, tracking accuracy, settling time, robustness, and control efficiency. By coupling a physically resolved droplet model with policy learning, the proposed approach moves from characterizing where levitation occurs to learning how to maintain it, providing a new setting for reinforcement learning in nonlinear physical systems with state-dependent dynamics.

TL;DR: We develop an RL framework for adaptive acoustic levitation of droplets beyond the Rayleigh regime. A physics-based model guides learning to adjust acoustic excitation for stable, robust, and efficient levitation across varying conditions.

Class-conditional conformal prediction promises that a screening model clears at most an $\alpha$ fraction of true positives. The promise holds only while deployment matches calibration within each class. When that is in doubt, the usual move is to watch unlabeled deployment scores for trouble. We show this cannot work in general and ask what it takes instead. A class-localized harmful shift and a harmless prevalence shift can produce the same unlabeled score distribution, so no unlabeled monitor beats a coin on both. Side information helps little: with a stable negative class and a prevalence prior, the unlabeled data bound the miss rate only to an interval that, on our data, is useless unless prevalence is known to about $\pm3\%$. Labels settle the question, and we bound how many are needed from both sides, including a lower bound that holds even for monitors that also watch the unlabeled stream. We study this in diabetic retinopathy screening on six public datasets. Calibrated on held-out eyes ($81\%$ from DDR's official validation split), the band auto-clears $17.7\%$ of referable eyes on DDR's official test split against a promised $5\%$ (exact test $p = 1.5\times10^{-12}$). Five standard label-free tools each misjudge at least one of five domains, and the most visible shifts, on Messidor-2 and DeepDRiD, do no harm. A betting monitor flags DDR after a median of $72$ random labels and EyePACS after $159$, between the lower bound and its own guarantee, and stays within its $5\%$ false-alarm budget on unharmed domains. At screening prevalence the same audit takes several hundred to a few thousand labels, and it requires labels graded to the calibration standard: $5\%$ random grading noise makes every unharmed domain look harmed unless the null is corrected for a known noise rate.

TL;DR: Unlabeled shift statistics cannot detect conformal coverage collapse; we prove the non-identifiability limits, bound the required audit labels, and evaluate betting monitors across six clinical datasets.

Interpretability-for-discovery pipelines routinely treat successful decoding of a concept from hidden activations as evidence that the model uses that concept for downstream tasks. We demonstrate that this inference from decodability to use fails mechanistically, and we quantify the magnitude of this failure by building a rigorous testbed in which a concept's causal contribution is zero by construction. A binary marker is stamped into real MNIST digits; in our label-independent regime, it is drawn independently of the label, ensuring no risk-minimising model can reduce its loss by reading the marker. Its true causal weight is exactly zero. Nevertheless, a linear probe recovers it at 0.8942 accuracy (0.3942 above chance)—an enormous false positive that would routinely be reported as a successful discovery of internal representation. Conversely, input-level intervention correctly returns a necessity indistinguishable from zero (-0.0007 ± 0.0013) in the null regime, while yielding 0.2031 ± 0.0124 in a label-coupled regime. Furthermore, a mathematical audit of representation ablation reveals it is mechanistically blind in this setting: projecting out the probe direction reports a necessity of 0.000067 ± 0.000623 even when input intervention proves the concept is actively used, representing an under-report of 3,046x. We propose the mandatory inclusion of null-calibrated interventional scores to validate discovery claims in neural networks.

TL;DR: Probing hidden activations for a concept produces massive false positives when the concept's true causal weight is zero; we mathematically audit estimators to show input intervention is null-calibrated.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly exposed to adaptive jailbreaking, particularly in high-stakes Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) domains. Although streaming probes enable real-time monitoring, they still make systematic errors. We identify a core issue: existing methods often rely on a few high-scoring tokens, leading to false alarms when sensitive CBRN terms appear in benign contexts. To address this, we introduce a streaming probing objective that requires multiple evidence tokens to consistently support a prediction, rather than relying on isolated spikes. This encourages more robust detection based on aggregated
signals instead of single-token cues. At a fixed 1% false-positive rate, our method improves the true-positive rate by 4.0%-35.55% relative to strong streaming baselines. We further observe substantial gains in AUROC, even when starting from near-saturated baseline performance (AUROC = 97.40%). We also show that probing Attention or MLP activations consistently outperforms residual-stream features. Finally, even when adversarial fine-tuning enables novel character-level ciphers, harmful intent remains detectable: probes developed for the base LLMs can be applied “plug-and-play” to these obfuscated attacks, achieving an AUROC of over 98.85%.

TL;DR: A multi-token evidence objective improves streaming detection by 4.0%-35.55% TPR at 1% FPR and achieves >98.85% AUROC against obfuscated attacks.

An activation steering edit should depend on the input exactly when the destination varies inside the class a query requests, and that is measurable before any rule is fitted or applied.

Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) adds one fixed direction to every input, the difference of the class means. Conditioning it on the requested class accounts for the between-class variation in the required displacement and leaves the within-class variation untouched, which no rule that reads only the source state can express. We study the impact of increasing input-dependence in the steering edit, moving from a difference of means to a destination retrieved per query—the mean of the 
k
 stored states nearest the query, inside the requested class—in which the two baselines are endpoints: at 
k
 equal to the class size the retrieved rule is the class-conditional difference of means.

We measure input-dependent steering on six substitution corpora that vary in whether the edit changes a word or a clause, and on an external benchmark, and find that input-dependent steering outperforms fixed-direction steering when the destination varies within the class. Retrieval wins at every layer of every substitution corpus in two models, and the level of input-dependence needed governs how to apply it: word-level edits are best made in the first tenth of the network from a few neighbours, clause-level edits at any depth from the class mean.

Where the class already determines the answer the class mean suffices and retrieval only matches it, though a fixed direction still fails there. Four quantities computed from the states alone identify the regime in which the edit should be applied.

TL;DR: Replacing activation steering's fixed direction with a destination retrieved per query wins at equal supervision, and the level of the concept being edited decides where in the network it helps and by how much.

Visual counting benchmarks report whether vision-language models produce the correct number, but not whether errors reflect perception or reasoning, nor what causes a reasoning failure. We introduce DecoyCount, 1,660 real-world images with pre-registered decoys across seven mechanisms, and identify a new reasoning failure we term visual-reasoning misalignment: models can execute the intended counting process when cued but fail to select it unaided; we quantify it with the reasoning-alignment gap, the paired accuracy gain from a matched cue. Despite possessing strong general reasoning, frontier VLMs remain below 50% accuracy on our benchmark, while matched cues improve accuracy by 11.8–22.1 percentage points, revealing substantial visual-reasoning misalignment. To test whether textual underspecification contributes to this misalignment, we introduce DecoyCount Multi-Hop, the first scenario-based multi-hop, multi-image counting benchmark; however, we find that its additional real-world context does not improve aggregate performance and rescues only a minority of neutral failures. Model scaling and increased inference-time reasoning improve accuracy but widen the gap; furthermore, agentic harnesses can exacerbate it. Thus stronger general reasoning does not guarantee aligned visual reasoning, with misalignment explaining one substantial component of the remaining deficit.

TL;DR: Our new benchmark isolate counting perception from reasoning by using visual decoys to expose a model's true reasoning alignment gap.

This paper investigates a technique for high-capacity associative memory with favorable scalability properties, based on the Kronecker product expansion of Sylvester Hadamard matrices.  Associations of key and value vectors in dimension $\text{log}_2 N$ are stored in a memory trace matrix of size $(\text{log}_2 N)\times N$, as opposed to $N$-dimensional vectors and $N\times N$ memory traces in more classical associative memory models.  The number of arithmetic operations for per-association storage/recall is also $\mathcal{O}(N \text{log}N)$.  For key and value vectors with binary $\pm 1$ elements, the model provably exhibits lossless recall of up to $N$ distinct associations.  However, we empirically observe robust recall under per-element Gaussian perturbations of binary key and value vectors with standard deviations up to $\approx 0.2$.  Lastly, this associative memory is fully differentiable, and we empirically assess its utility as a sub-module in larger deep learning models trained on downstream tasks involving memory, procedural knowledge, and algorithmic processing.

The tragedy of the commons poses a multiagent safety problem: reward-seeking agents can deplete a shared resource, and cooperation among its users does not itself specify how much must be preserved. We make preservation an explicit requirement by formulating a regenerative commons as a constrained Markov game or a constrained multi-agent MDP with a designer-specified depletion budget. We develop a nonstationary Lagrangian framework that constructs a policy sequence from solutions of unconstrained games or cooperative control problems. Extending earlier time-average constructions, we introduce average-epoch solution concepts for reset episodes with discounted rewards and terminal costs. We prove a reward-independent feasibility certificate, cooperative feasibility and approximate optimality against feasible policy mixtures, and an extension to unbiased sampled costs. For self-interested agents, a constrained Nash certificate quantifies the price-dispersion term introduced by deviations that redistribute budget across epochs. Under the stated assumptions on solver accuracy and multiplier updates, these results give constrained policy-sequence guarantees using solutions of unconstrained problems. Experiments with constrained IPPO and MAPPO in a Gordon--Schaefer fishery examine how depletion budgets shape stock retention, harvest rewards, and price adaptation.

Medical segmentation models predict where a lesion lies, but not what makes the marked tissue abnormal. Without an explanation in domain-specific terms, the model remains a black box that clinicians have no basis to trust. Concept bottleneck models address this by predicting named concepts first and computing the output from them, so the prediction is interpretable.
Existing concept bottlenecks need dense concept labels, either pixel-level annotations or scores from a foundation model. For many medical imaging tasks, neither is available for the concepts that experts use when searching for lesions. We present Concept2Mask, a concept bottleneck for segmentation in which each concept is a dense map, and the lesion mask is a linear function of these maps.  Only weak concept labels are required: the concept label says whether it is present anywhere in the lesion. The loss is built from clinically motivated assumptions about how the concepts relate to the lesion. We evaluate Concept2Mask on a subtle brain pathology that radiologists identify from a small set of imaging patterns  with clinical meaning, taking these patterns as the concepts, on data from two in-house cohorts and one public dataset. Concept2Mask outperforms strong baselines in detection and produces interpretable concept maps. The concept maps are not decorative: removing one concept channel degrades the segmentation of subjects who have that concept and leaves the other subjects almost unaffected. Against two baselines, Dice is lower but detection is better: Concept2Mask finds 96.2\% of lesions, against 81.4\% for the transformer ($p = 2\times10^{-10}$) and 66.7\% for nnU-Net ($p = 2\times10^{-20}$). No lesion found by either baseline is missed by Concept2Mask, which finds 34 lesions the transformer misses and 68 that nnU-Net misses, with $9\times$ fewer parameters than the transformer.

Deployed models can fail silently as the world they describe evolves. Attribution drift has served as an early warning in tabular data; we ask whether, in graph streams, a model's own explanations can forewarn the loss of nominal conformal coverage.
Doing so requires repairing the naive drift statistic twice. A vanishing edge loses mask mass regardless of whether the model relied on it, so we condition the importance on edge presence. Evolving graphs also break edge identity: a relabelling that changes nothing shifts the identity-based statistic by 0.69 on synthetic graphs and 0.83 on real ego-networks, whereas aggregating over structural roles brings both to 0.0 and stays well-defined when the support changes.
We test six pre-registered regimes on thirty seeds each. A two-channel monitor, tracking conditional mask mass and its distribution over roles, precedes coverage collapse by 8 to 14.5 steps across four gradual regimes (node addition, removal, replacement, and edge thinning), all surviving Holm correction. A sudden knockout yields the expected zero lead, and a harmless change triggers no alarm. Leads track the length of the transitional phase (Spearman 0.79 over 150 runs). On real transaction ego-networks, the untuned mass channel forewarns staged drift by 27 steps and is the only channel, attributional or structural, that never alarms on a stationary stream.
The main limitation is that the mass channel is blind to covariate drift, which breaks the guarantee in every run; the distributional channel detects it and also rescues the rewiring regime, so we report the two channels separately rather than as a union.

TL;DR: Label-free explanation drift forewarns conformal coverage collapse on evolving graphs, leading by 8–14 steps and never alarming on stationary streams.

Safe reinforcement learning often separates the quantity used to certify safety from the value function used to optimize the policy, so the certified behavior need not directly correspond to the policy's own objective.
We study this problem in solar-powered UGV navigation, where energy-aware decisions must remain viable under time-varying solar input.
We address this mismatch by formulating control as cost minimization and making the critic itself the safety certificate.
The critic is parameterized as an analytic distance to the target set multiplied by a bounded learned factor, which guarantees non-negativity, exact vanishing on the target set, and chosen class-$\mathcal{K}$ bounds for every parameter setting.
Thus, properness is enforced by architecture rather than assumed after training, while the same critic is used to estimate the policy's advantages.
Because the system is partially observed and driven by periodic solar forcing, per-step decrease is generally not admissible; instead, we certify finite-horizon contraction over each period and evaluate it using a scenario bound on held-out episodes.
The certificate contracts on $196$ of $200$ held-out periods, with no battery-depletion events, giving a $95\%$ confidence upper bound of $0.045$ on the per-period failure probability.
Ablations show that the cost formulation provides the required sign structure while the proper critic parameterization enforces the desired geometric bounds; in contrast, a merely non-negative critic violates the same bounds on $58.3\%$ of evaluated states.

TL;DR: We make the PPO critic itself a Lyapunov certificate by multiplying the analytic distance to the target set by a bounded learned factor, so properness holds by construction, and certify finite-horizon contraction on held-out episodes.

Repeated rollouts are needed to estimate the performance of stochastic LLM systems, including agents, but uniform repetition spends much of an evaluation budget on tasks that contribute little uncertainty to the reported score. The target metric may be capability, the probability of at least one success in $k$ independent attempts (pass@k), or reliability, the probability that all $k$ attempts succeed (pass^k). For capability, most of the uncertainty comes from tasks the system rarely solves; for reliability, it comes from tasks the system almost always solves. The tasks worth extra rollouts therefore depend on the metric and on the difficulty distribution. The natural way to exploit this is to allocate rollouts adaptively, choosing where to sample next from the outcomes observed so far. The usual combinatorial estimator, however, is unbiased only when each task's number of attempts is fixed in advance. Once the counts depend on the outcomes, the reported score can be biased. To avoid this, we propose a two-stage procedure that uses a small uniform pilot to estimate each task's contribution to uncertainty, then allocates the remaining budget to fresh rollouts accordingly, so the counts never depend on the outcomes they measure. Estimates from both stages are combined to retain the pilot information while preserving exact unbiasedness. We selected the allocation settings on synthetic task populations covering the full range of difficulty distributions. We then tested the procedure, with these settings fixed, on mathematical-reasoning benchmarks and on the agentic coding benchmark SWE-bench Lite. Savings are measured as the percentage of rollouts saved at matched root mean squared error (RMSE), including the pilot cost. Every test panel saves rollouts for pass@1 and pass^3 at every budget from 40 rollouts per task. On SWE-bench Lite, our procedure needs 22% fewer rollouts for pass@1 and 66% fewer for pass^3 to reach the RMSE of uniform sampling.

TL;DR: A two-stage allocation that plans extra rollouts from a pilot keeps pass@k and pass^k estimates unbiased and reaches the precision of uniform sampling with fewer rollouts.

As agents improve, users delegate increasingly complex tasks involving sequences of tool calls across multiple services. These user requests are often incomplete or constrained, requiring agents to ask for clarification or follow instructions that change how they ordinarily use tools and communicate. Moreover, users often make requests through end-user harnesses, such as Hermes and OpenClaw, which change how models act. Therefore, a tool-use benchmark for such tasks must use realistic service interfaces, support multi-turn user interaction, assess instruction-based behavioral steering and compare models across harnesses. Trustworthy evaluation also requires distinguishing agent failures from errors introduced by the infrastructure, harness integrations, user simulators, or verifiers. We present MULTIVERSE, a benchmark for cross-service delegation that simulates 35 real-world services with 809 tools in a self-contained sandbox. Its tasks include behavioral instructions and multi-turn settings that test whether agents seek missing information from a reticent user simulator. The benchmark compares twelve models on the same tasks under one bare harness (a simple loop) and four end-user harnesses. The strongest model–harness pair achieves a mean success rate of 69.8%. Instruction-following weaknesses differ across constraints: call budgets and final-response requirements have the highest average violation rates, while the most compliant model differs by instruction category. Agents struggle to obtain user-held information: in the multi-turn setting, 29.5% of attempts terminate without the agent consulting the user for information needed to solve the task. Among the models and settings evaluated, no harness is consistently best: a harness that helps one model can hurt another. Averaged across the evaluated models and settings, end-user harnesses perform nearly identically to the bare harness, despite large gains and losses for particular model–harness–setting combinations. We plan to release the benchmark and evaluation code and provide a leaderboard for the hidden test set.

The human brain contains billions of neurons connected by trillions of synapses, and its connectivity continually adapts. Inspired by biological development, Neural Developmental Programs (NDPs) construct artificial neural networks by optimising developmental rules rather than architectures directly. Standard NDPs grow networks through node replication, changing network size and connectivity together. We introduce Rewiring Neural Developmental Programs (R-NDPs), which instead construct policy networks by creating and removing connections among a fixed set of independently initialised nodes. Learned neural models propagate node states, select structural changes and predict connection weights. We also investigate a Hebbian extension in which developed node states encode plasticity parameters, allowing weights to adapt during policy execution. Across five reinforcement-learning control tasks and 30 evolutionary runs per condition, R-NDP without Hebbian learning generally matched or outperformed standard NDP. Hebbian learning had task-dependent effects: it improved target attainment on \textit{MountainCar} but did not consistently benefit the other tasks. These findings support connectivity-driven development as an alternative to network growth while showing that the value of synaptic plasticity depends on the task.

TL;DR: We introduce Rewiring Neural Developmental Programs (R-NDP), which develop reinforcement-learning policies by reorganising network connectivity and can incorporate Hebbian learning for within-lifetime adaptation.

Predictive biomarker discovery ranks patients by estimated treatment benefit and summarizes that ranking.
We parameterize these summaries using a rank kernel whose signed integral splits them into two families:
_spread_: which isolates benefit variation by removing the average effect, and _level_: which retains the average effect for subgroup thresholding.
Poor treatment-arm overlap and sparse clinical events distort both metrics.
Standard pipelines adjust base effect estimators but leave summary metrics uncorrected, forcing algorithms to optimize noise when overlap fails.
On null datasets lacking treatment heterogeneity, refining the rank partition inflates the uncorrected _spread_ claim,
while maximizing _level_ spuriously claims $80$% of restricted mean survival.
An exact de-bias removes the spread inflation at any stratum count.
For level objectives, a variance-dependent shrinkage curbs optimization bias by trading effect magnitude for selection stability,
removing $16.3\text{--}95.4$% of excess selection variance while discounting the noisiest strata by up to two-thirds on heteroscedastic test cases.
Neither correction alters underlying learning: corrected and uncorrected objectives select the same covariate in $99.7\%$ of $7{,}200$ paired fits.
For unrescuable cohorts, we add a model-free pre-fit gate, which at two rank strata rejects a cohort whose noise floor exceeds $63.9$ days.
Calibrated on $3{,}360$ fitted null cohorts, this floor marks where one in five de-biased fits claims half the reference effect on a null cohort, compared to $52.8$~days for uncorrected fits.
Neither cohort size nor overlap alters this $1.21\times$ extension except through the floor itself.
Because our safeguards evaluate the cohort and adjust the functional rather than altering the underlying estimator, both methods generalize to any effect model producing a ranked profile.

TL;DR: To stop biomarker algorithms from optimizing noise, we introduce model-agnostic gating and objective corrections that eliminate false discoveries while preserving true signal.

Recent agent benchmarks increasingly ground evaluation in executable environments, from code repair to web navigation, app APIs, and function calling. Yet completing consequential work beyond code requires more than producing a plausible response or valid tool call: agents must gather missing information over multiple turns, follow domain policies, coordinate dependent tools, and realize the correct persistent state transition without collateral effects. In this paper, we introduce Thinkingbox, a sandbox for tool-agent-user interaction that provides isolated MCP-compatible tool sessions, complete execution traces, and outcome evaluation over terminal backend state. Built on this sandbox, Thinkingbox-bench contains 507 policy-conditioned workflows across business scenarios, including retail, hospitality, auto insurance, neobank internal IT, and consulting IT/HR support. Each attempt is evaluated by task-specific executable checks that accept valid trajectories while rejecting wrong, missing, or extra effects; designated tasks additionally check required properties of the final response. Our experiments reveal that even the strongest proprietary and open-weight models show steep reliability drops: Claude Opus 5 falls from 66.50% pass@1 to 47.53% pass^20, and Kimi-K3 from 57.37% pass@1 to 13.41% pass^20. Moreover, many failed trials terminate cleanly after valid state-changing actions, so response- or tool-call-level signals poorly proxy end-to-end completion. Thinkingbox-bench reveals a large gap between occasionally finding a successful trajectory and reliably completing stateful business tasks.

TL;DR: We introduce Thinkingbox, a reusable sandbox, and Thinkingbox-bench, a 507-task benchmark for stateful business workflows, revealing a substantial gap between agents’ occasional success and reliable task completion.

Arterial stiffness, an independent predictor of cardiovascular events, can be measured non-invasively from guided waves launched along the arterial wall. Unlike bulk-wave measurements, these signals propagate as dispersive modes whose content depends jointly on geometry and material properties, challenging conventional model-based inversion in vivo. We examine whether a foundation model approach can instead learn transferable representations directly from the wave field. We pre-train a convolutional encoder without labels on simulations spanning a four-dimensional space of arterial geometry and viscoelastic material properties (35,280 in total, divided into training and held-out sets), using two self-supervised objectives, masked autoencoding (MAE) and a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), alongside a supervised reference trained on the shear modulus. The resulting representations are evaluated in three data domains of increasing realism: exact parameters in simulation, measured stiffness in tissue-mimicking phantoms, and clinical status from in vivo acquisitions in the common carotid artery (3,736 in 123 sessions from 105 subjects). To disentangle the value of pre-training from that of the architecture, we compare frozen representations with an untrained network of the same architecture. To assess whether they add information beyond the input, we also compare with a linear projection of the raw field and, for clinical discrimination, with physically interpretable dispersion-curve features. Using a parameter-free nearest-neighbour probe (k = 5), frozen MAE features achieve a mean AUROC of 0.81 over three pre-training seeds in discriminating healthy subjects from subjects with cardiovascular disease or risk factors, compared with 0.79 for the linear projection of the raw field, 0.72 for the dispersion-curve features, and 0.60 for the untrained network (mean over three initializations); MAE differs significantly only from the untrained network. In phantoms, however, the untrained network achieves the strongest shear-modulus recovery (mean  = 0.64 against $R^2 = 0.50$ for the strongest pre-trained encoder, MAE), suggesting that the convolutional architecture, through its inductive bias, is itself a strong baseline for this task. These results show that simulation pre-training can transfer clinically relevant information to in vivo classification, but that its benefits are task-dependent: MAE improves over the architecture alone for clinical discrimination under this probe, yet does not improve quantitative shear-modulus recovery in phantoms.

TL;DR: We show that a foundation model pre-trained on simulated arterial wave fields can transfer to clinical data, revealing task-dependent benefits over conventional model-based inversion and dispersion-curve features.

Semantic segmentation of large-scale aerial 3D point clouds requires both fine-grained geometric discrimination and reasoning over spatial structures that extend far beyond local neighborhoods. This is particularly challenging for aerial LiDAR and photogrammetric reconstructions, where point coordinates may be expressed under different orientations and where semantically related structures such as buildings, roads, vegetation, and infrastructure can span large spatial regions. Existing point-transformer methods model local geometry effectively, but positional information is typically encoded using conventional relative representations, while large-scale context is accumulated only indirectly through hierarchical propagation. To address these limitations, we propose the Quaternion Multiscale Context 3D Network (QMC-3DNet), which combines Quaternion Rotary Position Embedding (QuatRoPE) with a multiscale volumetric context pathway. QuatRoPE formulates query and key positional transformations as coordinate-dependent quaternion rotations, allowing relative 3D geometry to be encoded directly within query-key interactions without explicitly constructing pairwise positional tensors. Complementarily, the context pathway projects point features to structured 3D grids and incorporates a shared Haar Wavelet Neural Operator (Haar-WNO) to aggregate spatial information across multiple resolutions before fusing the resulting context back into the point representation through gated residual connections. Experiments on 3DAeroRelief and DALES show that QMC-3DNet is  effective across both photogrammetric and LiDAR point clouds, while ablation studies examine the contributions of QuatRoPE, Haar-WNO, multiscale depth, and context-operator choice. Together, these components provide a unified framework for combining relative 3D geometric encoding with explicit wide-context modeling for large-scale aerial point-cloud semantic segmentation.

Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly access external tools and services through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Current MCP deployments, however, verify only an agent's identity, not the set of tools that the agent is entitled to invoke. Moreover, the credential underlying this check is a software artifact, so a copy extracted from a compromised device carries the agent's full privileges. As agents grow more capable and autonomous in invoking tools, the impact of a single stolen credential grows with them. To address these issues, this paper proposes PRIMA (PUF-Rooted Identity-Bound MCP Agent Authorization), a hardware-rooted protocol that binds the tool authorization scope of an agent to its hardware identity, established by a Physical Unclonable Function (PUF). The server assigns the tool scope during enrollment and stores it against the PUF-derived identity of the agent, so the scope is never carried in any message the agent sends. Each session is opened by a fresh challenge to the PUF, and every subsequent tool invocation is checked against the scope bound to that identity, so an authenticated agent cannot extend its own privileges. The raw PUF response is retained by neither party, while nonces, timestamps and sequence numbers provide session freshness and replay protection. Anchoring identity and authorization in a single hardware-assisted primitive keeps verification overhead low, yielding a robust and lightweight protocol. Evaluation on an edge deployment shows 48.15% uniqueness and 99.8% reliability for the PUF, with approximately 32 ms of agent-side computation and 1.39 ms of server-side computation per session, the latter below the 1.50 ms and 3.80 ms reported for prior PUF-based schemes that verify identity alone and enforce no tool scope. Across 160 attack trials spanning eight scenarios, including unenrolled-device impersonation, session replay and privilege escalation through out-of-scope tool invocation, every trial produced the expected outcome, and all 400 tool-authorization decisions correctly enforced the enrolled scopes. These results demonstrate that hardware-rooted, identity-bound least-privilege authorization is practical for resource-constrained MCP agents, including Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) and smart healthcare deployments.

TL;DR: Authentication is not authorization: PRIMA roots an MCP agent's identity in a PUF and binds its tool permissions to that hardware, so a stolen credential opens nothing.

The exponential in softmax and SwiGLU is probably the highest-frequency non-
matmul operation in a transformer. Yet, unlike the matrix multiplications around
it, it is almost always computed at near-FP32 precision. We measure how much of
that precision is actually needed by truncating the mantissa of the exp2f result in-
side the inference kernels. Across Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B and Qwen3 235B,
and benchmarks spanning short-form reasoning to 100K-token contexts, both the
softmax exponential and SwiGLU tolerate removal of the entire mantissa, leaving
a bare power of two, with little to no accuracy degradation. Surprisingly, larger
models are more tolerant than smaller ones. First-order error-propagation bounds
are provided, showing that both softmax and sigmoid attenuate the exponential
error. Pushed to the limit, replacing softmax with hardmax collapses a pretrained
model, but annealing a temperature parameter recovers a functioning language
model. With hardmax, we can eliminate the exponential, one matrix multiplica-
tion, and the V-cache entirely, for an estimated 2x speedup of the attention l

TL;DR: Modern LLMs using transformer architecture can use very low precision exponenial functions with no noticeable degradation to accuracy.

Temporal knowledge graph extrapolation predicts future relational facts from past observations by combining structural regularities with recurring events. However, a gain in ranking accuracy alone does not explain whether a model benefits from informative historical evidence or from changes in competition among candidate entities. We study historical evidence fusion through a probabilistic framework that distinguishes candidate support, the probability mass assigned to that support, and the relative probabilities within it. The framework combines a normalized structural predictor with temporally discounted recurrence statistics and enables controlled comparisons of alternative history representations and fusion rules. Under a chronological evaluation protocol, we conduct multi-seed diagnostics on ICEWS14 and WIKI, including controls that retain retrieved candidates while replacing or permuting their historical weights. The results reveal dataset-dependent mechanisms: candidate-specific weights provide additional ranking gains on ICEWS14, whereas uniform and permuted alternatives reproduce much of the gain on WIKI. We further show that the correct answer's rank can improve without increasing its probability, exposing a distinction between recovering missing historical evidence and redistributing probability among competitors. Together, these findings provide a basis for designing and evaluating temporal predictors that account explicitly for both the availability of historical evidence and its effect on the predictive distribution.

TL;DR: We analyze how historical evidence shapes temporal knowledge graph predictions, distinguishing gains from candidate-specific information and probability redistribution among competing entities.

Vision-language models (VLMs) can explain their answers to clinical questions, yet these explanations need not reflect the visual evidence driving their predictions. Prompting methods such as chain-of-thought generate structured reasoning without guaranteeing its faithfulness, while causal attribution methods verify faithfulness only post hoc, at high per-example cost, and without teaching models to generate faithful explanations.
To address this gap, we introduce \textit{MedFaithAgent}, an agentic framework that makes causal faithfulness a trainable property of deployable VLMs. It identifies clinical concepts that are causally necessary, jointly sufficient, and visually grounded, using a counterfactual test calibrated against random equal-area removals and an actor–critic loop that repairs failing concepts. These verified explanations are distilled into a student model via supervised fine-tuning and verification-aligned reinforcement learning, enabling faithful explanations in a single forward pass. 
Since existing medical VQA benchmarks evaluate only answer correctness, we introduce \textit{MedFaithBench}, a clinically verified radiology benchmark spanning CT, MRI, and X-ray, annotated with causally verified concepts and grounded reasoning.
On MedFaithBench, the distilled student outperforms six prompting baselines, improving Faithfulness by 21\% and Causal Necessity by 50\% over chain-of-thought. These gains transfer to SLAKE, PathVQA, and the held-out PMC-VQA benchmark. These results show that causal faithfulness can be verified, distilled, and amortized into deployable medical VLMs.

Persistent memory allows language-model agents to retain user context, preferences, and task states across sessions, but remembered historical approvals frequently diverge from currently active human permissions. When stateful agents interact with emerging autonomous payment rails, an unverified memory record can trigger irreversible financial settlement. We formalize this vulnerability as memory-to-money authorization drift (MMAD): an internal memory error that translates into an unauthorized financial action. To systematically evaluate this failure mode, we introduce ghostpay v0.2, a paired benchmark of 1,440 synthetic episodes (720 matched risk/control pairs) spanning six failure classes, three payment rail modalities, four temporal horizons, and domain-disjoint partitions. We also design MAF (Memory-Authority Firewall), an architecture that decouples cognitive memory from an independently verified authority plane. Across the 1,152 held-out evaluation scenarios (576 pairs), heuristic and retrieval baselines exhibit high unauthorized execution rates (55.6%-60.6% UPER), whereas structured policy tracking and signed mandate verification eliminate unauthorized execution (0.0% UPER, 100.0% safe utility). In an audited exploratory pilot of 24 scenarios (12 matched pairs) evaluated on local open-weight models (llama3.2:1b and qwen2.5:1.5b), ungated agents unconditionally emitted payment requests across all risk scenarios (UPER = 100.0%), yielding 0.0% pair-safe utility, resistant to both provenance tags and governance prompts. Enforcing MAF eliminates unauthorized executions (0.0% UPER, paired McNemar p < 0.001), while legitimate payment completion is governed by model argument-schema fidelity. Our findings demonstrate that autonomous financial safety cannot rely on prompt governance or unstructured memory, requiring verifiable out-of-band authority gating.

Because of polysemanticity and superposition, it has been challenging to attribute
token understanding and generation to specific neurons. The information in the
transformer hidden states is so rich that the signs of the residual stream can be used
to surface the semantic content early in the neural network layers, and to control
what the model generates. We call this sign-pattern-driven interpretation approach
Bag of Dims (BoD). Using BoD, we read each dimension of the residual stream
individually. Since dimensions carry almost no shared information, a concept is
simply the set of dimensions that agree in sign. This lets us discover concepts
directly, without any training. A concept is detectable as early as the first few layers,
at AUC above 0.9 across the model families we tested, well before the answer it
resolves to becomes legible. The prediction capability of the signs is strong: setting
all magnitudes to unity preserves 56–94% top-5 next-token accuracy through the
language model head. Flipping a concept’s sign pattern during the live forward
pass suppresses that concept. This finding allows BoD to be used for model safety.
The concept suppression operates on the residual stream during prefill, before any
output tokens are generated, so harmful concepts in the input can be screened
and suppressed without a separate trained guard model, adding a safety check
at negligible extra cost within the existing forward pass. A separate and equally
cheap intervention instead steers a chosen concept into the generated text, without
any training. The BoD method depends on the transformers’ per-dimension sign
pattern, present across the residual stream, attention, and MLP subspaces, rather
than on any particular architecture, making it applicable to a wide range of models.

Multi-robot systems (MRS) will play an increasingly greater role in future robot operations, particularly in open-world environments typical of disaster recovery and planetary exploration. Planning for such MRS remains a formidable problem: coordination of multiple intelligent agents introduces novel challenges, in particular a large action space that increases combinatorially with the number of agents as well as unreliable inter-agent communication in open-world environments. Recently, visual language models (VLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot planning; VLMs allow users to flexibly express task specifications and semantic considerations through multi-modal interfaces, including natural language. Yet, the use of VLMs for planning and coordination of MRS remains an active area of research. We propose an architecture in which general-purpose VLMs jointly guide mobility and communication decisions of autonomous robotic agents, consuming the robots’ sensor streams; deciding which information should be shared among the agents; and issuing commands to an autonomous mobility stack. We demonstrate that grounding VLM decisions in role-specific contexts with local observations and dynamic persistent memory leads to dramatically improved task performance and scaling. We validate our framework through extensive simulations of a multi-agent mapping task, wherein a team of agents explores an unmapped region and task performance is measured by map reconstruction at a base station. Experiments show that the proposed architecture improves data packet delivery ratio and exploration coverage by up to 30.8% and 8.3%, respectively, compared to the strongest baseline, while demonstrating good scalability with increasing map size. We further provide design insights and recommendations through ablation studies and model comparisons within our proposed architecture.

Autoregressive decoding relies on the KV cache, whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length and caps batch size and throughput. Existing post-training methods exploit redundancy across tokens, layers, and feature dimensions, or lower numerical precision. We identify a complementary axis: within each attention head, values are largely predictable from their corresponding keys. We exploit this with value cache amortisation, which fits a lightweight per-head predictor at test time and stores residuals only for the tokens it reconstructs worst, giving $4\times$ near-lossless value compression. The predictor can be initialised by meta-learning for negligible prefill overhead, or fitted from scratch in settings that allow a one-off cost, such as multi-query inference. We pair value amortisation with cross-layer low-rank key compression to produce LowRAM, an asymmetric compression pipeline that stays close to lossless across three model families. By reconstructing only a selected subset of KV pairs at each decoding step, LowRAM can keep decoding overhead minimal and achieve up to $5\times$ higher peak decode throughput at $4\times$ compression. LowRAM further composes with quantisation and eviction, reaching $26.9\times$ compression at $94.5\%$ of baseline performance on long contexts. These results show that treating keys and values as structurally distinct enables efficient, aggressive, and composable KV cache compression.

Robot manipulation benchmarks score a single policy on a whole task, from finding the target to placing it, thus they cannot tell which policies have learned a skill that transfers. For instance, on LIBERO-PRO's position swap, eight policies that score 96.8–100% on LIBERO-Object all fall to 0–18%. On that account, we run each policy both end to end and inside SketcH, an open harness that locates a sketched target with sensors, moves the gripper next to it, and leaves only the grasp to the policy before it carries and places the object. Inside the harness, the eight policies differ in how well they grasp, and their success rates spread from 21% to 87%. In six of the eight policies, the features passed to the action head match the place of the gripper more closely than the object below it. Only the two π0.5 models and SimVLA move toward the object when the gripper hovers above it. X-VLA reads the location from its proprioception and VLA-Adapter from the scene camera's view of the arm, and both steer back toward where the object stood in training. For π0.5, the transferable grasp is learned within the first epoch and from about five demonstrations per object.

TL;DR: Only 2 of 8 VLAs learn a grasp that transfers to moved objects, and they are the ones that act on the object below the gripper instead of where it sat in training.

Wireless digital twins (DTs) rely on 3D environment models to predict radio propagation and support wireless-network decisions, yet these models are often initialized from imperfect 3D maps. Errors in building position, height, footprint, and orientation can therefore cause a high-fidelity propagation engine to simulate the wrong physical environment. In this paper, we study how a deployed wireless network can repair an existing DT using its own radio frequency (RF) measurements. In particular, we introduce Twin Residual Alignment and Calibration Engine (TRACE), a physics-grounded learning-based self-calibration framework that treats twin maintenance as residual alignment between the physical world and the current DT. Using the same sensor geometry and radio configuration as the physical measurements, TRACE uses ray tracing to generate corresponding RF observations from the current DT and compares them with the measured RF observations. The measured and simulated RF data are coherently backprojected onto a common metric world grid. For each building, TRACE extracts the same local region from both backprojections, centered at the building position specified by the current DT. TRACE then learns a multi-view corrector that combines evidence from multiple sensing nodes, accounts for their viewing geometry and the relative arrangement of buildings, and predicts a gated six-parameter geometric correction for each building. A key advantage of the TRACE design is that it suppresses shortcuts tied to absolute layout and sensor ordering, supports variable numbers of buildings and sensing nodes, and enables iterative correction through re-rendering. Across 5,400 held-out samples from unseen simulated scenes at $28$ GHz, TRACE reduces 3D position RMSE from $2.202$ m to $0.302$ m and yaw RMSE from $4.978^\circ$ to $0.894^\circ$. It also outperforms ViT and U-Net baselines under changes in layout, building count, sensing-node count, and SNR. On measured $28$ GHz RF data from the NIST outdoor courtyard, a model trained only on synthetic RF reduces mean planar wall-position error from $1.00$ m to $7.8$ cm, requiring neither measured-data fine-tuning nor ground-truth geometric labels for the measured data. These results show that the discrepancy between measured and twin-rendered RF observations can serve as a learning signal for repairing a wireless DT.

TL;DR: TRACE learns to self-calibrate imperfect wireless digital twins by comparing measured and twin-rendered radio frequency observations to correct building geometry, with direct sim-to-real transfer to measured 28 GHz data.

Butterfly Knife locates and numerically validates $A_2$ fold structure at
language-model token-pair decision boundaries. The fold normal form
specifies a local structure that persists under sufficiently small
smooth perturbations, making it an identifiable object for studying
safety-relevant decisions. A reduced screen classifies $216$ boundary points
on DistilGPT-2 and GPT-2 as fold candidates; two examples pass all seven
numerical validation criteria, including two-sheet continuation,
square-root scaling and cross-precision checks. For refuse/comply pairs,
$106$ of $121$ evaluable germs pass the same criteria across all seven
Qwen2.5-Instruct sizes from $0.5$B to $72$B, with median exponent $0.50$
at each size; $49$ concern the winning pair at the refined boundary.
An artifact-level join links $77$ certified germ identities to recorded
crossing measurements and $36$ certificate-bearing model--prompt pairs
to behavioural interventions. Separate scans identify refuse/comply
branches whose depth agrees with the onset of effective refusal-normal
ablation. Ablation produces judged
exploits across the size ladder; a $14$B follow-up raises the rate from
$1/19$ to $15/19$ by changing the sourcing layer. The controls remove
unequal activation magnitudes, leaving specificity at matched deletion
unresolved. The dose pilot is too coarsely resolved to establish an
advantage over a constant-dose baseline. The results make local fold
geometry experimentally accessible across model scales and connect its
refusal-related instances to measured safety outcomes.

TL;DR: We present a scanner to find the A_2 fold, it is stable under deformation, present in every transformer model we tested, and operationally relevant in safety behaviors at the minimum.

Applications of AI on edge devices are hampered by hardware limitations. To overcome these limitations, we re-frame sequence modeling through rotations on cooperating $SO(D)$ manifolds. Applied to sequence decoding, this enables stable recurrence over extended contexts that match standard Transformer baselines in perplexity with only $O(1)$ memory complexity at inference. In bypassing the context bottleneck of Transformers, Rotors offer a mathematically robust, deterministic and performant paradigm for real-time edge intelligence.

TL;DR: Fast pseudo-attentive edge inference via rotations on cooperating hyperspherical manifolds.

Recent advances in local computing hardware and small language models (SLMs) are making it increasingly practical to run capable language agents directly on personal devices. As these local models become strong enough to solve an increasing fraction of complex tasks, an appealing paradigm is to handle most computation locally while selectively delegating only the most difficult cases to a more capable cloud model. Realizing this paradigm, however, requires the local model to recognize its own capability boundary: it must determine when it can solve a task itself and when external assistance is necessary. In this work, we train such a self-orchestrating local model using reinforcement learning alone. The orchestrator can invoke a cloud expert as a tool at any point during its reasoning, incorporate the expert's response, and retain responsibility for producing the final answer.
