We extend GRPO with difficulty-aware reward shaping that discourages unnecessary expert calls on easy problems while encouraging delegation on difficult ones, thereby training the orchestrator to selectively seek assistance. We further introduce Random and Oracle bounds to characterize expected accuracy as a function of delegation rate. On AIME-2025, a Qwen3-4B-Instruct orchestrator paired with a GPT-OSS-20B expert delegates only 40% of problems while achieving 0.746 accuracy, approaching the expert-only accuracy of 0.78 and exceeding the Oracle bound. Despite being trained only on single-turn reasoning tasks, the learned delegation behavior transfers to the multi-turn personal-assistant benchmark Claw-Eval, where the orchestrator again exceeds the Oracle bound while escalating only a quarter of the tasks and consuming one-fifth of the expert's output tokens. Finally, we analyze the learned delegation behavior and show that replacing the expert with a stronger model improves accuracy without retraining the orchestrator, while scaling the orchestrator preserves the same selective delegation behavior.

TL;DR: We use a simple difficulty-aware RL reward to teach a small model both to solve more problems itself and to call a cloud expert only on hard ones, exceeding an oracle bound on math and agentic tasks.

Single-cell foundation models encode quantitative molecular states, whereas instruction-tuned language models provide flexible natural-language readout. Connecting them creates a cell–language form of the multimodal mirage: an accurate answer does not by itself establish that the decoder used the queried cell rather than prompt or language priors. We introduce CellSemantics, a continuous interface that maps frozen 1,280-dimensional Universal Cell Embeddings (UCE) through a two-stage Projector to 32 soft tokens consumed by frozen Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. The Projector is trained to retain relational and hierarchical structure and to support structured biological responses. We then intervene on the interface—replacing matched tokens with shuffled-cell, zero, or absent tokens—to make molecular evidence use measurable. Across five independently trained Projectors evaluated on 500 held-out Tabula Sapiens cells, correct-versus-shuffled gaps averaged 57.3 percentage points in broad-family macro accuracy and 51.6 points at mid-level resolution across three structured readout tasks. Against the best-performing label-free gene-text baseline, CellSemantics increased task-averaged mid-level macro accuracy from 35.4% to 55.2% while using 32 rather than approximately 143 evidence-token positions; broad-family performance was similar on average and task-dependent. Matched heads further showed that the interface retained UCE annotation separability. In simpler terms, CellSemantics makes cell states readable by a frozen language model and tests not only whether an answer is right, but whether it comes from the right cell.

TL;DR: CellSemantics makes cell states readable by a frozen LLM and tests whether its answers come from the matched cell.

Post-hoc conversion of a pretrained Transformer into a mostly convolutional
hybrid can reduce decoding cost and key--value (KV) cache memory, but such
conversions are commonly evaluated by how closely the student recovers the
teacher's perplexity. We show that perplexity recovery can substantially
overstate capability recovery. We replace most attention layers in
Pythia-1.4B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B with gated short-convolution mixers and
distill only the new parameters. On Pythia-1.4B with 6 of 24 attention layers retained, the resulting model
decodes 1.5--3.1$\times$ faster than a FlashAttention-3 teacher on an H100 and
uses a 4$\times$ smaller KV cache. However, retrieval recovers much later than
perplexity: increasing the retained attention budget from 8 to 10 layers raises
exact-key retrieval from 0.36 to 0.87, while perplexity changes only from
1.07$\times$ to 1.01$\times$ the teacher's. This retrieval transition persists
across larger distillation budgets and a different corpus, although its location
depends on the training recipe. Layer placement also matters substantially: at a fixed 6/24 attention budget,
retrieval ranges from 0.03 to 0.42 across placements. A short-convolution hybrid
pretrained from scratch succeeds on the same retrieval tasks, indicating that
the limitation is not inherent to the operator. Finally, near-teacher
in-domain perplexity does not guarantee out-of-domain quality, robust retrieval,
long-context behavior, or downstream accuracy. These results show that converted models should be evaluated jointly on
perplexity, retrieval robustness, long-context behavior, and downstream
performance.

TL;DR: Distilling Transformers into short-convolution hybrids recovers perplexity long before retrieval; harder probes lag further, and the sharp budget transition is Pythia-specific. Perplexity alone overstates converted models.

Brain-to-text decoders map fMRI to language through learned embeddings that are smaller and easier to share than raw recordings, but it is unknown whether these embeddings reveal whose brain produced them. We audit BP-GPT, an fMRI-to-text decoder, on eight participants retrained under a matched protocol. Raw functional connectivity identifies participants with 100\% top-1 accuracy (chance 12.5\%), and BP-GPT embeddings also reach 100\%, initially suggesting identity is fully preserved. However, BP-GPT trains a separate encoder per participant, so the model itself can leave a signature. Four observations confirm this: cross-participant embeddings share essentially no stimulus information, identification saturates at the encoder's first linear layer, between-subject differences account for 99.3\% of embedding variance, and subtracting each encoder's mean embedding alone collapses within-model identification to chance. Querying embeddings against profiles from independently seeded encoders isolates the signal that transfers across initializations: across twenty ordered pairs of five seed arms, accuracy falls to 54.3\% (subject-clustered 95\% CI 32.4-75.2\%; permutation $p=0.0001$), over four times chance but concentrated in a subset of participants. A classifier trained on four seed arms identifies participants in a fifth, unseen arm at 69.2\%, so pooling independent encoders strengthens rather than removes the transferable signal. An open-set verification attack that drops the labeled-gallery assumption confirms the same subset is vulnerable (AUC 0.742; per-participant equal error rate from 3.7\% to 44.9\%, Spearman $\rho=-0.88$ with closed-set identifiability). A targeted five-component subspace projection reduces cross-model identification on mean-pooled embeddings from 54.8\% to 7.5\% while retaining broadly comparable decoding quality in a preliminary UTS01 evaluation. Within-model identification therefore substantially overestimates re-identification risk in per-participant architectures, and the residual risk is highly uneven across individuals. Privacy audits of released representations should distinguish fingerprints introduced by the data from those introduced by the model.

TL;DR: BP-GPT’s apparent 100% identity leakage is largely driven by subject-specific encoder fingerprints, not neural identity alone.

Combining capabilities of multiple expert models trained starting from the same base checkpoint has become increasingly common in frontier language-model post-training. Recent trends suggest that multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) outperforms conventional off-policy methods.
  However, despite the higher inference and environment interaction costs incurred by MOPD, we find that much of its reported accuracy gain is due to certain training design choices and hyperparameter optimization, rather than the algorithm itself.
  We conduct a controlled self-distillation study across two multi-teacher settings, four models, and eleven benchmarks, comparing off-policy methods, namely supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and soft-label distillation, to hybrid teacher-prefix distillation and MOPD.
  We found that all four methods achieve \textit{nearly identical} accuracy. However, MOPD uses $14.8$--$23.1\times$ SFT's training GPU-hours.
  We also revisit four recently published comparisons between on-policy and off-policy distillation and find that the reported on-policy gains shrink substantially when SFT baselines are trained on rejection-sampled teacher trajectories and use independently tuned hyperparameters.
  As a training-free alternative, we also find that simple weight-merging methods can recover expert capabilities with minutes of CPU merging time, although their accuracy degrades as model size decreases and task interference increases.
  Overall, our results question recent gains reported due to MOPD and suggest careful tuning of more efficient off-policy baselines as a viable alternative.

When a previously learned task is relearned, recovery is defined at three levels: performance, function, and parameters. The first two have been studied in work on behavioral reversibility. We study the reversibility of parameter at the finest level: under random forward optimization, does a network still return toward its own previous weight states? The network is trained continuously on task cycles from A to B and back, and the full parameter history is recorded over more than 2,000 cycles and 40,000 independent training runs, each stopped at the same loss level. The results reveal an initial stage with disordered trajectories, then a stage with developing trajectories, and a final stage with stabilized periodicity. In this lifelong learning, periodicity provides evidence of weight reversibility, which proves stability at the behavioral level and may help establish a deterministic description of the mechanics of learning.

Combining verifier judgments, camera views, or human forecasts means deciding which sources to trust and how much evidence their agreement provides. Fusion rules are commonly learned from labeled examples, which may be unavailable on a new task. We argue that fusion is a measurement problem and propose Measured Fusion. Within-answer score variation measures attempt noise separately from persistent error. In a one-factor latent-class model, we establish when scores and dependent binary judges identify their joint likelihood without the need for labeled correctness. For equally informative, exchangeable Gaussian scores, the log-likelihood ratio reduces to Kish’s discounted sum, or an extremized mean; the true likelihood-ratio process inherits standard anytime-valid e-value guarantees for a candidate fixed in advance. Without correctness labels, Measured Fusion reaches 78.9% best-of-100 accuracy on Llama-70B GPQA, against 68.0% for Weaver tuned with labels on the same question folds, 66.8% for label-free FUSE and 79.4% for supervised logistic regression; modeling the eight judges’ shared error accounts for 10.2 points. On 891 SuperGPQA questions, label-free judge fusion reaches 46.02%, versus 46.46% for supervised logistic fusion and 46.24% for the strongest evaluated label-free pool. Reusing each panel’s frozen fit, eight-attempt selection exceeds Adaptive-Consistency’s accuracy by 4.6 to 9.8 points on all four Llama-70B panels. In a weekly replay of the four-year Good Judgment Project archive, pooling without outcomes recovers 92% of the Brier improvement that extremization fitted on an expanding history of resolved events achieves over the mean logit. With heads and calibration fixed, measured pooling has the lowest observed Scene-15 Brier of six pools on cross-entropy heads. Our calibrated multi-view pipeline exceeds TMC accuracy on three official benchmarks and matches or beats RCML in both comparisons.

TL;DR: Measured Fusion combines dependent sources without fusion labels and approaches supervised fusion across LLM verification, forecasting and multi-view classification.

We introduce a multi-turn interactive framework for reasoning evaluation that treats reasoning as active evidence acquisition and belief updating. Wherein, LLMs receive only the task rules, must issue targeted queries to a hidden environment, integrate partial observations over time, and decide when to submit a final answer. Beyond standard success rate and interaction efficiency, we evaluate contextual robustness under controlled contextual perturbations, and \emph{metacognitive adaptation} through \emph{counterfactual revision} and necessity judgment. We instantiate the framework as a benchmark of 474 executable games, each evaluated under five fixed configuration search spaces corresponding to five difficulty levels, and evaluate a broad set of frontier LLMs. Results show that the benchmark is highly discriminative, exposing large differences not only in success rate but also in interaction efficiency. Moreover, we empirically show that contextual perturbations cause moderate but consistent declines, whereas counterfactual revision and necessity judgment lead to much larger drops.

Continual learning for spiking neural networks (SNNs) is built on maintenance: every update is projected, regularized, or rehearsed so that a trained backbone keeps its earlier classes. The cost is paid on every step, including when a class the network already knows comes back. We ask how cheaply a gradient-free spiking learner can update when seen classes recur and what that costs in accuracy. Our method keeps a wide frozen random spiking expansion and a fixed random sketch and holds its readout as ridge sufficient statistics: each chunk is added to a Gram matrix and class sums, and the readout is solved once, with no gradient updates at deployment. A gated variant skips the write for a recurrence whose features are familiar and whose held-out accuracy is already high. On class-incremental streams with repetition over six datasets (frames, events, and audio spikes), five seeds, and baselines matched in width and stream, Our method (REWIRE) needs about 13$\times$ less modelled learner energy than Hebbian orthogonal projection (HLOP) and rehearsal, and about 2\,mJ per recurrence against 18 and 32\,mJ. Its backward transfer stays within 2 points of zero on five of the six datasets. The price is accuracy: it trails HLOP by 3.8 points on the eight-class streams and by 5.3 points on CIFAR-100, and ridge regression on the pretrained features alone is more accurate on the three natural-image datasets. On the spiking-audio stream SHD, it is 8.4 points above HLOP and 4.6 above rehearsal with the same memory. A ReLU random expansion of equal width matches the spiking one within 2 points, and skipping known recurrences helps every method, so the saving that remains is the cost of a write. We release the protocol, the cost account and the code.

TL;DR: REWIRE learns recurring classes in spiking neural networks (SNNs) without gradients, trading a few accuracy points for about 13 times less modelled learner energy than HLOP and rehearsal (SOTA).

Grouping latent features identified by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) may reveal how interactions among internal features are associated with vulnerabilities in large language models (LLMs). Understanding how these features are organized is important because model behavior emerges from coordinated feature activations. We study safety-relevant SAE features as structured groups rather than as isolated activations and ask three questions: (a) $\textit{When}$ harmful behavior occurs, do the associated activations form semantically coherent feature groups, or can behavior-altering interactions involve semantically distant features? (b) $\textit{What}$ is the minimal feature granularity required to induce safety failures, and can a single prompt token localize such feature subgroups? (c) $\textit{How}$ does the impact of feature subgrouping vary across malicious queries and conversational exchanges? We use external harmful-concept representations and token-level subspace similarity to identify prompt-conditioned SAE features, comparing cluster-based, hierarchical linkage-based, and single-token-driven grouping strategies. We amplify the identified feature subgroups and measure changes in harmfulness and generation quality. Across two adversarial benchmarks, SAE feature subgroups $\textit{substantially}$ alter model behavior. Feature subgroups localized using the token most strongly aligned with the harmful concept produce stronger steering effects than subgroups identified using multiple prompt tokens. This finding $\textit{challenges}$ prompt-level views of safety-relevant representations, suggesting that analyzing the prompt as a whole can miss safety vulnerabilities that are concentrated around a single token. Moreover, effective subgroups can contain semantically dissimilar features, showing that behavior-altering interactions need not form semantically coherent coalitions. We release our feature forensic toolkit \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Mechanistically_Steering-4720/README.md}{here} to support robustness testing of LLMs before deployment.

Understanding the rationale behind the decision-making process proves invaluable in various applications of AI and ML, such as robotics, healthcare, and industrial design. To make decision-making transparent, we define interpretable policies as list-based maps. Given the parameters of a Markov Decision Process and under a list-based definition of interpretability, we devise an algorithm, 'Value Interpretable Dynamic Treatment Regimes', that produces list-based policies as its output. We present theoretical bounds and algorithmic improvements for the same. We analyze the behaviour of the algorithm under 'tightness' conditions and provide convergence properties and potential improvements in this scenario. Furthermore, we show that the optimization problem can be formulated as a mixed-integer optimization problem. Further, we write the problem as a genetic algorithm for which we provide mixing time guarantees.

TL;DR: Model-based interpretable reinforcement learning algorithm where the optimal regions and actions are chosen in a greedy manner. Theoretical bounds are computed, and experiments are done for this and the related methods.

How much does a road graph help a traffic forecaster? The answer depends on what else the model already knows. We cross two inputs, a supplied road graph and a fixed random code that identifies each sensor, in separately trained Graph WaveNet models on METR-LA and PEMS04 with five paired training seeds. Without the code, the road graph lowers pooled test mean absolute error by 0.4338 and 1.5424. Once every sensor carries the code, the same graph lowers it by 0.1906 and 0.1366, a credit 2.3 and 11.3 times smaller, yet the graph's gain stays positive. Their gains overlap, and neither input replaces the other. A formal boundary shows why one comparison cannot stand in for the other: at the level of Bayes risk, the gain a component brings without identity in general neither bounds nor determines its gain beyond identity. Graph components should therefore be evaluated against an explicit sensor-identity baseline, with both comparisons reported side by side.

TL;DR: Once every sensor carries a fixed random identity code, the gain credited to a road graph in Graph WaveNet shrinks by a factor of 2.3 to 11.3, so graph components should be evaluated against an explicit identity baseline.

While tabular machine learning has witnessed substantial algorithmic advances, empirical evaluation remains predominantly confined to static and small-scale academic benchmarks (e.g., OpenML). These lab-centric setups rely on idealized, clean data distributions, obscuring the severe operational vulnerabilities of models deployed in non-stationary and hostile production environments such as industrial fraud defense, where misguided model selection directly translates into catastrophic financial losses and severe fraud exposure. To bridge this research-to-production gap, we introduce TabFraud, the first production-centric tabular benchmark derived from 15.3 billion fraud-exposed digital payment transactions. Spanning 547 fraud-oriented quantitative features across nine core payment scenarios, TabFraud formulates 22 curated train-test pairs governed by a flexible multi-split dataset protocol across five industrial stress-testing tracks: extreme data scaling, pervasive feature missingness, out-of-time (OOT) distribution shift, manual-review label noise, and zero-shot generalization. We extensively benchmark non-deep tree ensembles, task-specific deep architectures and emerging schema-agnostic tabular foundation models (e.g., TabPFN). Transcending an isolated global score (e.g., AUC, KS), we establish a production-aligned, multidimensional evaluation protocol encompassing operational utility (Recall@low-FPR), dynamic robustness, offline cost and online feasibility. Accompanied by a standardized development and evaluation toolkit, TabFraud provides a rigorous testbed for deployable, production-ready tabular intelligence.

TL;DR: An large-scale real-world tabular benchmark of payment fraud detection for production-ready tabular prediction model evaluation

Root cause analysis (RCA) in microservice systems identifies the faulty component, fault reason, and onset time from heterogeneous telemetry. Lightweight models can efficiently rank candidates but provide limited evidence for assessing their predictions, whereas direct LLM-based diagnosis may produce answers that are weakly grounded in the observations. Fault propagation further complicates RCA: anomalies from multiple events may coexist within an observation window, causing the predicted component, reason, and time to originate from different events or downstream symptoms.  We present RCASMol, a framework that separates evidence gathering from adjudication. Lightweight models and a behavior tree gather and verify evidence from the current monitoring data. RCASMol then aligns the fields requested by the task using component scope and shared metric or network-path evidence, and it screens events that behave as propagated symptoms through source--victim discrimination. The LLM compares the resulting candidates with their evidence and binding status, and a selection contract checks the selected identifiers. On the Bank, Market, and Telecom systems of the OpenRCA benchmark, RCASMol reaches exact accuracies of 46.00\%, 22.45\%, and 37.50\%, whereas an LLM that diagnoses from the same observations reaches exact accuracies of 28.00\%, 0.00\%, and 6.25\%, respectively. Removing the evidence constraint lowers exact accuracy by 16.00, 8.16, and 18.75 points on the three systems.

Preeclampsia is a major pregnancy complication for which earlier, minimally invasive risk detection remains clinically important. Our research investigates whether preeclampsia-associated information learned from placental transcriptomes can be transferred to maternal plasma cell-free RNA (cfRNA) across unpaired cohorts. Placental RNA-seq data from GSE234729 and maternal cfRNA data from GSE192902 were harmonised to 4,492 shared Reactome-covered genes. Placenta was treated as the labelled source domain and cfRNA as an unlabelled target domain. A Reactome-constrained Graph Convolutional Network was evaluated across various experiments like flat baselines, random-topology controls, post-hoc Optimal Transport (OT), Gromov-Wasserstein (GW), Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (FGW), and Integrated OT during representation learning. While direct transfer was modest, with logistic regression achieving AUROC 0.6027 and the Reactome-GCN 0.5301, repeated post-hoc alignment produced no robust improvement. In contrast, Integrated OT increased mean transductive AUROC from 0.4396 to 0.5904 and PR AUC from 0.3002 to 0.3735. When 30\% of cfRNA samples were excluded from adaptation, AUROC increased from 0.3779 to 0.5519. The results from the study suggest that cross-tissue alignment is more effective when incorporated during representation learning than when applied post hoc, while supporting only partial, non-clinical placenta-to-cfRNA transfer.

We study how to choose the field, strength, and timing of housekeeping-current injection (HCI) to reduce copying during diffusion sampling, while the score network stays fixed. 
HCI preserves a prescribed reference density but cannot correct the drift error with respect to it, so we add a transport current along the score gap. From one batch of baseline trajectories, a Gram matrix and a response vector give the optimal combination at a chosen drift strength.
This is the natural-gradient descent direction of the copy probability. We also show when a finite set of fields can reach the optimal reference-preserving direction. 
We verify the response formulas analytically with an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck calculation and test HCI numerically on a ring model. On CIFAR-10, HCI and a score-gap correction reduce copying while improving FID. On CelebA64, HCI reduces copying, while adding the gap reduces it further at a cost in KID.

TL;DR: We derive a natural-gradient method that optimizes a reference-preserving housekeeping current and a transport current from baseline trajectories, reducing training-data copying in diffusion models without retraining.

Language models are now increasingly used as safety classifiers in production
systems. Specialized safety classifiers, once trained and deployed, are fixed, and its
weights encode the policy it was trained on. However, policies now change often,
as agents gain new capabilities and new attack vectors appear, and each new policy
often has very little data to learn from. A frozen model asked to apply a new policy
from scratch often has low accuracy, and retraining a large model for every change
is slow and expensive. We propose Memory Descent, an external memory for
frozen language models that is learned by descent on a policy’s labelled examples.
Across five safety benchmarks, Memory Descent outperforms 12 previous memory
and prompt-optimization methods. On ATBench it reaches 52.2 diagnostic macro
F1, compared with 32.6 for the strongest published method and 43.3 for the trained
guard AgentDoG 1.5.

Machine unlearning has emerged as a critical ca-
pability for removing the influence of previously learned data
to satisfy privacy regulations, eliminate erroneous information,
and improve the trustworthiness of machine learning systems.
While existing machine unlearning methods have demonstrated
promising performance, they are primarily designed and eval-
uated in static learning settings. In contrast, many real-world
artificial intelligence applications operate in continual learning
environments, where models are continuously updated as new
data become available. In such adaptive systems, effective ma-
chine unlearning requires not only removing targeted knowledge
but also preserving the model’s ability to continue learning from
future data. This paper presents STAIR, a Stage-Aware Incre-
mental Unlearning framework designed for continual learning
systems that enables selective removal of previously learned
information without requiring complete model retraining. Unlike
conventional machine unlearning approaches that evaluate only
immediate forgetting performance, STAIR additionally evaluates
post-unlearning adaptation, assessing how selective forgetting
influences a model’s ability to effectively learn from subsequent
data. Furthermore, the proposed framework investigates how the
temporal stage at which information is learned affects forgetting
effectiveness, computational efficiency, and future model adapta-
tion. Extensive experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-
100 demonstrate that STAIR achieves predictive performance
comparable to full retraining while reducing unlearning time
by more than an order of magnitude. The experimental results
further reveal that the temporal position of learned information
significantly influences forgetting behavior, post-unlearning adap-
tation, and computational efficiency, providing new insights into
practical machine unlearning for continually evolving learning
systems.

Identifying acquisition artifacts in medical images is vital for quality control, yet device-generated quality scores capture them poorly. We formulate the problem of acquisition artifact identification as an in-distribution anomaly detection task, where the core challenge becomes separating acquisition artifacts from pathology. We introduce RetOCT-AD, an acquisition-quality scoring framework for retinal optical coherence tomography (OCT) that leverages a known set of synthetic imaging artifacts (degradations) and foundation-model representations for few-shot anomaly detection. We learn a nonlinear, transformer-based projector that maps degraded-image features to the corresponding clean-image features. Using prior knowledge of the synthetic degradations, we extract degradation associated components of the projection residuals to score acquisition artifacts. On synthetic degradations, RetOCT-AD outperforms all baselines. On 104 real B-scans, it agrees with two graders on 88.9\% of pairwise artifact comparisons, its score rises with the number of graded artifacts, and it is not raised by geographic atrophy or drusen across the test set.

TL;DR: We propose RetOCT-AD, a foundation model-based anomaly detection framework that identifies image acquisition artifacts in retinal OCT scans orthogonal to underlying pathologies

Language models often answer underspecified questions when they should clarify, but the ambiguity relevant to clarification is model-relative: a question matters as ambiguous only insofar as the model represents competing interpretations. We frame selective clarification as a representation--behaviour alignment problem: ambiguity is recoverable from hidden states, but model behaviour does not reliably act on it. We introduce BAIA, which uses a lightweight probe over frozen activations to construct ask-versus-answer supervision and align behaviour to representation. Across seven benchmarks, BAIA reduces mean in-domain false clarification from 19.9\% (APA) to 4.1\% while increasing ambiguous-query F1 from 79.9\% to 83.9\%, and transfers across domains. After fine-tuning, clarification behaviour tracks the frozen-base ambiguity signal more closely, suggesting that models can be trained to act on distinctions already represented internally.

TL;DR: Hidden-state probes separate ambiguity from answer difficulty far more reliably than output entropy; we use this internal signal to select fine-tuning data, aligning model behaviour with its internal representations.

Reduced EEG montages promise simpler acquisition, but comparing a reduced
montage with the full montage alone conflates two questions: how many elec-
trodes a decoder needs (compression), and whether choosing particular electrodes
helps beyond that number (selection). We evaluate the two separately. Using
a compact EEGNet-style decoder on imagined left- versus right-fist movement
from the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Dataset (106 participants;
subject-wise split of 74/16/16), we fixed a 90% retention criterion in advance,
selected the channel budget on validation participants only, evaluated it once on
held-out participants, and compared a training-only Fisher ranking with equal-
budget random subsets. Validation selected 32 of 64 channels, which retained
94.8% of full-montage Cohen’s κ (0.420 vs. 0.443). On held-out participants
the same budget retained 89.7% (0.292 vs. 0.326), and participant-level boot-
strap intervals (0.698–1.079) include 90%, so the test neither confirms nor rules
out the criterion. The Fisher ranking was never clearly separated from equal-
budget random subsets. With 20 subsets per budget, no one-sided p fell below
0.14; in a post-test, validation-only expansion to 100 subsets, the ranked mon-
tage sat at the 74th (k=16) and 87th (k=32) percentiles (p = 0.267 and 0.139).
Validation-only follow-ups point the same way: an eight-channel sensorimotor
montage outperformed the ranked montage on ten fresh seeds (∆κ = +0.120,
95% CI 0.088–0.151) but not random subsets of the same scalp strip, participant-
specific montages did not exceed random ones, and distillation was inconclusive.
Reduced-montage claims therefore need both equal-budget random baselines and
a held-out, uncertainty-aware check of the selected budget

TL;DR: We investigate how EEG channel selection and reduction affect the efficiency and reliability of motor-imagery brain–computer interface decoding.

Discovering organic molecules for semiconductors and energy storage and conversion requires searching a chemical space too large for exhaustive density-functional theory (DFT) calculations. Existing quantum-chemical datasets provide limited coverage of the low-gap π-conjugated molecules central to these applications, particularly with optimized 3D geometries at scale. We introduce 5.16 billion π-conjugated molecules assembled from ring cores and sidechain fragments, including cores from experimentally reported molecular semiconductors and redox-active molecules, with GFN2-xTB-optimized geometries, electronic properties, and generative lineage. The corpus is about three orders of magnitude larger than previous π-conjugated-molecule datasets with computed electronic properties, required ∼8 million CPU core-hours to generate, and occupies a distinct electronic regime, with a mean HOMO–LUMO gap of 2.3 eV compared with 5.1 eV for QM9 molecules evaluated using the same pipeline.

Because geometry optimization dominates the cost of constructing such a corpus, we use it to ask how much explicit 3D geometry and self-supervised pretraining each contribute to learned molecular representations. We compare fingerprint (1D), molecular-graph (2D), and geometry-aware (3D) encoders pretrained on matched subsets of the corpus, together with public self-supervised molecular models. Across fifteen DFT property-prediction tasks on a scaffold-disjoint benchmark of approximately 25,000 organic molecules, geometry-aware encoders achieve the lowest errors under both frozen and end-to-end evaluation. Most of this advantage arises from the 3D representation and equivariant inductive bias rather than from pretraining alone: after fine-tuning, 3D encoders given GFN2-xTB geometries outperform all evaluated fingerprint and graph models at as few as 2.1M parameters even from random initialization. Coordinate-denoising pretraining provides an additional 10–14% improvement for EquiformerV2-XL, while yielding smaller gains for lower-capacity 3D models. The tested self-supervised SMILES and graph representations provide no additional improvement over the 3D representation under frozen-feature fusion. Among the encoders pretrained in this work, the best fine-tuned 3D model achieves the lowest error on all fifteen DFT targets, including HOMO and LUMO errors 9.5% and 8.1% below the strongest refitted descriptor baseline and 20–29% below affine-calibrated GFN2-xTB predictions. These results separate the contributions of geometry, architecture, and pretraining, and show that accurate 3D molecular representations can provide a strong foundation for learning electronic properties across large π-conjugated chemical spaces.

TL;DR: We release 5.16 billion π-conjugated molecules with xTB-optimized 3D geometries and study how representation, scale, and coreset selection shape molecular pretraining; equivariant 3D models win on all fifteen DFT benchmarks

Whether access to a frontier language model materially increases a non-expert's ability to plan a chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) attack, beyond what public tools already provide, is a question that current evaluations answer in incompatible ways. They define non-experts, threat scope, baselines, scoring, and decision rules differently, so their results cannot be compared. We propose Threshold Exceedance Criteria (TEC) framework that fixes each of these choices in advance and treats them as separate, independently specifiable components of an uplift study. The framework distinguishes generative uplift, where the model helps write a plan from scratch, from revisionist uplift, where it helps improve a plan the participant already wrote. We applied it to a pre-release model with 527 non-expert participants across all four CBRN domains, in a three-arm design whose attack plans were scored by subject-matter experts blind to condition. The material-uplift criterion was exceeded only in the radiological domain, and only in the generative comparison. The result is specific to this model, these scenarios, and these thresholds; it was used to decide on pre-deployment mitigations, not to describe the deployed model. The reusable contribution is the framework, and we draw out what the study taught us about running such evaluations: decision rules must be fixed before data are collected, baselines stated, generative and revisionist effects estimated separately, and early signals kept apart from confirmed determinations.

TL;DR: Threshold Exceedance Criteria make CBRN uplift evaluations prespecified and comparable; applying them in  a large-scale expert-reviewed study separating generative from revisionist uplift, material uplift was confined to the radiological domain.

Computational models have explanatory power to understand cognition in individuals, but there is usually not enough training data to build such models with traditional machine learning.  However, alternative architectures that model neural and cognitive processes in more detail can be more easily fit to individuals and can lead to mechanistic insights into human behavior.  BiLex is such a computational model of the bilingual lexicon, containing a shared semantic system and phonetic language systems represented through self-organizing maps. In this study, BiLex was extended further into biological realism with excitatory and inhibitory lateral connections. This extension makes it possible to account for response times as well as common errors such as those based on semantic concept familiarity, typicality, and specificity. The Boston Naming Test was simulated in Spanish and English, and model performance approximated naming accuracy and error types in Spanish-English bilinguals with varying primary and secondary language histories. The results indicated that the approach captures semantic-level processes in bilingual lexical access, thus modeling the semantic cognition of individual subjects. In the future, such models may serve as a foundation for modeling impairments and treatment options.

TL;DR: Bilingual lexical-semantic naming processes and error behavior are modeled through a computational model with lateral connections.

Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) provides a common quadratic form for many discrete optimization problems, yet reaching strong solutions quickly remains difficult on large instances. We propose TReX (Tabu-based Replica Exchange), a GPU-resident parallel tabu-search solver designed to reduce this time to target. The central idea of TReX is not merely to run searches with different tabu tenures in parallel, but to move a continuing search among them. TReX runs multiple GPU-resident one-flip tabu searches with different tabu tenures and selectively exchanges continuing searches between adjacent tenure settings while preserving their search state. We evaluate TReX using one fixed configuration and ten seeds per instance on a single NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti 16 GB GPU, without instance-specific retuning. Geometric-mean target-attainment times are 6.16 ms across 60 binary quadratic programming instances from OR-Library and 19.1 ms across 23 instances from the Quadratic Programming Library. For high-dimensional random instances, the corresponding times are 1.112 s across 21 benchmark instances and 114.77 s across three generated instances with 10,000 variables; all 30 runs on the latter reach the specified reference targets. A five-condition ten-seed ablation on the 21 high-dimensional random benchmark instances further shows that conditional exchange modestly reduces capped geometric-mean time to hit (TTH) under homogeneous tenure (3.368 s to 3.295 s). Under heterogeneous tenure, conditional exchange reduces the same metric from 3.371 s to 1.070 s and outperforms all-accept exchange at 1.695 s. These results support the TReX design in which a continuing search selectively moves among different tabu tenures to accelerate target attainment.

TL;DR: On a single RTX 5070 Ti, TREx reaches the reference targets in all 243 B60/P21 runs, with geometric-mean time-to-targets of 6.04 ms and 1.004 s, respectively.

$Engineering design with large language models (LLMs) requires a clear connection between language-generated task descriptions and the dynamical conditions used to assess a controller. We present Control-Constrained Reasoning (CCR), an ontology-grounded framework for organizing this connection in controller synthesis. An LLM produces a structured design proposal, which is reconciled with a designated engineering specification. An executable knowledge layer uses ontology instances, validation shapes, and inference rules to identify control components and applicable constraint records. A Control Constraint Intermediate Representation (CCIR) passes these records to explicit numerical builders and external checks, while a runtime harness retains stage artifacts and coordinates bounded design revisions. In the implemented synthesis path, the LLM supplies an initial structured description; model construction, controller gains, implementation refinement, and evaluation metrics are computed by external modules. We instantiate CCR for boost and buck converters with constant-power loads and for a three-phase inverter. The detailed boost case combines switching-model evaluation, a recorded phase margin of $90.04^\circ$ and gain margin of 40.32~dB, and hardware load-step measurements. The three cases reuse the same proposal and execution interfaces with plant-specific knowledge. The resulting implementation provides traceable links among language-based specification handling, executable control knowledge, and numerical design records.$

Multimodal Sentiment Analysis (MSA) requires both efficient cross-modal interaction and well-aligned representations. Existing methods typically rely on dense pairwise attention, incurring substantial redundant parameters and computation, while contrastive learning aligns only at the sample level and ignores sentiment consistency, limiting sentiment discriminability. To address these issues, we propose a Low-rank Cross-modal Transformer with Two-stage Contrastive Learning (LCT-TCL). LCT captures cross-modal interactions through shared low-rank factor matrices, substantially reducing redundancy while yielding more effective fusion. TCL improves sentiment discriminability by aligning modalities before fusion to bridge modality gaps, and by organizing representations according to sentiment polarity after fusion, producing more sentiment-discriminative representations. On three widely used benchmarks (CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS), LCT-TCL achieves superior or comparable performance across multiple evaluation metrics, while requiring the fewest parameters and lowest FLOPs among Transformer-based methods.

TL;DR: LCT-TCL: a low-rank cross-modal Transformer with two-stage contrastive learning for efficient and sentiment-discriminative multimodal sentiment analysis.

Web agents can fail because information is missing from their observation, but also because they cannot identify the boundaries of information they have read. We separate these failures in controlled web tasks. In a 1,760-trial grid, canvas removed target text from all three tested structural observations while the target region remained visible to vision. The original vision deployments nevertheless failed all 40 canvas trials: every response contained the correct token with an adjacent marker appended. Follow-ups across four deployments show that greater visual separation, labeled components, and explicit output constraints reduce this failure. An additional 880-trial study varies target values, marker strings, positions, and typography: increasing the target--distractor gap from 8 to 96 pixels reduced delimitation errors by 80--85 percentage points in every deployment and improved task success. Labeled components yielded 0/240 observed delimitation errors in the original fixed-token study and 1/240 under instance variation; the latter was a truncated target without marker inclusion. Explicit-format prompts raised varied-canvas task success from 0/80 to 57/80. The central findings are that structural observations can omit information, reading the correct token does not ensure correct delimitation, and stronger boundaries or output constraints can substantially reduce failure. We distinguish structural text reachability, target-region visibility, recovered content, and completed actions; the findings concern versioned stacks and controlled tasks rather than a universal separation threshold.

TL;DR: We separate what web agents can observe from what they can accomplish, identifying observation gaps and answer-boundary errors.

Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce \textbf{introspective oversight}, which trains a model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual responses. We implement this by adding a separate observer channel that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.788). These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

TL;DR: Post-training in a new 3rd person role for oversight

Softmax attention scores a query against a key by their dot product, which grows with the norm of the key. One key with a large norm can therefore score highly against every query, and this is where attention sinks come from and why softmax needs a normalization layer or weight clipping to train under aggressive optimizers. We introduce JordanAttention, which scores a pair by the hyperbolic distance between them after lifting queries and keys to the unit hyperboloid of the Lorentz cone. A distance score is largest when key and query coincide, de- creases with their distance at a rate each head learns, and lets a key score highly only for queries near it. Since the Minkowski product of any two points on the hyperboloid is at least 1, the score stays bounded however large the weights grow. At GPT-2-small scale on FineWeb-Edu, with the optimizer, schedule and learning rate matched, JordanAttention has no attention sinks where softmax under Muon puts up to 83% of a layer’s attention on the first token; it matches softmax with QK-normalization and RoPE at the default key width, trains where softmax without the normalization fails, and trains without clipping in latent attention, where softmax collapses at every learning rate. As the key width shrinks it degrades at half the rate of softmax, with a width exponent of 0.49 against 0.84 and a lead of 0.09 nats at width 8 over three seeds. The kernel also factorizes exactly in Beltrami–Klein coordinates, and the resulting linear-time attention, with an exact 128-token window, matches the quadratic form and beats softmax at key width 8. A control study attributes the advantage to the distance-based similarity and the stability to the bound.

TL;DR: Replacing softmax with a Lorentz-cone kernel whose score is bounded by a geometric identity eliminates attention sinks, trains at 80x higher Muon learning rates, and admits an exact deterministic linear-time kernel expansion.

As tool-using agents have become increasingly prevalent in private workflows, they can take actions that exceed the authorized scope of a user's request. With this broader access comes the danger of prompt injection attacks, as well as agents simply overstepping on benign tasks. In our study, we test whether a language model can be trained to discern what a user has authorized and express it as a policy that is enforced on every tool call via a deterministic evaluator. To do this, we center our experiments on counterfactual pairs of requests that differ in a single change to what the user has authorized. Existing models score well on the single requests but perform noticeably worse on full pairs, with one trained model scoring 60.0% on single requests but only 27.6% on pairs. To address this, we compare SFT alone with SFT plus DPO, using negatives built by editing the correct policy or drawn from the model's own errors. None of the these training methods provides a clear fix. On the training family, we found that the edited-policy negatives cut down false allows from 10.7% with SFT alone to 1.2% while preserving authorized recall. However, on a separate transfer pilot, we found a similar decrease in false allows (from about 22% to 1.9%), but with the model also approving fewer legitimate requests, which may point to the model just learning to reject more. We ran one broader experiment, which showed a negative result: building negatives from the paired request did not reproduce the advantage.

TL;DR: Training LLMs to preserve user authorization in tool-use policies through counterfactual examples.

Agents can solve increasingly demanding tasks, yet real-world interaction can produce situations beyond their prior experience. Feedback supports continued learning, but the experience an agent can acquire is limited by the actions its environment allows. Can the agent use this experience to improve its opportunities for further learning? We propose Recursive Experience Learning (REL), which couples a learner with an agentic environment through two interacting loops. In the inner loop, a fast model learns from task feedback, while a meta model consolidates current and historical behavior. In the outer loop, the constructor uses interaction records and past revision outcomes to propose executable rule changes that add, replace, or deactivate available actions. REL assesses each candidate against the unchanged environment by continuing learning from a common learner state under matched resource budgets. Acceptance requires higher final task utility than the unchanged control while limiting measured capability loss on historical probes evaluated under the candidate rules. The validated checkpoint carries learning forward under a fixed task objective and evaluator. REL achieves 100\% correctness across 250 KernelBench workloads and a $1.85\times$ geometric-mean speedup over torch.compile on Level 3. On 40 CVDP problems, its 7B configuration solves 87.5\%, compared with 82.5\% for ACE-RTL with the same backbone. Sequential-task experiments and ablations support complementary benefits from learner continuation, rule evolution, and historical consolidation. These results support using experience to improve both current behavior and the action space available for subsequent learning.

TL;DR: REL couples continual reinforcement learning with environment evolution, using experience to improve policies and expand the interactions available for future learning.

Robots operating in cluttered spaces need whole-body collision awareness to avoid unintended contact with their surroundings. Existing visuomotor policies rely on cameras to perceive obstacles, which provide rich global scene context but suffer from partial observability due to occlusions. More fundamentally, whole-body collision awareness depends on the distance between each robot link and nearby obstacles, which changes continuously with the robot's configuration. Camera observations do not represent these distances directly, forcing policies to infer them implicitly from images, which makes collisions with links outside the end-effector difficult to anticipate. Distributed proximity sensing measures these distances directly and provides the raw material for a sense of the robot's own body. 
The challenge lies in representing dozens of small sensors distributed across the body into a signal that a policy can use. To address this, we present \emph{PC-ACT: Proximity Conditioned Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT)}, a policy that encodes each sensor's measurements into a token describing nearby geometry and its change over time, tags the token with the sensor's location on the body, and fuses these tokens with camera observations in ACT.  On a simulated Franka Research 3 equipped with whole-body time-of-flight sensors, PC-ACT reduces hazardous-contact exposure $5\times$ relative to standard ACT while increasing collision-free placement success. Finally, PC-ACT transfers zero-shot to sensor configurations featuring wider fields of view, $4\times$ lower frame rates, and $4\times$ fewer sensing zones. These results demonstrate that body-anchored proximity representations enable learned policies to acquire their own safety margins directly from demonstrations.

This work studies prediction parameterization for stochastic generative dynamics in diffusion models. Existing velocity-based generative models provide the simplicity of learning a single transport field, but their standard formulation is deterministic, whereas stochastic extensions generally require additional score information or an intermediate velocity-to-score reconstruction. To retain single-field prediction while directly supporting stochastic reverse dynamics, this paper introduces Mean Velocity Matching (MVM). MVM constructs a Gaussian perturbation process for which the conditional expectation of a restoration-oriented velocity, $(x_0-x_t)/t$, directly forms the reverse-SDE drift. Consequently, a single learned field is sufficient to parameterize the stochastic reverse process without separately estimating or reconstructing the score. Because direct regression of this velocity becomes unbounded near $t=0$, MVM further introduces a $\sqrt{t}$-scaled parameterization that preserves the reverse dynamics while yielding a bounded training target. The same learned field also induces a deterministic probability-flow ODE, enabling stochastic and deterministic sampling to be studied within a unified formulation. Experiments with Transformer-based generative models achieve an FID of $1.93$ at 65 NFE on ImageNet $32\times32$ and $2.10$ at 80 NFE on ImageNet $256\times256$. Controlled SDE--ODE comparisons further show that the ODE performs better under very low NFE, whereas the stochastic reverse process achieves lower FID when sufficient function evaluations are available. These results demonstrate that MVM provides a direct single-field parameterization of stochastic reverse dynamics while maintaining competitive generation quality.

TL;DR: Mean Velocity Matching establishes a new single-field paradigm for stochastic generative modeling, directly parameterizing reverse SDE dynamics without explicit score estimation.

We address the computational bottlenecks in Audio-Language Models (Audio LLMs), where the Whisper-style encoder must process long speech sequences prior to the text backbone. To alleviate this overhead, we propose \textbf{LITEALLM}, a post-hoc compression framework that replaces the encoder's dense linear layers with data-driven low-rank approximations derived from activation covariances. Using a compact multi-task calibration set covering ASR and general audio understanding, we utilize eigen-decomposition to project weights onto principal subspaces. A key innovation is a depth- and type-aware variance-retention schedule. This mechanism applies differential thresholds to attention and MLP blocks and linearly adapts criteria across layers, enabling aggressive compression in shallow layers while preserving semantic capacity in deeper ones. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that LITEALLM reduces encoding latency by approximately 20\% with negligible performance degradation (approximately 2\% relative drop). Our implementation is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LITEALLM-B408.

Comparing quantum and classical policies requires more than ranking their scores: feasibility, impact, and detection risk must be evaluated under a consistent protocol. We develop such a protocol for power-system state estimation and apply it to 360 policies across three networks. The study crosses compact quantum and parameter-matched classical policy cores with two optimizer families, using 30 paired seeds per network. Every learned perturbation passes the deterministic residual test, yet under calibrated measurement noise, mean alarm probabilities reach 12.5% against a nominal 5% false-positive rate. On the primary impact endpoint, the learned policies attain 6.9–23.2% of an offline feasible-control reference. After false-discovery-rate correction, one of twelve calibrated contrasts is statistically resolved: on IEEE 57, the classical geometry-aware policy has lower calibrated impact than its quantum counterpart. Because their update rules differ, this contrast does not isolate the effect of representation. A separate dense-meter sensitivity study yields maximum verified inner–outer bound gaps of 0.899% and 2.605%. Fourier reconstruction provides a structural audit of the selected circuit’s encoded-angle readout. These results show how feasibility, noisy detection, attained impact, and attribution can be assessed separately in power-system policy studies.

TL;DR: We present an evaluation protocol for quantum and classical power-system policies, assessing feasibility, impact, and detection risk across three networks.

Personalized language agents choose both what to remember about a person and how to use that memory. We separate these choices when predicting unseen answers to known interview questions. On 1,768 tasks from 188 people, a concrete memory built from a verified interview prefix outscores a trait description by 0.0158 (95% whole-person interval [0.0044, 0.0271]). Crossing both memories with one-shot generation and three-answer fusion, fusion lowers concrete-memory scores by 0.0123 ([-0.0189, -0.0056]); prompted and trained selectors do not detectably beat a random candidate. One call on the longer, unrewritten source record outscores every memory condition. Under a limited context budget, OwnWords retrieves the person's sentences with BM25 and answers in one call. It outperforms the written memory on 500 people outside the benchmark (+0.0127, [+0.0037, +0.0217]; an earlier held-out test was inconclusive) and across four budgets on 300 people (mean +0.0218, [+0.0138, +0.0298]), with the latter result repeated on 114 people. It does not detectably outperform recency truncation. These results compare evidence-construction procedures; they do not isolate the effect of verbatim wording. On Twin-2K-500, OwnWords predicts ordinal survey answers more closely than the written memory, but does not improve exact-choice accuracy and lowers it in one of two samples. Interview scores use a model-based content rubric without human ratings, and the original benchmark's participants were seen during development. These results characterize the tested procedures, not a general human-prediction ceiling.

TL;DR: For individual-answer prediction, tested multi-call workflows do not reliably help, while budget-matched excerpts offer a strong one-call alternative to written personal memories.

A coding agent repeatedly processes messages from earlier steps as it edits code and runs tests. We measure how total input tokens grow with the number of completed tool calls. Across 240 hosted runs on controlled bug-fixing tasks, a power-law fit gives an exponent of 1.24 ($95\%$ CI [1.19, 1.30]). A comparison of 431 completed runs across 3 models finds that the fitted local exponent increases with completed tool-call count. This rejects the hypothesis that input-token growth has the same exponent in shorter and longer runs within the range studied. Full history retention can produce an exponent below $2$ in short runs because repeatedly processing the fixed task prompt can outweigh the growing history. Measurements from individual model calls in the open-source OpenHands platform support this approximation, although we cannot identify the retention policy from the hosted measurements. We also compare full retention with compaction, which summarizes older history, on 159 paired tasks. Without a discount for reused input, full retention costs an estimated 1.40 times as much as compaction (geometric mean, $95\%$ CI [1.20, 1.66]). Repricing the same recorded runs with a 10-fold discount for reused input changes the ratio to 0.90 (geometric mean, $95\%$ CI [0.80, 1.02]), so we cannot establish a cost advantage for either policy under this pricing. Cost estimates must therefore account for how the fitted exponent changes with the number of completed tool calls and for the price of reused input.

TL;DR: Agent input growth varies with run depth, and cache pricing changes the cost benefit of context compaction.

Cell micromanipulation underpins biomedical procedures such as somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), where the demand for high precision and reduced manual variability has created an urgent need for robotic operation. However, robotic cell manipulation remains limited by the lack of anomaly detection and recovery in long-horizon, stage-dependent visual environments. Existing visual anomaly detectors are usually stage-agnostic and provide only opaque anomaly scores. To facilitate the study of this problem, we take SCNT, one of the most complex cell manipulations, as a representative case and introduce the SCNT-ADR-20k benchmark dataset. This dataset consists of 20,300 frames from 82 real SCNT manipulation sequences, annotated with operation stage labels, binary anomaly indicators and fine-grained recovery actions. Building upon this dataset, we propose SAFE-SCNT, a stage-aware retrieval-augmented framework for anomaly detection and recovery, which combines visual, stage, and textual knowledge through a retrieval mechanism. Experiments on the proposed benchmark show that SAFE-SCNT significantly outperforms existing methods in both anomaly detection accuracy and recovery performance.

TL;DR: We introduce SCNT-ADR-20k, a benchmark for anomaly detection and recovery in robotic somatic cell nuclear transfer, and propose SAFE-SCNT, a retrieval-augmented framework that significantly outperforms existing methods.

Steady-State Visually Evoked Potential (SSVEPs) provide a high-throughput testbed for neural decoding, yet real-world deployment is hindered by subject-specific calibration. We address this challenge by proposing DATCAN, a framework that embeds domain-specific invariances into contrastive learning while aligning feature statistics without supervision. DATCAN integrates three complementary components: (i) a harmonic-aware contrastive objective that encodes frequency-locked physiological priors directly into the embedding space, (ii) second-order covariance alignment (CORAL) that stabilizes cross-subject transfer through closed-form adaptation, and (iii) adaptive late fusion of interpretable classical heads (Task-Related Component Analysis, TRCA; Filter Bank Canonical Correlation Analysis (FBCCA) (Nakanishi et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2015) with normalized weighting. Contrastive pairing uses only source-subject labels: positives are other-subject trials evoked by the same known stimulus frequency (including harmonics), while negatives come from different frequencies. At inference, the TRCA/FBCCA heads score each frequency class, mapping embeddings to symbols without any target-subject calibration. Evaluated under strict leave-one-subject-out transfer, DATCAN achieves robust short-window decoding, sustaining >100 bits/min information transfer rate at 1 s-a regime where existing calibration-free baselines substantially underperform. Ablation and interpretability analyses confirm that each module contributes principled gains, yielding physiologically grounded, subject-invariant representations. Beyond Electroencephalogram(EEG), our results highlight a general recipe for calibration-free domain adaptation: encode physics-driven invariances in contrastive learning, align covariances without labels, and integrate interpretable ensembles. This blueprint extends naturally to other sequential and biosignal domains where distribution shift and data scarcity remain central obstacles.

Reproducibility: Code, preprocessing scripts, and evaluation notebooks with fixed seeds are provided in the supplementary material (anonymous).

TL;DR: DATCAN achieves robust calibration-free SSVEP decoding by combining harmonic-conditioned contrastive learning, covariance alignment, and adaptive late fusion.

Personal photographs can serve as emotional records, practical references, or tools for collecting and organizing ideas. These functions extend beyond depicted content and may go unmentioned when an owner considers an individual image. We hypothesize that explicitly representing relationships across a personal collection improves function prediction beyond image-only reasoning and flat collection context. We formulate prediction as a multilabel task using a vocabulary developed separately from evaluation participants. Our owner-annotation protocol asks the same questions about photographic use before and after neutral collection review, with all responses collected before exposure to model interpretations. We compare image-only inference with flat and relationally organized context linking recurring subjects and events. The contextual conditions use the same underlying evidence and matched budgets, with the multimodal model held fixed. Evaluation on held-out owners assesses generalization, event-level exclusions limit leakage, and repeated annotation measures response consistency. A focused analysis examines functions reported during collection review but omitted initially. The study tests whether relational organization makes behavioral information in personal collections more usable for multimodal inference, evaluated against independently elicited reports of photographic use.

TL;DR: We test whether organizing relationships across personal photo collections improves inference of photographic functions beyond image-only reasoning and flat context, using independently elicited owner reports.

Replanning should change how a tool-using agent completes a task, not what it is authorized to do. Yet rejecting one call leaves open whether the agent applies the associated constraint to a structurally different realization of the same protected effect. We study this problem as denial generalization, which asks whether a retained denial constrains structurally different realizations of the same protected effect. Our benchmark uses six representative transformation families to vary authorization-relevant relations while preserving the evaluated principal--resource effect. In controlled external-disclosure scenarios, the denial remains visible and effect-equivalent alternatives remain executable, with no new authorization granted. We distinguish path availability, observable discovery, and effect realization, and use a deterministic oracle to verify outcomes from environment state and execution records. Across Qwen3.7-Plus, Kimi K2.7 Code, GPT-5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5, post-denial protected-effect realization rates range from 42.4\% to 67.4\% under action-local denial. Transformation-dependent patterns persist when the underlying task is held fixed. A technical-failure control on Qwen shows that alternative-path discovery varies with the inference configuration. Effect-explicit denial reduces effect realization relative to a verbose action-local control. The largest associated behavioral change is a lower replanning rate, while realization remains frequent after an alternative route is discovered. These findings distinguish retaining a denial from consistently applying its associated constraint across alternative execution structures.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer new opportunities for traditional Chinese medicine (TCM). However, the privacy-sensitive nature of TCM data prevents centralized training, while the principle of syndrome differentiation and treatment requires models to preserve client-specific characteristics. These considerations make personalized federated fine-tuning a natural solution for enabling cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw data. Existing studies have explored personalization through factor-wise federated LoRA, assigning different sharing roles to individual low-rank factors. However, we find that factor similarity depends on initialization and internal coordinates, which may misdirect aggregation and weaken cross-client transfer. Client updates also mix transferable directions with local offsets, so excessive sharing can impair local adaptation while complete isolation forfeits transferable knowledge. Motivated by these findings, we propose Federated Low-Rank Subspace Personalization (FedLSP) for heterogeneous multimodal data. FedLSP learns a shared low-rank subspace from effective updates and represents local variation through client-specific offsets, enabling efficient knowledge sharing while preserving client-specific information. We evaluate FedLSP on a range of multimodal TCM tasks. Experimental results show that FedLSP consistently improves open-ended generation across heterogeneous clients and achieves the highest overall accuracy among the compared methods on external closed-set tasks.

TL;DR: FedLSP separates shared low-rank subspaces from client-specific coordinates for personalized federated adaptation under heterogeneous multimodal data.

Long-horizon web search tasks require agents to coordinate retrieval and reasoning across multiple steps. However, ReAct-style agents may overlook unresolved constraints and submit answers before sufficiently checking the supporting evidence. We propose **S**elf-**A**ssessment **G**uided **E**xploration (**SAGE**), a training-free framework that embeds two automatically triggered self-assessment modules into the ReAct loop using the same underlying language model. During search, **Trajectory Review** periodically assesses search progress and evidence coverage, identifying unresolved aspects of the question and suggesting subsequent search directions. Before submission, **Candidate Verification** evaluates the proposed answer against the question and collected evidence, allowing submission when a confidence threshold is met and otherwise providing feedback for further search or revision. Experiments across seven benchmarks and three models show that SAGE consistently improves accuracy over the ReAct baseline, while ablation studies indicate that the two modules provide complementary benefits in most settings. We hope these findings inspire further research within the community on self-assessment in long-horizon agentic tasks.

Transferability scores are used to choose a pretrained foundation model for a new task from a small labelled sample, including in medical imaging, where labels are scarce. Recent benchmarks report that in this setting some scores become degenerate: SFDA can assign the same score to every candidate model, and rankings change with the random draw of the sample. We explain when and why this happens and what can still be trusted. Scores such as SFDA and the H-score need the inverse of a covariance matrix; when the embedding dimension exceeds the number of labelled examples, the inverse does not exist, and implementations add ridge regularization. With 100 labels this holds for all 36 vision and language models we examine. We show that the score's value is then set by the regularization strength rather than by the data: dividing it by 100 multiplies the score by about 100, and bounded scores saturate at their maximum. The ranking of candidate models behaves differently. It does not depend on the regularization strength, and on natural images it agrees with a linear probe at least as well as the alternatives we test, provided the embeddings are normalized to a common scale and the computation is done in double precision. With a fixed regularization on unnormalized embeddings, the ranking mostly reflects embedding scale, and in single precision it can reverse. The commonly used pseudoinverse ranks worst. We give a simple check for regularization-dominated values and practical guidance for using these scores.

Unsupervised domain adaptation for 3D MRI segmentation is complicated by substantial appearance shifts across imaging domains, the absence of target-domain annotations, and limited access to source-domain data. We propose Bidirectional Semantic Harmonization (BSH), a framework that learns anatomy-preserving intensity transformations for cross-domain segmentation. BSH employs frozen reference-space segmentation models as semantic anchors and learns two complementary harmonization mappings between an ordered pair of source and target domains. The target-to-source mapping adapts unlabeled target images into the source semantic space using pseudo-label supervision, while the source-to-target mapping generates target-style source images with preserved annotations to provide clean supervision for refinement. By combining real target appearance with pseudo-semantic guidance and synthetic target-style appearance with accurate labels, BSH enables task-oriented harmonization without target-domain annotations. We evaluate BSH on public structural MRI datasets under reciprocal domain-transfer protocols using deliberately restricted source and target cohorts to emulate data-scarce medical imaging scenarios. The results demonstrate consistent improvements in cross-domain segmentation while preserving anatomically relevant structures.

TL;DR: We introduce BSH, a bidirectional semantic harmonization framework for unsupervised cross-domain 3D MRI segmentation.

Self-evolving agents are usually scored by endpoint Gain: held-out success after updating minus success before. We show that this credits a frozen rescore as evolution. On office-v1, a closed office-task pack with 40 held-out tasks, DeepSeek v4 Pro under no_evolve never changes its policy yet moves 17.5 percentage points across four held-out passes; one task is 2.5 points. Three text-update methods inspired by GEPA, ACE, and ExpeL, selected on validation before held-out was read, do not beat that rescore: their Gain minus the same-seed frozen Gain is -2.5, -3.3, and +4.2 points, inside the widest per-seed range, even where the accepted agent version changes. They also solve no task in three families the frozen policy never solves. Trace Evolution Bench (TEB) records that comparison. An update is accepted only when validation does not fall, held-out ids never enter the update, and a text update is not ranked with a weight update. The release has three frozen 80/20/40 packs: coding graded by closed-workspace unit tests (Chen et al., 2021), office graded by rule-bounded delivery, and manufacturing table QA over 12 pseudonymized real enterprise tables. The method matrix is office-only; coding and manufacturing report frozen repeats. The three packs are scored separately.

TL;DR: Endpoint Gain credits a frozen agent's 17.5-point rescore swing as evolution; TEB, with three frozen task packs, makes the frozen-versus-updated comparison executable.

Frontier LLMs are increasingly moving beyond their roles as question-answering systems to serve as agents that assist humans with professional work.
This shift calls for a comprehensive and systematic benchmark that aligns agent evaluation with real-world user needs and realistic workplace scenarios.
To this end, we construct the \textbf{Work360} dataset.
Drawing on real-world user data and reports on pillar industries, we identify $27$ primary domains encompassing $321$ subdomains.
We then engage $296$ experts to construct $20$ realistic and long-horizon tasks per domain, combining top-down guidance from domain knowledge frameworks with a bottom-up orientation toward authentic user needs.
We define long-horizon tasks and classify their complexity by expert labor time and tool-call counts; experts assign each task's complexity level, with model trial runs as supporting evidence.
Supported by reference deliverables, expert-written rubrics use $23{,}094$ scoring entries to assess task-specific requirements for content quality, practical usability, and, where relevant, visual presentation through objective checks and model-based judgments.
We evaluate eight frontier models on Work360, with the best-performing model achieving an overall score of only $52.16$ out of $100$.
Our analysis reveals that model strengths vary across domains and evaluation dimensions, while case studies expose failures to integrate task components into coherent, usable deliverables.
Work360 is not only useful for evaluating existing models, but also provides guidance for model training and the evolution of harness-based collaborative mechanisms.

TL;DR: Work360 evaluates LLM agents on 540 expert-authored, long-horizon professional tasks across 27 domains; the best of six frontier models scores only 51.3%, revealing persistent gaps in producing coherent, polished, and usable deliverables.

During RTL design, engineers must detect and localize bugs in increasingly large and complex codebases. Yet tracing a mismatch between specified and implemented behavior to the responsible RTL logic remains labor-intensive, often requiring repeated inspection of source code and signal waveforms. Existing LLM-based agents struggle to generate targeted tests from lengthy design specifications, trace mismatches through buggy code that omits the correct logic, and reject fixes that pass tests without correcting the originating bug. We present $\texttt{WIRE}$, a specification-driven framework for bug root-cause (BRC) localization in repository-level RTL designs. $\texttt{WIRE}$ first combines LLM priors with coverage-aware selection to prioritize RTL requirements and then generates fine-grained testbenches. It then applies temporal backtracing with local abstract syntax tree augmentation, which hypothesizes missing logic to continue backward tracing when causal dependencies are absent. Finally, $\texttt{WIRE}$ proposes modifications at traced candidate BRC locations and evaluates their effects on the target mismatch and causally related signals, filtering incidental fail-to-pass fixes. We also construct a repository-level BRC localization benchmark from real-world open-source RTL projects, comprising 341 tasks. On this benchmark, $\texttt{WIRE}$ achieves higher BRC localization performance than advanced baselines. We release our code at https://github.com/WIRE-ICLR2027/WIRE.
