Command-line interface (CLI) agents increasingly execute longer-horizon tasks, yet existing benchmarks either assume that user instructions remain fixed throughout execution or include user participation only as part of the trajectory without evaluating it separately. In this paper, we present RealCLI, a paired benchmark that unifies the evaluation of task execution and human--agent collaboration quality on realistic CLI tasks. To comprehensively measure collaboration quality, RealCLI builds a five-dimensional collaboration framework, refined into 22 sub-dimensions and 51 interaction scenario templates. To enable paired comparison between autonomous execution and human--agent collaboration, RealCLI provides two modes. RealCLI-Exec provides the complete specification, while RealCLI-Collab introduces a scripted user that delivers corrections, constraint revisions, authorization decisions, and other forms of participation. Across 33 configurations of frontier models and mainstream agent harnesses, RealCLI reveals clear capability gaps of frontier agents. The best configuration attains an average score of only 52.7\\%, and task effectiveness diverges sharply from collaboration quality. User interaction is not a reliable gain, and collaboration ability is consistently weak on steerability, trust calibration, and safety and risk awareness. Looking ahead, RealCLI provides a reproducible foundation for measuring and improving this capability.

Computational drug discovery commonly emphasizes the generation of novel molecular structures, although generated compounds may lack established safety information, synthetic accessibility, or clinical availability. We instead formulate target-specific drug repurposing as a molecular recommendation problem: given known ligands for a therapeutic target, the objective is to identify existing compounds that retain relevant molecular characteristics while exhibiting favorable target-specific binding affinity. We introduce DrugRank, an affinity-aware variational representation learning and retrieval framework designed for this setting. DrugRank jointly organizes its latent space according to molecular characteristics and experimentally measured binding affinity. RDKit molecular descriptors and Morgan fingerprints are encoded through a variational autoencoder (VAE) with modality-specific reconstruction objectives, while pointwise regression and pairwise ranking supervision encourage preservation of both affinity magnitude and relative ligand ordering. The resulting representation is used to retrieve and rank DrugCentral candidates around established therapeutic anchor ligands according to latent proximity and predicted target affinity. On held-out ChEMBL ligand datasets, target-specific DrugRank models achieve Spearman correlations of 0.780 for the orexin-1 receptor and 0.848 for the μ-opioid receptor. Retrieval analysis further reveals complementary roles for the two ranking signals: affinity-dominated ranking more strongly recovers compounds with known OPRM1 relevance, whereas increasing latent-space contribution retrieves candidates with greater structural similarity to the anchor. On the BACE benchmark, DrugRank achieves a mean ROC AUC of 0.8556 ± 0.0339 across 20 scaffold-based held-out evaluations. These results demonstrate the potential of jointly affinity- and structure-aware representations for anchor-guided retrieval and prioritization of existing compounds as target-specific drug repurposing candidates.

TL;DR: DrugRank is an affinity-aware molecular representation and retrieval framework that combines molecular reconstruction, affinity prediction, and ranking to prioritize existing compounds as target-specific drug repurposing candidates.

When can query-adaptive model teams outperform a fixed team, and when can a correct member's answer be recovered? We separate three bottlenecks: oracle headroom, selection regret, and resolution loss. Our conditional coverage estimator for model-team routing (coverage) estimates the conditional any-correct target by sharing linear query-by-expert parameters across subset targets, enforcing inclusion monotonicity, and searching feasible teams exactly. In the 50-seed held-out synthetic study with observable conditional dependence (seeds 100--149, fixed after development on earlier seeds), shared coverage achieves 93.83% any-correct coverage: paired gains of 1.33 percentage points over conditional independence [0.60, 2.08] and 1.08 percentage points over separate subset heads [0.38, 1.78]. Its gain over a selected fixed team is 0.88 percentage points [0.02, 1.73] and remains marginal. A distinct interaction-capable synthetic specification fails to improve over independence. On a conservatively verified five-model, 90-query MATH-500 diagnostic panel, a validation-selected fixed pair reaches the 82/90 hindsight coverage ceiling; the archived direct coverage route reaches 78/90. Direct coverage has four more selection misses but four fewer resolver losses than the fixed pair, so both realize 76/90 accuracy under one deterministic majority-vote resolver. Conditional coverage can help selection under learnable co-failure, but deployment gains also require headroom over fixed teams and effective answer resolution.

Relational knowledge distillation transfers a teacher's representation geometry, but evaluating all within-batch pairs requires quadratically many relation computations. Under a fixed budget, target weights and pair-sampling priority are distinct decisions. RAPID (Reliability-Aware Pair Importance Distillation) separates a normalized, label-aware target from an independently specified, importance-corrected pair proposal. Its instantiation uses calibrated teacher information and pilot-estimated student–teacher residuals. With detached proposals and unclipped inverse-probability correction, the sampled loss and stopped-proposal gradient are conditionally unbiased for the gated mini-batch objective. Pilot evaluations count toward the total relation budget. Across three paired seeds on AG News and SST-2, RAPID exceeds the cross-entropy student mean by 0.087 points on AG News and 1.41 points on SST-2, but reliability-gated uniform sampling has the highest observed mean on both. In a ten-batch SST-2 diagnostic, the tested adaptive proposal has greater loss-estimator spread and feature-gradient MSE than uniform sampling. A follow-up score and mixture sweep finds only small changes for near-uniform proposals in the initial-student setting, while stronger adaptive mixtures sharply reduce effective sample size. These findings show that unbiasedness does not guarantee lower variance and that target quality and proposal quality must be assessed separately.

CBC analysis is one of the most frequent and widely ordered diagnostic tests in clinical medicine, and often the first signal that decides which confirmatory tests a patient with a suspected hematological malignancy receives. ML is well positioned to support this decision, yet ML research on CBC data remains limited relative to imaging and genomic modalities, and existing efforts largely target narrow, single-condition, single-institution, fully-labeled settings. Real clinical practice, however, involves label scarcity, multi-institutional data, and conditions that fall outside any fixed taxonomy. This gap persists in large part because no dataset has existed to support the study of CBC-based ML under these conditions. We introduce OmniCBC, a corpus of about 210K unlabeled and 519 labeled CBC samples collected from two clinical institutions operating three Sysmex hematology analyzer models, with labels derived from clinician assessments spanning 25 hematological malignancy subtypes and a control class. OmniCBC pairs a large unlabeled pool with a comparatively small labeled subset, and spans multiple institutions and analyzer models. To make this heterogeneity measurable, we propose a three-way evaluation protocol, stratified, prospective, and cross-source, that approximately decomposes a model's generalization gap into temporal and source-attributable components, and define label-efficient and open-world tasks to standardize future evaluation. Benchmarking six representative supervised tabular methods, with bootstrap confidence intervals throughout, shows that all degrade on held-out sources, and that strong in-distribution performance does not guarantee robustness to source shift. We further analyze the latent structure of an autoencoder trained on the unlabeled pool as a first step toward label-efficient and open-world learning.

TL;DR: We introduce OmniCBC, a complete blood count dataset for hematological malignancy classification, along with an evaluation protocol and metric for measuring source-shift generalization.

Connectome-constrained models specify which neural interactions can occur, but not how much of that substrate a modeled computation uses. We formulate computational sufficiency as a task-conditioned frontier over retained-neuron cost, task degradation, and failure probability under a declared intervention. Two budgeted searches are evaluated against exact oracles, greedy elimination, and matched random removal. In a released 4,604-neuron walking model, a recovery benchmark at $\epsilon=0.35$ reaches the published 148-neuron circuit in five of seven search seeds and recovers it exactly in three. On 32 held-out draws the circuit has mean degradation 0.0168 and worst-draw degradation 0.332; a distribution-free 95% mean upper bound is 0.233, above $\epsilon=0.05$. In a 176,422-neuron male CNS rate model, the response-match task uses one fixed motor-readout trace. At $\epsilon=0.05$, H-CABES removes 62,844 neurons with search-cohort degradation 0.0069, versus mean degradation 0.727 for cost-matched random masks; its separate held-out 95% mean upper bound is 0.0114. At the permissive setting $\epsilon=\rho=0.5$, a mask with 93 additional neurons has held-out mean upper bound 0.466 and 7/30 failures ($U_{\mathrm{fail}}=0.394$). These are pointwise model-level results, not claims of biological necessity.

We propose DASCO (Dynamic Agent Scheduling with
Cost Optimization), a framework that unifies per-query
multi-agent system routing with explicit budget constraints.
DASCO introduces a cascaded cost-performance controller
that progressively constructs a budget-optimal MAS for each
query through three stages: (1) a collaboration determiner that
selects among topologies based on query difficulty and re-
maining budget; (2) a cascaded role allocator that assigns
specialized roles via structured probabilistic sequencing with
cost-aware penalties; and (3) a multinomial LLM router that
maps role-model affinities into per-agent backbone assign-
ments under hard budget constraints. Two empirical findings
shape the instantiation, and they narrow it: on the benchmarks
we study, the decisions that carry the gains are the topology
choice and the budget-masked backbone choice, while role
allocation reduces to a task-type constant—so we report the
cascade as the formulation and are explicit about which of
its stages our experiments actually test. Throughout, “points”
means percentage points of accuracy. First, the routing sig-
nal must be measured, not predicted: under a single-variable
comparison on our labeled training pool (same queries, same
label, same classifier, 5-fold cross-validation), query-text em-
beddings cannot determine whether a cheap model will solve
a query (66.8% balanced accuracy), whereas the behavior of
a few cheap trial calls—answer consistency, self-verification,
test pass rate—raises this to 84.1% overall and up to 94.9%
where the query carries executable tests, enabling a simple
supervised router to outperform every policy-gradient vari-
ant we trained. Second, the effective action space we recover
from these experiments—after six collapse runs over the full
combinatorial space and a set of live topology probes—is a
four-tier escalation ladder (cheapest single →mid-tier single
→strong single →strong homogeneous 3-agent chain), best
built by composing independently learned decision bound-
aries under a confidence gate. The multi-agent rung is load-
bearing: on the queries it selects, the chain solves 20 of 22
where the same strong model alone solves 9, and deleting the
chain action from the ladder—leaving a purely single-agent
model router—costs 1.7 points. Replacing the composed lad-
der with a single four-way classifier retrained end-to-end on
the identical tier labels loses 8.9 points, and live probes show
that placing cheap models inside multi-agent topologies de-
grades accuracy by 22–68 points on precisely the queries that
need collaboration.
Experiments on five benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH, Hu-
manEval, MBPP, MMLU; 946 held-out queries) with
real LLM API calls demonstrate that DASCO achieves:
(1) 90.4% overall accuracy, exceeding the budget-unaware
multi-agent router MasRouter (88.5%) at 2.3×lower cost;
(2) 91.6% on the four generative benchmarks (GSM8K,
MATH, HumanEval, MBPP; MMLU is multiple-choice and
is reported separately as zero-shot transfer) vs. a single
strong-model oracle’s 91.8% at 31% lower cost; and (3) a
22-point margin in overall accuracy over the cheapest single-
model baseline, driven by trial-based difficulty estimation

TL;DR: A cascaded controller that builds budget-optimal multi-agent LLM teams per query using measured difficulty signals, matching oracle accuracy at 31% lower cost and beating budget-unaware MAS routing by 1.9 points at 2.3× lower cost.

Specializing a language model can improve target-domain performance while degrading capabilities the student already possesses. Existing retention methods commonly add replay data or regularization, leaving the representation teaching signal itself unrestricted. We introduce COPD (Continue On-Policy Distillation), a capability-preserving on-policy representation distillation method. Protection-domain activations define an approximate null space, and only the teacher--student residual projected into this space contributes to the distillation loss. Protection prompts are used for basis estimation without adding a replay objective or an inference-time module. We evaluate mathematics specialization in two Qwen model families using MATH-500 and language-modeling, commonsense, and instruction-following probes. On Qwen3-8B, COPD reaches 76.2% MATH-500 with 66.14% LAMBADA in the high-target regime, extending the observed baseline frontier. Paired diagnostics show improved LAMBADA retention in both model families. WikiText-103 evaluations also show reduced degradation on an independent corpus. Representation analysis connects these gains with smaller final-layer movement in the protection subspace. Together, these results establish selective residual matching as a practical approach to controlling specialization and capability retention.

Deep multi-view clustering exploits complementary information across views to learn discriminative representations. However, repeated nonlinear transformations can dilute useful view-specific cues, while sample-level graph modeling incurs substantial computational costs and may propagate noise through unreliable connections. To address these challenges, we propose Dynamic Anchor Graph Attention Networks for Multi-View Clustering (DAGAT-MVC), which integrates residual view encoding, dynamic anchor graph attention, and cluster-level contrastive learning. Residual encoders retain informative view-specific features through shortcut paths and stabilize the optimization of deep view encoders. Rather than building a dense sample graph, DAGAT-MVC treats a compact set of learnable anchors as structural mediators. DAGAT-MVC adapts anchors to the evolving latent space through learnable perturbations. It then uses an attention mechanism to aggregate information from sample-associated anchors, enabling effective sample–anchor structural modeling. An anchor-aware contrastive objective aligns the resulting representations across individual views and the consensus space, while cluster-level contrastive learning promotes compact intra-cluster structure and separated inter-cluster semantics. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that DAGAT-MVC outperforms existing approaches.

TL;DR: DAGAT-MVC combines residual encoding, dynamic anchor graph attention, and contrastive learning for scalable multi-view clustering.

Language models accept million-token inputs yet often miss information far from the question. Hybrid models mix linear-attention layers with a few global layers, and new designs are often judged by the attention sink, the share of attention on the first token. This paper asks which designs let a hybrid learn retrieval early and keep the skill on longer inputs. Across 15 designs that each change one mechanism, 49 small models (up to 1.9 million parameters) are trained on a key-value retrieval task and tested at up to 64 times the training length. Existing designs face a trade-off. Attention-only models, including gated attention, sink logits and rectified softmax, learn within 1,900 steps but fail beyond twice the training length. Hybrids with the global layer last, as in Qwen3-Next and Kimi Linear, can extend to long inputs but learn late or never (13 of 20 runs learned). The proposed BKF (bound keys, global layer first) places the global layer first and adds a short convolution to the keys and values of that layer, so one attention step can link a question to the matching value. Only BKF both learned in every run by step 300 and held 98% recall at 64 times the training length, against 91% to 92% for global-last hybrids with the same length scale. The major finding is that layer order and key binding decide how early retrieval is learned, while sink size does not predict recall on long inputs.

TL;DR: Sink size does not predict long-context retrieval; placing the global layer first with bound keys makes small hybrid models learn retrieval in every run by step 300 and keep 98% recall at 64 times the training length.

Bilevel optimization couples upper-level decisions to a lower-level solution map. Safe-gradient-flow methods replace exact lower-level optimality with residual control, but their discrete implementations can require conservative steps. We study BBSGF, which combines a residual-induced halfspace direction, a Barzilai–Borwein spectral step formed from projected-direction differences, and a nonmonotone line search. Our analysis explicitly retains descent compatibility: under smoothness, compactness, direction continuity, and a uniform descent-angle condition, backtracking has a positive accepted-step lower bound and the full sequence of direction norms tends to zero. For a strongly convex lower problem, a pointwise error bound connects the direction norm and lower residual to the true bilevel hypergradient. Fixed positive residual tolerance yields conditional approximate, rather than exact, bilevel stationarity. We also quantify the perturbation from a positive denominator regularizer. Budget-accounted MNIST and frozen-feature CIFAR-10 experiments show task-dependent predictive and computational tradeoffs. Targeted spectral-pair controls improve Reg-HPO validation loss at smaller budgets, but do not establish uniform acceleration. Strongly convex diagnostics verify the error identities while showing negligible true-hypergradient progress on controlled CIFAR tasks. The method therefore offers an inexpensive filtered direction with explicit conditional guarantees, not an unconditional solution to stiff bilevel optimization.

Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of visual tasks, yet their substantial storage and computational costs hinder deployment on resource-constrained platforms. Post-training quantization (PTQ) offers an efficient solution without retraining, but existing methods typically rely on real or synthetic calibration samples and suffer from accuracy degradation at low bit-widths. We propose a novel strict Calibration-Free Post-Training Quantization (Calib-Free PTQ) paradigm which constructs quantization policies solely from the pretrained model. Our key insight is that a pretrained ViT is not statistically structureless: LayerNorm’s normalization constraints and learned affine parameters jointly encode a model-intrinsic prior from which quantization-relevant activation statistics can be derived without observing calibration features. Once calibration inputs are removed, however, conventional data-dependent sensitivity estimation also becomes unavailable. We further observe that the model's final prediction accuracy exhibits a sharp degradation when network modual components at various granularities are quantized below a certain bit-width. Guided by this finding, we propose an Adaptive Mixed-Precision Allocation (AMPA) method, which assigns different bit-widths to various network modual components to reduce precision while preserving accuracy-sensitive components. Experiments on ImageNet-1K show that our method achieves Top-1 accuracies of 80.262\%, 71.184\%, and 78.601\% on ViT-S, DeiT-T, and DeiT-S, respectively. Compared with representative data-free methods, our method improves Top-1 accuracy by an average of 1.9 percentage points on DeiT-T and DeiT-S. Compared with calibration-based PTQ methods, our method achieves comparable model sizes with only a small accuracy gap, while requiring neither real nor synthetic calibration samples. Our code will be publicly available.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in robotics manipulation, from architecture to data and to training, yet output action representation remains an axis understudied. Nearly all action outputs, from regression to flow-matching denoising, predict ``which single next action is the best''. However, such single-point action predictions could ignore the spatial structure of the action space: actions near a demonstrated action are nearly as reasonable as the demonstrated action itself, and this reasonableness decays as the distance grows, a graded structure that a point estimate can neither express nor learn from. To advance this, we introduce \textbf{ActionMap}, a voxel heatmap action head that drops into an existing VLA in place of its native action decoder. For each new action, the head predicts a voxel heatmap over the action space, where each voxel directly stores the probability of the corresponding action. Across simulation and real-world Franka manipulation, our heatmap head surpasses two architecturally distinct backbones at matched training steps (e.g., $97\%+$ LIBERO performance at 10k training steps over Jev-style and diffusion-expert-style VLAs), converges at comparable or faster rates, and remains markedly more data-efficient at low training data. The cross-backbone consistency indicates that action representation is a real lever for VLA performance, distinct from further backbone or recipe scaling. Project page: ...

Software engineering agents have shown promise in diverse development tasks, making their evaluation an important research topic. However, existing evaluations mainly report end-to-end test results or cover only a few execution stages. As a result, it is hard to tell where and why an agent succeeds or fails. To address this gap, we analyze the trajectories of agents on two representative tasks: implementing new requirements and fixing bugs. We find that these trajectories can be divided into six stages: requirement understanding, code exploration, plan generation, code modification, validation, and summarization. Based on this, we propose a comprehensive framework CodeTrace for trajectory evaluation. The framework unifies heterogeneous execution logs into stage-structured trajectories and designs 22 metrics. These metrics enable comprehensive analysis of trajectory behaviors at each stage, revealing differences in capabilities that end-to-end success rates cannot capture. We further construct execution trajectory graphs to compare different trajectories. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation on six agents (3 open and 3 closed agents) with two benchmarks. Finally, we use the evaluation feedback to optimize code agents, significantly improving their performance on both task types.

In agent frameworks such as OpenClaw, Skills are reusable modules that encapsulate tool use and workflow logic in natural language and code. Existing security scanners typically assess each Skill in isolation, yet security-relevant behaviors can be compositional: they may either form a complete threat within one Skill or constitute an incomplete threat fragment that becomes harmful when combined with capabilities exposed by other Skills. This creates an auditing gap between isolated per-Skill screening and explicit multi-Skill composition analysis. 
We present SkillWeaver, a compositional security auditing framework that decomposes agent threats into locally observable atomic behaviors and reasons about how these behaviors participate in threat paths. Given a single Skill, SkillWeaver identifies local security-relevant behaviors, constructs candidate complete threat paths or predefined compositional fragments, and validates their relations, context, and blocking conditions. This formulation supports conventional single-Skill threat detection while also exposing potential contributions to cross-Skill attacks without requiring the future collaborating Skills to be known at audit time.
On a source-reviewed evaluation set of 300 real-world Skills annotated for security risk and threat type, SkillWeaver achieves an F1 score of 0.540 and a recall of 0.819, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.7 F1 points. An in-the-wild analysis drawn from 18,141 unique analyzable Skills further uncovers source-supported threats and representative cross-Skill compositions, showing that meaningful partial threat structures identified from individual Skills can combine across compatible interfaces into complete attack paths.

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) can act as fast surrogates for patient-specific hemodynamic simulation, but training one PINN per patient from scratch is slow, and single deterministic surrogates give no indication of when a prediction should be trusted. We study cerebral-aneurysm hemodynamics (concentration $c$, velocity $\boldsymbol{u}=(u,v,w)$ and pressure $p$ fields governed by the incompressible Navier--Stokes and convection--diffusion equations) as a testbed for four complementary contributions to amortizing PINN training across a population of geometries and patients. (1) We show that a PINN warm-started from a universal model pre-trained across 30 synthetic geometries and then fine-tuned (transfer learning, TL) beats a patient-specific PINN trained from scratch at matched compute, and matches a from-scratch PINN given $5\times$ more epochs while using 80% less wall-clock time; an ensembled variant of transfer learning (Ensemble-TL) is validated on a real CT Scan dataset (98,786 points, 301 timesteps), where it attains the lowest mean relative-$L_2$ error (0.213) of six strategies tested. (2) We meta-train a first-order MAML initialization over synthetic patients and show it adapts to a new patient in 5-shot fine-tuning with 54% lower error than training from scratch, and reaches a fixed error target with a $20\times$ reduction in fine-tuning steps. (3) We introduce Physics-Residual Active Learning (PRAL), which combines predictive uncertainty, Navier--Stokes residual magnitude, and feature-space diversity into a single acquisition score; PRAL statistically significantly outperforms uncertainty-only and random acquisition across 25 held-out patients. (4) We build a calibrated deep-ensemble uncertainty estimate with post-hoc temperature scaling, reducing expected calibration error from 0.132 (from-scratch ensembles) to 0.046 (meta-initialized ensembles). An ablation over 20 patients confirms that meta-initialization and PRAL each contribute independently, and that physics-informed regularization by itself yields a smaller (+1%) but still positive benefit. Together, these four components turn single-patient PINN fitting into a population-level, few-shot, uncertainty-aware pipeline that is both faster and more reliable than training in isolation.

Wearable biosignals often vary more across subjects and sensors than with the physiological quantity they are intended to track. As a result, regression models can achieve low pooled error on held-out subjects by encoding subject identity rather than physiological change. We demonstrate this identity confounding in photoplethysmography-based blood pressure (BP) regression: subject-disjoint linear probes recover at most R² = 0.11 of systolic BP change from the latent representations of published encoders, with 40–83% of this decodability lost on unseen subjects. Moreover, stratifying error by the magnitude of BP change reveals severe failures above 60 mmHg that are obscured by pooled error. We constrain learning to within-subject change at three levels. First, the input pairs an event recording with a baseline recording from the same subject, and the target is their BP difference, removing subject-specific offsets. Second, each batch contains one pair from each of B subjects, preventing identity from determining the ordering structure. Third, the objective ranks paired embeddings according to BP change across subjects, while a decoder reconstructs the event signal from the pair, encouraging the paired representation to retain event-specific information. Pretrained on finger PPG from intensive-care and surgical cohorts and transferred to wrist PPG in clinical and daily-life settings, our model, MOrdereD, increases linear decodability of BP change to R² = 0.22, with only 9–14% loss on unseen subjects. In the clinical setting, it reduces error relative to a zero-change predictor by 34% across change strata and by 57% for changes above 60 mmHg, achieving 8.3 versus 11.0 mmHg pooled MAE and outperforming all baselines by at least 9 percentage points in macro skill. In daily life, the gain is 18%, although large changes remain poorly tracked. These results show that identity confounding can be substantially reduced when the input, batch construction, and objective are all explicitly designed around within-subject change, providing a more realistic estimate of what single-point-calibrated wearable BP models can achieve.

Large language models are now widely used worldwide, yet their understanding and reasoning about women’s harassment contexts remain limited, particularly in Asian contexts. Most publicly available women’s harassment datasets are monolingual, English-centric, or contain labels only at a coarse hate/not-hate level. We propose SheSafe-Bench, a comprehensive multilingual and code-mixed benchmark that focuses on women-directed harassment text in Asian contexts. SheSafe-Bench covers eight Indic language pairs commonly used in India: Hindi-English, Urdu-English, Bengali-English, Gujarati-English, Marathi-English, Odia-English, Tamil-English, and Nepali-English, comprising 8,750 comments collected from social media platforms such as Reddit and YouTube. 50% of the comments are naturally occurring code-mixed comments collected directly from social media, while the remaining 50% are monolingual comments that were manually converted into code-mixed comments by native-speaker annotators rather than through machine translation, in order to preserve the original meaning and intent of the comments.

This manual conversion was performed because naturally occurring data are often limited across different language pairs. It enables the creation of a balanced and sufficiently large dataset across multiple language pairs. Each of the 8,255  comments was manually labelled into one of six fine-grained categories: Sexual Harassment, Misogyny, Cyber Abuse, Violence, and Abortion,Depression  by two independent native-speaker annotators per language pair. We describe a structured and detailed pipeline covering data collection, cleaning, code-mixing verification, and quality control, and we specify an inter-annotator agreement and error-analysis protocol using Cohen’s κ. We test the benchmark on various open- and closed-source models.SheSafe-Bench aims to give a practical benchmark for evaluating how well language models understand women-directed harassment across diverse code-mixed Indic language contexts.

We study whether motion representations inspired by joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) preserve gait asymmetry when restoring complete windows of noisy 2D poses. Our adaptation of ideas from self-supervised learning uses paired synthetic motions and clean projected training references. Evaluation uses 14 development participants and three random training seeds. The main outcome is absolute error in recovering the change in knee-motion asymmetry between an original motion and its edited counterpart. A baseline that always predicts no change has mean error 5.81$\dg$, lower than all 16 trained variants with fixed penalties for failed measurements. Its error is 1.73$\dg$ lower than a model trained directly on joint coordinates (95\% interval [0.53, 3.15]$\dg$), although that model improves the noisy poses. The variant trained to predict differences between paired feature vectors has 0.37$\dg$ lower mean error than the variant predicting each vector separately. The 95\% interval [$-1.11$, 1.76]$\dg$ includes zero, leaving their relative accuracy uncertain. Adding training penalties for asymmetry-change errors and very short predicted limb segments increases mean knee-angle trajectory error in all eight model families. Giving less weight to the change penalty reduces trajectory error in the follow-up study. A post hoc geometric check finds more left--right assignment failures for the feature-difference variant despite its lower response-error estimate. These comparisons inform the evaluation of JEPA-inspired representations for future gait world models by testing measurement accuracy and geometric left--right assignment.

TL;DR: We use gait symmetry to explore how AI can preserve meaningful differences in human movement, guiding the development of motion models that measure how people move more faithfully.

We introduce a geometric learning formulation for B-SPIN, a B-spline path interaction network that represents multivariate functions through alternating products of a rectangular spline feature matrix and learned routing matrices. Each interaction branch is written as one scalar amplitude multiplied by Frobenius-unit matrix directions. This canonical form removes the continuous scale gauge of the unconstrained multilinear factorization while preserving its represented function class. The active parameter space is a product of matrix spheres, with an optional finite quotient accounting for residual sign symmetries. We derive its tangent spaces, metric, projection, exponential map, retraction, dimension, stability bounds, and path expansion. Two complementary solvers are developed. Canonical block coordinate descent (BCD) solves convex lifted ridge subproblems and then exactly restores the amplitude-direction representation. Joint Riemannian Gauss-Newton with conjugate gradients (RGN-CG) solves a damped normal equation over the full product tangent space using only Jacobian-vector and vector-Jacobian products. Our numerical study combines algebraic audits, controlled exact-recovery tests, and a parameter-matched comparison with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (KANs). RGN-CG reaches test $R^2\ge 0.999998$ on three exactly representable targets with a maximum sphere-constraint error of $1.19\times10^{-7}$. Across eight noisy synthetic tasks, B-SPIN wins all tasks: BCD obtains five wins and a mean test NRMSE of $0.034$, while RGN-CG wins the remaining three. B-SPIN also recovers active variables more faithfully than MLP and KAN. Real-data outcomes are mixed and do not establish universal superiority; on the three leakage-free datasets, KAN has the best mean rank. The study uses a single seed and is therefore exploratory. These results support B-SPIN as a compact and interpretable interaction model, and identify regularization, repeated evaluation, and scalable RGN preconditioning as the principal next steps.

TL;DR: B-SPIN is a compact, interpretable neural architecture that models multivariate interactions as B-spline paths and enables efficient matrix-free Riemannian second-order optimization.

Recurrent-depth models promise to trade inference-time iterations for computation by repeatedly applying a shared latent block. We ask what the iterated core actually contributes in a small recurrent latent model whose register state repeatedly cross-attends to its input. When the readout has direct token-level access to the input (a residual path), this path is necessary - removing it drops exact match (EM) to zero on every checkpoint - and carries most of the answer, while the example-specific core trajectory contributes a minority, seed-dependent share: in re-runs with a padding fix, shuffling it across examples costs 21% of EM (95% CI [4, 39], 4/5 seeds learn) without core input re-reading and 39% ([12, 64], 5/5) with it, a difference that is not significant. Linear and MLP probes on the core state do not exceed a positional-prior baseline in either case, so negative probes should not be read as absence. Without the residual path, the core computes iteratively: EM rises with iterations up to the training budget (0.24 at one step to 0.92 at eight), then degrades beyond it (0.11 at $8\times$ the budget) while the state norm grows and its direction keeps drifting without reaching a fixed point. A test-time norm rescaling beats a norm-matched placebo on every seed (McNemar $p<10^{-3}$), but its net gain is heterogeneous (mean $+0.29$ EM, seed-level 95% CI $[-0.29, 0.87]$, $n=3$). Outer normalization with a fixed-point penalty retains the solution up to $4\times$ the training depth when it is learned (2/6 seeds, exploratory). All results are small-scale and synthetic; success rates are reported as $k/n$ throughout.

TL;DR: In a recurrent latent-core model, a residual input path to the readout carries most of the answer while the iterated core contributes only partially; we diagnose this with causal interventions and study depth extrapolation and its partial repair.

In animals, an emotional state differs from a reflex partly because it outlasts its stimulus. In a transformer, apparent persistence may reflect continued access to the earlier text; a fixed-size recurrent state removes that access. We test how long an event keeps influencing three Mamba models (130M, 370M and 790M parameters) after its text is gone. Each model reads a threatening sentence or its neutral twin (48 matched pairs), then 64 tokens of unrelated filler, and we compare the log-probabilities of threat and calm words after a fixed stem. The effect survives. The models still separate the two conditions by +0.268, +0.236 and +0.168 nats, and which of the 48 pairs was read stays decodable from the cache (accuracy 0.88, 0.82 and 0.81; chance 0.021). Scrambling each passage's token order leaves 47% to 67% of that difference, and the part that depends on word order is separable from zero at 130M and 370M but not at 790M. The persistence is not specific to threat. In a preregistered control with 48 non-emotional mechanical events and their own readout words, the mechanical passages' residual against a no-passage run keeps a larger share of its initial size than the threatening passages' residual at every size (0.40, 0.45 and 0.37 against 0.27, 0.34 and 0.29). Editing the state along the mean threat-minus-neutral difference moves behavior at every size, and a preregistered test against 50 norm-matched random directions finds the edit specific at 130M and 370M but not at 790M. Two readouts need a second measure. In post hoc analyses, a hidden-state probe fitted at induction reports decay that is mostly shrinking variance, and with non-threat sentences as the reference, the threat-specific residual shrinks at 790M.

TL;DR: A threatening sentence still shifts Mamba's behavior 64 tokens after its text is gone, and a mechanical one keeps more of its initial effect; a state edit is specific at 130M and 370M under a preregistered test, not at 790M.

We present AutoSciML, a framework for automating scientific machine learning pipelines through retrieval-augmented generation over a knowledge base of physical dynamics. Unlike iterative search methods such as Bayesian optimization, AutoSciML encodes spatiotemporal data using pre-trained Masked Autoencoder embeddings and retrieves pre-computed Pareto-optimal configurations from a vector database. The Large Language Model functions as an intelligent interpreter: it maps natural-language user constraints to empirically verified method--hyperparameter pairs on the retrieved Pareto fronts. Evaluated on three target trajectories from three PDE families (Heat, Burgers, Advection) with five LLMs under four user-constraint scenarios, AutoSciML achieves a median 4.73$\times$ lower Relative L2 error than direct LLM recommendations, with improvements up to three orders of magnitude in low-data regimes where direct LLM configurations diverge. Against a Bayesian optimization baseline, AutoSciML shows comparable accuracy (3 wins / 3 losses over 6 test cases) while requiring 11--38$\times$ less compute per query, since the search cost is amortized into the offline library. The encoder additionally generalizes zero-shot to a PDE family held out from its training (Advection).

Dispersion-controlled multilayer optical coatings are used to control the properties of ultrashort laser pulses: they are the core building block of mirrors made of alternating thin transparent layers whose thicknesses determine how the stack reflects light as a function of wavelength. Because light is a complex-valued electric field, reflection adds a wavelength-dependent phase to it. The curvature of this phase, the group-delay dispersion (GDD), determines how the coating contributes to stretching or compressing an ultrashort pulse. Designing such a stack is a high-dimensional, non-convex optimization problem where the stack must simultaneously achieve, e.g., high reflectance and a prescribed GDD over a finite wavelength band. Gradient-based optimization is therefore highly sensitive to initialization since both objectives are derived from the same complex reflection coefficient $r(\lambda)$. We train a neural network to learn a continuous mapping from an optical specification — target reflectance, target GDD, and the wavelength band - directly to a complete layer stack, supervised by a differentiable physics model.
After training, the network maps the coating specifications to a candidate stack in a single forward pass. In order to improve design performance, this work adds a refinement step after the forward pass by optimizing the stack directly in the differentiable physics model. A design counts as successful if reflectance and GDD stay within the specified tolerance. A common starting point for a dispersive mirror design is a high-reflectivity, approximately dispersion-free stack based on the classical quarter-wave design, followed by numerical refinement. On a 63-point test target grid spanning the 800–1400\,nm design region, the learned initialization achieves an 82.5\% joint success rate, compared to 71.4\% for this quarter-wave baseline and 3.2\% for random initialization. Among common successful cases requiring refinement, the learned initialization requires roughly 7.4$\times$ fewer refinement steps than quarter-wave initialization over the same targets. These results show that a differentiable physics model can be used not only to optimize individual designs, but to amortize inverse design across a continuous family of optical targets.

TL;DR: We learn an amortized inverse-design model that maps optical targets directly to dispersion-controlled multilayer coatings, using differentiable physics to train without pre-optimized design labels.

Modeling cellular responses to perturbations requires learning representations that
integrate expression context across genes at broad transcriptomic coverage. We
introduce MDLA, a Masked discrete Diffusion model with non-causal Linear
Attention over gene identities and discretized expression counts. MDLA encodes
each cell as a queryable state, a unique memory of its expression profile, that
represents the single cell. Whereas transformer-based single-cell models obtain
cell representations from an added [cls] token or by pooling hidden representations
post hoc, this state is the only channel through which genes exchange context, so
the masked-diffusion loss shapes it directly, and its linear cost in gene number
keeps broad transcriptomic coverage tractable. Pretrained on the CZ CELLxGENE
Census, MDLA yields state readouts that outperform both mean-pooled hidden
representations and the embeddings of leading single-cell foundation models on
classifying COVID-19 infection status and Tabula Sapiens cell types. We then cast
perturbation prediction as conditional flow matching between the states of control
and perturbed cells. On the Replogle–Nadig Perturb-seq datasets, this approach
outperforms the state of the art for predicting held-out responses.

TL;DR: We use the attention state of a linear-attention masked diffusion model as the cell representation, and predict perturbation responses by flow matching between these states.
